(Benefit)

Reflect on the secret of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾: how these three letters are composed. When the alif is pronounced first, it is a hamzah, and it is the first of the articulation points, from the far end of the chest. The lam comes from the middle of the articulation points, and it is the letter most reliant on the tongue. The mim is the last of the letters, and its articulation point is the mouth. These three are the fundamental articulation points of the letters, namely the throat, the tongue and the lips, and they are arranged in the revelation from beginning, to middle, to end. These letters are thus the three base articulation points from which branch sixteen points of articulation, and from them come twenty-nine letters, upon which the speech of the earlier and later nations revolves. Moreover, it contains a wondrous secret: the alif is for the beginning, the lam for the middle and the mim for the end. Thus the three letters encompass the beginning, the end and the middle between them. Every surah that opens with these three letters includes the beginning of creation, its end and its middle. It therefore includes the fashioning of the world and its purpose, and the middle between beginning and end, which is legislation and commands. Reflect on this in al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Sajdah and al-Rum.

Also reflect on the pairing of the ta' with the sin and the ha' in the Qur'an. The ta' combines five of the attributes of letters that no other letter combines: jahr (voicing), shiddah (strength), istila' (elevation), and itbaq (emphasis). The sin is mahmus (unvoiced), rakhw (softness), mustafil (low), safir (whistling) and munfatih (open). It is not possible to add to the ta' a letter that opposes it, such as the sin or the ha'. So he mentioned the two letters that combine the attributes of letters. Also consider the surahs that contain single letters, and how you find the surah built upon the words of that letter. Among them is (Qaf). The surah is built upon the words of qaf: the Qur'an's mention, the mention of creation, the repetition of speech and its repeated review, nearness to the son of Adam, the two angels receiving the servant's words, the mention of the Watcher, the mention of the driver and the companion, casting into Hell, the advance warning of threat, the mention of the righteous, the mention of the heart and the generations, searching through the lands, the mention of "the saying" twice, the splitting of the earth, the casting of the firm mountains within it, the sprouting of the palm trees, provision, the mention of peoples, and the realization of the threat. Even if there were only the repetition of speech and dialogue, that would suffice. There is another secret: all the meanings of this surah correspond to what is in the letter qaf of strength, voicing, elevation and openness.

If you want more clarification of this, consider what the surah of (Sad) contains of its many disputes. Its first is the dispute of the disbelievers with the Prophet ﷺ, "Has he made the gods into one God?", up to the end of their words. Then the quarrel of the two litigants before David. Then the mutual disputing of the people of the Fire. Then the Exalted Assembly disputing about knowledge, which is the degrees and the expiations. Then the contention of Iblis and his objection to his Lord regarding His command to prostrate to Adam. Then his second dispute concerning his descendants, his oath that he will mislead them all, except the sincere among them. Let the discerning intelligent person reflect: would any surah other than (Sad) suit this, and any surah other than (Qaf) suit its letter? This is a drop from the sea of some of the secrets of these letters. And Allah knows best.

This [verse] involves two matters.

The first is that He guides by it those who have *taqwā* (God-consciousness) regarding what He had decreed before the Book was revealed. People, despite their differing creeds and sects, have settled in their minds that God, glory be to Him, dislikes injustice, abominations, and corruption on earth, abhors the one who does them, and loves justice, goodness, generosity, truthfulness, and reform on earth, and loves the one who does these things. So when the Book was revealed, God, glory be to Him, rewarded the people of righteousness by granting them success in believing in it, as a recompense for their piety and obedience, and He forsook the people of wickedness, depravity, and injustice by placing a barrier between them and being guided by it.

The second matter is that when the servant believes in the Book and is guided by it in general, accepts its commands, and affirms its reports, this becomes a cause of another guidance that is attained by him in detail. For guidance has no end: however far the servant advances in it, beyond that guidance there is another guidance, and beyond that another, without limit. So whenever the servant fears his Lord, he rises to another guidance, and he remains in increasing guidance as long as he remains in increasing taqwā. And whenever he forfeits a portion of taqwā, he loses a share of guidance in proportion to it. Thus, whenever he fears God, his guidance increases, and whenever he is guided, his taqwā increases.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿There has come to you from God a light and a clear Book, by which God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path﴾ [5:15–16]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance﴾ [42:13]. He said: ﴿The one who fears will be reminded﴾ [87:10]. He said: ﴿None will take heed except the one who turns back﴾ [40:13]. He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them because of their faith﴾ [10:9]. So He guided them first to faith, and when they believed, He guided them to faith, guidance after guidance. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And God increases in guidance those who are guided﴾ [19:76].

(A Benefit)

The difference between *shakk* (doubt) and *rayb* (disquiet/suspicion) lies in several aspects:

First: it is said *shakkun murīb* (a disquieting doubt), but it is not said *raybun mushakkik* (a doubting disquiet).

Second: one says *rāban-ī amrun kadhā* (a matter disquieted me), but one does not say *shakkanī* (it made me doubt).

Third: one says *rābahu yarībuhu* when it disturbs and troubles him. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he passed by a sick person (*ẓanī*) lying at the base of a tree: "Let no one disquiet him." It would not be appropriate here to say "let no one make him doubt."

Fourth: one does not say of a person who doubts the rising or setting of the sun, the beginning of the month, or the time of prayer that he is *murtāb* (disquieted) regarding that, even if he is in doubt about it.

Fifth: *rayb* is the opposite of tranquillity and certainty; it is unease, agitation, and disturbance, just as certainty and tranquillity are stability and settledness.

Sixth: one says *rābanī majīʾuhu wa dhahābuhu wa fiʿluhu* (his coming, his going, and his action disquieted me), and one does not say *shakkanī*. Doubt is the cause of disquiet, for a person first doubts, and his doubt leads him to disquiet. Thus doubt is the beginning of disquiet, just as knowledge is the beginning of certainty, *al-istinjāʾ*.

(Another Benefit)

His saying: "This is insights from your Lord" [7:203] is general and unrestricted, while His saying: "and a guidance and mercy for a people who have certainty" is specific to the people of certainty.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [10:57].

A parallel to it in particularity is His saying: ﴿a guidance for those who have taqwā﴾ [2:2], and His saying: ﴿by which God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace﴾ [5:16].

A parallel also is His saying: ﴿This is an exposition for mankind, and a guidance and admonition for those who have taqwā﴾ [3:138].

He has informed that it is a guidance general to all the responsible, saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, though guidance has already come to them from their Lord﴾ [53:23].

So He, glory be to Him, informed that the Qur'an is insights for all people. *Baṣāʾir* is the plural of *baṣīra*, which is a form *faʿīla* in the sense of *mufʿila*, that is, making [things] seen for those who see. From this is His saying: ﴿And We gave Thamūd the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [17:59], that is, a clear sign that necessitates insight.

The verb *abṣara* is used both intransitively and transitively. One says *abṣartuhu* meaning "I showed him," and *abṣartuhu* meaning "I saw him." So *mubṣira* in the verse means "seen," not "seeing." Those who took it to mean "seeing" erred in the verse and were bewildered as to its meaning.

For it is said *baṣara bihi* and *abṣarahu*, so it takes the preposition *bāʾ* at times and the *hamza* at other times. Then one says *abṣartuhu kadhā*, meaning "I showed him it," just as one says *baṣṣartuhu bihi* ("I made him see it") and *baṣara huwa bihi* ("he saw it").

So here there is *baṣīra*, *tabṣira*, and *mubṣira*. *Baṣīra* is the clear [sign] that makes one see; *tabṣira* is a verbal noun like *tadhkira*, and that which necessitates insight is also called by it, so one says "this verse is a *tabṣira*," because it is the instrument of insight and what necessitates it.

So the Qur'an is *baṣīra* and *tabṣira*, and *hudā* (guidance) and *shifāʾ* (healing) and *raḥma* (mercy), in a general sense and in a specific sense. For this reason God, glory be to Him, mentions both this and that: it is a guidance for the worlds, an admonition for the God-conscious, a guidance for the God-conscious, a healing for the worlds, a healing for the believers, an admonition for the worlds, and an admonition for the God-conscious. So it is in itself guidance and mercy, healing and admonition.

Whoever is guided by it, takes admonition, and is healed, is like one who uses the medicine by which healing is attained; it is medicine for him in actuality. If he does not use it, it is medicine for him in potentiality. So too is guidance: the Qur'an is guidance in actuality for whoever is guided by it, and in potentiality for whoever is not guided by it. Only the God-conscious and certain believers are guided by it, are shown mercy, and take admonition.

*Hudā* in origin is the verbal noun of *hadā yahdī hudan*.

Whoever does not act upon his knowledge is not guided, as in the report: "Whoever increases in knowledge but does not increase in guidance increases from God only in distance." But it is called *hudā* because it is its nature to guide. This is better than the view of one who said it is *hudā* in the sense of *hādin* (one who guides), a verbal noun used in the sense of an active participle, like *ʿadl* meaning *ʿādil* (just), *zawr* meaning *zāʾir* (visitor), and *rajul ṣawm* meaning *ṣāʾim* (fasting man), for God, glory be to Him, has informed that He guides by it.

So God is the Guide (*al-Hādī*), and His Book is the guidance (*al-Hudā*) by which He guides, upon the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ).

So here are three things: an agent, a receptive recipient, and an instrument. The agent is God, the Exalted. The recipient is the heart of the servant. The instrument is that by which guidance is achieved, namely the revealed Book. God, glory be to Him, guides His creation with guidance, just as one says *dallahum dalāla* ("he guided them to it"), *arshadahum irshādan* ("he directed them"), and *bayyana lahum bayānan* ("he made clear to them").

The point is that the receptive place is the heart of the servant who is God-conscious, who turns in repentance to his Lord, who fears Him, who seeks His pleasure and flees from His wrath. When God guides him, it is as though the effect of His action reaches a receptive place, so it is affected by it, and it becomes for him guidance, healing, mercy, and admonition, in existence, in action, and in acceptance. But when the place is not receptive, the guidance reaches it but has no effect on it, just as nourishment reaches a place not receptive to being nourished; it has no effect on it, but only increases it in weakness and corruption along with its corruption. As He, the Exalted, said in the sūra He revealed: ﴿As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in filth upon their filth﴾ [9:124–125]. And He said: ﴿And We send down from the Qur'an that which is a healing and mercy for the believers, but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [17:82].

So the failure of guidance occurs sometimes because the place does not accept it, sometimes because the instrument of guidance is lacking, and sometimes because the agent, who is the Guide, does not act. Guidance in reality is achieved only when these three matters come together.

He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And had He made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse﴾ [8:23].

So He, glory be to Him, informed that He has cut off from them the source of guidance, which is making their hearts hear and understand what benefits them, because the place does not accept it, for there is no good in it. For a man only submits to the truth through the good that is in him, through inclining toward it, seeking it, loving it, being eager for it, and rejoicing in attaining it. These people have nothing of that in their hearts, so the guidance reached them and fell upon them, as rain falling from the sky reaches hard, elevated ground that holds no water and grows no herbage: it is neither receptive to water nor to growth. The water in itself is mercy and life, but there is no acceptance of it in that ground.

Then God affirmed this meaning regarding them by His saying: ﴿And had He made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse﴾ [8:23].

So He informed that in them, along with the lack of acceptance and understanding, there is another calamity, which is arrogance, aversion, and corrupt intention. Had they understood, they would not have submitted, nor followed the truth, nor acted upon it. So the guidance regarding these people is the guidance of exposition and establishing proof, not the guidance of success and direction. Thus the guidance did not connect with mercy in their case.

As for the believers, the guidance connected with mercy in their case, so the Qur'an became for them guidance and mercy, while for those others it is guidance without mercy.

The mercy that accompanies guidance regarding the believers is both immediate and deferred.

As for the immediate mercy, it is what God gives them in this world: love of goodness and piety, tasting the sweetness of faith, finding its delight, and the joy and happiness that God has guided them to what others have strayed from and disagreed about regarding the truth. They move about in the light of His guidance and walk with it among people, and they see others bewildered in darkness. So they are the most joyful of people in what their Lord has given them of guidance. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of God and His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate"﴾ [10:58].

So God, glory be to Him, commanded His believing, guided servants to rejoice in His bounty and mercy.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 3:**

**(Benefit)**

Reflect on the wisdom in the strictness at the beginning of the obligation followed by ease at its end, after the soul has been prepared for resolve and compliance. The servant thereby gains two things: the reward for his resolve and for preparing his soul to comply, and the ease and facility of what God has lightened for him.

Among examples of this: God commanded His Messenger fifty prayers on the night of the Ascension (al-Isra'), then lightened them and graciously made them five.

Among examples: He first commanded them to endure one against ten, then lightened that for them to one against two.

Among examples: He forbade them in fasting that, if one of them slept, he could eat or have intercourse afterward, then lightened this for them.

Among examples: He obligated them to give charity before privately consulting His Messenger. When they prepared their souls for this, He lightened it for them by permitting them to do so without it until dawn.

Among examples: the waiting period of one year was lightened to four months and ten days. This is like what occurs in trials through commands. Trials also occur through divine decree and destiny: the servant is made to bear strictness first, then it is lightened for him. The wisdom in this is that the second is made easier by the first, and the second is met with contentment and witnessing of grace and mercy.

Kings sometimes do something close to this with some of their subjects. Those who are extorted are demanded a great deal, which they may be unable to bear, and then it is reduced to less, so their souls willingly submit to humility and it becomes easy for them. Similarly, some porters add to a load things they do not need, then those things are removed, so that carrying the remainder becomes easy for them.

The point is that this is a door of wisdom in creation and command, and the opposite also occurs in command, decree and destiny. He moves His servants gradually from what is easy to what is more severe, so that the severity does not come on them suddenly, so that they cannot bear it and do not submit to it.

This is like His gradual imposition of the laws, one after another, rather than having them all commanded at once. Likewise with the prohibitions. Among examples: they were first commanded to pray two rak'ahs at a time, then when they became accustomed to it, two more rak'ahs were added for the settled (non-travel) prayer.

Among examples: they were first commanded to fast and were given the choice between fasting and paying the expiation (fidyah). When they became accustomed to it, they were commanded to fast definitively.

Among examples: they were first given permission to fight without it being obligated upon them. When their souls settled on it and they experienced its good outcome and fruit, they were commanded to it as an obligation.

The wisdom of this gradual method is training in accepting the rulings, submitting to them, and complying with them little by little. Similarly, such a thing occurs in His decree and destiny. What is decreed for His servant is necessarily so, as demanded by His praiseworthiness and wisdom. He tests him first with the lighter, then raises him to what is above it until he completes what has been prescribed for him of it. For this reason the servant may strive at the beginning of a trial to repel and remove it, yet it only grows more severe, because it is like an illness at its onset and its growth. The intelligent person first submits to it, humbles himself, abases himself before his Lord, and extends his neck in humble submission to His might, until the greatest part of it passes over him and overwhelms him, and night announces the morning. Then, when he strives to remove it, the means assist him. Whoever reflects on this in creation benefits greatly. There is no power and no strength except with God, the Exalted.

**(Section)**

It suffices the intelligent, perceptive person with a living heart to contemplate one branch of the branches of command and prohibition, namely the prayer (salah), and what it contains of striking wisdoms, hidden and apparent benefits, and advantages connected to the heart, the spirit, the body and the faculties. If all the wise men of the world gathered and exhausted their powers and minds, they would not encompass the details of its wisdom, secrets and praiseworthy ends. Rather, they would all fall short before the secrets of al-Fatihah (the Opening chapter) and what it contains of divine knowledge, lordly wisdom, beneficial sciences, complete monotheism (tawhid), and praise of God through the fundamentals of His names and attributes. It also mentions the categories of creation in relation to their ends and means. And there is in its preliminaries and conditions wondrous wisdom: purifying the limbs, garments and place; taking adornment; facing His House, which He made a guide for mankind; emptying the heart; sincerity of intention; and opening it with a word comprehensive of the meanings of servanthood, indicating the fundamentals of praise and its branches. It expels from the heart turning toward anything else and attending to other than Him.

So the worshipper presents himself in his heart standing before a Majestic Great One, greater than everything, more glorious than everything, mightier than everything, without any cause. In His grandeur are the heavens and what they shade, and the earth and what it carries, and all the worlds. Faces are humbled before Him, necks submit to Him, and the tyrants are abased before Him. He is the Subduer of His servants, watching over them, knowing what their breasts conceal, hearing their speech and seeing their places. Nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him.

Then he begins to glorify Him, praise Him, mention His blessed name, His exalted majesty, and His singularity in divinity. Then he begins to praise Him with the best praise by which He may be praised: His praise, His lordship over the worlds, His beneficence toward them, His mercy upon them, and glorifying Him with the great sovereignty on the Day when no sovereign exists except Him, when He gathers the first and the last in one plain and recompenses them for their deeds.

Then he affirms Him in the two kinds of tawhid: the tawhid of His lordship, by seeking help from Him, and the tawhid of His divinity, by worship to Him. Then he asks Him for the best thing requested and the most sublime thing sought absolutely, which is guidance to the Straight Path (al-sirat al-mustaqim), which He set up for His prophets, messengers and their followers. He made it a path leading whoever travels it to Him and to His Garden. It is the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His blessing, by making them recognize the truth and making them followers of it, rather than the path of those who earned His anger, who recognized the truth but did not follow it, and the path of those who went astray from knowing it and following it.

Thus it includes knowledge of the Lord, the path leading to Him, and the goal after arrival. It includes praise, supplication, and the most noble ends, which are servanthood, and the closest means to it, which is seeking help. The means is placed before the object of help to indicate that it is specific to Him, and that this belongs only to Him, the Glorified. It also mentions divinity, lordship and mercy. Thus He is praised, worshipped in His divinity, creates, provides, causes death and gives life, governs the kingdom, misguides whoever deserves misguidance, is angry with whoever deserves anger by His lordship and wisdom, bestows favour, shows mercy, is generous, pardons, forgives, guides, and accepts repentance by His mercy.

How many kinds of knowledge, sciences, tawhid and realities of faith are in this surah, by God!

Then he proceeds, after that, to recite the spring of hearts, the healing of breasts, the light of insights, and the life of spirits, which is the speech of the Lord of the worlds. He alights thereby in whatever gardens he wills, of flourishing groves and wondrous orchards, whose flowers are radiant, whose fruits are fresh, whose clusters have been made easy to pick and made accessible to the one who reaches for them. So he gathers from those fruits good, which he is commanded to do, and evil, from which he is forbidden; and wisdom, admonition, insight, reminder, lesson; confirmation of truth and refutation of falsehood; removal of doubt; an answer to a question; clarification of what is obscure; encouragement toward the causes of success and happiness; warning against the causes of loss and misery; a call to guidance and turning away from perdition. They descend upon the hearts like rain upon a land that has no life without it, and they take their place in them as spirits take their place in bodies. What bliss, delight of eye, joy of heart, exultation and gladness are not attained in this intimate conversation! And the Lord, the Exalted, hears His speech flowing on the tongue of His servant, and says: "My servant has praised Me; My servant has extolled Me; My servant has glorified Me."

Then he returns to magnifying his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. He finds his Lord's covenant of reminder: that He is greater than everything in truth of His servanthood and what He deserves to be treated with. Then he returns bowing, his back bent in submission to His greatness, humbled before His might, subdued before His dominion, glorifying Him by mentioning His great name. He has exalted His greatness above the state of the servant, his abasement and his submission. He has met that greatness with this humility, bowing and submission. He has lowered himself, bowed his head, folded his back, while his Lord is above him, seeing his submission and abasement and hearing his speech. So it is a pillar of magnification and exaltation, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"As for bowing, then magnify the Lord therein."

Then he returns to his standing position, praising his Lord and extolling Him with His most perfect, most comprehensive and most inclusive praises, extolling Him as the One deserving praise and glory, acknowledging his servanthood, testifying to His oneness, and affirming that none can withhold what He gives, and none can give what He withholds, and that the fortune of the fortunate and their wealth and shares will not benefit them against Him, however great they are.

Then he returns to his magnification and prostrates before Him on the most noble part of himself, which is the face, rubbing it in the dust in abasement before Him, humbling himself and submitting. Every limb of the body has taken its share of this submission, even the tips of the fingers and the ends of the toes. He is commanded to prostrate with his garments and hair too, so that they are not withheld. He is also commanded that his limbs not be carried upon one another, and that he place his forehead on the earth, and touch his face to the ground, and that his head be the lowest part of him, in completion of submission and humbling before the One to whom all might and all greatness belong. This is the very least of what is due to Him from His servant. Even if he remained in this state from the moment he was created until he died, he would not have fulfilled his Lord's right over him.

Then he is commanded to glorify his Lord, the Most High (Sabbih isma rabbika al-a'la), so he mentions His exaltedness, glorified be He, in the state of lowness, and declares Him free of such a state. The One who is above everything and exalted above everything is exempt from lowness in every sense; rather He is the Most High in every sense of height. And since this is the utmost of the servant's abasement, submission and humility, the Lord is nearest to him in this state. So he is commanded to strive in supplication, because of the Nearness of the Near, the Responsive. God, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Prostrate yourself and draw near﴾.

The bowing serves as a prelude before the prostration and a preparation for it. He moves from one submission to a more complete, perfect submission, higher in rank than it. He separates them with a pillar that is purposeful in itself, in which he strives with praise, extolling and glorification. He placed between one submission and the submission before it and the submission after it. He made the submission of prostration come after praise, extolling and glory, just as the submission of bowing came after that. So reflect on this wondrous order, and this movement through the stations of servanthood: how he moves from the station of praising the Lord with His finest attributes and names and most perfect praises, to the One before whom he submits and humbles himself, that He has this praise. He carries his submission into his station in a manner suited to that station and fitting for it. Thus he remembers his Lord's greatness in the state of his submission, and His loftiness in the state of his lowness.

Since the noblest of the prayer's remembrances is the Qur'an, he began with the noblest state of man, which is the standing posture, in which he stands erect in the best form. And since the best of its physical pillars is prostration, he prescribed it with the attribute of repetition. He made the conclusion and end of the rak'ah, where it terminates, correspond to the opening of the rak'ah with the Qur'an, and its closing with prostration, which is the first surah with which revelation began: it began with recitation and ended with prostration.

Between these two submissions, he prescribed that he sit in the posture of servants and ask his Lord to forgive him, have mercy on him, provide for him, guide him and grant him well-being. These supplications encompass for him the good of his worldly life and his Hereafter. Then he prescribed the repetition of this rak'ah time after time, just as he prescribed the repetition of remembrances and supplications time after time, so that by the first he may prepare himself to complete what follows, and by what follows he may make up for what preceded it, and so that the heart may be filled with this nourishment, and take its full share of the medicine to counter it. For the station of prayer in relation to the heart is the station of food and medicine. When one who is extremely hungry takes a morsel or two, their sufficiency and satisfaction of his hunger is very little. Likewise the sick person who needs a quantity of medicine sufficient for him: if he takes a qirat of it, his illness is not wholly removed, though it is reduced to that extent. Nothing provides nourishment or healing to the heart like prayer. For the health and cure of the heart, it is like the nourishment and medicine of the body.

Then, when he completes his prayer, he is prescribed to sit in the sitting of the abased, humble servant before his master, and to praise Him with the best greetings (al-tahiyyat), and to greet the one who brought this great portion and through whose hands the nation received it. Then he greets himself and all the servants of God who share in this servanthood with him. Then he recites the testimony of truth (the shahadah). Then he returns to send blessings upon the one who taught the nation this good and guided them to it. Then he is prescribed to ask for his needs and to supplicate with whatever he wishes, for as long as he is before his Lord, turned toward Him.

When he has done so, he is permitted to leave it by greeting those who share the prayer with him. This is in addition to what the states and knowledge contain, from the first station to the last. You will not find any station on the journey to God, or any station of the knowers, except that it is within the prayer. What we have mentioned of its nature is like a drop from an ocean. How, then, can it be said that it is mere obligation, not prescribed for any wisdom or purpose intended by the Lawgiver, but pure hardship and burden and difficulty resting upon bare will, without purpose or benefit whatsoever, mere compulsion and imposition, and not a cause of any benefit of this world or the Hereafter?

Then reflect on the chapters of the Sharia, its means and its ends. You will find them filled with intended wisdoms and praiseworthy goals for which they were prescribed. Were it not for these, people would be like cattle, or even worse in condition. How much wisdom and benefit there is in purification, for the heart and the body! It gladdens the heart, invigorates the limbs, lightens the burdens that nature has imposed, and cleanses the soul of the filth of transgressions. It purifies the heart, the spirit and the body. And in the ghusl of major impurity (janabah) there is additional softness and renewal for the body, similar to what is dissolved from it through impurity, which is among the most beneficial things.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 6:

Al-Suhayli said:

His words: ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them, it is the same for them﴾

Since they do not care about the warning, and it does not benefit them, and nothing from it enters their hearts, it takes on the status of something asked about, whether it occurred or did not. Therefore the alif is not called the alif of equalization (alif al-taswiya), as some have done; rather it is the alif of interrogation (alif al-istifham) in the sense for which it was established. The coming of "andharta-hum" (you warned them) and "ad'awtumuhum" (you called them) in the past tense has not ceased to be so.

If it is said: Why did it come in the past tense, namely "andharta-hum," and likewise "ad'awtumuhum am antum samitun" (whether you called them or you are silent), and "wa-aqama Zayd am qa'ada" (Zayd stood or sat), and it did not come in the present or future tense?

The answer has two aspects.

The first: the sentence carries the meaning of a condition (shart), and a condition is placed after a future verb in the past tense. You say: "in qama Zayd ghadan qumtu" (if Zayd stands tomorrow, I will stand). Here that meaning is impossible; it is as if you said: "in qama Zayd aw qa'ada lam ubali" (if Zayd stands or sits, I do not care), and the people will not benefit whether you warn them or do not warn them. Therefore it came in the past tense. Al-Farisi said something other than this, but close to it in wording. He said: the alif of interrogation resembles "in" which is for the conditional, because the interrogation is necessary just as the condition is not realized when the conditioned is absent. This expression is faulty in several respects, too long to mention. Had he seen the meaning we have mentioned, it would have been more fitting, though in my view it is also flawed, because the meaning of the condition requires the future specifically, not the present or past.

As for His words: ﴿It is the same for you whether you called them﴾ and ﴿It is the same for them whether you warned them﴾, they are not restricted to the future; rather equality in lack of concern exists in every state, and it is even more evident in the present tense verb. A present tense verb never comes after a conditional particle in any way.

The verification of the answer is that you say: We have established in the results of thought a principle, which is that the verb was not derived from the verbal noun (masdar) in an annexed form except to indicate that the noun is the subject of the predicate, namely the doer to whom the masdar is annexed. Its patterns do not vary after it is derived from the masdar except because of differences in the states of the event, whether past or future. If the speaker intends not to restrict the event to one time rather than another, nor to one future state rather than a past state, but to make it absolute, he uses the past tense form, which has no additions, so that it is lighter on the tongue and closer to the verbal noun from which it is derived. Do you not see that they say: "la af'aluhu ma laha barq wa-ma tara ta'ir" (I will not do it as long as lightning flashes and a bird flies), using only the past tense, because they wanted an absolute, unrestricted duration; and that one does not do this thing during the period of lightning flashing or a bird flying, and similar things. So they did not go beyond the past tense, because they did not intend a future or present in particular.

If you say: "They do not intend a past either, so how did it come in the past tense?"

We say: it has been joined with "la ukallimuhu wa-la af'aluhu" (I will not speak to him or do it), which shows that his saying "ma laha barq" does not intend a flash that has ended and ceased; it intends only the coincidence of the negated act with the other act over an absolute and continuous duration. So in "ma laha barq" there is nothing but the meaning of flashing, except that the verbal noun was dropped so that lightning becomes the subject of the predicate, as has preceded. Whenever you intend this and do not intend a restriction to a time, the past tense form is more worthy and more appropriate.

Likewise His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warned them﴾: He annexed the warning to the addressed one who is the subject of the predicate, and derived from "al-indhar" the verb to indicate that the addressee is the doer of the warning. He left the verb in the past tense because it is absolute in all time, and because the people did not care about this, nor were they in a state of caring. So there was no meaning in introducing the four additions, since the intent is not to restrict the act to a time nor to specify it to a state.

If you say: does the past tense form restrict it to cessation?

I say: it is a matter of two cases (hadath hadithayn). What we have mentioned suffices as an answer, together with what is in His words: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warned them﴾ of the establishment of this attribute in them, and its occurrence now and in the outcome. So you do not say "it is the same for your two garments or your two slaves" if the equality was in the past and they are now different. This indication negates the cessation that is imagined in the past tense form, just as the present tense form in your saying "la ukallimuhu ma damati al-samawat wa-al-ard" (I will not speak to him as long as the heavens and earth endure) negates the cessation imagined in "dama." When cessation is negated and the four additions are negated, the event remains absolute and unrestricted in both matters.

Reflect on this and you will find it correct.

If it is said: If you permit that the sealing, the locking and the covering are a punishment and a requital for the crimes, and for the disbelief and turning away that precedes the commission of crimes?

It is said: This is a point in which most people err, and they attribute to God, glorified is He, what contradicts the requirement of His names and attributes. The Qur'an from beginning to end only indicates that the sealing, the locking and the veil were not done by the Lord, glorified is He, to His servant from the first moment, when He commanded him to believe or made it clear to him. Rather He did it after repeated calling by Him, and emphasis in clarification and guidance, and repeated turning away from them, and excess in disbelief and obstinacy. Then He seals their hearts and places a seal upon them, so they do not accept guidance after that. The first turning away and disbelief was not with a seal or sealing; it was a choice. When it was repeated from them it became a nature and a disposition. Reflect on this meaning in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sight is a covering, and for them is a great punishment﴾. It is well known that this is not a ruling that encompasses all disbelievers; rather, most of those who believed and affirmed the messengers had been disbelievers before that, and God did not seal their hearts and their hearing. So these verses concern specific groups of disbelievers, whom God treated this way as a punishment from Him in this world, with this kind of hastened punishment, just as He punished some with transformation into apes and swine, and some with the effacing of their eyes. He, glorified is He, punishes with the effacing of hearts just as He punishes with the effacing of eyes. He, glorified is He, sometimes punishes with straying from truth as a lasting and continuous punishment, and sometimes with it for a time, then He pardons His servant and guides him, just as He punishes with torment in that way too.

(Grammatical difficulties)

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for you whether you called them or you are silent﴾

These are among the matters whose grammatical analysis (i'rab) has puzzled the masters of Arabic, and their opinions have differed on it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Sawa' is a noun in the sense of equality, described by it as the masdars are described," and from it is His saying: ﴿Come to a word that is equal between us and you﴾ and His saying: ﴿in four days, equal for those who ask﴾, meaning level. Its being raised is because it is the predicate of "inna," and ﴿a-anzarta-hum am lam tundhirhum﴾ is in the place of nominative, as the subject, as if it were: "inna li-l-ladhina kafaru mustawin 'alayhim inzaruka wa-'adamuhu" (for those who disbelieve, your warning and its absence are level for them), as you say: "inna Zaydan mukhtasimun akhuhu wa-ibn 'ammihi" (Zayd's brother and cousin are disputing). Or ﴿a-anzarta-hum am lam tundhirhum﴾ is in the place of the inceptive (mubtada'), and "sawa'" is a predicate preceding it, meaning "sawa' 'alayhim inzaruka wa-'adamuhu" (your warning and its absence are equal for them), and the sentence is the predicate of "inna."

If you say: The verb is always a predicate, not something predicated about, so how is it correct that it is predicated about in this sentence?

I say: It is of the kind of speech in which the side of the wording is abandoned in favour of the side of the meaning. We have found the Arabs inclining markedly toward meanings in some places of their speech. Among that is their saying: "la ta'kul al-samaka wa-tashrab al-laban," meaning: let not the eating of fish and the drinking of milk be from you.

And if the apparent wording is on what is not valid, such as conjoining a noun to a verb, and the particle of interrogation and "am" being bare, in the sense of equality, while the meaning of interrogation has been wholly stripped from them.

Sibawayh said: "This followed the form of the interrogative particle, as it followed the form of the vocative particle in your saying: 'Allahumma aghfir lana ayyatuha al-'isaba' (O God, forgive us, O company)."

He means that this followed the form of interrogation while there is no interrogation, just as that followed the form of the vocative while there is no vocative. The meaning of equality is their equality in the knowledge of the one asked about, because it is known that one of the two matters exists, either the warning or its absence, but not specifically; and both are known by an unspecified knowledge.

I say: This is his view and the view of a group of grammarians. It has been objected to what they stated, that it necessarily follows for the one who holds it that he permits "sawa'a qumta am qa'adta" without saying "'alayya" or "'alayka," and that he permits "sayyan adhahaba Zayd am jalasa" and "yatafiqani aqama Zayd am qa'ada," and what is similar to this, which is not permitted in speech and has not been transmitted from anyone, because the estimate they posited applies to this.

Another group said: "sawa'" here is an inceptive (mubtada'), and the interrogative sentence is in the place of the predicate.

They only said this although "sawa'" is indefinite, because a sentence is never in the place of an inceptive, nor in the place of a subject.

It was objected to them that when a sentence is a predicate there must be a pronoun in it returning to the inceptive, so where is the pronoun returning to "sawa'" here?

They answered this by saying that "sawa'," though it is an inceptive in wording, is a predicate in meaning, because the meaning is "the warning and its absence are equal for them." They said: it is not necessary that a pronoun return from the inceptive to the predicate; so since "sawa'" is a predicate in meaning and not in wording, the meaning was observed.

A parallel to this is their saying: "darbi Zaydan qa'iman" (my striking Zayd standing), for no pronoun returns to "darbi" from the state that takes the place of the predicate, because its meaning is "strike Zayd, or I struck Zayd," and a verb has no pronoun returning to it. So likewise what is in its meaning and strength.

A parallel also is "a-qa'imun akhuka" (is your brother standing?), because "akhuka," though it takes the place of the predicate, is a doer in meaning, and "qa'im" has the meaning of the verb that raises the doer. So these meanings were observed in these places, and the side of the wording was abandoned in favour of the side of the meaning. The inceptive's ruling remained requiring nominative in wording, and the inceptive contains a meaning differing from the meaning of inception, so that meaning was given its ruling, and no pronoun returned to the wording, and the wording of the inceptive was given the ruling of inception and was raised.

This is the view of this other group. It was objected to it, after acknowledging its goodness and strength, that the Arabs never spoke in this way with "sawa'" except when they joined it with the pronoun in the genitive after "'ala," as in "sawa'un 'alaykum" (equal for you), "sawa'un 'alayhim" (equal for them), and "sawa'un 'alayya" (equal for me). If they extend what they established for "sawa'" to whether it is joined with "'ala" or not, it is not so; and if they restrict it to what is joined with "'ala," they have not explained the secret of this restriction.

A third group, among them al-Suhayli, and this is his wording: "Since the Arabs do not say 'sayyan aqamta am qa'adta' nor 'mithlan' nor 'shabihan,' and they say that only with 'sawa'' together with the genitive after 'ala,' it became necessary to search for the secret in this, and for the intent of the people in this speech, and for equality between what, and in which attributes, of the two named things described as equal. We found that the meaning and intent of the speech is only the equality of lack of concern regarding standing or sitting, or warning or not warning. If they wanted equality in an attribute existing in the essence, they would say 'sawa' al-iqamah wa-al-shukhus' (equal are the staying and the departing), just as they say 'sawa' Zayd wa-'Amr' and 'sayyan' and 'mithlan,' meaning their equality in the attribute of their essences. So when you want to make two matters equal in lack of concern, and in not turning your heart to them, and that they have become cheap to you and insignificant to you, you say: 'sawa' 'alayya af'alu am lam yaf'al' (it is the same for me whether he does or does not do it), just as you say: 'la ubali af'alu am lam yaf'al' (I do not care whether I do or do not do it); because caring is an action of the heart, and actions of the heart are cancelled when followed by the interrogated sentences or the sentence emphasized with the lam. You say: 'la adri aqama Zayd am qa'ada' (I do not know whether Zayd stood or sat), and it is followed by 'la-yaqumanna Zayd' (Zayd will certainly stand), but these heart-actions are not cancelled until their doer is mentioned in wording or in meaning, and then it is in the place of the object of knowledge." Then he said: "When this is established, 'sawa'' is an inceptive in wording, and '('ala' and 'alaykum' or 'alayhim') is genitive in wording, and it is the doer in meaning, which is the content of the speaker's intent, since your saying 'sawa' 'alayya' means 'la ubali' (I do not care), and in 'ubali' there is a doer, and that doer pronoun is the one in the genitive after 'ala' in meaning, because the two matters are equal upon you only in lack of concern. If you are not concerned with them, you do not turn your heart to them, and if you do not turn, it is as if you said: 'la adri aqamta am qa'adta' (I do not know whether you stood or sat). So when the interrogative sentence became in the sense of the object of an action of the heart, it did not require that there be in it a pronoun returning to what precedes it, since before it there is in reality only the meaning of a verb that operates on it as its object, and the pronoun of its operator.

Were it not for your saying '('alayya' and 'alaykum),' that meaning would not be strengthened, nor would it operate on the sentence; but because the genitive is attached, it becomes in the ruling of what is spoken, and the genitive becomes the doer in meaning, like the doer in 'alimtu' (I knew), 'darayta' (you knew), and 'baliyta' (you cared). Do you not see how the genitive in their saying 'lahu sawt sawt ghurab' (he has a sound, the sound of a crow) takes the place of the doer in 'yusawit,' so that it is as if you had uttered 'yusawit,' and so 'sawt ghurab' is put in the accusative? And when you say 'alayhi nawh al-hamam' (upon him is the cooing of doves), you make 'nawh al-hamam' nominative, because the pronoun in the genitive after 'ala' is not the doer that wails, as it was in your saying 'lahu sawt sawt ghurab.' So likewise the genitive in 'sawa' 'alayhim' is the doer that is in your saying 'la yubaluna wa-la yaltafitun' (they do not care and do not turn), since equality is only in lack of concern and turning. The speaker intends nothing other than this, so the doer is mentioned and the caring is its object, and so the interrogative sentence became an object."

**Al-Khatm** (sealing). Al-Azhari said: its original meaning is covering. One says *khatama al-badhr fi al-ard* ("he sealed the seed in the ground") when he covers it.

Abu Ishaq said: *khatama* and *taba'a* (both meaning "to seal") have one meaning in the language, which is covering something and making it secure so that nothing can enter it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ Likewise His saying: ﴿And Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾.

I say: *al-khatm* and *al-taba'* share what has been mentioned, and differ in another meaning. *Al-taba'* is a seal that becomes a natural disposition and innate character, so it is a lasting effect that does not depart.

If it is said: How do you interpret the verses of sealing (*taba'*), veiling and misguidance in the Qur'an, when they seem to imply that the Lord, glory be to Him, compels the wretched to their misguidance?

We say: If Allah grants the resolution of this difficulty and the answer to this question, then no obscurity will remain for those with insight. So we say, first: those whom Allah, glory be to Him, informed of the sealing upon their hearts were addressed as believers, and were required to submit to Islam and to adhere to the rulings, with the requirement of obligation and invitation, while they were described as having ability, power and preference, as has already been established. Whoever believes that they were prevented, compelled, barred by force and invited, then in his view the obligation is like what would happen if a man's hands and feet were bound with ropes, he were thrown into the sea, and then it was said to him, "Do not get wet." This is a matter that no one attributes to the Messengers' laws except one who is at fault in himself and audacious toward his Lord. In the view of this speaker there is no difference between the command of subjection and the command of creation in His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾, and His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, and between the command of obligation. When this is invalid, then the correct way of speaking about these verses, in whose true meanings most sects have gone astray, is this: Allah, when He wills good for a servant, perfects his intellect and completes his insight, then turns away from him the obstacles and impulses, removes from him the impediments, grants him companions of good, eases for him its paths, cuts off from him the distractions and causes of heedlessness, and destines for him what brings him near to the acts of nearness, so he meets them, then becomes accustomed to them and trained in them. And when Allah wills evil for His servant, He decrees for him what distances him from good and drives him away from it, prepares for him the means of persisting in error, makes him love to pursue desires, exposes him to calamities, and whenever the calls of the soul prevail over him, the calls of good are suppressed. Then he continues in evils through the ages, and reaches their abysses, while whisperings, the promptings of Satan and the outbursts of the commanding soul (*al-nafs al-ammara bi'l-su'*) cooperate against him, so heedlessness spreads a veil over his heart by the decree and measure of Allah. That is the sealing (*al-taba'*), the sealing (*al-khatm*) and the coverings (*al-akinna*).

I will give an example of this. Suppose a young man, recent in his maturity, whom no schools have refined and no experiences have seasoned, who is at the height of his youthfulness and desire, who has gained a portion of worldly goods and been given a touch of beauty, and no guardian has stood over him to restrain him from the pits of ruin or prevent him from entangling himself in the nets of passion. Companions of corruption meet him while he is in the arrogance of his youth, speaking to himself of lasting a long time. How close such a description is to casting off restraint, hastening toward the characteristics of the wicked. Yet with all this he is a chooser who prefers; he is not compelled to sins and slips, nor is he barred from obedience, and he has the intellect that makes him deserving of blame if he disobeys. Whoever is in this state, it is not rationally impossible to obligate him, for he is not prevented. But if Allah's decree of evil has preceded for him, then he is going toward the decisive judgment of Allah and His final decree, convicted by the proof of Allah, unless Allah covers him with His mercy, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful. What I have mentioned is clear in the meanings of the verses, and no one who has been granted success doubts it.

If it is said: How can the Wise desire folly?

We have explained that actions are equal with respect to one who neither benefits nor is harmed. But when He informs that He obligates His servants and demands them, and removes their excuses, then His word is true and His speech is sincere. The closest thing they could oppose it with is that the wise among us, when he sees his slave-girls and servants mingling with one another while they are committing what is forbidden to them in his sight and hearing, does not find it good to leave them in their state. The Lord, glory be to Him, sees the evil of their deeds and draws them on step by step from where they do not know. Then he said: "I have exhausted my breath. But if I found someone to explain to me this chapter in acquiring this knowledge, it would be dearer to me, by the Lord who watches over every soul for what it has earned, than the kingship of the world in its entirety for as long as it lasts." End of his words, verbatim.

This is a fine middle position between the two groups. Most of his companions rejected it, including al-Ansari, the commentator on *al-Irshad*, and others. They said: it is closer to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), and the dispute between him and them returns only to the name. They also said this is something he stood alone in. However, he left unaddressed certain matters. Among them: he denied that Allah dislikes what He has decreed of sins, on the basis of his principle that everything He wills is beloved to Him; and that if He has decreed disbelief, wickedness and disobedience, then He wills it and loves it and does not dislike it. And if the power and choice of the servant are effective in bringing about the act in his view, by the decree of the Lord, glory be to Him, then he was right in this and excelled. But the claim that Allah, glory be to Him, loves disbelief, wickedness and disobedience and does not dislike them when they occur, is a statement of utmost falsehood, opposed to clear reason and transmitted text. What led him to it is his saying that love is will and desire, and that whatever He desires He loves. Whoever does not distinguish between desire (*mashi'a*) and love (*mahabba*) is bound to one of two false positions, from which he must not escape.

The first is that Allah, glory be to Him, loves disbelief, wickedness and disobedience. The second is that He did not desire, decree or ordain these things. Each of the two correlates has been held by a group. One group said: He does not love them or approve of them, so He did not desire them or ordain them. Another group said: they occur by His desire and will, so He loves them and approves of them. Both groups agree on this principle and differ on its consequence.

Allah, glory be to Him, has rebuked those who argued for His love from His desire in three places in His Book: in Surah al-An'am, al-Nahl and al-Zukhruf. He said: ﴿The ones who associated partners will say, "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything." Likewise denied those before them until they tasted Our might. Say, "Do you have any knowledge that you can bring out for us? You follow only assumption, and you are only conjecturing."﴾

He related the same of them in al-Nahl, then said: ﴿Likewise did those before them. Then is there upon the messengers except clear notification?﴾

And He said in al-Zukhruf: ﴿And they say, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they are only guessing.﴾

They argued for His love of their polytheism and His approval of it by His having allowed it, and that had He not loved it and approved of it, He would not have willed it from them. They also set this against His command and prohibition and the call of the messengers. They said: how does He command a thing whose opposite He has willed from us? How does He dislike from us a thing whose occurrence He has willed? Had He disliked it, He would not have enabled us to do it, and He would have prevented between us and it. So Allah, glory be to Him, declared them liars in this, and informed that this is a denial of His messengers, and that His messengers all agree that He dislikes their polytheism, hates it and abhors it; and that were it not for His hatred and dislike, He would not have made the polytheists taste His punishment, for He does not punish His servant for what He loves. Then He demanded of them knowledge to confirm their doctrine, that Allah permitted it and loves it and approves of it. But the mere fact that He permits them by decree does not indicate this to any sane person; otherwise oppression, abominations, striving in the earth with corruption and tyranny would be beloved and approved to Him. Then He informed that their basis for this is only assumption, which is the most false of speech, and that for this reason they were people of conjecture and lying. Then He informed, glory be to Him, that He has the conclusive proof against them from two directions. The first is the intellects He placed in them, by which they distinguish between good and evil, truth and falsehood, and the hearing and sight, which are the instruments for perceiving truth and by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. The second is the sending of His messengers, the sending down of His books, and His enabling them to believe and submit. He did not hold them accountable for only one of the two, but for both together, for the perfection of His justice and to cut off every excuse from every side. For this reason He called His proof against them "conclusive" (*al-baligha*), meaning it has reached the furthest extent of clarity, such that no argument remains for any speaker and no excuse for any apologist. Whoever offers Him a sound excuse, He accepts it. Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿So if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾, and that nothing occurs except by His will. This is part of the completeness of His conclusive proof, for if a thing is impossible because He has not willed it, then its existence is necessary when He wills it. What He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. This is among the greatest proofs of monotheism and among the clearest proofs of the falsehood of what you are upon, of polytheism and taking rivals besides Him. What you have argued from His will for your polytheism is among the most manifest proofs of its falsehood and corruption. Had they mentioned the decree and the will as an affirmation of His oneness, an expression of need and recourse to Him, a disavowal of power and strength except through Him, and a desire for Him to relieve them of what, had He willed that it not occur from them, it would not have occurred, that would have benefited them and opened for them the door of guidance. But they mentioned it as an opposition to His command and as a nullification of the call of the messengers, so it only increased them in error.

The point is that He, glory be to Him, has distinguished between His proof (*hujja*) and His will (*mashi'a*). Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, in his *Maqalat* (*Doctrines*), relates the consensus of the People of the Sunna and Hadith (*Ahl al-Sunna wa'l-Hadith*) upon this. What Ibn Fawrak related from him in his summary of his *Maqalat* is that he used to distinguish between these. He said: "He did not distinguish between love (*wudd*) and affection (*hubb*), will (*irada*) and desire (*mashi'a*), approval (*rida*) and preference (*ikhtiyar*). He did not say that any of them is specific to certain objects over others, but he said that each of them has the meaning of its companion, with a restriction that removes ambiguity: that the believer is loved by Allah to be a believer, among the people of good, as He knew; and the disbeliever is also willed to be a disbeliever, as He knew, among the people of evil; and He loves that this be so, as He knew. He said the same concerning approval, selection and choice, and he restricted the wording with this so that no error would be imagined in it." End of quotation.

What the People of Hadith and Sunna, all of them, the jurists entirely, the majority of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) and the Sufis agree upon is that He, glory be to Him, dislikes some entities, actions and attributes, even though they occur by His will. He hates them and abhors them, as He hates the essence of Iblis and the essences of his troops and hates their deeds, and does not love that, even though it exists by His will. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾; ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾; ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾; ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾; ﴿And do not transgress; indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾; ﴿If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free of need of you; and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾.

So this is an report of His not loving these matters and not approving of them after they occur. This is explicit in refuting the view of one who interprets the texts as meaning that He does not love them from one who has not committed them, and loves them when they are committed, so He loves them from the one who committed them and does not love them from the one who did not. This is among the greatest falsehoods and lies against Allah. Rather, He, glory be to Him, dislikes them and hates them before they occur, while they occur, and after they occur, for they are ugly and vile, and Allah is exalted above loving the ugly and the vile. Rather, they are the most hateful thing to Him. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿All of that, its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾.

He, glory be to Him, has informed that He dislikes the obedience of the hypocrites, and for this reason He discourages them from it. How, then, would He love their hypocrisy and approve of it, and make its people beloved to Him, chosen by Him, and approved by Him? From this false principle arose their saying that actions are equal in relation to the Lord, glory be to Him, and that they are not divided in themselves into good and bad. Thus there is no difference in relation to Him, glory be to Him, between gratitude and disbelief. For this reason they said that thanking Him for His blessings is not obligatory by reason. On this principle they said that His will is the very same as His love, that whatever He wills He loves, approves and chooses. After this principle was rooted, they could not say that He hates the entities and actions He created and loves some of them. Rather, everything He does and creates is beloved to Him, and what is hated and abhorred is only what He has not willed and has not created. They established this principle only out of concern to protect the decree (*qadar*), so they used it to build the Law and the decree, and they committed themselves, for its sake, to consequences by which they cast doubt on the decree and wisdom, and for its sake they denied clear reason. They equated the most hideous ugliness and the most beautiful goodness in the reality of the matter, saying: they are equal, with no difference between them except by the bare command and prohibition. So lying, oppression, transgression and aggression are, in their view, equal to truthfulness, justice and benevolence in reality. There is nothing in this that requires its goodness, and nothing in that which requires its ugliness. They made this doctrine a badge of the People of the Sunna, and made the opposite view the doctrine of the people of innovation, the Mu'tazila and others.

By the life of God, this is among the most false of positions, and the most opposed to causes. It holds that He does nothing through anything, and it denies the powers, natures and instincts, and that things can be causes or have an effect. This closed to them the door of correctness in the questions of the decree. They committed themselves to these false principles, and to consequences that are more manifestly false, and these consequences are from the first thing that shows the corruption and falsehood of these principles, for the falsehood of a consequence stems from the falsehood of what it entails.

(Section)

Here are a number of things by which He punished the disbelievers by preventing them from faith: sealing (*khatm*), stamping (*taba'*), coverings (*akinna*), veils (*ghita'*), sheaths (*ghilaf*), curtains (*hijab*), deafness (*waqr*), blindfolding (*ghisha'a*), rust (*ran*), fetters (*ghull*), barriers (*sadd*), locks (*qufl*), deafness (*summ*), dumbness (*bakm*), blindness (*ama*), turning away (*sadd*), diverting (*sarf*), binding upon the heart (*shadd 'ala al-qalb*), misguidance (*dalal*), heedlessness (*ighfal*), sickness (*maradh*), the turning of hearts (*taqlib al-af'ida*), the intervening between a person and his heart (*hawl bayn al-mar' wa-qalbihi*), the deviation of hearts (*izaghat al-qulub*), abandonment (*khidhlan*), reversal (*irkas*), discouragement (*tathbit*), beautifying (*tazyin*), not willing their guidance and purification, causing their hearts to die after life has been created in them, so they remain in original death, withholding light from them so they remain in original darkness, making the heart hard so that the image and form of guidance are not impressed upon it, and making the chest narrow and constricted so that it does not accept faith.

Some of these return to the heart, such as sealing, stamping, locking, coverings, heedlessness, sickness and similar. Some return to his messenger, which conveys guidance to it, such as deafness and heaviness. Some return to his forerunner and scout, such as blindness and blindfolding. Some return to his interpreter and messenger who conveys from Him, such as verbal dumbness, which is the result of heart dumbness. So when the heart is dumb, the tongue is dumb. Do not listen to one who says these are metaphors and figures of speech, for he speaks according to the measure of his knowledge and understanding of Allah and His messenger. For this speaker, the reality of the action is that it is of iron, sealing is with wax or clay, sickness is fever with shivering, colic or other bodily illnesses, death is merely the departure of the spirit from the body, and blindness is the loss of the light of the eye by which one sees. This group is among the people most veiled. These matters, when attributed to their locus, are according to that locus. The relation of the lock of the heart to the heart is like the relation of the lock of a door to the door. Likewise the seal and stamp upon it are, in relation to it, like the seal and stamp upon the door, the chest, and similar. Likewise the relation of deafness and blindness to the ear and eye. Likewise its death and life are like the death and life of the body. Rather, these matters are more binding upon the heart than upon the body. So if it were said that they are literal of the heart and figurative of the sensible bodies, it would be like the saying of these people and stronger than it, and both are false. So blindness, dumbness, death and locking are literal for the heart. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but blind are the hearts within the breasts﴾. The meaning is that this is the greatest blindness and its origin. This is like His saying, may blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ): "Usury is only in delayed exchange (*nasi'a*)." And His saying: "Water is only from water." And His saying: "Richness is not from abundance of goods; richness is richness of the soul." And His saying: "The poor man is not one who is turned away by a morsel or two, or a date or two; the poor man is one who finds nothing sufficient for him and is not noticed so that charity is given to him." And His saying: "The strong man is not the one who overthrows others; the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry." He did not intend to deny the name from these things, but He intended that these are more deserving of these names and more worthy of them than those who are named by them. Likewise His saying: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but blind are the hearts within the breasts﴾. Close to this is His saying: ﴿Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah and the Last Day...﴾, the verse.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 7 (part 2 of 2):

"On both interpretations, the heart is truly ascribed blindness, and so is everything else that is attributed to it. Since the heart is the sovereign of the limbs, which are its soldiers, it is what moves and employs them, and volition, the faculties, and voluntary motion all issue from it, these metaphors are primary, while the limbs follow. Let us therefore mention these matters in detail and where they occur in the Qur'an, for the sealing (al-khatm) has already been discussed."

Al-Azhari said: "Its root meaning is covering, as when one covers seed in the earth (khatama al-badhr fi al-ard) by burying it."

Abu Ishaq said: "The meaning of khatama and taba'a (sealing and stamping) in the language is one and the same: it is covering over a thing and making it secure, so that nothing enters it, as the Exalted said: ﴿Or is it that there are locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad 47:24], and likewise His saying: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:87]."

I say: sealing (al-khatm) and stamping (al-tab') share what has been mentioned, and they differ in another respect, namely that the stamp (al-tab') is a seal that becomes a disposition and a natural trait, so it is a lasting effect that does not separate from its object.

God has torn away the veils of the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) and exposed their secrets in the Qur'an, and He has made their affairs clear to His servants so that they may be on guard against them and against their people. In the opening of Surah al-Baqarah He mentioned the three groups of mankind: the believers, the disbelievers, and the hypocrites. He mentioned four verses about the believers, two about the disbelievers, and thirteen verses about the hypocrites, because of their great number, the general trial they pose, and the severity of their harm to Islam and its people. The affliction that Islam suffers from them is extremely severe, because they are attributed to it and to its support and loyalty, yet in reality they are its enemies. They express their hostility in every form, and the ignorant man thinks it is knowledge and reform, when in fact it is the utmost ignorance and corruption.

How many a stronghold of Islam have they demolished! How many a fortress of it have they uprooted at its foundations and laid waste! How much knowledge of it have they obliterated! How many a banner of it, raised high, have they brought down! How many times have they struck at the roots of its plantings with the mattocks of doubts, to uproot them! How many times have they blinded the springs of its watering-places with their opinions, to bury and cut them off!

Islam and its people therefore remain in a state of tribulation and affliction at their hands. Their doubts keep assailing it with raid after raid, and they claim that by this they are reformers. ﴿Surely it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 12]. ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect His light, though the disbelievers hate it﴾ [al-Saff: 8].

They have agreed to abandon revelation, and so they are united in refusing to be guided by it. ﴿But they have divided their affair among themselves into sects, each party rejoicing in what it has﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 53]. ﴿Some of them inspire others with ornate speech as deception﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. And for this reason ﴿they have taken this Qur'an as something to be abandoned﴾ [al-Furqan: 30].

The landmarks of faith in their hearts have been effaced, so they do not recognise them. Its places of worship have fallen into ruin in their view, so they do not maintain them. Its bright stars have set from their hearts, so they do not love them. Its sun has been eclipsed when the darknesses of their opinions and thoughts gathered, so they do not see it. They have not accepted the guidance of God with which He sent His Messenger, they have not raised their heads to it, and they have seen no harm in turning away from it toward their own opinions and thoughts. They have stripped the texts of revelation of their authority over reality, removed them from their rightful rule over certainty, and launched against them raids of false interpretations. Ambush after ambush keeps issuing against them from among them. The texts came down upon them as a guest comes down upon base people, and they received them with none of the acceptance and honour that was due to them. They received them from afar, pushing them away from their chests and backs, saying: "You have no passage with us; and if you must pass, then only by way of mere transit." They prepared against them every kind of equipment and all manner of rules, and when the texts descended upon their courtyard they said: "What have we to do with mere verbal surfaces that give us no certainty at all?" As for their common folk, they said: "It is enough for us what we found our successors (khalaf) upon, namely the later scholars, for they know these matters better than the early predecessors (al-salaf) and are more skilled in the methods of proof and argument." But those earlier ones were overcome by simplicity and soundness of heart. They did not devote themselves to laying down the foundations of speculative method; rather, they directed their resolve to doing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden. So the method of the later scholars is more knowledgeable and more judicious, while the method of the earlier predecessors is more ignorant, but safer.

They have placed the texts of the Sunnah and the Qur'an in the position of a caliph in this age: his name is on the coinage and in the sermon atop the pulpits, raised high, but the ruling that takes effect belongs to someone else. So his judgement is neither accepted nor heard.

They have dressed themselves in the garments of the people of faith while their hearts belong to the people of deviation and loss, of rancour and disbelief. Their outward appearance is that of the helpers, but their inner selves have sided with the disbelievers. Their tongues are the tongues of those who make peace, but their hearts are the hearts of those who wage war. And they say: ﴿We believe in God and the Last Day,﴾ but ﴿they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8].

Their capital is deceit and cunning, their merchandise is lying and treachery. In their worldly reckoning they believe that both parties are content with them, and that they are secure among them. ﴿They deceive God and those who believe, but they deceive none but themselves, and they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9].

The diseases of doubts and desires have worn down their hearts and destroyed them, and evil intentions have overpowered their wills and their purposes and corrupted them. Their corruption has reached the point of ruin, so that even the skilled physicians have been unable to cure it. ﴿In their hearts is a disease, and God has increased their disease; and for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10].

Whoever has the claws of their suspicions fastened upon the skin of his faith, they tear it to every kind of shred. Whoever has the sparks of their trial lodged in his heart, they cast him into the torment of the blaze. Whoever has the doubts of their deception enter his ears, they stand between his heart and assent. Their corruption on earth is great, and most people are heedless of it. ﴿When it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers." Surely it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11-12].

In their view, whoever holds fast to the Book and the Sunnah is a man of mere outward forms, deprived of his share of reason, and one who adheres to the texts is like a donkey carrying books: his concern is only to carry what is transmitted. The merchandise of the merchant of revelation is unsaleable among them, and what he brings is not accepted by them. The followers of the Prophetic way are foolish in their eyes, and in their private gatherings and assemblies they consider them ill-omened. ﴿When it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" Surely it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 13].

Each of them has two faces: one face with which he meets the believers, and another with which he turns back to his fellow atheists. He has two tongues: one which the Muslims accept at face value, and another through which he translates his hidden secret. ﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they go apart to their devils, they say, "Surely we are with you; we were only mocking"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14].
