Then Allah, glorified and exalted, struck for them another parable, one concerning water, and said, exalted is He: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky, within which are darknesses, thunder, and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].

He likened their share of the light and life with which Allah sent His Messenger (ﷺ) to the share of one who kindles a fire, which was extinguished from him just when he most needed it, its light departed, and he was left in the darkness, bewildered and lost, unable to find the way or know the path. And He likened them to the people of the rain-cloud (ṣayyib), which is the rain that pours down (yaṣūbu), that is, descends from high to low. He likened the guidance with which He guided His servants to the rain-cloud, because hearts come alive through it just as the earth comes alive through rain. And the share of the hypocrites from this guidance is likened to the share of one who obtains from the rain-cloud nothing but darknesses, thunder and lightning, and has no share in what lies beyond that, which is the purpose of the rain-cloud: the life of lands, servants, trees and animals. The darknesses within it, and that thunder and lightning, are sought for something other than themselves; they are a means to the full benefit of that rain-cloud. The ignorant person, because of the extremity of his ignorance, limits himself to perceiving what is in the rain-cloud of darkness, thunder and lightning, and the consequences of these: intense cold, a traveller halted from his journey, and a craftsman halted from his craft. He has no insight that penetrates to what the outcome of that rain-cloud will be of life and general benefit. Such is the condition of everyone of short sight and weak intellect, whose gaze does not pass beyond the apparent disliked matter to what lies behind it of everything beloved.

This is the condition of most of creation, except those whose insight is sound. When one of weak insight sees what is involved in jihad of toil, hardships, exposure to the loss of life, severe wounds, the blame of the blamers, and enmity from those whose enmity he fears, he does not advance upon it, because he has not witnessed the praiseworthy consequences and the ends toward which the competitors race and for which the rivals compete. Likewise, one who resolves upon the journey of Hajj to the Sacred House, and knows of that journey nothing but the hardship of travel, separation from family and homeland, enduring hardships, and parting from familiar things, and his gaze and insight do not pass beyond the end, outcome and consequence of that journey, does not set out on it and does not resolve upon it. The condition of these is the condition of one of weak insight and faith, who sees in the Qur'an the promise and the threat, the restraints and prohibitions, and the commands that are burdensome to souls, which wean them from suckling at the breast of familiar things and desires. Weaning is the hardest and most difficult thing for a child, and all people are children of intellect except one who has reached the stage of wise, discerning men and has attained the truth in knowledge, action and recognition. This is the one who looks beyond the rain-cloud, at what is within it of thunder, lightning and thunderbolts, and knows that it is the life of existence.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "One may say: He likened the religion of Islam to the rain-cloud, because hearts come alive through it just as the earth comes alive through rain. What is connected to it of the likeness of the disbelievers to the darknesses, what is in it of promise and threat to thunder and lightning, and what afflicts the disbelievers of terrors, calamities and trials from the people of Islam to thunderbolts. The meaning: 'or like the people of a rain-cloud,' and what is meant is 'like a people whom the sky seized in this attribute, and who suffered from it what they suffered.'"

He said: "The correct view, upon which the scholars of eloquence (ʿulamāʾ al-bayān) agree and do not overstep, is that both similes are composite similes (al-tamthīlāt al-murakkaba), not discrete ones, in which each single element is not forced to be assigned a separate likeness. This is the decisive statement and the firm doctrine. Its explanation is that the Arabs take things individually, each separated from the other, so that this does not take hold of that, and then they liken them to their counterparts, as in the Qur'an, where He likened a state resulting from a collection of things that have become interlocked and bound together until they became one thing, to another like it, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the donkey that carries books﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 5], and so on. The purpose is to liken the condition of the Jews in their ignorance of what they had of the Torah and its manifest signs, to the condition of the donkey in its ignorance of what it carries of books of wisdom. For the donkey, the two conditions are equal: one who carries books of wisdom and one who carries other burdens, and it perceives nothing of that except the toil and fatigue that pass over its back. And like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And strike for them the parable of the life of this world: like water which We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it, then it became dry stubble which the winds scatter﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]. The meaning is the brevity of the splendour of this world, like the brevity of the lasting of this green growth.

As for the view that the likeness is meant to be of individual items to individual items, not bound to one another, with their final outcome being one thing, that is not correct. Likewise, when He described the hypocrites' falling into their error, and the bewilderment and confusion in which they were entangled, their bewilderment and the severity of the matter for them were likened to what one suffers whose fire has been extinguished after being kindled in the darkness of night; and likewise one whom the sky seizes on a dark night, with thunder, lightning and fear of thunderbolts." He said: "If you ask: which of the two similes is more eloquent? I say: the second, because it is more indicative of the extremity of bewilderment, the severity of the matter and its frightfulness. For this reason it is placed last, since they proceed in such matters from the lighter to the more severe."

(Section)

These two parables comprise great wisdoms:

First: the one who is illuminated by fire is illuminated by a light from another source, not from himself. When that fire goes out, he remains in darkness. So too the hypocrite, who professes with his tongue without belief and love in his heart and without firm conviction, has the light he possesses as something borrowed.

Second: the light of fire requires, to continue, a material that sustains it, and that material is for the light like food for a living creature. Likewise the light of faith requires a material of beneficial knowledge and righteous action by which it stands and endures through their continuance. When the material of faith is cut off, it is extinguished, just as fire is put out when its fuel runs out.

Third: darkness is of two kinds: a continuous darkness that was never preceded by light, and a darkness that arises after light, and this is the more severe of the two and the most grievous for whoever has it as his portion. The darkness of the hypocrite is darkness after illumination, so his condition is likened to the condition of one who kindled a fire and was left in darkness after the light. As for the disbeliever, he is in darkness and has never emerged from it at all.

Fourth: in this parable there is an announcement and an alert concerning their state in the Hereafter: they will be given an apparent light, as their light in this world was apparent, and then that light will be extinguished just when they most need it, since it has no lasting material to sustain it. They will remain on the Bridge in darkness, unable to cross, for no one can cross it except with a steadfast light that accompanies him until he traverses the Bridge. If that light has no material of beneficial knowledge and righteous action, Allah, exalted is He, takes it away at the moment its owner most needs it. Thus the parable corresponds to their state in this world and to their state on the Day of Resurrection, when the lights are distributed beyond the Bridge: the light of the believers remains, and the light of the hypocrites is extinguished.

From here you learn the secret in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah took away their light...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and He did not say "He removed their light." If you want further explanation and clarification, then reflect upon what Muslim narrated in his Ṣaḥīḥ from the hadith of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhumā).

He was asked about the crossing (al-wurūd), and said: "We will come on the Day of Resurrection upon a hill above the people," he said: "The nations will be summoned with their idols and what they used to worship, the first after the first. Then our Lord, blessed and exalted, will come to us after that and say: 'Whom are you waiting for?' They will say: 'We are waiting for our Lord.' He will say: 'I am your Lord.' They will say: 'Until we look at You.' Then He will manifest Himself to them, laughing." He said: "Then He will set off with them, and they will follow Him, and each person among them, whether hypocrite or believer, will be given a light. Then they will follow Him, and on the Bridge of Hell there are hooks and thorny plants that seize whom Allah wills. Then the light of the hypocrites will be extinguished, and then the believers will be saved. The first group to be saved will have faces like the full moon on the night of the full moon, seventy thousand of them, who will not be reckoned. Then those who follow them, like the lights of a star in the sky. Then likewise, then intercession will be opened, and they will intercede until whoever said 'There is no god but Allah' and had in his heart good weighing a barley-grain comes out of the Fire, and they will be placed at the courtyard of Paradise, and the people of Paradise will sprinkle water upon them." And he mentioned the rest of the hadith.

Reflect upon his words: "He will set off, and they will follow Him, and each person among them is given a light, the hypocrite and the believer," then reflect upon His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses, they do not see﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and so on.

Reflect upon their state when their lights are extinguished and they remain in darkness, while the believers have gone in the light of their faith, following their Lord, mighty and majestic. Reflect upon His saying (ﷺ) in the hadith of intercession: "Let every nation follow what it used to worship." So every polytheist follows the god he used to worship. The monotheist is worthy of following the true God, besides whom every object of worship is false. Reflect upon His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when a shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration, but they will not be able﴾ [al-Qalam: 42].

He mentioned this verse in the hadith of intercession at this point, and His saying in the hadith: "Then His shin will be uncovered." This addition clarifies what is meant by the shin mentioned in the verse. Reflect also upon the mention of His setting off and His being followed, exalted is He, after this. This opens for you a door of the secrets of Monotheism, the understanding of the Qur'an, and the way Allah, glorified and exalted, deals with the people of His Oneness, who worshipped Him alone and associated nothing with Him. This is the treatment with which He dealt with the people of polytheism in return: each nation went with its object of worship, and it set off with it and followed it to the Fire, while the true God set off and His friends and worshippers followed Him. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, in whom the eyes of the people of Monotheism are gladdened in this world and the Hereafter, and who parted from people in it when they most needed them.

Another of these wisdoms: the first parable includes the occurrence of darkness, which is misguidance and bewilderment, whose opposite is guidance. The second parable includes the occurrence of fear, whose opposite is security. So there is neither guidance nor security for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing, those are the ones for whom is security, and they are guided﴾ [al-An'am: 82].

Ibn ʿAbbās and others among the early Muslims (al-salaf) said: The likeness of these people in their hypocrisy is like the likeness of a man who kindled a fire on a dark night in a desert, warmed himself, saw what was around him, and guarded against what he feared. While he was in that state, his fire went out, and he remained in darkness, afraid and bewildered. So too the hypocrites, by professing the word of faith, were secure regarding their property and children, married believers, inherited from them and shared spoils with them; that was their light. When they die, they return to darkness and fear.

Mujāhid said: "The kindling of the fire for them is their turning toward the Muslims and guidance, and the extinguishing of their light is their turning toward the polytheists and misguidance." That illumination and the extinguishing of the light have been explained as being in this world, have been explained as being in the barzakh, and have been explained as being on the Day of Resurrection. The correct view is that this is their condition in all three abodes: since they were thus in this world, they are recompensed in the barzakh and on the Day of Resurrection with the like of their state: ﴿a recompense in proportion﴾ [al-Naba': 26], ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. For the returning state comes back upon the servant with what was present for him in this world. For this reason the Day of Recompense is so named: ﴿Whoever was blind in this world will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray in the way﴾ [al-Isra': 72], ﴿and Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾ [Maryam: 76], and so on.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 19 (part 2 of 3)

The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated that the completeness of what a person enjoys of the good things in the Hereafter corresponds to the completeness of the deeds he performed in this world. (. . . . ) He (ﷺ) saw a cluster of poor-quality dates (hashaf) hanging in the mosque for charity, and said: "The owner of this will eat hashaf on the Day of Resurrection." He thereby informed that his recompense will be of the same kind as his deed, so he will be repaid for that charity with hashaf of the same kind.

This subject opens for you great doors of understanding the Return (al-ma'ad, the Resurrection) and the differences among people in their states there, and the various matters that occur in it. Among them:

The lightness and heaviness of the burden on the servant's back when he rises from his grave. It corresponds to the lightness or heaviness of his burden of sins: if it is light, it will be light; if it is heavy, it will be heavy.

Among them: his being shaded by the shadow of the Throne, or his being exposed to the heat and the sun. If he had, in this world, sincere righteous deeds and faith that shade him from the heat of shirk, sins and injustice, he will be shaded there in the shade of his deeds beneath the Throne of the Most Merciful. But if he was exposed here to prohibitions, transgressions, innovations and immorality, he will be exposed there to intense heat.

Among them: the length of his standing at the place of gathering, and its hardship upon him, and its being made easy for him. If he stood long in prayer by night and day for Allah, and bore hardships for the sake of His pleasure and obedience, the standing on that day will be light for him, and easy, and if he preferred comfort here, ease and idleness and luxury, the standing there will be long for him and its hardship will be intense upon him.

Allah, the Exalted, has indicated this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Qur'an to you in stages. So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever. And mention the name of your Lord morning and afternoon, and during part of the night prostrate to Him and exalt Him through the long night. Indeed, these love the immediate world and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾ (76:23–27)

So whoever glorifies Allah through the long night, that day will not be heavy upon him; rather it will be the lightest thing for him.

Among them: the heaviness of his scale there corresponds to his bearing the weight of the truth in this world, not merely to the abundance of deeds. The scale is made heavy only by following the truth, being patient upon it, giving it when asked, and taking it when it is given, as the Siddiq (Abu Bakr) said in his advice to 'Umar: "Know that Allah has a right by night which He does not accept by day, and a right by day which He does not accept by night. And know that the scales of those whose scales are heavy were made heavy only by their following the truth and its being heavy upon them in the life of this world. It is right that a scale into which the truth is placed should be heavy. And the scales of those whose scales are light on the Day of Resurrection were made light only by their following falsehood in the life of this world, its lightness upon them. It is right that a scale into which nothing but falsehood is placed should be light."

Among them: the people's coming to the Basin (al-hawd) and their drinking from it on the Day of the Great Thirst corresponds to their coming to the sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their drinking from it. Whoever came to it in this world, drank from it and quenched his thirst fully, will come to his Basin there and drink from it and be fully satisfied. He (ﷺ) has two great basins: a basin in this world, which is his sunnah and what he brought, and a basin in the Hereafter. So those who drink from this basin in this world are those who drink from his Basin on the Day of Resurrection. Some drink and some are deprived, some drink little and some drink much. Those whom he and the angels drive away from his Basin on the Day of Resurrection are those who used to drive themselves and their followers away from his sunnah, preferring other things over it. Whoever was thirsty for his sunnah in this world and had no drink from it, will be more thirsty in the Hereafter and his liver will burn more. A man will meet another and say: "O so-and-so, did you drink?" He will say: "Yes, by Allah." He will say: "But by Allah I did not drink, woe to my thirst!"

So come forward, O thirsty one, and the coming is possible. If you do not come, know that you are doomed. And if Ridwan does not give you a sip to drink, he will give it to you while you are thirsty, my friend. And if you do not come to his Basin in this abode, you will be turned away from it on the day you meet him, O you who are turned away.

Among them: his distribution of lights in the darkness beyond the Bridge. The servant is given light there according to the strength of the light of his faith, his certainty, his sincerity, and his following of the Messenger in the life of this world. Among them are those whose light is like the sun, and below that like the moon, and below that like the brightest star in the sky in brilliance.

Among them are those whose light is like a lamp, in strength and weakness and what lies between.

Among them are those given a light on the tip of the big toe of his foot, which shines at times and goes out at others, according to the amount of the light of faith he had in the life of this world. This is that same light which Allah brought forth for His servant in the Hereafter, manifest, seen with the eyes. No one else is illuminated by it, and no one walks except by the light of himself. If he has light, he walks in his light; if he has no light at all, the light of others does not benefit him.

Since the hypocrite in this world had a manifest light that was not steady nor connected to his inner self, and had no source of faith, he is given in the Hereafter a manifest light with no source, and then it is extinguished from him at the moment he most needs it.

Among them: their passing over the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) in speed and slowness corresponds to the speed and slowness of their journey on the straight path of Allah in this world. The fastest of them in journeying here will be the fastest there, and the slowest here will be the slowest there. The firmest of them in standing on the straight path here will be the firmest there. Whoever was snatched by the hooks of desires, doubts and misguided innovations here, will be snatched there by hooks like the thorns of the sa'dan plant. The effect of the hooks on him there will correspond to his desires, doubts and innovations here. So there are the saved, untouched; the scratched, who will be saved; and the cast-down, that is, cut by the hooks and piled into the Fire, just as those hooks affected them in this world: ﴿a recompense in accordance [with their deeds]﴾ (78:26), and ﴿your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ (41:46).

The point is that Allah, blessed and exalted, set forth for His servants the two parables, the watery and the fiery, in Surat al-Baqarah, in Surat al-Ra'd, and in Surat al-Nur, because the two parables contain life and illumination. The believer has a living heart and an illuminated one; the disbeliever and the hypocrite have a dead heart and a dark one. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness, never to emerge from it?﴾ (6:122), and the Exalted said: ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike, nor are darknesses and light, nor shade and heat, nor are the living and the dead alike﴾ (35:19–22). So He made whoever is guided by His guidance and illuminated by His light a seeing, living person in a shade that protects him from the heat of doubts, misguidance, innovations and shirk, illuminated by His light. And the other is blind and dead, in the heat of disbelief, shirk and misguidance, immersed in darknesses. And the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, or faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ (42:52).

(A subtle point)

The Exalted said: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾, and did not say "their fire." Fire has burning and illumination; He took away from it the illumination and kept for them its harm and burning. Likewise is the state of the hypocrites: the light of their faith was taken away by hypocrisy, and there remained in their hearts the heat of disbelief, doubts and suspicions, boiling in their hearts. Their hearts were roasted by its heat, its harm, its poisons and its blaze in this world, and Allah the Exalted will burn them with it on the Day of Resurrection, a Fire sealed shut, reaching the hearts (104:6–7).

This is the parable of one whom the light of faith never touched in this world, but rather came out of it and left it after having been illuminated by it. This is the state of the hypocrite: he recognized, then denied; he affirmed, then rejected. He is in darknesses: deaf, dumb, blind, as the Exalted said concerning their fellow disbelievers: ﴿Those who denied Our signs are deaf and dumb in darknesses﴾ (6:39). And the Exalted said: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry: deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ (2:171).

Allah the Exalted likened the state of the hypocrites in their departing from the light after it had illuminated them to the state of one who kindles a fire and then its light goes away from him after it had illuminated what was around him. This is because the hypocrites, by mixing with the Muslims, praying with them, fasting with them, hearing the Qur'an, and witnessing the signs and landmarks of Islam, had witnessed the illumination and seen the light with their own eyes.

For this reason the Exalted said concerning them: ﴿so they do not return﴾ (2:18), because they departed from Islam after having been clothed in it and illuminated by it, so they do not return to it.

And the Exalted said concerning the disbelievers: ﴿so they do not understand﴾, because they never understood Islam, never entered it, and were never illuminated by it. Rather, they remain in the darknesses of disbelief: deaf, dumb, blind.

Glory be to the One who made His speech a cure for the diseases of the breasts, calling to faith and its realities, calling to eternal life and everlasting bliss, and guiding to the path of right guidance.

The caller to faith would have been heard if he had reached attentive ears, and the admonitions of the Qur'an would have healed if they had met empty hearts. But the winds of doubts and desires swept over the hearts and extinguished their lamps, and the hands of heedlessness and ignorance took hold of them, closing the doors of their guidance and losing their keys. Their earnings covered them, so speech benefited them nothing, and they were intoxicated with the desires of error and the doubts of falsehood, so they no longer listened to reproach.

They were admonished with admonitions more piercing than spears and arrows, but they died in the sea of ignorance and heedlessness, captive to passion and desire. And a wounded one who is dead feels no pain.

As for deafness and heaviness of hearing, it is in the saying of Allah: ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾ (2:18).

And His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He has made them deaf and blinded their vision﴾ (47:23).

And His saying: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray. Those are the heedless﴾ (7:179).

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness upon them. Those are called from a far place﴾ (41:44).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "In their ears is deafness from hearing the Qur'an, and it is blindness upon them: Allah has blinded their hearts so they do not understand. Those are called from a far place, like the beast that understands nothing but a call and a cry."

Mujahid said: "Far from their hearts."

Al-Farra' said: "You say to a man who does not understand, in this way: you are being called from a far place." He said: "It is mentioned in the tafsir: it is as if they are being called from the sky and do not hear." End of quote.

The meaning is that they do not hear and do not understand, just as one who is called from a far place does not hear and does not understand.

As for dumbness, the Exalted said: ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾. "Bukm" (dumb) is the plural of "abkam," which is one who does not speak.

Dumbness is of two kinds: dumbness of the heart and dumbness of the tongue, just as speech is of two kinds: speech of the heart and speech of the tongue. The more severe of the two is dumbness of the heart, just as its blindness and deafness are more severe than blindness of the eye and deafness of the ear.

So Allah, glorified is He, described them as not understanding the truth, and their tongues not speaking it.

Knowledge enters through three doors: the hearing, the sight, and the heart. These three doors were sealed against them: the hearing was sealed by deafness, the sight by blindness, and the heart by dumbness. Its counterpart is the Exalted's saying: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾ (7:179). And Allah, glorified is He, combined the three in His saying: ﴿And We made for them hearing and sight and hearts, but their hearing, their sight and their hearts availed them nothing at all, since they used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ (46:26).

So when He, glorified is He, wills the guidance of a servant, He opens his heart, his hearing and his sight. And when He wills his misguidance, He makes him deaf, blind and dumb. And success is from Allah.

﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾ (2:19).

As-sayyib: the rain that pours (yusawwib) from the sky, meaning that it descends from it swiftly. It is a parable for the Qur'an, by which the hearts live, like the rain by which the earth, the plants and the animals live. The believers understood this from it and knew the life that would come to them through it, which has no equal. The thunder and lightning did not prevent them from it: the thunder and lightning are the threat, the warning, the punishments and the penalties with which Allah warned those who opposed His command.

He informed that He sends it down upon those who deny the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or the harsh commands within it, like fighting the enemies and patience upon the command, or the burdensome commands upon the souls that go against their desires; these are like the darknesses, the thunder and the lightning.

But whoever knows the places of the rain and the life that comes through it does not feel lonely because of the darkness, thunder and lightning that accompany it. Rather he takes comfort in it and rejoices in it, because of what he hopes to gain from it of life and fertility.

As for the hypocrite, his heart is blinded; his sight does not pass beyond the darkness. He sees nothing but a flash that almost snatches away sight, and a great threat, and darkness. So he feels lonely because of this and is afraid of it. He puts his fingers in his ears so as not to hear the sound of the thunder, and the sight of that flash and the intensity of its glare and the magnitude of its light terrify him. He fears that it will snatch away his sight, because his sight is too weak to stand before it. So he is in darkness, hearing the sounds of the crashing thunder and seeing that snatching flash. If what is before him is lit, he walks in its light; if the light disappears, he stands bewildered, not knowing where to go. Because of his ignorance, he does not know that this is one of the necessary features of the rain by which the earth and plants live, and that his own life is in himself. Rather, he perceives nothing but thunder, lightning and darkness, and has no awareness of what lies beyond that. So loneliness is inseparable from him, and terror and fright never leave him.

And as for the one who is familiar with the downpour, who knows what good, life, and benefit come from it, and knows that it must bring thunder, lightning, and darkness caused by the clouds, he is at ease with that. It does not frighten him, and it does not prevent him from taking his share of the downpour.

This is an exact parable for the downpour that Jibril (ﷺ) brought down from the Lord of the worlds, blessed and exalted, upon the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that through it hearts and all existence might be given life. His wisdom required that it be accompanied by clouds, thunder, and lightning, just as rain is accompanied by water: a perfect wisdom and ordered causes, arranged by the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The share of the hypocrite from that downpour was therefore only its clouds, its thunder, and its lightning. He did not know what lay behind them. So he was frightened by what the believers found reassuring, he doubted what the people of certainty were at peace with, and he questioned what those who see and know were sure of. His sight, in the parable of fire, was like the sight of a bat at midday, and his hearing, in the parable of water, was like the hearing of one who dies from the sound of thunder. It is mentioned that some animals die from hearing thunder.

When such minds, ears, and eyes are struck by satanic doubts, false imaginings, and deceptive assumptions, these roam within them and dominate them, rise and fall within them, their domain expands, and their talk and speech multiply. They fill the ears with their nonsense and the earth with their writings. How many there are who respond to them, accept them, uphold their cause, defend their territory, fight under their banners, and swell their numbers!

Because of the widespread affliction they cause and the harm their words do to hearts, Allah has exposed them in His Book to the utmost degree, has unveiled their veils to the fullest extent, and has made clear their signs, their deeds, and their words. The Mighty and Majestic has continued to say: "And among them… and among them… and among them…" until their affair became plain, their realities became clear, and their secrets were revealed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 21–22 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾

This is an argument of the utmost clarity and the highest degree of explanation, covering all the objectives of the fundamentals of religion: the affirmation of the Creator and of His attributes of perfection, namely His power, knowledge, will, life, wisdom and acts; the origination of the world; and the affirmation of the two kinds of His Oneness (tawhid), the Oneness of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah), which entails that He alone is the Lord, the Creator, the Originator, and the Oneness of Godhead (tawhid al-uluhiyyah), which entails that He alone is the God who is worshipped, loved, and to whom alone worship, humility, submission and love are fitting. Then, after that, He established the prophethood of His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) with the most eloquent, best, most complete establishment, furthest from any opposition. Thereby the truthfulness of His Messenger in all that he says is established, and he has informed about the Return, Paradise and Hell, so the soundness of that is established by necessity.

These verses thus established all of these objectives in the best manner. He opened them with His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾, which is an address to all the children of Adam, who all share in its relation to them. Then He said: ﴿Worship your Lord﴾, commanding them to worship their Lord. Within this phrase lies the decisive proof of the obligation of worshipping Him, for if He is our Lord, who nurtures us by His blessing and beneficence, the owner of our essences, our necks and our souls, and every atom of the servant is His property in pure and true ownership, and He has nurtured him by His kindness to him and His favour upon him, then worshipping Him and thanking Him is obligatory upon him. For this reason He said: ﴿Worship your Lord﴾ and did not say "your God." The Lord is the Master, the Owner, the Benefactor, the Nurturer, the Reformer, and God, Exalted is He, is the Lord in all these senses. Nothing is more necessary in intellects and natural dispositions than worshipping One who is such, alone, without partner.

Then He said: ﴿who created you﴾, thereby also alerting to the obligation of worshipping Him alone, namely that He brought them out from non-existence into existence, produced, invented and originated them alone without partner, by their acknowledgment and confession, as He said in another place of the Qur'an: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God."﴾ So if He alone is the Creator, how could He not be the sole object of worship, and how could they set up a partner with Him in worship while you confess that He has no partner in creation?

This is the method of the Qur'an: it argues from the Oneness of Lordship to the Oneness of Godhead. Then He said: ﴿and those before you﴾, thereby alerting that He alone is the Creator of you, of your fathers, and of those who preceded you, and that none shared with Him in the creation of those before you or of you. His creation of them entails the perfection of His power, will, knowledge, wisdom and life, and that entails all the rest of His attributes of perfection and sublime qualities. Thus this includes the affirmation of His attributes and acts and His oneness in His attributes, so there is no likeness to Him in them, and in His acts, so there is no partner with Him in them. Then He mentioned the purpose of creating them, which is that they should fear Him, so that they obey Him and do not disobey Him, remember Him and do not forget Him, thank Him and do not disbelieve in Him. This is the reality of taqwa of Him. As for His saying: ﴿that you may become righteous﴾ (la'allakum tattaqun), it has been said that it is a reason for the command; it has been said that it is a reason for the creation; and it has been said that the meaning is "worship Him so that you may fear Him by worshipping Him"; and it has been said that the meaning is "He created you so that you may fear Him." The last is more apparent, for several reasons:

First: taqwa is worship, and a thing cannot be the cause of itself.

Second: its parallel is His saying: ﴿I created the jinn and mankind only that they may worship Me.﴾

Third: creation is closer in wording to His saying ﴿that you may become righteous﴾ than the command is.

For the one who supports the first view, he may say: it is not impossible that His saying "that you may become righteous" is a reason for the command to worship; its parallel is His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾. So this is a reason for the prescription of fasting, and it is not impossible that it be a reason for both matters together, and this is the most fitting for the verse, and God knows best.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾.

He mentioned here another proof, which includes the argument from His wisdom in His creatures. The first includes the basic creation and origination and is called the proof of invention and origination; the second includes the observed wisdoms in His creation and is called the proof of providence and wisdom. He, Exalted is He, often repeats these two kinds of argument in the Qur'an. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿God is He who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you, and subjected to you the ships to run in the sea by His command, and subjected to you the rivers, and subjected to you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses, and subjected to you the night and the day﴾. He mentions the creation of the heavens and the earth, then mentions the benefits and wisdoms of the creatures. Its parallel is also His saying: ﴿Is He who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delight, which were not yours to make grow their trees? Is there a god with God? Rather, they are a people who ascribe equality [to Him]. Is He who made the earth a place of settlement and made within it rivers and made for it firmly set mountains and made between the two seas a barrier?﴾ up to the end of the verses.

Moreover, in these verses there are secrets and wisdoms, as much as the minds of all the worlds can grasp and comprehend; perhaps there will pass by you, God willing, an alert to a slight fragrance of that.

Similar to this also is His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of the night and the day, the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people, the water that God sends down from the sky and with it revives the earth after its death and disperses therein every creature, and the directing of the winds and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are signs for a people who reason﴾. This is abundant in the Qur'an for whoever reflects upon it.

In Surat al-Baqarah He mentioned the settled world, which is the earth, its ceiling, which is the sky, and the basic benefits of the servants, which is the water He sent down from the sky. Thus He mentioned the dwelling and the dweller and what they need of their welfare. By His making the earth a bed, He alerted to the completeness of His wisdom in that He prepared it for the settling of animals upon it, making it a bed, a cradle, a carpet and a resting place. He made its ceiling a firm, level building, without any gap, disparity or defect. Then He said: ﴿So do not set up rivals to God while you know﴾. Consider this conclusion and the strength of its connection to those premises before it, and how the intellect attains it at first glance, free of every doubt, suspicion and flaw. Every speaker, arguer and disputant, when he exaggerates in establishing what he establishes and prolongs it and extends his discourse about it, his ultimate aim, if what he says is sound, is to arrive at some of what is in the Qur'an. So reflect upon what lies beneath these words of decisive proof for the Oneness of God: that is, if God alone is the One who did these deeds, how can they set up rivals to Him, when you know that He has no rival who shares with Him in His acts? The miraculousness of the Qur'an lies in its eloquence.

When He had established the two kinds of Oneness, He moved on to prophethood, saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call your witnesses other than God, if you are truthful﴾.

If doubt arises in you concerning the noble Qur'an and the truthfulness of the one who brought it, and you say that it is fabricated, then produce one surah resembling it. This is an address to all the people of the earth. It is impossible that any one of them should bring speech that he fabricates and invents of his own accord, then challenge all the people of the earth together to oppose him in the smallest part of it, which is three verses, out of several thousand, and then all creatures be unable to do so. Indeed, those who sought to oppose it produced what was among the strongest evidences of its truthfulness, for they brought something that sensible people are ashamed to hear and judge to be vile, repulsive and base. It is like one who displays a perfume that no one has ever smelled the like of, and challenges all creatures, kings and commoners alike, to bring a grain of perfume like it; the sensible are ashamed and recognise their inability, while the fools bring foul, rotten dung and say, "We have brought the like of what you brought." Does this add anything to what he brought but strength, proof, greatness and majesty? God, Exalted is He, reinforced this rebuke, reproach and challenge by saying: ﴿and call your witnesses other than God, if you are truthful﴾, just as one who challenges an opponent says, "Strive against me with everyone you are able to, from your companions, helpers and allies, and leave none of them out until you seek help from them." No one would undertake this except the most ignorant, foolish and feeble-minded of the world, unless he was not confident of the truth of what he claims, or the most perfect, excellent, truthful and trustworthy of men in what he says. The Prophet (ﷺ) would recite this verse and its like to all kinds of creatures, the unlettered and the scripture-people, Arabs and non-Arabs, saying: "You will never be able to do that, and you will never do it." So they turned to war and to accepting the killing of their beloved ones, the orphaning of children, the slaughter of souls and the admission of incapacity to oppose it. Had they been able to bring one surah, they would not have turned from it to choose warfare, the orphaning of children, the killing of souls and the confession of inability to oppose it.

There are several aspects to the establishment of prophethood through this verse:

This is the first of them.

The second: his undertaking this matter and recording it upon all creatures with a general recording until the Day of Resurrection, that they will never do it. No one would undertake this and announce it except on the basis of knowledge free of doubt, grounded in revelation from God, Exalted is He; otherwise human knowledge and power would be too weak for it.

The third: consideration of the very thing he challenged with, and what it contains of matters which human faculties cannot bring the like of; its eloquence, its arrangement and its rhetoric is one instance of its miraculousness.

This aspect is a miracle for whoever hears it, reflects upon it and understands it; and by the first two aspects it is a miracle for everyone to whom its report reaches, even if he does not understand it or reflect upon it. So reflect upon this point concerning the miraculousness of the Qur'an, and you will recognise in it the shortcoming and failing of many speakers in explaining its miraculousness. They have not fulfilled a tenth of its due. Some restricted its miraculousness to the diversion of motives from opposing it while being able to do so; some restricted it to the bare eloquence and rhetoric; some to the divergence of its style of arrangement from the styles of speech; some to what it contains of informing about the unseen; and other inadequate sayings which neither heal nor benefit. Its miraculousness is beyond all of that and above all of that.

When this proof has established prophethood, it becomes obligatory upon people to affirm the Messenger in his report and to obey his command. He has informed about God, His names, attributes and acts, and about the Return, Paradise and Hell, so the soundness of that is established with certainty. Thus He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, which has been prepared for the disbelievers. And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾.

﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call your witnesses other than God, if you are truthful (23). But if you do not and you will never do it, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, which has been prepared for the disbelievers (24)﴾

(Issue)

It is well known among the grammarians, the jurists of legal theory and the jurists that the particle (in, إنْ) is attached only to what may or may not occur, as in your saying: "If you come to me, I will honour you," and it is not attached to what is certain to occur; so one does not say "If the sun rises, I will come to you," but rather "When the sun rises, I will come to you" (idha, إذا). Each of the two may be attached to the other. Some of the legal theorists found this problematic, saying: "In has come in the Qur'an with what is certain to occur, such as His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, while He, Exalted is He, knows that the disbelievers are in doubt about it; and His saying ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it, then fear the Fire﴾, and it is certain that they will not do it." He answered this by saying: the divine attributes do not enter into the Arabic conventions; rather the Arabic conventions are built upon the attributes of creatures, and God revealed the Qur'an in the language of the Arabs and according to their manner. So whatever was good in the custom of the Arabs, the Qur'an was revealed in that form, and whatever was ugly was not revealed in the Qur'an. Thus whatever is customarily uncertain among people may be attached to (in), whether by God or by another, whether it is known to the speaker or the hearer or not. Likewise it is good for one of us to say, "If Zayd is in the house, honour him," while knowing that Zayd is in the house, because Zayd's being in the house is customarily uncertain.

This is the governing principle for what is attached to (in), and the problem is thereby resolved.

I say: this objection does not arise, for what the people (the scholars) said is that what is certain to occur must be attached to (idha), whereas what may or may not occur is what is attached to (in), even if after its occurrence it becomes certain. Once you understand this, reflect upon His saying: ﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy from Us, they rejoice in it; but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful﴾. Consider how He used (idha) for the attaining of mercy, which is certain to reach them from God, and used (in) for the befalling of evil, since what God pardons is more numerous; and He used the past tense verb, which indicates the certainty of occurrence, for mercy, and the future tense, which indicates that the evil is not certain to occur, for the arrival of evil.

Consider also how He used, for the arrival of mercy, the verb of tasting, which indicates the direct contact of mercy with them, and that it is tasted by them; tasting is the most particular and intense kind of contact. Consider how He used, for mercy, the preposition of the starting point, attached to Himself, saying ﴿from Us, mercy﴾, and for evil He used the preposition of causation (bi, ب) attached to the earning of their hands. Consider how He emphasised the first clause, which included the tasting of mercy, with (in), and not the second clause. The secrets of the noble Qur'an are far more numerous and greater than human minds can encompass.

Consider His saying: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish except Him﴾. Note how He used (idha) here, since the touching of harm to them at sea is certain, in contrast to His saying: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is despairing and hopeless﴾, where He did not restrict the touching of evil but left it unrestricted. And when He restricted it to the sea, where it is certain, He used the particle (idha). Consider His saying: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws to one side; but when evil touches him, he is full of despairing supplication﴾... how He used here (idha), which signals the certainty of occurrence that entails despair, for despair arises only when the touch of evil is realised; so using (idha) here conveys the intended meaning more than (in) would. In contrast is His saying: ﴿And when evil touches him, he has lengthy supplication﴾, for he, through his shortness of patience and weakness of endurance, whenever he anticipates evil, turns away and prolongs supplication; and when it is realised, he becomes despairing. Such secrets in the Qur'an are not attained except by a gift from God and an understanding that He gives to a servant through His Book.

If you say: what do you make of His saying: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, then for her is half of what he left﴾, and death is certain? I reply: the conditional is not on death in general, but on a particular death, namely a death without children.

If you say: what do you make of His saying: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you, and be grateful to God, if you are indeed worshipping Him﴾, and His saying: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned, if you are believers in His signs﴾, and the Arabs say: "If you are my son, obey me"? And in the hadith concerning greeting the dead: "And we, if God wills, will certainly join you" (narrated by Muslim), and the joining is certain; and in the words of the testator: "If I die, a third of my wealth is charity."

Ibn al-Qayyim said: As for His words, ﴿If you are indeed those who worship Him﴾, the reason the particle (in) (ʾin, "if") is apt here is argument and binding the listener to a conclusion. The meaning is: your worship of Allah entails your thankfulness to Him; indeed, it is thankfulness itself. So if you are committed to His worship and included among its adherents, then eat of His provision and give thanks for His blessings.

This kind of construction is frequently used in argumentation, as when you say to a man: "If Allah is your Lord and your Creator, then do not disobey Him; if the meeting with Allah is true, then prepare for it; if Paradise is true, then provide for the journey to it." This is better than the answer of those who said that (in) here stands in place of (idh, "when"). Rather, it refers to their joining the believers and their arrival at the place where those others have gone. As for the testator's saying, "If I die, then a third of my wealth is charity," the reason is that although death is certain, since its time is not known and the span of hope for life is long, it is treated as something doubtful. This is the reality indicated by the conditions of people, for no sensible person is certain of death and content to remain in a state in which he never loves to die. As one of the early Muslims said: "I have never seen a certainty without doubt more like a doubt without certainty than death."

On this basis some scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-maʿānī) interpreted ﴿Then after that you will surely die. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised up﴾. They emphasized the death with the particle of emphasis (lam) and used the active participle, which indicates permanence, while for the resurrection they used the verb and did not emphasize it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 21–22 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾

This is an argument of the utmost clarity and the highest degree of explanation, covering all the objectives of the fundamentals of religion: the affirmation of the Creator and of His attributes of perfection, namely His power, knowledge, will, life, wisdom and acts; the origination of the world; and the affirmation of the two kinds of His Oneness (tawhid), the Oneness of Lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah), which entails that He alone is the Lord, the Creator, the Originator, and the Oneness of Godhead (tawhid al-uluhiyyah), which entails that He alone is the God who is worshipped, loved, and to whom alone worship, humility, submission and love are fitting. Then, after that, He established the prophethood of His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) with the most eloquent, best, most complete establishment, furthest from any opposition. Thereby the truthfulness of His Messenger in all that he says is established, and he has informed about the Return, Paradise and Hell, so the soundness of that is established by necessity.

These verses thus established all of these objectives in the best manner. He opened them with His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾, which is an address to all the children of Adam, who all share in its relation to them. Then He said: ﴿Worship your Lord﴾, commanding them to worship their Lord. Within this phrase lies the decisive proof of the obligation of worshipping Him, for if He is our Lord, who nurtures us by His blessing and beneficence, the owner of our essences, our necks and our souls, and every atom of the servant is His property in pure and true ownership, and He has nurtured him by His kindness to him and His favour upon him, then worshipping Him and thanking Him is obligatory upon him. For this reason He said: ﴿Worship your Lord﴾ and did not say "your God." The Lord is the Master, the Owner, the Benefactor, the Nurturer, the Reformer, and God, Exalted is He, is the Lord in all these senses. Nothing is more necessary in intellects and natural dispositions than worshipping One who is such, alone, without partner.

Then He said: ﴿who created you﴾, thereby also alerting to the obligation of worshipping Him alone, namely that He brought them out from non-existence into existence, produced, invented and originated them alone without partner, by their acknowledgment and confession, as He said in another place of the Qur'an: ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God."﴾ So if He alone is the Creator, how could He not be the sole object of worship, and how could they set up a partner with Him in worship while you confess that He has no partner in creation?

This is the method of the Qur'an: it argues from the Oneness of Lordship to the Oneness of Godhead. Then He said: ﴿and those before you﴾, thereby alerting that He alone is the Creator of you, of your fathers, and of those who preceded you, and that none shared with Him in the creation of those before you or of you. His creation of them entails the perfection of His power, will, knowledge, wisdom and life, and that entails all the rest of His attributes of perfection and sublime qualities. Thus this includes the affirmation of His attributes and acts and His oneness in His attributes, so there is no likeness to Him in them, and in His acts, so there is no partner with Him in them. Then He mentioned the purpose of creating them, which is that they should fear Him, so that they obey Him and do not disobey Him, remember Him and do not forget Him, thank Him and do not disbelieve in Him. This is the reality of taqwa of Him. As for His saying: ﴿that you may become righteous﴾ (la'allakum tattaqun), it has been said that it is a reason for the command; it has been said that it is a reason for the creation; and it has been said that the meaning is "worship Him so that you may fear Him by worshipping Him"; and it has been said that the meaning is "He created you so that you may fear Him." The last is more apparent, for several reasons:

First: taqwa is worship, and a thing cannot be the cause of itself.

Second: its parallel is His saying: ﴿I created the jinn and mankind only that they may worship Me.﴾

Third: creation is closer in wording to His saying ﴿that you may become righteous﴾ than the command is.

For the one who supports the first view, he may say: it is not impossible that His saying "that you may become righteous" is a reason for the command to worship; its parallel is His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾. So this is a reason for the prescription of fasting, and it is not impossible that it be a reason for both matters together, and this is the most fitting for the verse, and God knows best.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾.

He mentioned here another proof, which includes the argument from His wisdom in His creatures. The first includes the basic creation and origination and is called the proof of invention and origination; the second includes the observed wisdoms in His creation and is called the proof of providence and wisdom. He, Exalted is He, often repeats these two kinds of argument in the Qur'an. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿God is He who created the heavens and the earth and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you, and subjected to you the ships to run in the sea by His command, and subjected to you the rivers, and subjected to you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses, and subjected to you the night and the day﴾. He mentions the creation of the heavens and the earth, then mentions the benefits and wisdoms of the creatures. Its parallel is also His saying: ﴿Is He who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delight, which were not yours to make grow their trees? Is there a god with God? Rather, they are a people who ascribe equality [to Him]. Is He who made the earth a place of settlement and made within it rivers and made for it firmly set mountains and made between the two seas a barrier?﴾ up to the end of the verses.

Moreover, in these verses there are secrets and wisdoms, as much as the minds of all the worlds can grasp and comprehend; perhaps there will pass by you, God willing, an alert to a slight fragrance of that.

Similar to this also is His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of the night and the day, the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people, the water that God sends down from the sky and with it revives the earth after its death and disperses therein every creature, and the directing of the winds and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are signs for a people who reason﴾. This is abundant in the Qur'an for whoever reflects upon it.

In Surat al-Baqarah He mentioned the settled world, which is the earth, its ceiling, which is the sky, and the basic benefits of the servants, which is the water He sent down from the sky. Thus He mentioned the dwelling and the dweller and what they need of their welfare. By His making the earth a bed, He alerted to the completeness of His wisdom in that He prepared it for the settling of animals upon it, making it a bed, a cradle, a carpet and a resting place. He made its ceiling a firm, level building, without any gap, disparity or defect. Then He said: ﴿So do not set up rivals to God while you know﴾. Consider this conclusion and the strength of its connection to those premises before it, and how the intellect attains it at first glance, free of every doubt, suspicion and flaw. Every speaker, arguer and disputant, when he exaggerates in establishing what he establishes and prolongs it and extends his discourse about it, his ultimate aim, if what he says is sound, is to arrive at some of what is in the Qur'an. So reflect upon what lies beneath these words of decisive proof for the Oneness of God: that is, if God alone is the One who did these deeds, how can they set up rivals to Him, when you know that He has no rival who shares with Him in His acts? The miraculousness of the Qur'an lies in its eloquence.

When He had established the two kinds of Oneness, He moved on to prophethood, saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call your witnesses other than God, if you are truthful﴾.

This is an address to all the people of the earth. It is impossible that any one of them should bring speech that he fabricates and invents of his own accord, then challenge all the people of the earth together to oppose him in the smallest part of it, which is three verses, out of several thousand, and then all creatures be unable to do so. Indeed, those who sought to oppose it produced what was among the strongest evidences of its truthfulness, for they brought something that sensible people are ashamed to hear and judge to be vile, repulsive and base. It is like one who displays a perfume that no one has ever smelled the like of, and challenges all creatures, kings and commoners alike, to bring a grain of perfume like it; the sensible are ashamed and recognise their inability, while the fools bring foul, rotten dung and say, "We have brought the like of what you brought." Does this add anything to what he brought but strength, proof, greatness and majesty? God, Exalted is He, reinforced this rebuke, reproach and challenge by saying: ﴿and call your witnesses other than God, if you are truthful﴾, just as one who challenges an opponent says, "Strive against me with everyone you are able to, from your companions, helpers and allies, and leave none of them out until you seek help from them." (Benefits and Gems)

Their saying ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾ means: its likeness and counterpart, not its very same thing. Does it mean that this is like what we were provided with in the world, of fruits and produce, or that this is like what was given to us before in Paradise?

Two opinions have been reported on this. In the tafsir of al-Suddi, from Abu Malik and Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning ﴿They will say, "This is what we were provided with before"﴾, they said: they were brought fruit in Paradise, and when they looked at it they said, "This is what we were provided with before," in the world. Mujahid said: "It resembles it." Ibn Zayd said: "This is what we were provided with before in the world." ﴿And they will be given it in semblance﴾, meaning they recognize it.

Others said: "This is what we were provided with before" refers to the fruit of Paradise given before this, because of the great resemblance between some of it and the rest in colour and taste. The proponents of this view offered several arguments.

The first: the resemblance among the fruits of Paradise to one another is greater than the resemblance between them and the fruits of this world.

The second, which Ibn Jarir related from them: "One of the reasons of those who say this is that whenever a fruit is plucked from Paradise, another like it returns in its place, just as it was."
Al-Husayn related to us: Ibn Bashshar related to us, Ibn Mahdi related to us, Sufyan related to us: I heard Ibn Murrah narrate from Abu Ubaydah, and he mentioned the fruit of Paradise, and said: "Whenever a fruit is plucked, another returns in its place."

The third argument: His saying ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾, which serves as a kind of explanation and the cause motivating their saying "This is what we were provided with before."

The fourth argument: it is known that not everything in Paradise's fruit was given to them in the world, and many of its people do not know the fruits of this world nor have they seen them.

Another group, including Ibn Jarir and others, preferred the other view and argued with several points.

Ibn Jarir said: "What confirms the soundness of the view of those who say that the meaning of ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾ is in the world is that Allah, mighty is His praise, said: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a fruit from it, a provision﴾, they say, 'This is what we were provided with before,' and He did not specify that this saying is in some cases and not others. Since He, mighty is His remembrance, told us that this is their saying whenever they are provided with a fruit, then there is no doubt that this is their saying with the first provision they receive of its fruits, after entering Paradise and settling in it, having had no fruit of it before. Since there is no doubt that this was their saying at its beginning, as it is their saying in its middle and what follows, it is known that it is impossible that they would say, for the first provision they received of the fruits of Paradise, 'This is what we were provided with before, this fruit of Paradise,' and how could they say that for the first provision of its fruit when they had no other before it? 'This is what we were provided with before,' lest some deviant or misguided person clothe them in the saying of falsehood from which Allah has purified them, or someone object that this saying is not theirs for the first provision they receive of its fruit, thereby rejecting what Allah has made sound without establishing evidence that this applies to some states of theirs and not others. It has thus become clear that the meaning of the verse is: whenever they are provided with a fruit of Paradise, in Paradise, they say, 'This is what we were provided with before,' in the world."

I say: The proponents of the first view restrict this general statement to other than the first provision, due to the indication of reason and context, and this is not unusual in the method of the Qur'an. You are necessarily compelled to make specifications of several kinds too:

The first: many fruits of Paradise, those which have no counterpart in the world, are not described by this saying.

The second: many of its people have not been provided with all the fruits of the world that have a counterpart in Paradise.

The third: it is known that they will not continue saying this forever, saying with every single fruit they eat, "This is what we were provided with in the world," and continuing this speech endlessly. The Mighty Qur'an did not intend this meaning, nor is it among the things that concern them regarding their bliss and pleasure. Rather, it is a clear statement that departs from what is customary and understood by the addressee.

Its meaning is that some of it resembles the rest: its first is not better than its last, and it is not subject to what befalls the fruits of this world when trees age and grow old, such as diminished yield, small fruit and other things. Rather, its first is like its last, and its last is like its first; all of it is choice, resembling one another. This is the meaning of their saying. There is no contradiction with what Allah the Exalted has stated, nor any attribution of falsehood to the people of Paradise in any way. What is necessary for them of specification is necessary for you in its like, and more. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, mighty and majestic, ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾: al-Hasan said: "All of it is choice, with no inferior part. Do you not see how you consider some of the fruit of this world inferior, while in Paradise there is no inferiority?" Qatadah said: "Choice, with nothing inferior in it, for the fruits of this world are cleaned and some of them are rejected." Ibn Juraij and a group said likewise. On this view, the meaning of semblance is agreement and equality.

Another group, including Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, and some Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said: "Similar in colour and appearance, but not similar in taste." Mujahid said: "Its colour is similar, its taste different." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said likewise. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said: "The grass of Paradise is saffron, and its sand is musk. The young servants will go round them with fruit, and they will eat it, then they will bring them the like of it, and they will say, 'This is what you brought us just now,' and the attendants will say, 'Eat, for the colour is one and the taste is different.'" This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a fruit from it, a provision, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they will be given it in semblance﴾.

Another group said: the meaning of the verse is that Paradise's fruit resembles the fruit of this world, except that the fruit of Paradise is more excellent and more pleasant. Ibn Wahb said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: "They recognize its names as they did in the world: apple is called apple, pomegranate is called pomegranate. They say in Paradise, 'This is what we were provided with before,' and they will be given it in semblance, recognizing it, though it is not the same in taste." Ibn Jarir chose this view. He said: "Our evidence against the view of him who says that the meaning of the verse is 'This is what we were provided with before,' i.e., in Paradise, is the evidence against the view of him who opposes our interpretation of His saying, ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾: that Allah the Exalted informed us of the reason why the people said, 'This is what we were provided with before,' and that they were given it in semblance."

I say: This does not prove the falsehood of their view, for the reasons already mentioned. And He said: ﴿Gardens of Eden, their doors opened for them, reclining therein, calling therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾. He said: ﴿Calling therein for every fruit, secure﴾, which indicates their security from its ending and its harm. He said: ﴿And that is the Garden which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do. For you therein is abundant fruit﴾. He said: ﴿And fruit abundant, neither cut off nor forbidden﴾, meaning it is not available at one time and unavailable at another, nor is it withheld from whoever desires it. He said: ﴿So he is in a pleasant life, in a lofty garden, its clusters near at hand﴾. "Qutuf" is the plural of "qitf," which is what is plucked; "qitf" with a fatha is the act of plucking. Meaning, its fruits are near, close to whoever reaches for them, so he takes them however he wishes. Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: "He reaches for the fruit while lying down." He said: ﴿And near upon them are its shades, and its clusters are lowered in subjugation﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "When one intends to reach for its fruit, it bends down to him until he reaches what he wants." Others said: "Close to them, made subservient however they wish; they take from it standing, sitting, and reclining." This is like His saying: ﴿its clusters are near﴾. The meaning of "tadhlil" of the clusters is facilitating their reach. The people of Madinah say: "dhallala al-nakhl," meaning they smoothed its roots and extracted them from the palm frond so that it is easy to reach.

Abd Allah ibn al-Imam Ahmad said: Uqbah ibn Mukram al-Ammi related to me: Rabi' ibn Ibrahim ibn Alayh related to us: Awf related to us, from Qassamah ibn Zuhayr, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah sent Adam down from Paradise, peace be upon him, and taught him the craft of everything, and provided him with fruit of Paradise. So these fruits of yours are from the fruit of Paradise, except that these change, while those do not change." It has already been mentioned that the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary has fruit like large water-jars.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Paradise was displayed to me, so that if I had taken a cluster from it, I would have taken it." In another wording: "I reached out and took a cluster from it, but my hand fell short of it."

Abu Khaythamah said: Abd Allah ibn Ja'far related to us, Ubayd Allah related to us, Ibn Aqil related to us, from Jabir, who said: While we were in the noon prayer, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stepped forward and we stepped forward with him. Then he reached out to take something, then he drew back. When he finished the prayer, Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, today in your prayer you did something you did not usually do." He said: "Paradise was displayed to me, with its splendour and freshness, and I reached out and took a cluster of grapes to bring to you, but it was prevented between me and it. Had I brought it to you, you would have eaten from it for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, and it would not have diminished."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: Sufyan related to us, from Hammad, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The fruit of Paradise is like water-jars and buckets, whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, softer than butter, and it has no stone."

Sa'id ibn Mansur said: Shurayk related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: "The people of Paradise eat from its fruit standing, sitting, and reclining, in whatever state they wish."

Al-Bazzar said in his Musnad: Ahmad ibn al-Faraj al-Himsi related to us, Uthman ibn Sa'id ibn Kathir ibn Dinar al-Himsi related to us, Muhammad ibn al-Muhajir related to us, from al-Dahhak al-Ma'afiri, from Sulayman ibn Musa, who said: Kurayb related to me that he heard Usamah ibn Zayd say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is there anyone who would strive for Paradise? For Paradise has no barrier. By the Lord of the Ka'bah, it is a light that gleams, a fragrant herb that sways, a lofty palace, a flowing river, a ripe fruit, a beautiful and lovely spouse, many garments, in a place of permanence forever, in a sound abode, with fruit and greenery and joy and blessing, in a lofty, radiant dwelling." They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, we are those who strive for it." He said: "Say, 'If Allah wills.'" The people said: "If Allah wills."

Al-Bazzar said: "We do not know of anyone who narrated this hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) except Usamah, and we do not know of any chain for it from Usamah except this one, nor do we know that anyone narrated it from al-Dahhak al-Ma'afiri except this man, Muhammad ibn al-Muhajir."

In the hadith of Laqit ibn Sabrah, which Abd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated in his father's Musnad and others, I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what will the people of Paradise be given to drink?" He said: "Rivers of purified honey, and rivers of wine with no headache nor regret, and rivers of milk whose taste never changes, and water that does not go stale, and fruit, by the life of your Lord, of what they know, and better than its like with it. As for the fragrant herb, it is every plant of pleasant scent." Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah said: "It is our basil, but a sprig of Paradise's basil is brought and we smell it."

(Benefit)

Al-Thana' (praise) is from the glad tidings, and the good dream is from the glad tidings, and the angels' giving glad tidings to one at death is from the glad tidings. And Paradise is among the greatest of glad tidings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾.

And the Exalted said: ﴿And rejoice in the Garden which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

It is said: it is called that because it affects the skin of the face (bashrah al-wajh).

Therefore it is of two kinds: glad tidings that gladden, which affect the face with brightness and joy, and glad tidings that sadden, which affect it with dejection and frowning. But when it is used without qualification, it means joy. When it is qualified, it takes the sense of its qualifier.

His saying: "And it is purer than joy (farah)." He argued for this by saying that joys are often mixed with sorrows, meaning their opposite is often blended with them, unlike gladness (surur).

It is said: gladness too is often mixed with grief and sorrows, so there is no difference.

His saying: "For this reason the Qur'an came using its name for the joys of this world in several places."

He means: Allah the Exalted attributed joy to the conditions of this world in His saying: ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and in His saying: ﴿Do not rejoice; indeed Allah does not love the rejoicers﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and His saying: ﴿Indeed he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10]. For the joys of this world are never freed from their sorrows and afflictions at all. Rather, there is no joy except that it is accompanied by a prior, concurrent, or subsequent sorrow. Joy is never pure; there must be a sorrow accompanying it. But joy may overpower grief so that its rule and pain are submerged in its presence, and vice versa.

It is said: The Qur'an also came using joy regarding the affairs of the Hereafter in several places, such as His saying: ﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170], and His saying: ﴿Say: in the bounty of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. So there is no difference between them in this respect that he mentioned.

His saying: "The word surur occurs in the Qur'an in two places concerning the state of the Hereafter."
