They said: The difference between His saying ﴿Go down to a city﴾ and His saying ﴿Go down from it﴾ is that the first is for the end and limit of the descent, while "descend from it" includes its starting point and beginning, which has no effect on what we are discussing, for "descended from such-and-such to such-and-such" implies moving from a high place to a low place. So what effect does the beginning and end of the descent have in determining the place of descent as the Eternal Garden?

They said: As for the story of Musa and his blaming Adam for bringing him out of the Garden, this does not indicate that it is the Eternal Garden. And your saying that it is not conceivable that Musa would blame Adam for bringing himself and his offspring out of a garden on the earth is a reproach that benefits nothing.

Do you think that was a garden like any of these cut-off, wretched gardens, subject to calamities, toil, fatigue, thirst, plowing, irrigation, pollination, and all the forms of hardship that befall these gardens?

There is no doubt that Musa, peace be upon him, is more knowing and more exalted than to blame Adam for leaving and bringing out his offspring from a garden of this description. But whoever says this, the garden was one that no calamity reaches, whose fruits are never cut off, whose rivers never dry up, whose dwellers never hunger, thirst, are exposed to the sun, or go naked, and in which toil, fatigue, and misery never touch them. Blaming a person for causing his own departure from such a garden is fitting.

They said: As for Adam's excuse, peace be upon him, on the Day of Resurrection to the people of the gathering, that his sin was what expelled him from the Garden, so it is not fitting for him to ask for its opening for them, this does not necessitate that it is the very one from which he was expelled. Rather, if it were other than it, the excuse would be even stronger, for if the expulsion from a garden other than the Eternal Garden occurred because of sin, how is it fitting to ask for the Eternal Garden and intercession in it, having been expelled from another by sin?

This is the standing place of the views of both parties and the final stage of the steps of the two groups. Whoever has a share of knowledge in this matter, let him seek it, for this is the time of need for it. And whoever knows the limit of his stride and the measure of his stock, let him leave the matter to its knowing one, and not be content for himself with diminishing and belittling him. Let him be among those who stand on the hillocks, the observers of war, if he is not among those who advance, retreat, thrust, and strike. For the stallions have met, the rivals have clashed, and the arena has grown narrow for them in this field of contest:

"When the stallions meet in a clamor, how is the condition of the weak one in the middle?"

These are the core arguments of the two groups, passing by your door and being brought to you, and these are the wares of the merchants of scholarship being hawked in the market of slump, not the market of hype. Whoever lacks any means of clarity and insight in it should not lack from one who has exhausted his capacity and spent his effort the excuse of being correct or pardoned. Let him not be content for himself with the worst of the two shares and the basest of the two portions: ignorance of the truth and its means, and enmity toward its people and seekers. When the sought thing is great and you lack a knowing, sincere companion, then travel with your resolve beyond the dead, and hold fast to the teacher of Ibrahim. For in this matter we have mentioned such transmissions, proofs, and wondrous subtleties as may not be found in any of the books of the authors, and its worth is known only by the virtuous and fair.

From Allah, the Glorified, is the seeking of aid, upon Him is reliance, to Him is recourse, for He does not disappoint one who relies upon Him, nor does He waste one who seeks refuge in Him and entrusts his affair to Him. He is our sufficiency and the best Disposer of affairs.

(Section)

When He, glorified is He, brought him down from the Garden and exposed him and his offspring to various kinds of trials and tribulations, He gave them better than what He had withheld: His covenant, which He made to him and his offspring, and informed that whoever among them holds fast to it reaches His pleasure and the abode of His honor. He, the Exalted, said after his expulsion from it:

﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you. And if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance—there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve." (38)﴾

And in the other verse: ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, some of you enemies to others. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be distressed. And whoever turns away from My remembrance—indeed, for him is a depressed life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind." (124) He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, while I was [once] seeing?" (125) [Allah] will say, "Thus came to you Our verses, but you forgot them; and thus, this Day, you are forgotten." (126)﴾

So when He, glorified is He, broke him by bringing him down from the Garden, He mended him and his offspring with this covenant which He made to them. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me﴾. This is the conditional "in" reinforced with "ma", which indicates the generality of time.

The meaning is: at whatever time and whatever moment guidance comes to you from Me. He made the answer of this condition a conditional sentence, which is His saying: ﴿whoever follows My guidance, there is no going astray and no misery﴾, just as you say, "If you visit me, then whoever brings me news of your arrival, he is free."

The answer of the condition may be a complete sentence, either a pure statement like your saying, "If you visit me, I will honor you," or a statement linked to the condition like this, or emphasized with an oath, or with "in" and "la," as in His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, indeed you are polytheists.﴾

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 38 (part 8 of 8):

And as for the imperative (talab), as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you ask, ask of Allah; and if you seek help, seek help from Allah,"
and his saying: "And when you meet them, then be steadfast,"
and the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when you have come out of the state of ihram, then hunt﴾, and ﴿When the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. This type most often comes with idha (إذا), which signifies the certainty of the occurrence of the condition, for a secret: it indicates that the demand is certain upon the certainty of the condition. So whenever the condition is certain, the demand is certain. Thus idha, which indicates the certainty of the condition, is used, and so the certainty of the demand is known when it occurs.

It may occasionally come with in (إن), as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work."﴾

As for a nominal sentence (jumla insha'iyya), as in his saying to his disbelieving slave: "If you become Muslim, you are free," and to his wife: "If you do such-and-such, you are divorced."

This is an act of manumission and divorce upon the existence of the condition according to one opinion, or an act performed at the time of the conditional statement, with its effect being delayed until the condition exists, according to another opinion.

On either view, the response to the condition is a nominal sentence (insha'i). The point is that the response to the condition in the mentioned verse is a conditional sentence, namely his saying ﴿So whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾. This condition requires the connection of the first sentence to the second as the connection of cause to effect and of means to result. So the condition, which is the necessitating cause and the requirer of the response, which is the necessary consequence, if there is mutual necessity between them from both sides, then the existence of each without the other is impossible, like entering Paradise through Islam, and the removal of fear, grief, error and misery along with following desire. These are the general conditions of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, for they are causes and reasons, and a ruling is negated when its cause is negated.

If the necessity between them is from only one side, then the condition is a specific necessitating thing and the response is a general necessary consequence. So whenever the specific necessitating condition is fulfilled, the general necessary response is fulfilled, but the converse is not necessary, as one says: "If this is a human, then it is an animal," and "If the sale is valid, then ownership is established."

This is the predominant form in qiyas al-dalala (inference by indication), where the condition is an indicator of the response, so its existence necessitates the existence of the response, because the response is its necessary consequence, and the existence of the necessitating thing entails the existence of the necessary consequence. Its non-existence does not necessitate the non-existence of the response. If this condition occurs between a cause and an effect, then if the ruling is caused by several causes, this is valid, and the response may be more general than the condition, as in your saying: "If this is an apostate, then his blood is lawful," for the lawfulness of blood is more general than its lawfulness through apostasy. Except that it may be said that the ruling of the specific cause is negated upon its negation, and if the ruling is established by another cause, then it is another ruling.

As for the ruling of a specific cause, it is impossible that it be negated while it is absent. In that case, the necessity returns from both sides, and the existence of each of the condition and the response necessitates the existence of the other, and its non-existence necessitates the non-existence of the other.

The full verification of this lies in the question of explaining one ruling by two causes, about which people have a well-known dispute.

The decisive resolution of it is that if the one ruling is one in kind, such as the lawfulness of blood, the establishment of ownership, and the nullification of purity, then it is permissible to explain it by different causes.

And if the ruling is one in its specific instance, such as the lawfulness of blood through apostasy, and the establishment of ownership through sale or inheritance, and the like, then it is not permissible to explain it by two different causes. By this detail the confusion in this question disappears. And Allah knows best.

Whoever reflects upon the evidences of the two groups will find that everything used by the one who holds that a ruling is explained by different causes only indicates the explanation of the one in kind by them, and everything used by the one who negates explaining a ruling by two causes is only complete as evidence for negating the explanation of the one in specific instance by both. So the two positions, upon verification, return to one thing.

The point is that Allah, glorified is He, made following His guidance and His covenant, which He made with Adam, a cause and a requirer of the absence of fear, grief, error and misery. This response is established by the establishment of the condition and negated by its negation, as previously explained.

And the negation of fear and grief from the one who follows guidance is a negation of all kinds of evil, for the disliked thing that befalls the servant, whenever he knows of its occurrence, he fears that it will befall him, and when it befalls him, he grieves over what has afflicted him. So he is constantly in fear and grief, and everyone who fears grieves, and everyone who grieves fears. Each of fear and grief is over the loss of what is loved or the occurrence of what is hated. So the divisions are four: fear of losing what is loved, and the occurrence of what is hated; and this is the sum of all evil. Allah, glorified is He, negated all of that from the one who follows His guidance, which He sent down upon the tongues of His messengers. In negating fear, He used the noun that indicates negation of permanence and necessity, for the people of Paradise must experience fear in this world, in the intermediate state, and on the Day of Resurrection, when Adam and other prophets say, "Myself, myself." So He informed that they, although they fear, there is no fear upon them, meaning that the fear they feared will not reach them. In negating grief He used the present verb, which indicates the negation of renewal and occurrence, meaning that grief will not reach them, nor will it arise for them when they do not remember what has passed from them. Rather, they are in constant joy, and no grief over what has escaped them will befall them.

As for fear, since its attachment is to the future and not to the past, its negation indicates that it does not reach them at all, meaning what they feared will neither touch them nor visit them. And Allah knows best.

The one who grieves grieves in the future over what has passed, and the one who fears fears in the present over what is to come.

﴿So there is no fear upon them﴾: meaning what they feared will not reach them, and no grief over what has escaped them will arise for them.

And in the other verse He said: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance will not go astray, nor will he be distressed﴾, negating two things from the one who follows His guidance: going astray and misery.

Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Allah guaranteed for whoever recites the Qur'an and acts upon what is in it that he will not go astray in this world nor be miserable in the Hereafter. Then he recited: ﴿And if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor be distressed﴾. The verse negates the very name of going astray and misery from the one who follows guidance absolutely, so the verse implies that he will not go astray in this world nor be miserable, and will not go astray in the Hereafter nor be miserable there. The stages are four: guidance and misery in this world, and guidance and misery in the Hereafter. But Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned in each abode the more apparent of its two stages. So he mentioned going astray in this world, since it is more apparent to us and closer than mentioning going astray in the Hereafter.

Also, the going astray of this world is the most severe going astray in the Hereafter, and the misery of the Hereafter necessarily entails going astray there. So by each stage he alerted to the other: by negating the going astray of this world he alerted to the negation of the going astray of the Hereafter, for the servant dies upon what he lived upon, and is resurrected upon what he died upon. Allah, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind. (124) He will say: "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind while I had been seeing?" (125) He will say: "Thus came to you Our signs, but you forgot them, and thus today you are forgotten." (126)﴾

And in another verse He said: ﴿And whoever was blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter and more astray in way﴾. So He informed that whoever was astray in this abode will be more astray in the Hereafter.

As for the negation of the misery of this world, it may be said that since going astray in it has been negated from him and guidance has been attained for him, and guidance in it comes with the coolness of certainty, tranquility of heart, tasting the sweetness of faith, finding the joy and delight of the heart in it, and in it being blessed, and the heart becoming alive through faith, illumined by it, strong through it, having obtained through it its nourishment, its satisfaction, its healing, its life, its light, its strength, its pleasure and its bliss, which is among the greatest kinds of bliss and the best of good things and the greatest of pleasures. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do. (97)﴾ This is the report of the most truthful of the truthful, and its reality to its people is the certainty of sight, indeed it is the truth of certainty. Every one who does righteousness must have Allah cause him to live a good life according to his faith and deed. But the coarse and boorish mistake the meaning of life, supposing it to be enjoyment of kinds of food, drink, clothing and marriage, or the pleasure of leadership, wealth, subduing enemies and indulging in varieties of desires.

There is no doubt that this is a pleasure shared with animals, and indeed the share of many animals of it may be greater than the share of a human. Whoever has no pleasure except that which predators, beasts and cattle share with him is one who is called from a far place. But where is this pleasure from the pleasure of a matter which, when its joy mixes with the hearts, consoles one for children, women, homelands, wealth, brothers and dwellings, and he is content to leave them all and go out from them entirely, and exposes himself to kinds of hardships and difficulties, while he is adorned with this and his chest is expanded by it, so that killing his son, his father, his companion or his brother becomes pleasing to him, and the blame of no blamer takes him in that. So much so that one of them meets the spear with his chest and says: "I have triumphed by the Lord of the Ka'bah," and another prolongs his life until he gets his sustenance from his hand and says: "Indeed, it is a long life if I am patient until I eat it," then advances to death joyful and glad.

Another, despite his poverty, says: "If the kings and the sons of kings knew what we are upon, they would fight us over it with swords."

Another says: "There pass through the heart moments in which it dances with joy."

And one of the knowers said: "There pass over me moments in which I say: If the people of Paradise are in such a state, then they are indeed in a pleasant life."

And whoever reflects upon the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he forbade them from continuous fasting (wisal), and they said: "You practise continuous fasting," he said: "I am not like your state; I spend the night with my Lord, He feeds me and gives me drink," knows that this is the food and drink of the spirits, and what overflows upon them of kinds of joy, pleasure, happiness and bliss, of which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was at the highest peak; and whoever else clings to its dust sees the kingdom of this world and its bliss, in comparison to it, as scattered dust, indeed as vanity and deception.

And whoever said that he (ﷺ) used to eat and drink food and drink by which his body was nourished has erred, for several reasons. First: he said, "I spend the night with my Lord, He feeds me and gives me drink," and if it were eating and drinking it would not be continuous fasting nor fasting at all.

Second: the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them that they are not like his state in continuous fasting, for when they practise it they are harmed by it. As for him, when he practises it he is not harmed by continuous fasting. Had he been eating and drinking, the answer would have been: "I also do not practise continuous fasting, but I eat and drink as you eat and drink." Since he confirmed them in their saying "You practise continuous fasting" and did not deny it to them, this shows that he was practising continuous fasting and that he was not eating or drinking in a way that breaks the fast.

Third: had it been eating and drinking that breaks the fast, the answer distinguishing between them and him would not be valid, for then he and they would be equal in not practising continuous fasting. How then could the answer be valid with his saying "I am not like your state"? This is a matter that most people know: when the heart obtains what gladdens and delights it, by attaining its desire and the union with its beloved, or what grieves and saddens and distresses it, it becomes preoccupied and is diverted from food and drink, so much so that many lovers pass days without eating anything, and their souls do not seek food. And one who said it in this sense has expressed it clearly:

"For her there are tales of your remembrance that occupy her, diverting her from drink and from provision.
For her there is a light by your face by which she is illumined, and from your speech behind her is a driver.
When she complains of the weariness of the journey, or the spirit of arrival counts her, she revives at the appointed time."

The point is that guidance necessarily entails the happiness of this world, the goodness of life and immediate bliss, a matter witnessed by the senses and by inner experience.

As for the happiness of the Hereafter, it is unseen and known by faith. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned it because it is more important, being the desired end, while the going astray of this world is more apparent, and by being saved from it one is saved from every evil, and it is the most severe going astray and misery of the Hereafter. Therefore he mentioned it alone. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 45:

It is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: Allah, the Exalted, says: "Every deed of the son of Adam is for himself except fasting, for it is for Me, and I will reward it."

In another wording: "Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied, a good deed being rewarded tenfold its like. Allah, the Exalted, said: except fasting, for it is for Me, and I will reward it."

This is only because it is patience (sabr) of the self and restraining it from its desires, as is shown in the same hadith: he leaves his desire, his food and his drink for My sake. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ), when asked about the best of deeds, said: "Upon you is fasting, for there is nothing equal to it." Since patience is the restraining of the self from answering the call of desire, and this is the reality of fasting, for it restrains the self from answering the call of the desire for food, drink and intercourse, the Companions and early scholars explained patience in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾, as meaning fasting, and Ramadan was named "the month of patience."

Some of the early scholars (salaf) said: Fasting is half of patience. This is because patience is the restraining of the self from answering the call of desire and anger. The self desires a thing for the pleasure of attaining it, and it becomes angry out of aversion to what pains it. Fasting is patience against the demands of desire only, namely the desire of the belly and the private parts, not the demands of anger. Yet the completeness and perfection of fasting is the self's patience against answering the call of both. The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated this in the sound hadith, his saying: "When one of you is fasting on a day of fasting, let him not behave foolishly or shout. If someone reviles him or fights with him, let him say: I am fasting."

He thus guided to the moderating of the forces of desire and anger, and that the fasting person should guard himself from their corrupting his fast. The one corrupts his fast, and the other nullifies his reward, as he said in another hadith: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need that he should give up his food and drink."

They said: Sufficient for the excellence of patience over gratitude is the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they patiently endured; they are the ones who are the winners﴾. He made their success the recompense of their patience. And the Exalted said, ﴿And Allah is with the patient﴾: nothing equals His being with His servant. As some of the knowers (ʿarifin) said: The patient have gone with the good of this world and the Hereafter, for they attained the companionship of Allah.

And the Exalted said, ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, for indeed you are in Our eyes﴾. This includes protection, safeguarding and preservation for the one who is patient for His decree.

He has promised the patient three things, each of which is better than the world and what is in it: His blessings (salawat) upon them, His mercy upon them, and singling them out for guidance, in His saying, ﴿Those upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and they are the guided﴾. This implies that guidance is confined to them. He also informed that patience is among the determined matters (ʿazm al-umur) in two verses of His Book, and He commanded His Messenger to emulate the patience of the steadfast messengers (ulu al-ʿazm).

This has been mentioned previously.

They said: The evidence indicates that asceticism in the world and moderation in it, as far as possible, is preferable to abundance of it; asceticism in it is the state of the patient, and abundance of it is the state of the grateful. They said: The Messiah, upon him be peace, was asked about two men who passed by a treasure, one of whom passed over it without turning towards it, while the other took it and spent it in obedience to Allah, the Exalted. Which of them is better?

He said: The one who did not turn to it and turned away from it is better in the sight of Allah.

They said: What confirms this is that the keys to the treasures of the earth were offered to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not take them, saying: "Rather, I would be hungry one day and satisfied one day." Had he taken them, he would have spent them in seeking Allah's pleasure and obedience, yet he preferred the station of patience and asceticism regarding them. They said: It is known that human perfection lies in three matters: knowledge that one knows, deeds that one performs, and states that follow from one's knowledge and deeds. The best of knowledge, deeds and states is knowledge of Allah, His names, attributes and acts, and acting in accordance with His pleasure, and the heart's being drawn to Him through love, fear and hope. This is the most noble thing in this world, and its reward is the most noble thing in the Hereafter. The most exalted aims are knowing Allah, loving Him, intimacy with His nearness, longing for meeting Him, and delighting in His remembrance. This is the highest happiness of this world and the Hereafter, and this is the end that is sought for its own sake. The servant perceives fully that this is the very essence of happiness only when the veil is lifted for him, he departs the world and enters the Hereafter. Otherwise, while in this world, even if he perceives it to some degree, his perception of it is not complete, because of the obstacles upon him and the trials with which he is tested. Otherwise, happiness in reality is nothing but this. All knowledge and understanding follows this knowledge and is sought for its sake, and the excellence of knowledge varies according to how far it leads to this knowledge and how far it is from it. So every knowledge that leads more closely to knowledge of Allah, His names and attributes is higher than what is below it. Likewise with the states of the heart: every state that is closer to the goal for which it was created is more noble than what is below it. Likewise with deeds: every deed that is closer to attaining this goal is better than others. For this reason, prayer and jihad are among the best deeds, being the most direct in leading to the goal. This is how it must be, for whatever thing is closer to the end is better than what is far from it.

(Section)

As for the eighth issue, namely that He singled out the people of felicity for guidance to the exclusion of others: this is a matter on which people differed, and their disputation extended on both sides. The question is whether God bestows any blessing (ni'mah) upon the disbeliever or not. The one who negates it argues from this and from His saying: ﴿And whoever obeys God and the Messenger, those are with the ones whom God has blessed, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous; and excellent are those as companions.﴾ He singled out these for blessing, which indicates that others are not blessed. He also argues from His saying to His believing servants: ﴿and that I may complete My favor upon you﴾, and from the fact that blessing contradicts retribution and punishment, so what blessing is there for one created for everlasting torment? The one who affirms it argues from His saying: ﴿And if you should count the favors of God, you could not enumerate them﴾; and from His saying to the Children of Israel: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾, and this is address to them in a state of their disbelief; and from His saying in Surat al-Nahl, in which He enumerates His common blessings upon His servants from its beginning until His saying: ﴿Thus He completes His favor upon you that you may submit. But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear notification. They recognize the favor of God; then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.﴾ This is an explicit text that admits of no alternative interpretation. They also argue that the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, all live within the blessing of God, and every person acknowledges to God that he lives only within His blessing; this is known necessarily among all categories of the children of Adam, except one who is obstinate and denies God's right and disbelieves His blessing.

The decisive resolution of the question is that absolute blessing (al-ni'mah al-mutlaqah) is specific to the people of faith, with none sharing it with them, whereas general blessing (mutlaq al-ni'mah) is common to all creation, the righteous and the wicked, believer and disbeliever. The complete absolute blessing is that which is connected to the felicity of eternity and to everlasting delight; this is not shared. General blessing is common and shared. So if the negator intends to deny absolute blessing to the disbeliever, he is mistaken; and if he intends to affirm general blessing, he is correct. Thereby the evidences harmonize, the dispute disappears, and it becomes clear that each of the two groups has both error and correctness. And God is the Granter of success to what is right.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾, He reminds them of His blessing upon their forefathers. For this reason He enumerates them one by one: that He delivered them from the people of Pharaoh, that He split the sea for them, that He appointed Moses for forty nights, after which they went astray, then He turned to them in forgiveness and pardoned them, that He shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quails, and other blessings that He enumerates to them. These were for their predecessors and forefathers, so He commanded them to remember them, so that their remembrance of them would lead them to obedience to Him, to faith in His messengers, and to heed the warning of His punishment with what He punished those who did not believe in His messenger nor submitted to His religion and obedience. His blessing upon their forefathers was a blessing from Him upon them that demanded gratitude from them. So how do you substitute for gratitude for it your disbelief in My messenger, your denial of him, and your enmity toward him? This does not indicate that His complete absolute blessing was present for them in the state of their disbelief. And God knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We said﴾, ﴿And when We delivered you﴾, ﴿And when We parted﴾ (the sea). This occurs very frequently with the conjunctive wa (and) without mentioning a governing word that governs (idh) (the temporal "when"). This is because the discourse is in the context of enumerating blessings and repeating the narratives, so the conjunctive wa points to them as if they were mentioned explicitly, since the addressee knows the intended meaning. When this was obscure to some of the literalist grammarians (al-Zahiriyya al-nuhat), they said that wa is here superfluous (za'ida), and that is not the case. Among this category is the wa that carries the meaning of rubba (perhaps/how many), for you find it frequently at the beginning of speech, as an indication by them of enumerating what follows it, whether of boasting, praise, or other things. All of these are meanings concealed within the soul, and these particles are conjoined to them. Sometimes they state that concealed meaning explicitly, as in the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "Leave what is in your soul, even if they give you fatwas about it and give you fatwas."

From this category is the frequent omission of the responses (jawab) in the Qur'an, because the wa indicates them, the addressee knowing that the wa is conjunctive, and that it is only used to conjoin to something. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they took him away and agreed to put him into the depths of the well﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they reached it, its gates were opened﴾.

This domain is broad in the language. This is what there is on this question. This very matter had occurred to me in person at the station in Mecca, and it was circulating in my soul, and I turned away from it deliberately, because I had not seen it in the discussions of the scholars. Then I saw it afterward in two learned grammarians, one of whom hovered around it, and what was reported, and I do not know his name, and the second is Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli, may Allah have mercy on him, for he uncovered it and stated it explicitly. When realities become apparent, be the happiest of people with them, even if the ignorant spurn them. And Allah is the Granter of success in what is correct.

Ibn Jarir said: The Sabi'i (sabi') is one who newly adopts a religion other than his own, like an apostate from among the people of Islam who leaves his religion. Every person who leaves the religion he was upon for another is called a sabi' by the Arabs. From this it is said: "Fulan sabi'a, yasba'u, sabi'an" (so-and-so turned away, i.e., changed his religion). It is also said: "Sabi'at al-nujum" (the stars rose) when they appear, and "Sabi'a 'alayna Fulan" (so-and-so rose up over us) when he came into view.

I say: The Sabi'ah (Sabians) are a great nation, among whom are the fortunate and the wretched. They are one of the nations divided into believers and disbelievers. The nations before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) are of two types:

The first type are disbelievers and wretched entirely; none among them is fortunate, such as the worshippers of idols and the Magians (Majus).

The second type are divided into fortunate and wretched, and they are the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians.

Allah, glorified is He, has mentioned both types in His Book, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians and the Sabians—whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾

He said likewise in al-Ma'idah. And He said in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners [with Allah]—indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is Witness over all things.﴾ [al-Hajj: 17]. Here He did not say "whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day," because He mentioned with them the Magians and those who associated partners. So He mentioned six nations, of which two are wretched, and four are divided into wretched and fortunate. Where He promised the people of faith and righteous deeds among them a reward, He mentioned only four nations, and no more.

Thus, in the verse of separation (judgment) between the nations He included the two nations with them, and in the verse of promise of reward He did not include them with them. So it is known that the Sabians include the believer and the disbeliever, the wretched and the fortunate. This is an ancient nation, older than the Jews and the Christians, and they are of types: Sabians who are ḥunafa' (upright), and Sabians who are polytheists.

Harran was the seat of the kingdom of these people before the Messiah, and they had books, compositions and sciences. In Baghdad there was a large group of them, among them Ibrahim ibn Hilal al-Sabi, author of "al-Rasa'il," who was upon their religion and fasted Ramadan with the Muslims. Most of them were philosophers, and they have famous doctrines recorded by the authors of the heresiographies (al-maqalat).

The summary of their position is that they do not deny the prophets, nor do they make it obligatory to follow them. In their view, whoever follows them is fortunate and saved, and whoever attains by his intellect what they called to and agrees with them in it and acts by their precepts is fortunate, even if he is not bound to them.

Thus, according to them: the call of the prophets is true, but it does not specify one path to salvation. They acknowledge that the world has a Maker, a Governor, Wise, transcendent above resemblance to created things. But many of them, or most of them, said: "We are unable to reach His majesty without intermediaries, and it is necessary to draw near to Him through the mediation of the spiritual beings, holy and purified from corporeal matter, free from bodily powers, exalted above spatial movements and temporal changes; indeed they are created upon purity and made upon sanctification."

(The Proof of the Prohibition of Legal Stratagems)

The summary of this is that forbidden stratagems (hiyal) are a form of deceiving God, and deceiving God is prohibited. As for the first premise: the Companions and the Successors, who are the most knowledgeable of the Ummah in the words of God and His Messenger and their meanings, named that deception (khida'). As for the second premise: God censured the people of deception, and informed that their deception is only against themselves, that there is a sickness in their hearts, and that He Exalted deceives them. All of this is a punishment for them. The matter of deception rests on two foundations: the first is displaying an act for other than the purpose for which it was made; the second is displaying a statement for other than the purpose for which it was laid down. This applies to forbidden stratagems. God Exalted punished those who devised stratagems to cancel the share of the needy at harvest time by cutting their garden for themselves and destroying its fruit. How much more so, then, one who devises stratagems to cancel the obligations of God and the rights of His creatures? He also cursed the people of the Sabbath and transformed them into apes and swine because of their stratagem to do what He had forbidden them.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said, regarding the words of God Exalted: ﴿And you have already known those who transgressed among you in the Sabbath﴾

He said: They cast the fish on the Sabbath, then left them in the water, and retrieved them afterward, cooked them, and ate them. By God, the most ill-fated meal is a meal that hastened punishment in this world and hastened torment in the Hereafter. By God, those fish were not greater in the sight of God than the blood of Muslim people, except that He hastened [punishment] for these and deferred it for those.

His saying "they cast them on the Sabbath" means they devised a way for them to fall into the water on the Sabbath day, as others have explained: they dug pools for them, then opened them on Friday evening. It does not mean they personally cast them on Saturday; for had they dared to do that, they would have retrieved them. Our Shaykh said: These people did not disbelieve in the Torah or in Moses; they only acted through interpretation and stratagem, whose outward appearance is the appearance of piety while its reality is transgression. For this reason, God knows best, they were transformed into apes, because the form of the ape has some resemblance to the form of man, and in some of the attributes mentioned of it there is a resemblance to him, yet it differs from him in definition and reality. When those transgressors distorted God's religion such that they held only to what resembles religion in some outward aspect and not its reality, God transformed them into apes that resemble man in some outward aspect and not in reality, as a fitting recompense.

This is reinforced by the fact that the Children of Israel consumed usury and people's wealth falsely, which is greater than eating game on a specific day, yet those were not punished with transformation as were those who made the forbidden lawful through stratagem. Because those were greater in sin, their punishment was greater. They were like the hypocrites who do what they do and do not acknowledge the sin; rather their creed and their deeds have become corrupt. This is unlike one who consumes usury, people's wealth falsely, and forbidden game while knowing its prohibition, for his disobedience is accompanied by his acknowledgment of the prohibition, his fear of God, his seeking forgiveness, his repentance at some point, his acknowledgment that he is a sinful disobedient, the breaking of his heart from the humiliation of disobedience, his disdain for himself, his hope for his Lord's forgiveness, and his counting himself among the sinners who err. All of this is faith which leads its possessor to good, unlike the deceiver, the schemer, who devises stratagems against the heart of God's religion.

For this reason the Prophet ﷺ warned his Ummah against committing stratagems, saying: "Do not commit what the Jews committed, lest you make the prohibitions of God lawful by the slightest stratagems." God Exalted has informed that He made this town, or this deed which they did, a deterrent for what lay before it and after it, and an admonition for the God-fearing.

It is fitting, then, for one who fears God and dreads His punishment to beware of making God's prohibitions lawful through all kinds of cunning and stratagem, and to know that what he displays of trickery and deception in words and deeds will not save him from God, and to know that God has a Day on which men will be overturned, mountains will be blown away, terrors will follow one another, limbs and joints will bear witness, hidden things will be tested, and consciences will be revealed; on which falsehood becomes apparent, secrets become public, the concealed becomes exposed, the unknown becomes known, and what is in the breasts is brought out and revealed, just as what is in the graves is scattered and brought forth; and on which the rulings of the Lord Exalted will apply to intentions and purposes, just as His rulings in this abode applied to outward statements and movements. On the Day when faces will turn white because of what was in their owners' hearts of sincere counsel to God, His Messenger, His Book, and of righteousness, truthfulness, and sincerity toward the Great, the Exalted; and faces will turn black because of what was in their owners' hearts of deceit, fraud, lying, scheming, and stratagem. There the deceivers will know that they were deceiving only themselves, and playing with their religion, and that they were scheming only against themselves, and they did not perceive it.

Then, of their worst ignorance and wrongdoing is their saying to their prophet: ﴿Now you have brought the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71].

If they meant by it: "You had not brought the truth before that concerning the matter of the cow," then that is apostasy and manifest disbelief. And if they meant: "Now you have made clear to us the complete explanation in specifying the cow commanded to be slaughtered," then that is manifest ignorance, for the explanation had already been given by His saying:

﴿Indeed, God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67].

For there is no ambiguity in the command, nor in the act, nor in the animal slaughtered. The Messenger of God ﷺ had brought the truth from the very first time.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: Some of the predecessors claimed that the people apostatized from their religion and disbelieved by their saying to Moses, "Now you have brought the truth," and he claimed that this was a denial by them that Moses, peace be upon him, had brought them the truth regarding the cow before that, and that this was disbelief from them. He said: The matter is not as he said in our view, because they had submitted in obedience by slaughtering it, even though their saying which they spoke to Moses was ignorance from them and a slip of theirs.

Ignorance (al-jahl) is of two kinds: the absence of knowledge of the beneficial truth, and the absence of acting upon its requirement and its demand. Both are called ignorance linguistically, conventionally, legally, and in reality. Moses said, ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾, when his people said to him, ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾, meaning, "from among the mockers." Joseph the Truthful said, ﴿And unless You turn away from me their scheming, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf: 33], meaning, "from among those who commit what You have forbidden." And the Exalted said, ﴿Allah accepts repentance only from those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [al-Nisa': 17]. Qatadah said: "The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed that everything for which Allah is disobeyed is ignorance." Another said: "The Companions agreed that whoever disobeys Allah is ignorant." And the poet said:

Let no one among us act in ignorance toward us,
lest we act in ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant.

The failure to observe knowledge is called ignorance either because it has not benefited the one who possesses it, so it is treated as if it were ignorance, or because of his ignorance of the evil that the consequences of his action will bring.

(Section)

Among the Shaytan's manipulations of the Jews during the lifetime of their prophet is also what Allah, the Exalted, related in His Book about the story of the slain man whom they killed and then disputed about, until they were commanded to slaughter a cow and strike the body with part of it.

The story contains several kinds of lessons:

First: its report is among the signs of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family.

Second: it indicates the prophethood of Musa (Moses), and that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.

Third: it indicates the soundness of what all the messengers agreed upon, from the first of them to the last of them: the resurrection of bodies and the raising of the dead from their graves.

Fourth: it establishes the Chooser who acts by choice, who knows everything, is capable of everything, is just, to whom injustice and oppression cannot be attributed, and is wise, to whom futility cannot be attributed.

Fifth: the establishment, upon His servants, of various kinds of signs, proofs and arguments by diverse means, as an increase in guidance for those who seek guidance, and as a clear excuse and warning for the astray.

Sixth: that one should not meet the command of Allah, the Exalted, with obstinacy and excessive questioning, but should hasten to comply. When they were commanded to slaughter a cow, it was obligatory for them to hasten to comply by slaughtering any cow whatsoever, for the command to that is neither vague nor problematic; rather, it is like His saying: "Free a slave, feed a poor man, fast a day," and the like. Therefore, whoever argued from this verse for the permissibility of delaying clarification beyond the time of address has erred, for the verse is independent of separate clarification, clear in itself. But when they became obstinate and insistent, He made it strict upon them.

Abu Ja'far Ibn Jarir said, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: "If the people, when they were commanded to slaughter a cow, had taken any cow from among the cattle and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them. But they made it hard upon themselves, so Allah made it hard upon them."

Seventh: that it is not permissible to meet a command of Allah, whose wisdom the one commanded does not know, with denial. That is a kind of disbelief. When their prophet said to them: "Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter a cow" [al-Baqarah: 67],

they met this command with their saying: "Do you make us a laughingstock?" [al-Baqarah: 67].

Since they did not know the wisdom in the connection of this command with what they had asked about, they said: "Do you make us a laughingstock?" [al-Baqarah: 67].

This is from the utmost of their ignorance of Allah and His messenger. For he informed them of Allah's command to them in this matter, and he was not the one who commanded it. And had he been the one who commanded it, it would not have been permissible for one who believes in the messenger to meet his command with this. So when he said to them: "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant" [al-Baqarah: 67],

and they were certain that Allah had commanded this, they began to be obstinate by asking about its specific description and color. When they were informed of that, they returned to asking a third time about its specific description. When it was made definite for them and no ambiguity remained, they hesitated in compliance and nearly did not carry it out.

Then, among the worst of their ignorance and wrongdoing was their saying to their prophet: "Now you have come with the truth" [al-Baqarah: 71].

If they meant by this: "You did not come with the truth before that concerning the matter of the cow," then that is an apostasy and clear disbelief. And if they meant: "You have now made the complete clarification in specifying the cow to be slaughtered," then that is clear ignorance, for the clarification had already been achieved by his saying:

"Indeed Allah commands you to slaughter a cow" [al-Baqarah: 67].

For there is no vagueness in the command, nor in the act, nor in the slaughtered animal. Thus the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had brought the truth from the very first time.

Muhammad Ibn Jarir said: Some of the predecessors used to claim that the people apostatized from their religion and disbelieved by their saying to Musa, "Now you have come with the truth," and he claimed that this was a denial by them that Musa, peace be upon him, had brought them the truth concerning the cow before that, and that this was disbelief from them. He said: "The matter is not as he said, in our view, because they had already submitted in obedience by slaughtering it, though their saying that they said to Musa was ignorance on their part and one of their blunders."

Eighth: the report of the hardness and severity of the hearts of the community, and the non-establishment of faith within them.

'Abd al-Samad Ibn Ma'qil said, from Wahb: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: "After Allah, the Exalted, brought the dead man to life and he informed them of his killer, they denied the killing, and said: 'By Allah, we did not kill him,' after they had seen the signs and the truth." Allah, the Exalted, said: "Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones or even harder in hardness" [al-Baqarah: 74].

Ninth: the requital of the oppressive transgressor with the opposite of his intention, both legally and by decree. The killer intended the inheritance of the slain man and the averting of killing from himself, so Allah, the Exalted, exposed and disgraced him, and deprived him of the inheritance of the slain man.

Tenth: that the Children of Israel were tested with the cow twice among all the animals: they were tested by worshipping the calf, and they were tested by the command to slaughter a cow. The cow is among the most dull-witted of animals, to the extent that it is used as a proverb.

Apparently, this story came after the story of the calf. In the command to slaughter the cow there is a reminder that this kind of animal, which does not refuse slaughter, plowing, or irrigation, is not fit to be a god worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted, and that it is only fit for slaughter, plowing, irrigation, and labor.
