Among them is His saying in the sacred hadith: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it."

Among them is His saying: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit," and the hadith continues.

So the servant continually gains profit with his Lord, better than what he has sent forward. The one who draws near to Him with his heart, soul and deeds, his Lord opens for him a life unlike the kinds of life people have. Rather, the life of one who is not so compared to his life is like the life of an embryo in its mother's womb compared to the life of the people of this world and their pleasures in it, indeed greater than that.

This is a model of one who has surpassed the nobility and excellence of this life. Even if knowledge of this brings its possessor a good life, how much more so when the heart is dyed by it and it becomes a state constantly inherent in its essence. So Allah is the One sought for help.

This life is in truth the life of this world and its bliss. Whoever loses it, his loss of his natural life is more fitting for him.

"This is the life of the young man; if it is lost, his losing life is more fitting for him."

There is no life except the life of the lovers, those whose eyes are comforted by their Beloved, whose souls are at peace with Him, whose hearts are reassured by Him, who find intimacy in His nearness and delight in His love. In the heart there is a need that nothing fills except the love of Allah, turning to Him and returning to Him, and its disarray is never gathered except by that. Whoever does not attain this, his whole life is worries and griefs, pains and regrets. If he has lofty resolve, his soul is torn apart over the world with regrets, for his resolve is not content in it with what is lowly. And if he is base and despicable, his life is like the life of the most degraded animals. Eyes are not comforted except by love of the First Beloved.

"Shift your heart wherever you wish among desires; love is only for the First Beloved."

"How many a dwelling on earth a young man grows accustomed to, yet his longing is always for the first dwelling."

(Section: The religion is built on two foundations, remembrance and gratitude)

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you; and be grateful to Me and do not deny Me﴾.

And the Prophet said to Mu'adh: "By Allah, I love you, so do not neglect to say after every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well."

Remembrance here does not mean merely the remembrance of the tongue, but the remembrance of the heart and the tongue together. His remembrance includes the remembrance of His names, His attributes, the remembrance of His command and prohibition, and remembrance of Him through His speech. That requires knowing Him, believing in Him and in the attributes of His perfection and the descriptions of His majesty, and praising Him with all kinds of praise. This is not complete except through affirming His oneness. So true remembrance of Him entails all of this, and entails mention of His blessings, His favors, and His kindness to His creatures.

As for gratitude, it is the performance of His obedience and drawing near to Him by all kinds of what He loves, outwardly and inwardly. These two matters are the essence of religion. His remembrance necessitates knowledge of Him, and His gratitude includes obedience to Him. These two are the end for which jinn and humankind, the heavens and the earth were created, for which rewards and punishments were established, the Books were sent down and the Messengers sent. They are the truth by which the heavens and the earth and what is between them were created. Its opposite is falsehood and vanity, from which He is exalted and sanctified, and which is the assumption of His enemies about Him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain; that is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾. He said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them playing. We did not create them except with truth﴾. He said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth, and indeed the Hour is coming﴾. He said, after mentioning His signs at the beginning of Surah Yunus: ﴿Allah did not create that except with truth﴾. He said: ﴿Does man think he will be left neglected?﴾. He said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾. He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except to worship Me﴾. ﴿It is Allah who created seven heavens and of the earth their like; the command descends among them that you may know that Allah is over all things competent and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾.

He said: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for the people, and the sacred month and the offerings and the garlands. That is so that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾.

Thus it is established by what has been mentioned that the ultimate purpose of creation and command is that He be remembered and thanked: remembered so that He is not forgotten, and thanked so that He is not denied. He, glory be to Him, remembers whoever remembers Him and is grateful to whoever is grateful to Him. His remembrance of His servant is a cause of the servant's remembrance of Him, and the servant's gratitude is a cause of increase from His bounty. Remembrance belongs to the heart and tongue; gratitude is for the heart in love and turning in repentance, for the tongue in praise and commendation, and for the limbs in obedience and service.

**(Benefit)**

He, glorified is He, joined patience (sabr) to the pillars of Islam and to all the stations of faith. He joined it to prayer, as in His saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

He joined it to righteous deeds in general, as in His saying ﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds﴾.

He made it the companion of God-consciousness (taqwa), as in His saying ﴿Indeed, whoever is mindful of God and is patient﴾.

He made it the companion of gratitude, as in His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful person﴾.

He made it the companion of truth, as in His saying ﴿and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience﴾.

He made it the companion of mercy, as in His saying ﴿and advise one another to patience and advise one another to compassion﴾.

He made it the companion of certainty, as in His saying ﴿Because they were patient and used to be certain of Our signs﴾.

He made it the companion of truthfulness, as in His saying ﴿the truthful men and the truthful women, the patient men and the patient women﴾.

He made it the cause of His love, His companionship, His help, His aid, and a good reward. Some of this suffices as a mark of its honour and excellence. And God knows best.

**[Section: The Station of Patience]**

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of patience.

Imam Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: "Patience is mentioned in the Qur'an in about ninety places."

It is obligatory by the consensus (ijma') of the Muslim community. It is half of faith, for faith consists of two halves: half patience and half gratitude.

It is mentioned in the Qur'an in sixteen forms.

The first: the command to it, such as His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer﴾, and His saying, ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]. And His saying, ﴿Be patient and endure﴾ [Al 'Imran: 200], and His saying, ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except by God﴾ [al-Nahl: 127].

The second: the prohibition of its opposite, such as His saying, ﴿So be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]; and His saying, ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾ [al-Anfal: 15], for turning one's back is abandoning patience and steadfastness. And His saying, ﴿And do not nullify your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 33], for nullifying them is abandoning patience in completing them. And His saying, ﴿And do not weaken and do not grieve﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], for weakness comes from lack of patience.

The third: praise of its people, such as His saying, ﴿the patient and the truthful﴾ [Al 'Imran: 17], and the verse, and His saying, ﴿and the patient in misfortune and hardship and in time of battle; those are the ones who have been truthful, and those are the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

This is abundant in the Qur'an.

The fourth: His, glorified is He, declaring His love for them, such as His saying, ﴿And God loves the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146].

The fifth: His declaring His companionship (ma'iyyah) with them. This is a special companionship, which includes protecting them, helping them, and strengthening them. It is not a general companionship, which is the companionship of knowledge and encompassing. Such as His saying, ﴿And be patient; indeed, God is with the patient﴾ [al-Anfal: 46], and His saying, ﴿And God is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249].

The sixth: His informing that patience is good for its possessors, such as His saying, ﴿And if you are patient, it is better for those who are patient﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], and His saying, ﴿And that you be patient is better for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 25].

The seventh: the declaration that they will be rewarded for their best deeds, such as His saying, ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient with their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 96].

The eighth: His, glorified is He, declaring that He will reward them without account, such as His saying, ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10].

The ninth: the giving of good tidings to the people of patience, such as His saying, ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155].

The tenth: the guarantee of victory and support for them, such as His saying, ﴿Yes, if you are patient and mindful of God, and they come at you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked [for battle]﴾ [Al 'Imran: 125]. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Know that victory comes with patience."

The eleventh: His informing that the people of patience are the people of firm resolve, such as His saying, ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [al-Shura: 43].

The twelfth: the information that none attains righteous deeds, their reward, and great portions except the people of patience, such as His saying, ﴿Woe to you! The reward of God is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds, but none receives it except the patient﴾ [al-Qasas: 80], and His saying, ﴿And none receives it except those who are patient, and none receives it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35].

The thirteenth: the information that only the people of patience benefit from the signs and lessons. Such as His saying to Moses, ﴿Bring your people out of darkness into light and remind them of the days of God. Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful person﴾ [Ibrahim: 5]; and His saying about the people of Saba': ﴿So We made them as narratives and scattered them completely. Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful person﴾ [Saba': 19]; and His saying in Surat al-Shura: ﴿And among His signs are the ships sailing the sea like mountains. If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless upon its surface. Indeed in that are signs for every patient, grateful person﴾ [al-Shura: 32].

The fourteenth: the information that the sought-after success, the deliverance from what is feared and dreaded, and the entry into Paradise are attained only through patience, such as His saying, ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23].

The fifteenth: that it brings its possessor the rank of leadership (imamah). I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God sanctify his soul, say: "Through patience and certainty, leadership in religion is attained." Then he recited His saying, ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and used to be certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Sajdah: 24].

The sixteenth: its being joined to the stations of Islam and faith, just as God, glorified is He, joined it to certainty, faith, God-consciousness, reliance on God, gratitude, righteous deeds, and mercy.

For this reason, patience in faith is like the head in the body, and there is no faith for one who has no patience, just as there is no body for one who has no head. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said: "The best life we ever experienced was through patience." The Prophet (ﷺ) informed in a sound hadith that patience is a light (diya'). And he said: "Whoever seeks to be patient, God will make him patient."

In a sound hadith: "How wondrous is the affair of the believer! Indeed, all his affairs are good, and this is not the case for anyone except the believer. If something pleasant befalls him, he is grateful, and that is good for him. And if something harmful befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him."

And he said to the black woman who used to suffer from seizures and asked him to pray for her: "If you wish, be patient and you will have Paradise; or if you wish, I will supplicate God to cure you." She said: "I suffer exposure, so pray to God that I not be exposed." So he prayed for her.

He commanded the Ansar, may God be pleased with them all, to be patient with the favouritism (athrah) they would encounter after him, until they meet him at the Basin (al-hawd).

He commanded patience at the encounter with the enemy. He commanded patience at the time of calamity. And he informed that patience is only at the first shock.

The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the afflicted person with what is most beneficial for him, which is patience and seeking the reward (ihtisab) [from God].

For this lightens his affliction and multiplies his reward. Whereas impatience, complaining, and grumbling increase the affliction and cancel the reward.

The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that patience is entirely good, and he said: "No one is given a gift better or more expansive than patience."

(Chapter)

It is related in the Musnad, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No one is afflicted by a calamity and then says: 'Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return. O Allah, reward me in my affliction and replace it for me with something better,' except that Allah will reward him in his affliction and replace for him something better than it."

This statement is among the most effective remedies for the afflicted, and the most beneficial for him in this world and the next, for it contains two great principles. When the servant truly realises these two principles, he finds consolation for his affliction.

The first: the servant, his family and his wealth belong to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in truth. He has placed them with the servant as a loan (ʿāriyah). When He takes them back, He is like the lender who takes his property back from the borrower. Moreover, a thing is enclosed between two nonexistences: a nonexistence before it and a nonexistence after it, and the servant's possession of it is a loaned enjoyment for a brief time. Furthermore, the servant is not the one who brought it into existence from non-existence, such that it would be his property in truth, nor is he the one who protects it from calamities after its existence, nor does he preserve its existence. Thus he has no real influence over it and no true ownership. Furthermore, he disposes of it only by command, as a servant who is commanded and forbidden, not as an owner. For this reason, he is permitted to dispose of it only in ways that accord with the command of its true Owner.

The second: the servant's destination and return is to Allah, his true Master. He must leave the world behind him and come to his Lord alone, just as He created him the first time: without family, without wealth, without tribe, but with his good deeds and his bad deeds. If this is the beginning of the servant and what he was given, and his end, then how can he rejoice in what exists or grieve over what is lost? So reflection upon his origin and his return is among the greatest remedies for this disease. And among its remedies is that he know with certainty that what befell him was never going to miss him, and what missed him was never going to befall him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves but that it is in a Book before We bring it into being. Indeed that is easy for Allah. [This is] so that you won't despair over what has eluded you and not exult over what He has given you. And Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful﴾ [al-Hadid: 22].

And among its remedies is that he look at what he has been afflicted with, and find that his Lord has left him its like or something better, and has stored up for him—if he is patient and content—what is greater than the loss of that calamity by manifold multiples, and that had He willed, He could have made it greater than it is.

And among its remedies is that he extinguish the fire of his calamity with the cool of consoling himself by the example of others who are afflicted, and let him know that "in every valley there are the Banū Saʿd" (i.e., everyone has their trouble). Let him look to the right: does he see anything but trial? Then let him turn to the left: does he see anything but regret? If he searched the whole world, he would find among its people only one who is tested: either by the loss of something beloved or the arrival of something hateful. The evils of this world are like dream-visions or a passing shade: if they make you laugh briefly, they make you weep much; if they please you for a day, they grieve you for an age; if they grant enjoyment briefly, they withhold it for long. Whenever it fills a home with blessings, it fills it with lessons; and whenever it gives someone a day of joy, it hides for him a day of sorrow. Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "For every joy there is a sorrow, and no house is filled with joy except that it is filled with sorrow." Ibn Sirin said: "Laughter never occurs except that weeping follows it."

Hind bint al-Nuʿmān said: "We saw ourselves as among the most honoured of people and the most powerful in dominion, then the sun had not set before we saw ourselves as the lowest of people." It is true, from Allah, that He does not fill a home with blessings except that He fills it with lessons.

A man asked her to tell him about her situation, and she said: "We awoke in the morning, and there was no one among the Arabs who did not hope for us; then we evening came, and there was no one among the Arabs who did not pity us."

Her sister Ḥurqa bint al-Nuʿmān once wept while she was in her might. She was asked: "What makes you weep? Perhaps someone has harmed you?" She said: "No, but I saw a brightness among my people, and rarely does a home fill with joy except that it fills with sorrow."

Isḥāq ibn Ṭalḥa said: "I entered upon her one day and said to her: 'How have you found the tears of kings?' She said: 'What we are in today is better than what we were in yesterday. We find in the Books that no household lives in blessing except that after it they will be given a lesson; and that fortune never revealed itself to a people with a day they love except that it hid for them a day they hate.'" Then she said:

"While we were governing the people, and the affair was ours,
Suddenly we among them became commoners, dividing what is left."
"Fie upon a world whose bliss does not endure,
It turns us about in turns and transforms us."

Among its remedies is that he know that excessive grief does not turn it back; rather it multiplies it, and in reality it is an increase of the illness.

Among its remedies is that he know that the loss of the reward of patience and submission—which is the blessings, mercy and guidance that Allah guaranteed for patience and for saying "Istirjāʿ"—is in reality greater than the calamity itself.

Among its remedies is that he know that excessive grief gratifies his enemy, grieves his friend, angers his Lord, pleases his Satan, nullifies his reward, and weakens his soul. Whereas if he is patient and seeks Allah's reward, he wears down his Satan and turns him away humiliated, pleases his Lord, delights his friend, displeases his enemy, bears part of the burden for his brothers, and consoles them before they console him. This is steadfastness and the supreme perfection, not slapping cheeks, tearing collars, calling for destruction and ruin, or raging against what has been decreed.

Among its remedies: that he know that the joy and delight which patience and seeking reward bring him are many times greater than what he would have gained by keeping what he was afflicted with, had it remained with him. And it suffices him in this the "House of Praise" that will be built for him in Paradise in return for his praise of his Lord and his saying "Istirjāʿ." So let him consider: which of the two calamities is greater—the calamity of the immediate world, or the calamity of missing the House of Praise in the Garden of Eternity? In al-Tirmidhī, it is related with a raised chain: "On the Day of Resurrection, some people will wish that their skins had been cut with scissors in this world, because of what they see of the reward of the people of trials."

And some of the early generations said: "Were it not for the calamities of this world, we would arrive at the Resurrection bankrupt."

Among its remedies: that he refresh his heart with the spirit of hope for a replacement from Allah, for everything has a substitute except Allah, and for Him there is no substitute, as it has been said:

"For everything, if you lose it, there is a substitute,
But for what you lose from Allah, there is no substitute."

Among its remedies: that he know that his share of the calamity is what it produces in him. Whoever is content, for him is contentment, and whoever is angry, for him is anger. So your share of it is what it has brought about in you, so choose the best of shares or the worst. If it produces in him anger and disbelief, he is written in the register of the lost; if it produces in him impatience and neglect of an obligation or commission of a prohibited act, he is written in the register of the negligent; if it produces in him complaint and lack of patience, he is written in the register of the defrauded; if it produces in him objection against Allah and disparagement of His wisdom, then he has knocked at the door of heresy or entered it; if it produces in him patience and steadfastness for Allah's sake, he is written in the register of the patient; if it produces in him contentment with Allah, he is written in the register of the content; if it produces in him praise and thankfulness, he is written in the register of the thankful, and is under the banner of praise with those who praise; if it produces in him love and longing for the meeting with his Lord, he is written in the register of the sincere lovers.

In the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad and in al-Tirmidhī, from the hadith of Maḥmūd ibn Labīd, raised: "When Allah loves a people, He tests them; whoever is content, for him is contentment, and whoever is angry, for him is anger." Aḥmad added: "And whoever wails, for him is wailing."

Among its remedies: that he know that however far he goes in grief, his final state will be to a patience of compulsion, which is neither praised nor rewarded. Some sages said: "The intelligent person does on the first day of a calamity what the ignorant does after days." And whoever does not endure with the patience of the noble will console himself with the consolation of animals.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ, raised: "Patience is at the first shock." Al-Ashʿath ibn Qays said: "If you are patient out of faith and seeking reward, well and good; otherwise you will console yourself with the consolation of animals."

Among its remedies: that he know that the most beneficial medicine for him is conformity with his Lord and God in what He loves and is pleased with for him. The特性 and secret of love is conformity with the beloved. Whoever claims to love a beloved, then becomes angry at what He loves and loves what He hates, has testified against himself to his lie and has become hateful to his beloved.

Abū al-Dardāʾ said: "When Allah decrees a decree, He loves to be pleased with it." ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn used to say during his illness: "The most beloved to me is what is most beloved to Him." Likewise Abū al-ʿĀliyah said.

This is a remedy and treatment that works only with lovers, and not everyone can be treated by it.

Among its remedies: that he weigh the two greatest pleasures and enjoyments, and the more lasting of them: the pleasure of enjoying what he was afflicted with, and the pleasure of enjoying Allah's reward for him. If the preponderance appears to him and he prefers the preponderant, let him praise Allah for His success. But if he prefers the outweighed in every respect, let him know that his calamity in his intellect, heart and religion is greater than the calamity he suffered in his worldly life.

Among its remedies: that he know that the One who tested him with it is the most Wise of the wise and the most Merciful of the merciful, and that He, glorified be He, did not send the affliction to him to destroy him with it, nor to punish him with it, nor to uproot him; rather He visited him with it to test his patience, his contentment with Him and his faith, and to hear his humble supplication and pleading, and to see him prostrate at His door, seeking refuge in His presence, with a broken heart before Him, raising the tales of his complaint to Him.

Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qādir said: "My son, calamity did not come to destroy you; it came only to test your patience and your faith. My son, fate is a beast of prey, and a beast of prey does not eat carrion."

The point is that calamity is the furnace of the servant in which his essence is smelted: either he comes out pure gold, or he comes out entirely dross, as it has been said:

"We smelted it, thinking it silver,
But the furnace revealed the dross of the iron."

If this furnace does not benefit him in this world, then before him is the greater furnace. So when the servant knows that his being put into the furnace of this world and its smelting is better for him than that furnace and smelting, and that one of the two furnaces is inevitable, let him recognise the value of Allah's blessing upon him in the immediate furnace.

Among its remedies: that he know that, were it not for the afflictions and calamities of this world, the servant would be struck by the diseases of pride, self-admiration, tyranny and hardness of heart, which would be the cause of his destruction, in the present and the future. So from the mercy of the Most Merciful of the merciful is that He visits him from time to time with various kinds of medicines of calamities, which serve as a protection for him from these diseases, a preservation of the soundness of his servitude, and a purging of the corrupt, vile and destructive substances within him. Glory be to Him who shows mercy through His trial and tests through His blessings, as it has been said:

"He bestows blessing through affliction, however great it be,
And Allah tests some people with blessings."

Were it not that He, glorified be He, heals His servants with the medicines of trials and tests, they would transgress, rebel and become arrogant. And when Allah, glorified be He, wishes good for a servant, He gives him a medicine of trial and testing according to his condition, by which He purges him of the destructive diseases, until, when He has refined him, purified him and cleansed him, He qualifies him for the noblest stations of this world, which is His servitude, and the highest reward of the Hereafter, which is seeing Him and nearness to Him.

Among its remedies: that he know that the bitterness of this world is itself the sweetness of the Hereafter, and the sweetness of this world is itself the bitterness of the Hereafter, as Allah, glorified be He, reverses them thus. And that moving from a bitterness that ends to an everlasting sweetness is better for him than the reverse. If this is hidden from you, then look at the words of the Truthful and Truly-Reported One (ﷺ): "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and Hellfire is surrounded by desires."

In this station the minds of creatures differ, and the true natures of men appear, and most of them...

He preferred the fleeting sweetness over the lasting sweetness that never ends, and he would not endure the bitterness of an hour for the sweetness of eternity, nor the humiliation of an hour for the honor of eternity, nor the trial of an hour for the well-being of eternity. For the present is, to him, something witnessed, while what is awaited is unseen, his faith is weak, and the authority of desire rules him. From this arises the preference for the hasty world and the rejection of the Hereafter. This is the state of the gaze that rests on the surface of things, their beginnings and first appearances. As for the piercing gaze that tears through the veils of the hasty world and passes beyond them to their outcomes and final ends, it has a different standing.

So call your soul to what Allah has prepared for His friends and for those who obey Him: the enduring bliss, the everlasting happiness, the greatest triumph. And call it to what He has prepared for the people of idleness and neglect: disgrace, punishment, and perpetual regrets. Then choose which of the two divisions is more fitting for you. Each acts according to his own disposition, and each person inclines toward what suits him and what is better for him. Do not consider this treatment tedious, for the great need for it, on the part of both the physician and the patient, has compelled its extension. And success is from Allah.

(Section)
Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Abdullah ibn Lahi'ah informed us, from Ata' ibn Dinar, that Sa'id ibn Jubayr said:
"Patience is the servant's acknowledgment before Allah of what has befallen him from Him, his seeking reward from Allah, and his hope for His recompense. A man may feign composure while he is in fact distressed; yet only patience is seen from him."

His words "acknowledgment of the servant before Allah of what has befallen him from Him" are an explanation of His words ﴿Indeed, we belong to Allah﴾, so he acknowledges that he is a possession of Allah, Whose owner disposes of him as He wills. His words "hoping for what is with Allah" are an explanation of His words ﴿and indeed to Him we shall return﴾, meaning that we will be returned to Him, and He will recompense us for our patience, and the reward for the calamity will not be lost. His words "A man may feign composure while he is in fact distressed" mean that patience is not mere feigned composure; rather it is restraining the heart from resentment toward what has been decreed and restraining the tongue from complaint. Whoever feigns composure while his heart is resentful of the decree is not patient.

Yunus ibn Yazid said: I asked Rabi'ah ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman, "What is the limit of patience?" He said: "That on the day calamity befalls you, you be like you were before it befell you."

Qays ibn al-Hajjaj, regarding Allah's words ﴿so be patient with beautiful patience﴾, said: "It is that the one afflicted be among the people without being recognized as the one who is afflicted."

Shammar, whenever he consoled a afflicted person, would say: "Be patient with what your Lord has decreed."

Abu Aqil said: "I saw Salim ibn Abdullah ibn Umar, with a whip in his hand and wearing a waist-wrapper, at the death of Waqid ibn Abdullah ibn Umar, and whenever he heard a wailing woman he struck her with the whip."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Mihran narrated to me, saying: A woman of Quraysh said:
"By He who alone is eternal, and none is equal to Him in the inaccessible might,
If the beginning of patience is bitter in its taste, it yields from its consequence sweet fruit."

He said: Amr ibn Bukayr recited to me:
"I was patient, and patience was the better outcome; what use is grief to me, that I should grieve?
I held back the tears of my eye until I returned them to my gaze, though the eye weeps in the heart."

He said: Ahmad ibn Musa al-Thaqafi recited to me:
"I was told that Khawlah had grieved yesterday because the calamities of time had befallen her.
Do not grieve, O Khawlah, and be patient, for the noble have been built upon patience."

He said: Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Taymi narrated to me that a man consoled another man over his son, saying: "Allah's promise is due only to the one who is patient for His sake. So do not add to the calamity that has befallen you the loss of the reward, for that is the greater of the two calamities upon you, and the more painful of your two misfortunes. Peace."

Ibn Abi al-Simak consoled a man and said: "Upon you is patience; by it the one who seeks reward acts, and to grief returns the one who wails."

Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz said: "As for contentment, it is a rare or inaccessible station, but Allah has placed in patience a good support."

When Abd al-Malik's son died, he prayed over him and then said: "May Allah have mercy on you; you were indeed a minister to me and a helper to me." He said: While people wept, not a drop fell from his eyes.

Mutarrif ibn Abdullah was afflicted in a son of his, and people came to console him. He went out to them with the best cheerfulness, then said: "Indeed I am ashamed before Allah to be abased by a calamity."

Amr ibn Dinar said: Ubayd ibn Umayr said: "Grief is not that the eye sheds tears and the heart grieves; rather grief is the evil word and the evil thought."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Harawi narrated to me: "A precious son of mine died, so I said to his mother: 'Fear Allah, seek reward, and be patient.'
She said: 'My calamity is too great for me to spoil it with grief.'"

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Umar ibn Bukayr informed me, from a shaykh of Quraysh, that: al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn, father of Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan, died, while Ubayd Allah was then judge and governor of Basra. Many people came to console him, so they discussed what distinguishes a man's grief from his patience, and they agreed that if he abandons anything he used to do, then he has grieved.

Khalid ibn Abi Uthman al-Qurashi said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr used to console me over my son. He saw me circling the House while veiled, so he uncovered the veil from my head and said: "Submissiveness is a form of grief."

(Section)
As for the view of many jurists among our companions and others, that there is no harm in the afflicted person placing a cloth on his head by which he is recognized, saying that consolation is a sunnah and that this facilitates his being recognized so that he may be consoled, there is room for scrutiny in this. Our shaykh rejected it, and there is no doubt that the early generations did not do anything of the kind, nor was this reported from any of the Companions or the Successors. The earlier reports are all explicit in refuting this view.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh also rejected giving up wearing what one habitually wears, and said it is a form of grief.

In sum, their custom was not to change anything of their attire before the calamity, nor to abandon what they used to do. All of this contradicts patience. And Allah, glory be to Him, knows best.

(Benefit)
His ﷺ saying: "Whoever consoles one who is afflicted, he has the like of his reward."

Some have found this problematic and said: The hardship of calamity is far greater than the equivalence of the consoler's consolation, given that his heart remains cool?

Ibn Aqil, may Allah have mercy on him, answered with a very wonderful response. He said: "The aim is not what some say to one another, such as 'May Allah lengthen your life, may you live and remain,' or 'May Allah prolong your life,' and the like. Rather, the aim is one who sets out to a heart that has been disturbed and agitated by the pain of the calamity, which has nearly settled into resentment, speaking in despair and falling into sin. He treats that heart with verses of threat, the reward of patience, and the blame of grief until he removes what is in it or lessens it, and so it is consoled. Thus the reward of the one who comforts becomes like the reward of the one afflicted, for each of them repelled grief: the afflicted one endured it through patience, and the consoler worked through the means of treating the pain of sorrow."

(Anecdote)
When al-Abbas died, people refrained from consoling his son Abdullah, out of reverence and honor for him, until a man from the desert came and recited to him:
"Be patient, and we shall be patient with you, for the patience of the subjects follows the patience of the head.
Your patience after al-Abbas is better than him, and Allah is better than you for al-Abbas."
He said: So he was relieved, and people turned to console him.

(Benefit)
Some scholars consoled a man over his young child, saying: "Part of you has entered Paradise, so strive that the rest of you not be left behind from it."

I say: There is some question about the permissibility of this testimony. For although we do not doubt that the children of believers are in Paradise, we do not testify that any specific child is there, just as we testify that believers in general are in Paradise, but we do not testify that any specific person is there except those whom the text has named. On this basis is to be understood the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, when she testified that a child of the Ansar was a sparrow of the sparrows of Paradise, and the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "And how do you know?..."

So we say to this consoler likewise: "And how do you know that some of the one consoled has entered Paradise?"

The essence of the matter is the distinction between the specific and the general, regarding children and adults. And Allah knows best.

(Fā'idah)

The statement that ṣalāh from Allah means raḥmah (mercy) is false, for three reasons.

First: Allah, exalted is He, distinguished between them in His saying: ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy﴾.

Second: asking for mercy is prescribed for every Muslim, whereas ṣalāh (blessing) is specific to the Prophet, and it is his right and the right of his family. For this reason many scholars prohibited invoking ṣalāh upon any specific person other than him, whereas no one has prohibited invoking mercy upon a specific person.

Third: the mercy of Allah is general, encompassing everything, while His ṣalāh is specific to the elect of His servants.

As for the ṣalāh of the servants in the sense of du'ā' (supplication), the statement that it means du'ā' is problematic for several reasons.

First, du'ā' may be for good or for evil, whereas ṣalāh occurs only in good.

Second, if you say da'awtu (I supplicated), it is transitive with the preposition lām, while ṣallaytu (I prayed/blessed) is transitive only with ʿalā, and da'ā transitive with ʿalā does not mean ṣallā.

Third, the act of du'ā' requires one who is supplicated to and one for whom it is made: you say, "I supplicated to Allah for you with good," whereas the act of ṣalāh does not require that. You do not say, "I prayed Allah upon you" or "for you." This shows that it does not have the same meaning. What greater divergence could be clearer than this? But imitation (taqlīd) blinds one from perceiving realities, so beware of inclining to its earth.

On the derivation of ṣalāh: I have seen a good statement by Abū al-Qāsim al-Suhaylī on the derivation of ṣalāh, and this is his wording. He said: The meaning of ṣalāh, wherever the word is used, returns to tenderness (ḥanw) and compassion (ʿaṭf). However, tenderness and compassion may be perceptible or intelligible. Thus, from it, what befits Allah's majesty is attributed to Him, and what is exalted above Him is negated. Just as highness (ʿulūw) is perceptible and intelligible, the perceptible aspect of it is the attributes of bodies, and the intelligible aspect is the attribute of the Lord of majesty and honour. This meaning is abundant and found in the attributes, and the abundant may be an attribute of perceptible things and an attribute of intelligible things. It is one of the names of the Lord, exalted is He, and He is sanctified above resemblance to bodies and likeness to created beings. The meaning attributed to Him from these is intelligible, not perceptible. Once this is established, ṣalāh is called ʿaṭf (compassion) and ḥanw (tenderness). You say, "O Allah, incline Your compassion toward us," meaning, "have mercy upon us."

The poet said:

"I have not ceased in my gentleness toward him and my inclining toward him, as a mother inclines toward her child."

The mercy of servants is a tenderness in the heart; when the one who shows mercy finds it within himself, he inclines toward the one he pities and bends over him. The mercy of Allah toward His servants is generosity and bounty; so when He blesses someone, He has bestowed favour upon him and conferred blessing. When these acts come from Allah or from the servant, they are transitive with ʿalā and restricted to good, not departing from it to anything else. All of them thus return to one meaning, except that they are in the sense of supplication, and ṣalāh in the sense of mercy is intelligible bending, not perceptible. Its fruit from the servant is du'ā', since he cannot do more than that; its fruit from Allah is benevolence and bounty. Thus the meaning of ṣalāh has not differed; only its resulting fruits have differed. The ṣalāh that consists of rukūʿ and sujūd is perceptible bending, so the meaning there differs only in respect of the intelligible and the perceptible, and this is not a difference in reality. That is why all of them are transitive with ʿalā and agree in the word derived from ṣalāh, and one may not say ṣallaytu ʿalā al-ʿaduww (I prayed upon the enemy) meaning "I supplicated against him." The meaning of ṣalāh has thus become more tender and more eloquent than the meaning of mercy, though it returns to it, for not every merciful person bends over the one he pities or inclines toward him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verses 159–160:

The repentance of these sinners for their corrupt beliefs is by strictly following the Sunnah (the Prophet's way). It is not enough for them to do only that. They must also make clear the corruption of the innovation (bid'ah) they were upon, since repentance from a sin is by doing its opposite. For this reason, God Almighty made the condition for the repentance of those who conceal what God sent down to be the clarification of "the clear proofs and the guidance" (al-bayan). Because their sin was concealment, their repentance from it is through clarification. God Almighty says: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear for the people in the Book, those are cursed by God and cursed by those who curse. Except for those who repent, make amends, and clarify. Those I will turn back to, and I am the Ever-Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 159–160]. The sin of the innovator is greater than the sin of the concealer, because the latter concealed the truth, whereas the former concealed it and called to its opposite. So every innovator is a concealer, but not every concealer is an innovator.

He made the condition for the repentance of the hypocrite (munafiq) to be sincerity (ikhlas), because his sin is hypocrisy and showing off (riya'). God says: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 145]. Then He says: ﴿Except for those who repent, make amends, hold fast to God, and make their religion sincerely for God. Those are with the believers, and God will give the believers a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 146].

For this reason, the sounder of the two opinions is that the repentance of the one who falsely accuses (qadhif) is by retracting his accusation against himself, because this is the opposite of the sin he committed, and he violated the honour of a chaste Muslim. Repentance is not achieved from him except by retracting his statement against himself, so that the shame he attached to the accused by the false accusation is removed. This is the purpose of repentance.

As for the one who says that his repentance is to say, "I seek God's forgiveness for the accusation," and to acknowledge its prohibition, this is a weak opinion. This brings no benefit to the accused, and the clearing of his honour from what was charged against him is not achieved by it. Therefore the purpose of repentance from this sin is not achieved by it. This sin involves two rights: a right of God, which is the prohibition of false accusation, so his repentance from it is by seeking God's forgiveness, acknowledging the prohibition of false accusation, regretting it, and resolving not to return to it; and a right of the servant, which is attaching shame to him. So his repentance from that is by declaring himself a liar. Thus repentance from this sin is by both matters together.

If it is said: If he is truthful, having witnessed the act of adultery and reported it, how is it permissible for him to call himself a liar and accuse himself of falsehood, and for that to be part of his repentance?

It is said: This is the difficulty for which the proponent of this view said what he said, namely that his repentance is the acknowledgment of the prohibition of false accusation and seeking forgiveness for it. This is a point that requires clarifying the sense of "lying" by which God judged the accuser and reported that he is a liar in God's sight, even if his report corresponds to reality. So we say:

"Lying" (kadhib) is used in two senses. The first is a report that does not correspond to what it reports, and this is of two kinds: deliberate lying (kadhib 'amd) and mistaken lying (kadhib khata'). Deliberate lying is well known. Mistaken lying is like the statement of Abu al-Sanabil ibn Ba'kak in his legal opinion for a widow who had given birth, that she may not remarry until four months and ten days have passed for her. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Abu al-Sanabil has lied." From the same usage is his ﷺ saying, "Whoever said it has lied," said to one who said: "The deeds of 'Amir have come to nothing," since he had killed himself by mistake. Also from the same usage is the statement of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit: "Abu Muhammad has lied," when he said: "The witr (odd-numbered night prayer) is obligatory." All of this is mistaken lying, and its meaning is that the one who said it was mistaken.

The second kind of lying is a report that it is not permissible to make, even if it corresponds to what it reports, such as the report of the accuser who alone saw the act of adultery and reports it. He is a liar in God's judgment, even if his report corresponds to what it reports. For this reason God said: ﴿Then, since they did not bring witnesses, those are the liars in the sight of God﴾ [al-Nur: 13]. So God's judgment in such a case is that he be punished with the punishment of the slanderer and liar, even if his report corresponds to the facts. Accordingly, his repentance is not realized until he acknowledges that he is a liar in God's sight, as God reported about him. If he does not acknowledge that he is a liar, while God has declared him a liar, then what repentance does he have? Is this anything but sheer persistence and open defiance of God's judgment that He has passed upon him?

(Section)

God Almighty, glorified is He and exalted is His majesty, has rebuked them and reproached them through His Messenger for distortion, concealment, and hiding. He says: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you mix the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?﴾

He says: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear for the people in the Book, those are cursed by God and cursed by those who curse﴾.

He says: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and sell it for a small price, they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire. God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and they will have a painful punishment﴾.

He says: ﴿O People of the Book, Our Messenger has come to you, making clear to you much of what you used to hide of the Book and pardoning much. There has come to you from God a light and a clear Book, by which God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace, and brings them out of darknesses into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path﴾.

As for distortion (tahrif): God Almighty has informed us of it in many places. Likewise is twisting the tongue with the Book so that the listener thinks it is from the Book when it is not. These are five matters:

The first: mixing truth with falsehood (labs al-haqq bi'l-batil), which is blending them such that the truth cannot be distinguished from falsehood.

The second: concealing the truth (kitman al-haqq).

The third: hiding it (ikhfa'), which is close to concealing it.

The fourth: altering words from their places (tahrif al-kalim 'an mawadi'ihi), which is of two kinds: altering their wording and altering their meaning.

The fifth: twisting the tongue with it (layy al-lisan bihi), so that the revealed wording becomes confused with other words for the listener.

These matters they committed only for purposes that prompted them to do so.

When they opposed the Messenger, denied his prophethood, rejected him, and fought him, they were much closer to denying his description and attributes, concealing that, removing it from its places, and interpreting it in other than its proper sense. And so they did. But because the glad tidings (bisharat) were many and varied, they were overcome in concealing and disclosing them, so they resorted to distorting the interpretation and removing its meaning from what it can only refer to, and applying them to something non-existent that God has not created and that has no existence at all.

(Benefit)

The Lord, exalted is He, calls His servants in the Qur'an to know Him by two means:

The first is contemplation of His creations (mafʿūlāt), and the second is reflection upon His verses (āyāt) and pondering them. Those are His visible signs (āyātuhu al-mashhūda), and these are His audible, intelligible signs (āyātuhu al-masmūʿa al-maʿqūla).

The first type is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ships that sail through the sea with that which benefits people...﴾ up to its end, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, are signs for people of understanding.﴾

This is abundant in the Qur'an. The second is like His saying: ﴿Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ and His saying: ﴿Have they not pondered the word?﴾ and His saying: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses.﴾ This too is abundant.

As for creations, they indicate actions, and actions indicate attributes, for a creation points to the one who made its action, and that necessarily entails His existence, power, will and knowledge, since it is impossible for a voluntary act to proceed from one who is non-existent, or from an existent who has no power, no life, no knowledge and no will.

Then, the diverse specifications found in creations indicate the will of the Agent and that His act is not by mere nature, such that it would be one uniform thing never repeated. What is in them of benefits, wisdom and praiseworthy ends indicates His wisdom, exalted is He. What is in them of benefit, kindness and goodness indicates His mercy. What is in them of seizing, vengeance and punishment indicates His anger. What is in them of honour, nearness and care indicates His love. What is in them of humiliation, distancing and forsaking indicates His hatred and abhorrence. What is in them of a thing's beginning in utmost deficiency and weakness, then its being driven to its completion and end, indicates the occurrence of the return (maʿād). What is in them of the conditions of plants and animals, and the movement of waters, is evidence of the possibility of the return. What is in them of the manifest traces of mercy and blessing upon His creatures is evidence of the soundness of prophethood. What is in them of perfections, which if they were absent would render it deficient, is evidence that the Giver of those perfections is more deserving of them. Thus His creations are among the most indicative things of His attributes and of the truthfulness of what His messengers related about Him.

The created things bear witness, confirming the audible verses and directing attention to reasoning from the verses that are created. The Exalted said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ That is, that the Qur'an is true. He informed that He would surely show them from His visible signs what makes clear to them that His recited verses are true. Then He informed that the sufficiency of His testimony for the truth of His report is by what He established of proofs and demonstrations for the truthfulness of His Messenger. So His verses bear witness to his truthfulness, and He is the Witness who testifies to the truthfulness of His Messenger through His verses; He is the Witness and the one witnessed for, the Proof and the one proven. He is the Proof by Himself for Himself, as one of the knowers said: "How can I seek a proof for One who is the proof of everything? Whatever proof I seek for Him, I find Him more manifest than it." For this reason the messengers said to their peoples: ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ He is more known than every known thing and clearer than every proof. Things are in reality known through Him, though He is known through them in the sense of reasoning and inference from His acts and His judgments.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 1 of 3):

He informed that whoever loves something other than Allah as he loves Allah, the Exalted, is among those who take rivals (andad, sing. nidd) besides Allah. This is a rival in love, not in creation and lordship. No one among the people of the earth has affirmed this rival in lordship, unlike the rival in love. Most people of the earth have taken rivals besides Allah in love and in veneration.

Then He said: ﴿And those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165].

There are two interpretations of the verse:

The first: "And those who believe are stronger in love for Allah" than the possessors of rivals are for their rivals and their gods, which they love and venerate besides Allah.

The second: "And those who believe are stronger in love for Allah" than the love of the polytheists who associate rivals with Allah. The love of the believers is pure, while the love of the possessors of rivals has been diminished by a share given to their rivals. Pure love is stronger than shared love.

These two interpretations are based on the two interpretations of His saying, ﴿they love them as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], for it has two interpretations:

The first: they love them as they love Allah. Thus He affirms for them the love of Allah, but it is a love in which they associate rivals with Allah.

The second: the meaning is that they love their rivals as the believers love Allah. Then He explained that the love of the believers for Allah is stronger than the love of the possessors of rivals for their rivals.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) preferred the first interpretation and used to say: They were blamed only for setting up equals between Allah and their rivals in love, and not devoting it sincerely to Allah as the believers do.

This equalizing is what is mentioned in His saying, reporting about them, when they say in the Fire to their gods and rivals, while those gods are brought along with them into the punishment: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 97-98].

It is known that they did not equate them with the Lord of the worlds in creation and lordship. They only equated them with Him in love and veneration.

This is also the "equalizing" mentioned in His saying: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

That is, they set up others as equal to Him in worship, which is love and veneration. This is the more correct of the two interpretations.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in another place:

It is known that they did not equate those (gods) with Him, glorified is He, in creation, provision, causing death, giving life, sovereignty, or power. They only equated them with Him in love, in devotion (ta'alluh), and in submission and humility before them. This is the utmost ignorance and injustice. How can dust be equated with the Lord of lords? How can slaves be equated with the Owner of necks? How can the one who is by himself poor, weak, incapable, and needy, who has from himself nothing but non-existence, be equated with the one who is self-sufficient, who is by himself powerful, whose self-sufficiency, power, sovereignty, existence, beneficence, knowledge, mercy, and absolute perfect completeness are necessary attributes of His essence?

What injustice is more hideous than this? And what judgment is more oppressive than it? He has made equal to His creation the One who has no equal, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

So the polytheist equated the One who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light with one who does not possess for himself or for others an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth. Oh, what an equalizing that contains the greatest and most hideous injustice!

(A subtle point)

It is related that al-Fudayl entered upon his daughter during her illness, and she said to him: "O father, do you love me?"

He said: "Yes."

She said: "There is no god but Allah. By Allah, I did not think this of you, and I did not think you loved anyone along with Allah. Rather, single out Allah with love, and let there be for me from you mercy."

That is, let your love for me be the love of mercy, which Allah placed in the heart of a father for his child, not a love alongside Allah.

So there is a right of love that belongs to Allah alone, and no other shares it with Him. The most unjust injustice is placing that love in other than its proper place, and associating others with Allah in it.

Let the discerning person reflect upon this chapter, for it is among the most beneficial chapters of this book, if Allah wills.

[Section: The difference between love for Allah and love alongside Allah]

This is one of the most important distinctions, and everyone needs, indeed is compelled, to distinguish between this and that. Love for Allah is among the perfections of faith, while love alongside Allah is the very essence of shirk.

The difference between them is that the lover in love for Allah follows the love of Allah. When His love takes firm hold of the servant's heart, that love necessitates that he loves what Allah loves. When he loves what his Lord and Protector loves, that love is for Him and in Him, just as he loves His messengers, prophets, angels, and friends, because He, the Exalted, loves them; and he hates those who hate them, because He, the Exalted, hates them. The sign of this love and hatred for Allah's sake is that his hatred does not turn into hatred for Allah's sake, and his love for Allah's beloved does not turn into hatred when he receives from him what he dislikes and what pains him, whether by mistake or intentionally, while the person is obedient to Allah in it, or interpreting, or striving in judgment, or rebellious and deviating. The whole religion revolves around four principles: love and hatred, and what follows from them, action and abstention. Whoever's love, hatred, action, and abstention are all for Allah has perfected faith, such that when he loves, he loves Allah; when he hates, he hates for Allah; when he acts, he acts for Allah; and when he abstains, he abstains for Allah. Whatever is lacking from these four categories is a deficiency in his faith and religion, however he may reckon it.

This is in contrast to love alongside Allah, which is of two kinds. One kind undermines the foundation of monotheism (tawhid) and is shirk. The other kind undermines the completeness of sincerity (ikhlas) and love for Allah, but does not expel one from Islam.

The first is like the love of the polytheists for their idols and rivals, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah﴾.

These polytheists love their idols, images, and gods alongside Allah as they love Allah. This is a love of devotion and servitude, accompanied by fear, hope, worship, and supplication. This love is the pure shirk that Allah does not forgive, and faith is not complete except by opposing these rivals, having intense hatred for them and for their adherents, opposing them, fighting them. For this purpose Allah sent all His messengers, revealed all His books, created the Fire for the people of this shirkī love, and created Paradise for those who fight its people and oppose them for His sake and seeking His pleasure. Whoever worships anything from the time it is presented to him until he is laid in his grave has taken a god and a protector besides Allah and has associated others with Him, whatever that object of worship may be; and he will surely disavow it at the time he needs it most.

The second kind is love for what Allah has made attractive to souls: women, children, gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilled land. A person loves these with the love of desire, like the love of the hungry for food and the thirsty for water. This love is of three kinds. If he loves them as a means of reaching Allah and seeks help through them in pleasing Him, he is rewarded for it and it is of the category of love for Allah, as a means of reaching Him. He enjoys them, and this was the state of the most perfect of creation, to whom women and perfume were made beloved from the world. His love for them was an aid to him in loving Allah, conveying His message, and carrying out His command. If he loves them because they suit his nature, desire, and will, and he does not prefer them over what Allah loves and is pleased with, but obtains them according to natural inclination, they fall within the category of permissible things, and he is not punished for that; yet it diminishes the completeness of his love for Allah and of love in Him. And if they are his aim, his purpose, and his striving to attain and possess them, and he prefers them over what Allah loves and is pleased with, he is one who wrongs himself, following his desire.

The first is the love of the foremost (al-sabiqun).
The second is the love of the moderate (al-muqtasidun).
The third is the love of the wrongdoers (al-zalimun).

Reflect upon this subject and what it contains of unity and distinction, for it is the battleground of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah) and the soul at peace (al-nafs al-mutma'innah). Whoever is guided is guided by Allah.

[Section: On lovers leaving the lesser of two beloveds out of desire for the higher of them]

This is a chapter that only noble, dignified, proud souls enter, which are not content with the base and do not sell the higher for the lower, like the sale of the helpless one who is deceived. The captivating beauty of a deceptive adornment does not possess them, even though it is accompanied by various kinds of ugliness. As one of the Bedouins said when he looked at a veiled woman:

"If Allah blesses a garment,
then may Allah not bless the veil."

"It shows you the eyes of the wild oryx, lowered,
and uncovers a sight more hideous."

Another said:

"Let not the veil you see deceive you,
for beneath the veil lies a grievous disease."

The proud soul is not content with the base, and Allah, glorified is He, has condemned peoples who exchanged food for a lesser food, and He rebuked them for it. He said: ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and that is evidence of the baseness of the soul and its lack of worth.

Al-Asma'i said: A Bedouin man was alone with a woman and intended a sinful act. When he had her in his power, he drew back, and then began saying:

"A man who sells a Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth
for the narrow space between your thighs
is indeed one who has little insight in measurement."

Abu Asma' said: A man entered a thicket and said: "If I were alone here with a sin, who would see me?" Then he heard a voice that filled what lies between the two lava plains of the thicket: ﴿Does He not know who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk: 14].

Imam Ahmad said: Haddathana Haytham, that is Ibn Kharijah, haddathana Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Adi al-Bahrani, from Yazid ibn Maysarah, who said: Indeed Allah, the Exalted, says: "O young man who abandons his desire for Me and spends his youth for My sake, you are with Me like some of My angels."

Ibrahim ibn al-Junayd mentioned that a man solicited a woman for herself. She said to him: "You have heard the Qur'an and the hadith, so you are the most knowledgeable." He said: "Then close the doors." She closed them. When he approached her, she said: "There is one door I have not closed." He said: "Which door?" She said: "The door between you and Allah." So he did not approach her.

He also mentioned, from a Bedouin, who said: "I went out on one of the dark nights, and I came upon a girl who looked like a signpost. I wanted her for herself. She said: 'Woe to you! Did you have no restraining intellect when you had no prohibiting religion?' I said: 'By Allah, no one sees us except the stars.' She said: 'Then where is their Maker?'"

(Section)

Wilayah (loving allegiance) has love as its root. There is no allegiance except with love, just as enmity has hatred as its root. Allah is the Protector (wali) of those who believe, and they are His friends. They show allegiance to Him through their love for Him, and He shows allegiance to them through His love for them. Thus Allah shows allegiance to His believing servant in proportion to His love for him.

For this reason He, glorified is He, denounced those who take protectors besides Him, in contrast to those who show allegiance to His protectors, for they do not take them besides Him; rather, their allegiance to them is part of the completeness of their allegiance to Him.

He has denounced those who equated Him with others in love, and He informed that whoever does so has taken rivals besides Him, loving them as he loves Allah. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah, but those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165].

He also reported about those who equated Him with rivals in love, that they will say in the Fire to those they worshipped: ﴿By Allah, we were indeed in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 97-98].

With this monotheism in love, Allah, glorified is He, sent all His messengers, revealed all His books, and the call of all the messengers from the first to the last was unanimous upon it. For its sake the heavens, the earth, Paradise, and the Fire were created: He made Paradise for its people, and the Fire for those who associate others with Him in it.

The Prophet (ﷺ) swore that: "No servant truly believes until he loves Me more than his child, his parent, and all people." So how about love for the Lord, majestic is His majesty? He said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him): "No, until I am dearer to you than yourself." That is, you do not believe until your love reaches this extent.

If the Prophet (ﷺ) has a greater claim upon us than our own selves in love and its requirements, is not the Lord, majestic is His majesty, and sanctified are His names, more worthy of our love and worship than our own selves? Everything that comes from Him to His believing servant calls to loving Him, of what the servant loves and dislikes: His giving and withholding, His well-being and His trial, His restriction and expansion, His justice and His grace, His causing death and giving life, His gentleness and His goodness, His mercy and His kindness, His concealing and His pardoning, His forbearance and His patience with His servant, His answering of his supplication, His removal of his distress, His relief of his anguish, and His relief of his sorrow, without any need on His part for him, but rather with His complete independence from him in every respect. All of this calls hearts to devotion to Him and to love for Him. Moreover, His enabling His servant to disobey Him and His helping him in it, and His concealing it until he has fulfilled his need from it, and His protecting and guarding him, and His fulfilling his need from disobedience to Him while He helps him and he seeks help through His blessings, are among the strongest incentives to love for Him. If a created being did even the least of these things for another created being, the other's heart would not be able to withhold love for him. So how would the servant not love with all his heart and limbs the One who does good to him continually, with every breath, despite his wrongdoing? His good comes down to him, and his evil rises up to Him. He makes Himself beloved to him through His blessings while He is free of need for him, and the servant makes himself hateful to Him through sins while he is in need of Him. Neither His goodness, kindness, and favors to him prevent him from disobeying Him, nor does the servant's disobedience and baseness cut off his Lord's goodness to him.

The basest baseness, then, is that hearts turn away from loving One of such a description, and attach themselves to the love of others.

Moreover, every created being you love, or who loves you, only wants you for himself and for his own purpose from you. But Allah, glorified and exalted is He, wants you for your own sake, as in the divine report: "My servant, everyone wants you for himself, but I want you for your own sake."

How then is the servant not ashamed that his Lord should be for him in this station, while he turns away from Him, occupied with love for another, his heart completely absorbed by love for someone other than Him?

And also, whoever deals with you among the creatures, if he does not profit from you, will not deal with you, and he must have some kind of profit. The Lord, exalted is He, deals with you only so that you may gain from Him the greatest and highest profit. A dirham is repaid tenfold, up to seven hundred times, and up to many multiples, while a sin is counted as one, and it is the thing most swiftly erased.

And also, He, glory be to Him, created you for Himself, and created everything for you, in this world and the Hereafter. So who has a better claim than Him to having one's utmost capacity exhausted in His love and one's effort expended in seeking His good pleasure?

And also, your requests, indeed the requests of all creatures together, are with Him. He is the most generous of the generous and the most noble of the noble. He gives His servant before he asks, beyond what he hopes for. He appreciates the little deed and makes it grow, and He forgives the great number of slips and erases them. ﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him; every day He is in some affair﴾. Hearing one voice does not distract Him from another, the multitude of requests does not confuse Him, and He is not wearied by the insistence of the insistent. Rather, He loves those who persist in supplication, He loves to be asked, and He becomes angry when He is not asked. He is shy before His servant where the servant is not shy before Him, He covers him where he does not cover himself, and He has mercy on him where he does not have mercy on himself. He called him by His blessings, His kindness and His favors to His honor and His good pleasure, but he refused. So He sent His messengers in pursuit of him, and sent with them His covenant to him. Then He Himself, glory be to Him, descended to him, and said: "Whoever asks Me, I will give him; whoever seeks My forgiveness, I will forgive him?" As it has been said:

"I call you, but you refuse union;
I send My messenger in pursuit;
I descend to you Myself;
I meet you in sleep."

How could hearts not love the One who brings good deeds only He brings, and who removes bad deeds only He removes, who answers supplications, pardons stumbles, forgives sins, conceals faults, relieves distresses, responds to cries for help, and grants wishes, other than Him?

So He is the most worthy of being remembered, the most worthy of being thanked, the most worthy of being worshipped, and the most worthy of being praised. He is the most helpful of those sought, the most compassionate of those who rule, the most generous of those asked, the most expansive of those who give, the most merciful of those asked for mercy, the most honorable of those sought, the mightiest of those resorted to, and the most sufficient of those relied upon. He is more merciful to His servant than a mother is to her child, and more joyful at the repentance of the penitent than one who has lost his riding beast, which carries his food and drink, in a deadly desert, who had despaired of life and then found it again.

He is the King, with no partner. He is the One, with no equal. Everything perishes except His Face. He is obeyed only by His permission, and disobeyed only with His knowledge. He is obeyed, so He is thanked; and by His success and His blessing He is obeyed. He is disobeyed, so He forgives and pardons, though His right is neglected. He is the nearest witness, the most glorious guardian, the most faithful to covenant, and the most just upholder of justice. He comes between souls, takes hold of foreheads, records deeds, and determines the terms of life. Hearts are open to Him, the secret is manifest to Him, the unseen is uncovered to Him, and every person is in need of Him. Faces are humbled before the light of His Face, and hearts are incapable of grasping His essence. Natural dispositions and all the proofs point to the impossibility of His like and His equal. The darknesses are illuminated by the light of His Face; the earth and the heavens are lit by Him; all created beings are set right through Him. He does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers justice and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His Face would burn up whatever His sight reaches of His creation:

"The one who gives His love in full does not exchange it for another,
even if he were to possess all of existence entire."

(Benefit)
His love, exalted is He, indeed that He be more beloved to the servant than everything else absolutely, is among the greatest obligations of the religion, its greatest foundation, and its most sublime principle. Whoever loves alongside Him a creature in the same way that he loves Him, then he is among the shirk that is not forgiven for its owner, and no deed is accepted with it.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides Allah, equals, whom they love as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾.

And if the servant is not among the people of faith until Allah and His Messenger are more beloved to him than his own self, his family, his children, his parents and all people, and his love follows the love of Allah, then what is the thought about the love of Him, glory be to Him?

And He, glory be to Him, did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Him, a worship that encompasses the perfection of His exaltation and humility before Him. For this reason He sent His messengers, sent down His books, and legislated His laws.

Upon this were reward and punishment established, Paradise and Hell founded, and people divided into the wretched and the happy. And just as He, glory be to Him, "there is nothing like unto Him," so His love and His veneration are not like the love, veneration and fear of any other.

The creature, whenever you fear him, you become estranged from him and flee from him. Allah, glory be to Him, whenever you fear Him, you find intimacy with Him and flee to Him. The creature is feared for his injustice and his aggression, whereas the Lord, glory be to Him, is feared only for His justice and His equity.

And likewise with love. The love of a creature, if it is not for Allah, is a torment for the lover and a burden upon him. What he suffers from it of pain is greater than the pleasure he obtains from it, and the further it is from Allah, the greater its pain and torment.

Besides this, in the love of a creature there is turning away from you, mistreatment of you, failure to fulfill its promise to you, either because of the competition of others who love him, or because of his dislike and enmity toward you, or because of his preoccupation with his own interests and what he loves more than you, or because of other calamities.

As for the love of the Lord, glory be to Him, its nature is other than this, for there is nothing more beloved to hearts than their Creator and Originator. He is their God and their object of worship, their Protector and their Master, their Lord and their Manager, their Provider, their Giver of death and life. So the love of Him is the bliss of souls, the life of spirits, the joy of selves, the sustenance of hearts, the light of minds, the coolness of eyes, and the cultivation of the inner self. There is nothing sweeter, more delightful, more pleasant, more joyful or more blissful to sound hearts, good spirits and pure minds than His love, intimacy with Him, longing for His meeting, and the sweetness that the believer finds in his heart from this, which is above every sweetness. The bliss that he attains from it is more complete than every bliss, and the pleasure that reaches him is higher than every pleasure. As one who had experienced it described his state, saying: "There are moments when a passing thought comes to the heart, in which I say: If the people of Paradise are in such a state, then they are indeed in a pleasant life."

Another said: "There are moments when the heart is so stirred that it trembles with joy at its intimacy with Allah and its love for Him."
