Another said: "The poor people of heedlessness left this world without tasting the best of what is in it."

Another said: "If the kings and the sons of kings knew what we are in, they would fight us over it with swords."

The finding and tasting of these matters is in proportion to the strength and weakness of love, and in proportion to the perception of the beauty of the Beloved and nearness to Him. Whenever love is more perfect, perception of the Beloved more complete, and nearness to Him more abundant, the sweetness, pleasure, joy and bliss are stronger.

Whoever knows Allah, glory be to Him, and His names and attributes more, desires Him more, loves Him more, and draws nearer to Him, finds in his heart from this sweetness what cannot be expressed, and it is known only by taste and ecstatic finding. When the heart tastes this, it cannot prefer anything else in love over it, nor any of its kin. The more love for Him grows, the more servitude, humility, submission and tenderness toward Him grow, and freedom from the bondage of anything else.

The heart does not prosper, nor is it set right, nor does it enjoy bliss, nor rejoice, nor take pleasure, nor find rest, nor become still, except through the worship of its Lord, love of Him, and turning to Him in repentance. Even if it obtained everything in creation that it takes pleasure in, it would not be at peace with them nor find rest in them; rather they would only increase its poverty and restlessness, until it attains what it was created for and prepared for: that Allah alone be the ultimate goal of its desire and the final end of its seeking. For in it there is an intrinsic need for its Lord and its God, insofar as He is its object of worship, its beloved, its God and its sought one, just as in it there is an intrinsic need for Him insofar as He is its Lord, its Creator, its Provider and its Manager. Whenever the love of Allah takes firm root in the heart and grows strong within it, it expels from it the worship of anything other than Him and its servitude to it.

"So it becomes free, in honor and protection,
its lights and its radiance upon its face."

There is no believer who does not have in his heart love for Allah, the Exalted, and tranquility in remembering Him, delight in knowing Him, joy and pleasure in His remembrance, longing for His meeting, and intimacy with His nearness, even if he does not perceive it, because his heart is occupied with other things and turned toward what preoccupies it. For the existence of a thing is other than sensing and being aware of it.

The strength and weakness of this, its increase and decrease, is in accordance with the strength, weakness, increase and decrease of faith.

And whenever Allah alone is not the ultimate goal of the servant's desire and the final end of his aim, and He is not the Beloved desired by him in essence and in primary intention, while everything else he loves, desires and seeks only as a consequence of Him, then he has not fulfilled the testimony that there is no god but Allah. There is in him deficiency, defect and shirk to the extent of that, and he has, as a consequence of that, pain, regret and punishment in proportion to what he has missed of it.

And even if he strives for this goal by every means, and knocks on every door, but is not seeking help from Allah, not relying upon Him, not in need of Him for its attainment, and not certain that it is attained only by His success, His will and His help, and there is no path to it for him other than that in any way, then his goal will not be attained. For what Allah wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. Nothing brings one to Him except Him, nothing guides to Him except Him, He is not worshipped except by His help, and He is not obeyed except by His will.

﴿For whoever among you wills to go straight. But you do not will except that Allah wills, the Lord of the worlds﴾ [At-Takwir: 28-29].

(Section)
The whole of the revealed books of Allah, from first to last, revolve around commanding that love and its requirements, and forbidding the love of what opposes it and clings to it, and striking parables and comparisons for the people of the two loves, and mentioning their stories, their outcomes, their stations, their rewards and their punishments. No one finds the sweetness of faith, indeed no one tastes its flavor, except one in whom Allah and His Messenger are more beloved than anything else, as in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Three qualities whoever has them finds the sweetness of faith" — and in another wording: "No one tastes the flavor of faith except one who has three qualities: that Allah and His Messenger be more beloved to him than anything else; that he love a person only for the sake of Allah; and that he hate to return to disbelief after Allah has rescued him from it, just as he hates to be thrown into the Fire."

And in the two Sahihs also, from him, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until I am more beloved to him than his father, his child and all people."

For this reason, the call of the messengers, from the first of them to the last, agreed upon the worship of Allah alone, without partner.

The root of worship, its completion and its perfection is love, and the singling out of the Lord, glory be to Him, with it, so that the servant does not associate anyone else with Him in it.

The word that contains these two foundations is the word by which no one enters Islam except by it, and by bringing which alone his blood and property are protected, and by whose realization in the heart and the tongue alone one is saved from the punishment of Allah, and whose mention is the best of remembrance, as in the Sahih of Ibn Hibban from him (ﷺ): "The best of remembrance is: There is no god but Allah."

The verse that contains it, and that shows its excellence, is the chief of the verses of the Qur'an, and the surah specifically devoted to its realization equals a third of the Qur'an. By it Allah, glory be to Him, sent all His messengers, sent down all His books, and legislated all His laws, in fulfillment of its right and its perfection. It is the word by which the servant draws near to his Lord and enters into His protection. It is the refuge of His friends and His enemies alike, for when His enemies are touched by harm on land and sea, they turn to His monotheism, disown their shirk, and call upon Him, making their religion sincerely for Him. As for His friends, it is their refuge in the hardships of this world and the Hereafter.

For this reason, the supplications of the distressed were: "There is no god but Allah, the Mighty, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the Noble Throne."

And the supplication of Dhu al-Nun, by which no distressed person called without Allah relieving his distress: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been of the wrongdoers."

Thawban, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When something alarmed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would say: 'Allah is my Lord; I do not associate anything with Him.'" And in another wording he said: "He is Allah; there is no partner for Him."

Asma bint Umais, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught me words to say at times of distress: Allah, Allah is my Lord; I do not associate anything with Him."

And in the Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from his father, from his grandfather, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The supplication of Yunus when he called out in the belly of the whale: 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.' No Muslim has ever supplicated with it for anything except that it was answered for him."

And in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, marfu': "The supplication of the distressed: O Allah, Your mercy I hope for, so do not leave me to myself for the blink of an eye, set right all my affairs for me; there is no god but You."

So tawhid (monotheism) is the refuge of seekers, the place of flight for fugitives, the salvation of the distressed, and the aid of those in dire need. Its reality is singling out the Lord, glory be to Him, with love, veneration, exaltation, humility and submission.

(Section)
When it is known that every movement has its root in love and will, there must be a beloved that is desired for its own sake, not sought and loved for the sake of something else. For if every beloved were loved for the sake of something else, it would necessitate either an infinite regress or an endless chain of causes and ends, and that is invalid by the consensus of the rational. A thing may be loved from one aspect and not from another, but there is nothing loved for its essence from every aspect except Allah, mighty and majestic, alone, to whom alone divinity is fitting. For if there were in the heavens and the earth gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted. The divinity by which the messengers called their peoples to the monotheism of the Lord is worship and devotion.

Among its requirements is the monotheism of Lordship, which the polytheists acknowledged, and Allah argued against them with it, for acknowledging it necessarily entails acknowledging the monotheism of divinity.

(Another benefit)
Beneficial love is of three kinds: love of Allah; love for the sake of Allah; and love of what helps one to obey Allah, the Exalted, and to avoid His disobedience.

Harmful love is of three kinds: love alongside Allah; love of what Allah hates; and love of what severs one's love from the love of Allah, the Exalted, or diminishes it.

These are six kinds, upon which the loves of creation revolve.

The love of Allah, mighty and majestic, is the root of all praiseworthy loves, the root of faith and tawhid, and the two other kinds follow from it.

And love alongside Allah is the root of shirk and of all blameworthy loves, and the two other kinds follow from it.

Love of forbidden images and infatuation with them is among the things that bring about shirk. The closer a servant is to shirk and the further from sincerity (ikhlas), the stronger his love for images of beauty becomes; and the more sincere and the stronger his tawhid, the further he is from infatuation with images. For this reason, the wife of al-ʿAzīz was afflicted with the infatuation that befell her, because of her shirk. Yusuf al-Siddiq (peace be upon him) was saved from it by his sincerity. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our chosen, sincere servants.﴾ [Yusuf: 24].

So "evil" (al-sūʾ) is infatuation, and "immorality" (al-fahshāʾ) is adultery. The sincere one has purified his love for Allah, so Allah purifies him from the trial of infatuation with images. The polytheist, however, has a heart attached to other than Allah; he has not purified his tawhid or his love for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

[Section: The Categories of the Beloved]

The beloved is of two kinds: that which is loved for its own sake (maḥbūb li-nafsihi), and that which is loved for the sake of something else (maḥbūb li-ghayrihi).

That which is loved for the sake of something else must necessarily end at that which is loved for its own sake, to avoid an impossible infinite regress (tasalsul). Everything other than the true Beloved is loved for the sake of something else. Nothing is loved for its own essence except Allah alone. Everything else that is loved is loved only as a consequence of the love of the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, such as the love of His angels, His prophets, and His friends (awliyāʾ), for their love follows from His love, subhanahu, and is among its necessary consequences.

Indeed, the love of the Beloved necessitates the love of what He loves. This is a matter that must be given careful attention, for it is the point at which one distinguishes between beneficial love for other than Allah and that which does not benefit and may even harm.

Know that none is loved for his own essence except one whose perfection is among the necessary attributes of his essence, and whose divinity (ilāhiyya), lordship (rubūbiyya), and self-sufficiency (ghinā) are among the necessary attributes of his essence. As for all else, it is only hated and disliked because it opposes what He loves and contradicts it. The degree of its hatred and dislike corresponds to the strength or weakness of this opposition. Whatever is more opposed to what He loves is more hated, whether it is a substance, an attribute, an action, a will, or other than these. This is a just balance by which the Lord's approval and disapproval, His allegiance and enmity, are weighed. So when we see a person loving what the Lord, the Exalted, hates and hating what He loves, we know that in him there is enmity toward Him to that degree. And when we see a person loving what the Lord loves and hating what He hates, and whenever a thing is more beloved to the Lord, it is more beloved to him and preferred by him, and whenever a thing is more hateful to the Lord, it is more hateful to him and more distant from him, we know that in him there is allegiance to the Lord to that degree.

So hold fast to this principle in yourself and in others, for loyalty (al-wilāya) is an expression of agreeing with the Praiseworthy Friend in what He loves and what He abhors, and it is not by abundance of fasting, nor prayer, nor asceticism, nor spiritual discipline.

The beloved for the sake of something else is also of two kinds:

The first: that which the lover delights in attaining and possessing.

The second: that which causes him pain, yet he endures it because it leads to the beloved, like drinking a bitter medicine. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216].

So He, subhanahu, informed that fighting is hateful to them even though it is good for them, because it leads to the greatest and most beneficial beloved. The souls, under ease, comfort, and luxury, consider that an evil for them, because it leads to the loss of the beloved. The intelligent person does not look at the immediate pleasure of a beloved and prefer it, nor at the immediate pain of a hateful thing and turn away from it, for that may be an evil for him; rather, it may bring upon him extreme pain and deprive him of the greatest pleasure. Indeed, the wise of this world bear hardships that are hateful for the sake of the pleasure that follows them, even if it is cut off.

Thus there are four matters: a hateful thing that leads to a hateful thing; a hateful thing that leads to a beloved thing; a beloved thing that leads to a beloved thing; and a beloved thing that leads to a hateful thing. The beloved that leads to the beloved has the motive to act gathered in it from two angles, and the hateful that leads to a hateful has the motive to abstain gathered in it from two angles.

The remaining two kinds are pulled between two motives, and they are the arena of trial and testing. The soul prefers whichever of the two is nearer to it, namely the immediate, while the intellect and faith prefer whichever is more beneficial and more enduring. The heart is between the two motives, inclining to this at one time and to that at another, and here is the place of trial, legally and by divine decree. The motive of intellect and faith calls out at every moment: "Hasten to success" (ḥayya ʿala al-falāḥ); "At dawn the people praise the night journey" (ʿinda al-ṣabāḥ yaḥmadu al-qawmu al-surā); and at death the servant praises his piety (al-tuqā). But if the darkness of the night of love grows intense and the authority of desire and will dominates, it says: "O soul, be patient, for it is only an hour, then it passes, and all of this goes away and vanishes."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 166:

The ties that were severed from them are the bonds that were with other than God and for other than God. They were severed from them when they were most in need of them. This is because when those aims dissolved and became void, their means dissolved and became void too. Means become void when their ends become void, and they vanish when those ends vanish. "Everything perishes except His Face" (﴿كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]), and every deed is void except that which is intended for His Face. Every effort directed toward other than Him is void and vanishing. This is as people observe in this world: the vanishing of the effort, work, toil and service that a servant performs for a ruler, a commander, a man of position, or a man of wealth. When the one for whom he worked is gone, that work ceases, that effort becomes void, and nothing remains in his hand but deprivation. For this reason God Most High says on the Day of Resurrection: "Is it not just of Me that I grant every man what he used to take as his protector in the world?"

So the worshippers of idols and images have their idols and images as their protectors, and they fall with them into the Fire. The worshippers of the sun and the moon have their gods; when the sun is folded up and the stars scatter, that worship vanishes, becomes void, and turns into regret for them: ﴿Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not come out of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]. For this reason the polytheist is the greatest loser in bargain and the most cheated on the Day of his return. He is referred to a bankrupt who is utterly bankrupt, indeed to nothing, whereas the monotheist's referral is to the wealthy, generous Creditor. How far apart are the two referrals!

God Most High says: ﴿And the ties were cut off from them﴾.

ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "Affection."

Mujāhid said: "Their association in the world."

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "That is, the kinship ties were cut off from them, and their dwellings were scattered among them in the Fire."

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "The deeds."

All of these are true. The means are the connections that existed between them in the world, and they were severed from them when they most needed them.

As for the means of the sincere monotheists devoted to God, they remain connected to them, and their connection endures as long as their object of worship and love endures.

For a means follows its end in lasting and in being severed.

Section: [The conflict of followers and leaders]

This is the ruling concerning the followers and the leaders who are polytheists in error. As for followers who oppose their leaders, deviating from their way, and who claim to follow them while not actually following their way, they are the ones mentioned in God's words: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and the ties between them are cut off. And those who followed will say, "If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not come out of the Fire﴾. Those leaders were upon guidance, while their followers claimed that they were on their way and method, yet they opposed them, travelling a path other than theirs, claiming that they loved them and that their love would benefit them despite their opposition. So on the Day of Resurrection they disown them, for they had taken them as allies besides God and assumed that this taking would benefit them.

This is the state of everyone who takes intimates and allies besides God and His Messenger, allying with them, opposing for their sake, being pleased for their sake and angered for their sake. All his deeds are void; he sees them on the Day of Resurrection as regrets upon him, despite their abundance and the severity of his exertion and toil in them, because he did not devote his loyalty and enmity, his love and hatred, and his support and preference, to God and His Messenger. So God, Mighty and Majestic, nullifies all that deed and severs those means. On the Day of Resurrection every connection, bond, affection and alliance that was for other than God Most High will be cut off, and there will remain only the means linking the servant to his Lord, which is his share of emigration to Him and to His Messenger, and the singling out of his worship for Him alone with its requirements of love, hatred, giving, withholding, allegiance, enmity, drawing near and distancing; and the singling out of following His Messenger and abandoning the words of others, abandoning what contradicts what he brought, turning away from it, not attending to it, and singling out his following of him in a pure manner free of any taint of turning to anyone else, let alone associating anyone with him, let alone preferring the word of another over his.

This is the means that does not sever its possessor, and this is the relation between the servant and his Lord: the relation of pure servanthood. It is his true bond, and every other attachment will pass away, and to it all things return:

"Shift your heart wherever you wish among desires; love is only for the first Beloved."

"How many dwellings on earth does a young man grow fond of, yet his longing is always for the first dwelling."

This is the relation that benefits the servant; nothing else benefits him in the three abodes: the abode of this world, the abode of the barzakh, and the abode of settlement. There is no stability, life, bliss or success for him except through this relation. It is the means connecting the servant with God. The one who said it well:

"When the bond of union between them is severed, the lovers have a bond that is never severed.
And when the shattering of the people's union occurs between them, the lovers have a union that is never shattered."

The point is that on the Day of Resurrection God, glory be to Him, severs all the means, bonds and connections that existed among creatures in the world. Only the means and connection between the servant and God remain, which is the means of pure servanthood. It has no existence or realization except by singling out the following of the Messengers, peace and blessings of God be upon them, for this servanthood came only through their tongues and is known only through them, and there is no path to it except by following them. God Most High says: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. These are the deeds they did in the world that were not according to the Sunnah of His Messengers and their way, and that were not for His Face; God makes them scattered dust. Their doer gains nothing from them at all. This is among the greatest regrets for the servant on the Day of Resurrection: that he sees all his striving lost, having gained nothing from it, when the doer most needs his deed. The people of beneficial striving are made happy by their striving.

This parable includes "the one who calls out" (nāʿiq), meaning one who makes a sound to a flock of sheep and other animals, and "the one called to" (manʿūq bihi), meaning the animals. It has been said that the nāʿiq is the worshipper, who is the caller to the idol, and the idol is the one called to. The situation of the disbelievers in their supplication is like that of someone who calls out to what cannot hear him. This is the view of a group of scholars, including ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd and others.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshāf, al-Zamakhsharī's commentary) and a group with him found this view problematic. They said: God's words ﴿except calling and crying out﴾ do not support it, because idols do not hear calling or crying out.

Three answers have been given to this objection:

First: the particle "illā" (except) is superfluous, and the meaning is "what hears nothing but calling and crying out." They said that al-Aṣmaʿī mentioned this in the line of the poet:

*"Gaunt she-camels that never cease except kneeling"*

meaning "that never cease kneeling." But this answer is unsound, because "illā" is not added to speech as a superfluous element.

Second: the comparison is made with the general act of calling, not with the specific qualities of the one called.

Third: the meaning is that the likeness of these people in calling upon their gods, which do not understand their calling, is like the likeness of one who calls out to his flock. He gains nothing from his calling, except that he is himself in calling and crying out. Likewise, the polytheist gains from his calling and worship nothing but toil.

It has also been said: the meaning is that the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of animals that understand nothing of what the shepherd says beyond the sound. Thus the shepherd is the caller of the disbelievers, and the disbelievers are the animals that are called.

Sībawayh said: the meaning is "and your likeness, O Muḥammad, and the likeness of those who disbelieve is like the likeness of the one who calls out and the one called to." According to his view, the meaning is: "and the likeness of those who disbelieve and their caller is like the likeness of the sheep and the one who calls to them."

You may take this as a compound comparison (al-tashbīh al-murakkab) or as a divided comparison (al-tashbīh al-mufarraq). If you take it as compound, it is a comparison of the disbelievers in their lack of understanding and their failure to benefit, with sheep to which the shepherd calls out, so they understand nothing from his speech except the bare sound, which is calling and crying out. If you take it as divided, then "those who disbelieve" stand in the position of the animals, the call of their caller to the path and guidance stands in the position of the one who calls out to them, their being called to guidance stands in the position of the calling-out, and their perception of mere calling and crying out is like the perception of animals of the mere sound of the one who calls. And God knows best.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not understand﴾. And He says about the disbelievers: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they will not return﴾.

So the disbeliever does not understand, but the hypocrite saw, then became blind; he knew, then pretended ignorance; he acknowledged, then denied; he believed, then disbelieved. Whoever is like this is greater in disbelief, more corrupt of heart, and more insolent toward God and His messengers, so he deserves the lowest level of the Fire.

There is also another meaning in this, which is that what drove them to hypocrisy was the seeking of honour and status between the two groups. They wanted to please the believers so that they would honour them, and to please the disbelievers so that they would honour them as well.

From here their trial came upon them, for they wanted the honour of both groups. They had no aim in faith, in Islam, or in obeying God and His messenger. Rather, their inclination, their partiality and their direction were towards the disbelievers. So they were repaid for that with the greatest humiliation, which is that their abode was placed at the lowest of the lowest, beneath the disbelievers. Hence what the hypocrites were described with, namely deceiving God and His messenger and the believers, mocking the people of faith, lying, playing with religion, and showing that they were of the believers while concealing in their hearts (what was contrary), made their disbelief grievous, so they deserved the lowest level of the Fire.

For this reason, when God, exalted is He, mentioned the categories of creation at the beginning of the surah (2:2–20), He divided them into: a believer outwardly and inwardly; a disbeliever outwardly and inwardly; and a believer outwardly but a disbeliever inwardly, who are the hypocrites. He mentioned three verses concerning the believers (2:3–5) and two verses concerning the disbelievers (2:6–7).

When He reached the mention of the hypocrites, He mentioned about them some dozen verses (2:8–20), in which He blamed them to the utmost degree, exposed their faults, their ugliness and their disgrace. He informed that they are the foolish, the corrupters on earth, the deceivers, the mockers, the losers in their exchanging guidance for error, and that they are deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not return. He also said that they have sickness in their hearts, and that God increases their sickness. He left out no blame or defect without blaming them for it. This indicates the intensity of His hatred for them, His detestation of them, and His enmity towards them, and that they are the most hated of His enemies to Him. Thus His overwhelming wisdom is manifest in singling out this class for the lowest level of the Fire.

We seek refuge in God from the likeness of their condition, and we ask Him for His well-being and His mercy. Whoever reflects on what God has described the hypocrites with in the Qur'an of blameworthy qualities will know that they are most deserving of the lowest level of the Fire. He described them as deceiving Him and His servants, and described their hearts as diseased, which is the disease of doubts and suspicions. He described them as corrupting on earth, mocking His religion and His servants, transgressing, exchanging guidance for error, being deaf, dumb, blind, bewildered, and lazy in His worship, committing fornication, remembering Him little, and wavering between the believers and the disbelievers, neither to these nor to those.

Ibn al-Qayyim's Commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 2, verse 172

If you ask: what do you make of His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided you and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him you worship﴾

and His saying: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, if you are believers in His verses﴾

and the Arabs say: "If you are my son, then obey me."

And in the hadith concerning greeting the dead: "And we, if Allah wills, will certainly join you" (narrated by Muslim).

And joining (them) is certain. And in the words of the one making a bequest: "If I die, then a third of my wealth is charity."

I say: As for His saying ﴿if it is Him you worship﴾, the purpose for which the use of (in, إنْ) here is appropriate is argument and binding proof. The meaning is: your worship of Allah necessarily entails your gratitude to Him; indeed, it is gratitude itself. So if you are committed to His worship and included among its adherents, then eat of His provision and give thanks for His blessings. This is often used in argumentation, as you say to a man: "If Allah is your Lord and Creator, then do not disobey Him; if the meeting with Allah is true, then prepare for it; if Paradise is true, then provide for the journey to it." This is better than the answer of those who said that (in, إنْ) here stands in the place of (idh, إذ, "since"). The same applies to His saying ﴿if you are believers in His verses﴾, and to their saying "if you are my son, then obey me," and similar examples.

As for His saying "And we, if Allah wills, will certainly join you," the conditional here is not for death in general, but for their joining the believers and their arrival at where they have arrived.

As for the words of the one making a bequest, "If I die, then a third of my wealth is charity": although death is certain, since its time is not known, and the span (of life) is long and the hope of living is extended, it is treated as something doubtful. This is the reality indicated by the conditions of the servants, for no sensible person is certain of death and content to remain in a state in which he never loves to die. As one of the early Muslims said: "I have never seen a certainty without doubt more resembling a doubt without certainty than death."

On this basis some scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) interpreted ﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be resurrected﴾: they emphasized the death with the lam, used the active participle which indicates permanence, and for the resurrection used the verb without emphasizing it.

(Benefit)

Whoever has been afflicted has only been afflicted through neglecting gratitude and neglecting neediness and supplication. No one attains success through Allah's will and help except by standing in gratitude and sincere neediness and supplication. The foundation of all this is patience, for it stands to faith in the position of the head to the body; when the head is cut off, the body cannot survive.

Among the examples of transgression (al-‘udwan) is exceeding what is permitted of carrion in a state of necessity (darurah), by going beyond what is allowed of it, such as eating to satiety, whereas it is only permitted to him to ward off the pangs of hunger (sadd al-ramaq), according to one of the two opinions in the school of Ahmad, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah.

Malik permitted him to eat to satiety and to take provision when he is in need of it. But if he has become independent of it, and eats it in order to protect his wealth and out of stinginess about buying a slaughtered animal or the like, then eating it is transgression. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring [it] nor exceeding [the limit], then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173]

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: he does not eat it without necessity, and does not exceed his satiety. It was also said: "neither desiring" means neither seeking it while he finds other than it; "nor exceeding" means not going beyond the limit set for him concerning it, so that he eats until he is satisfied, rather than only warding off hunger. Muqatil said: not regarding it as lawful (mustahill) for himself, nor taking provision from it.

It was also said: he does not transgress by going beyond the limit set for him concerning it, nor does he exceed by falling short in eating it until he perishes; for he would then have transgressed the limit of Allah by either exceeding it or falling short of it. This one is sinful and that one is sinful. Masruq said: whoever is compelled to eat carrion, blood, or the flesh of swine, and does not eat or drink until he dies, enters the Fire. This is the more correct of the two opinions regarding the verse. Ibn 'Abbas, his companions, and al-Shafi'i said: "neither desiring nor exceeding" means not rebelling against the ruler (al-sultan) and not exceeding while on a journey (safar), so that a journey of disobedience (safar ma'siyah) does not qualify, and on this basis they held that one who is disobedient by his journey is not granted the concession (la yatarakhkhas).

The first opinion is more correct, for ten reasons, and this is not the place to mention them, since the verse makes no reference to travel, either by negation or affirmation, nor to rebellion against the imam. It is not specific to that, nor was it revealed for that purpose. It is general with regard to both the resident and the traveller. The transgression (al-baghy) and aggression (al-'udwan) in it refer to the eating that is the object of the prohibition, not to some external matter unconnected to eating. Also, a parallel to this is His saying in another verse: ﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. So this is the transgressor and the aggressor, and "inclining toward sin" means tending toward the forbidden quantity of eating it. This is the condition without which it is not permitted to him. Also, it is permitted only out of necessity, so the permission is measured by its measure; and He informed them that exceeding it is transgression, aggression, and sin, so the permission granted by necessity does not make it lawful. And Allah knows best.

The "sin" (ithm) and "aggression" ('udwan) are the same as the "sin" (ithm) and "transgression" (baghy) mentioned in Surat al-A'raf, although baghy is most commonly used with respect to the rights of people and domination over them.

Accordingly, when baghy is joined with 'udwan, baghy is their oppression by means of what is forbidden in kind, such as theft, lying, slander, and initiating harm, while 'udwan is exceeding the right in exacting it to something greater than it. Thus baghy and 'udwan with regard to people are like ithm and 'udwan within the limits of Allah.

Here there are four matters: a right of Allah and a limit for it, and a right of His servants and a limit for it. So baghy, 'udwan, and zulm are crossing both limits to what lies beyond them, or falling short of them, so that one does not reach them.

Allah has gathered the qualities of righteousness (al-birr) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets...﴾.

So He, glorified be He, informed that righteousness is faith in Allah, in His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day. These are the five fundamental articles of faith (usul al-iman), without which faith has no foundation. [Righteousness also includes] the outward legal obligations (shara'i') of establishing prayer, paying zakah, and obligatory expenditures, and the inner deeds of the heart which are its realities, such as patience and fulfilling covenants. Thus these qualities encompass all divisions of religion: its realities and its legal observances, the deeds connected to the limbs and to the heart, and the five fundamental articles of faith. Then He, glorified be He, informed about this that these are precisely the qualities of taqwa (God-consciousness), saying:

﴿Those are the ones who are true, and those are the God-conscious (al-muttaqun).﴾

As for taqwa, its reality is acting in obedience to Allah out of faith and seeking reward (ihtisab), in both commands and prohibitions. So one does what Allah has commanded, out of faith in the command and belief in His promise, and abstains from what Allah has forbidden, out of faith in the prohibition and fear of His threat. As Talq ibn Habib said: "When strife occurs, extinguish it with taqwa." They said: "And what is taqwa?" He said: "That you act in obedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you abandon disobedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah."

This is the best thing that has been said in defining taqwa.

Every action has a starting point and an end. An act does not become obedience and a means of drawing near to Allah unless its source is faith, so that the motive behind it is pure faith, not habit, not desire, not seeking praise and status, or anything else. Rather, its starting point must be pure faith and its end the reward of Allah and seeking His pleasure, and this is ihtisab.

﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾

Within this address there is something that serves as an answer to an implied question: "Does not the destruction of this noble structure, and the inflicting of pain on this soul and its destruction, in the case of the killer, multiply the corruption of killing? So for what wisdom was this issued by One whose mercy encompasses all things, and whose wisdom dazzles the intellects?" The address contains the answer to this in His words: ﴿And in retaliation (qiṣāṣ) there is life for you﴾.

This is because when the killer imagines that he will be killed in retaliation for the one he killed, he refrains from killing and holds back, and prefers the love of his own life and soul. Thus there is life in it for him and for the one he intended to kill.

From another aspect: when a man from their clan or tribe was killed, they would kill in return anyone they found from the killer's clan, his kin and his tribe. In this there was corruption and destruction whose harm spread widely and whose burden grew heavy. So God Most High prescribed retaliation (qiṣāṣ), and that none be killed in return for the slain except his killer. In this there is life for his clan, his kin and his relatives. The life is not in retaliation insofar as it is a killing, but insofar as it is retaliation: the killer alone is taken for the slain, and not another. So retaliation contains life in both respects.

Reflect upon what lies beneath these noble words of majesty, conciseness, eloquence, clarity and great meaning.

The verse opens with His words "for you" (lakum), which indicates that the benefit of retaliation is specific to you and returns to you. Its prescription was therefore only a mercy upon you and a kindness to you, so its benefit and its wisdom are for you, except for the One whose harm and benefit cannot reach the servants.

Then He follows it with "in retaliation" (fī al-qiṣāṣ), as a declaration that the life that results is only in justice, which is that the killer is treated as he treated the slain.

Al-qiṣāṣ in the language means equivalence, and its essence goes back to following. From it is His words Most High: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him"﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ: 11), meaning follow his trace.

From it also is His words: ﴿So they both returned, retracing their footsteps﴾ (al-Kahf: 64), meaning they traced back the path and followed it.

From it also: "qaṣṣa al-ḥadīth" and "iqtiṣāṣuhu" (relating a narrative and recounting it), because one part of it follows another in mention. Thus the requital of the offender was called qiṣāṣ, because it follows his trace, so that it is done to him as he did. This is one of the things by which it is inferred that the offender should be treated as he did, so that he is killed in the same manner as he killed, in order to realize the meaning of qiṣāṣ.

(A benefit)

Were it not for retaliation, the world would be corrupted, and people would destroy one another, both by initiating and by carrying out. So in retaliation there is a repelling of the corruption of audacity towards blood, both through the crime and through the carrying out of punishment.

The Arabs in their pre-Islamic time used to say: "Killing is the most effective deterrent to killing."

By the shedding of blood, blood is protected. Filth is not washed away by filth; rather, the crime is a filth and retaliation is a purification. If there is no alternative to the death of the killer, and of him who deserves to be killed, then his death by the sword is more beneficial for him in this world and in the next. Death by it is the swiftest, easiest and least painful of deaths. So his death by it is a benefit for him, for the heirs of the slain, and for people in general. This is similar to the destruction of an animal by slaughtering it for the benefit of a human being, which is good, even though slaughtering it causes harm to the animal. The benefits arising from its slaughter are many times greater than the corruption of its destruction.

Then this corrupt question shows its corruption and falsity through the death which God has decreed upon His servants, and in which He made all of them equal. Were it not for it, life would not be pleasant, provisions would not suffice, dwellings, cities, markets and roads would become too cramped for them. In parting from the one who is hated there is as much pleasure and ease as there is in union with the beloved. Death is a deliverance for the living, death is a relief for each of the two from the other, and an exit from the abode of trial and testing, and a door to entering the abode of life.

[The secret of why punishments were not always made of the same kind as the sins]

If it is said: how do you claim that these punishments are attached to the intellects and in accordance with the benefits, when you know that after disbelief in God there is nothing more monstrous, and nothing more ugly, than the shedding of blood? So how do you deter from the shedding of blood by shedding it? Is the example of this anything but removing filth with filth? Moreover, if that were approved, it would be more fitting that the clothes of one who burns the clothes of another be burned, that the animal of one who slaughters the animal of another be slaughtered, that the house of one who ruins the house of another be ruined, and that one who is insulted be permitted to insult his insulter. What, in clear reason, is the difference between this and killing the one who killed another, or cutting off the limb of one who cut off a limb? If the shedding of the first blood is a corruption, and cutting off the limb likewise, then how is that corruption removed by the shedding of a second blood and the cutting off of a second limb? Is this anything but doubling the corruption and multiplying it? And if the first corruption were removed by this second corruption, there would be in that what there would be; for how can one corruption be removed by a corruption that is its counterpart in every respect? How, then, when the first cannot be removed at all? The proof of this is what we mentioned: the corruption of burning clothes, slaughtering livestock, ruining houses and cutting down trees is not removed by the like of it. Then how is it good that a thief be punished by cutting off the hand with which he committed the theft, but it is not good that the fornicator be punished by cutting off his private part with which he committed fornication, nor the slanderer by cutting off his tongue with which he committed slander, nor the forger against the ruler and the Muslims by cutting off his fingertips with which he committed forgery, nor the one who looks at what is not lawful for him by gouging out his eye with which he committed the forbidden? It is known that the matter of these punishments, in kind, measure and cause, is not a matter of analogy; rather it is pure will, and to God belongs the disposal of His creation. He does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

The answer, with God is the granting of success and support, is in two ways: a general one and a detailed one. As for the general: whoever legislated these punishments and arranged them according to their causes, in kind and measure, is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Wisest of the wise, the most Knowing of the knowers, the One who encompasses all things in knowledge, who knows what has been, what will be, and what would not be, and how it would be were it to be. His knowledge encompasses the aspects of benefit, subtle and grand, hidden and manifest, both what is possible for human beings to perceive and what is not. These specifications and measures are not outside the aspects of wisdom and praiseworthy ends, just as the specifications and measures found in His creation are likewise. This is in His creation, and that is in His command, and both originate from the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom, and His placing of everything in the place which nothing but it befits and which nothing but it requires. Just as He placed the power of sight and the light for the seeing in the eye, the power of hearing in the ear, the power of smell in the nose, the power of speech in the tongue and the lips, the power of grasping in the hand, the power of walking in the foot, and assigned to each animal and other creature what befits it and what is good for it to be given of its limbs, forms, attributes and measure. His perfection and firm ordering encompass everything His creation encompasses, as He said Most High: ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾ (an-Naml: 88). Since He, glory be to Him, perfected His creation to the utmost perfection and ordered it to the utmost ordering, then His command being in the utmost perfection and ordering is more fitting and more deserving. Whoever does not know this in detail should not, in summary, deny it, and his ignorance of God's wisdom in His creation and His command, and of their perfection, and of their issuing from pure knowledge and wisdom, does not justify his denying it in reality.

Glory be to God, how great is the injustice and ignorance of man! If he objected to any craftsman in a craft of which his knowledge and understanding fall short, and asked him about the causes, instruments, actions and measures specific to his craft, and how each of these was exactly as it is, neither greater nor smaller nor in any other form, he would mock him and ridicule him, and marvel at the feebleness of his mind and the scarcity of his knowledge.

This is what he has prepared by sharing that craft with him, and reaching what he reached in it, and exceeding it and correcting him in it. Yet the craftsman is not immune from weakness, deficiency, lack of comprehensiveness and ignorance; rather that is ever present with him. Still, he cannot but submit to him, acknowledge his wisdom, confess his own ignorance, and admit his inability to reach what he reached of that. So how is it that this does not suffice with the Wisest of the wise, the most Knowing of the knowers, and the One who perfected everything and made it firm, and placed it in accordance with wisdom and benefit? This aspect alone was sufficient to repel every doubt and answer every question. This is other than the path taken by those who deny judgment and causation. Yet, with all this, we will undertake a detailed answer, according to our capacity and what suits our deficient knowledge, our rigid understanding, our weak minds and our limited expressions. So we say, and with God is the granting of success:

[Deterring corrupters is approved by the intellects]

As for his saying: "How do you deter from the shedding of blood by shedding it, when that is like removing filth with filth?" It is a question of extreme feebleness and corruption. The first thing said to its asker is: do you see that deterring the corrupters and the criminals from their corruption and crimes, and restraining their aggression, is approved by the intellects and in accordance with the benefits of the servants, or do you not see it so? If he says, "I do not see it so," that spares us the burden of answering him, for he has confessed against himself to opposing all the peoples of the children of Adam, with their differing creeds, sects, religions and opinions. Were it not for the punishment of the criminals and corrupters, people would destroy one another, the order of the world would be corrupted, and the condition of beasts, cattle and wild animals would become better than the condition of the children of Adam. If he says, "Rather, the benefit is not complete except by that," it is said to him: it is known that the punishment of criminals and corrupters is not complete except by something painful that deters them, and makes the offender an example and a lesson for whoever wishes to do the same as he did. At this point, there must be a destruction of some part of him in proportion to his crime, in greatness and smallness, in fewness and abundance.

[Uniformity in punishments despite differing crimes is not befitting to wisdom]

It is known by the innate understanding of the intellects that uniformity in punishments despite the differing of crimes is not approved, but rather contrary to wisdom and benefit. For if one made them all equal in the lightest of punishments, the benefit of deterrence would not be achieved; and if one made them all equal in the most severe of them, it would be contrary to mercy and wisdom, since it is not befitting to kill for a glance and a kiss, or to cut off a hand for stealing a grain or a dinar.

Likewise, disparity among punishments despite the equality of crimes is ugly in natures and intellects, and both are rejected by the wisdom of the Lord Most High, His justice and His kindness to His creation. So He imposed punishment at times by the destruction of the soul, when the crime reaches in its enormity the extreme of ugliness, such as a crime against the soul, the religion, or a crime whose harm is general. The corruption in this punishment is particular, and the benefit achieved by it is many times greater than that corruption, as He Most High said: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous﴾ (al-Baqarah: 179). Were it not for retaliation, the world would be corrupted, and people would destroy one another, both by initiating and by carrying out. So in retaliation there is a repelling of the corruption of audacity towards blood, both through the crime and through the carrying out of punishment.

The Arabs in their pre-Islamic time used to say: "Killing is the most effective deterrent to killing."

By the shedding of blood, blood is protected. Filth is not washed away by filth; rather, the crime is a filth and retaliation is a purification. If there is no alternative to the death of the killer, and of him who deserves to be killed, then his death by the sword is more beneficial for him in this world and in the next. Death by it is the swiftest, easiest and least painful of deaths. So his death by it is a benefit for him, for the heirs of the slain, and for people in general. This is similar to the destruction of an animal by slaughtering it for the benefit of a human being, which is good, even though slaughtering it causes harm to the animal. The benefits arising from its slaughter are many times greater than the corruption of its destruction. Then this corrupt question shows its corruption and falsity through the death which God has decreed upon His servants, and in which He made all of them equal. Were it not for it, life would not be pleasant, provisions would not suffice, and dwellings, cities, markets and roads would become too cramped for them. In parting from the one who is hated there is as much pleasure and ease as there is in union with the beloved. Death is a deliverance for the living, death is a relief for each of the two from the other, and an exit from the abode of trial and testing and a door to entering the abode of life.

A poet said:

May God reward death on our behalf with good, for it is
kinder to us than every kind one and more tender.

It hastens the release of souls from harm,
and brings them near to the abode that is most noble.

How much, then, is the blessing that Allah, glory be to Him, bestows upon His servants, the living and the dead, in death, which cannot be counted! How much more so when it contains purification for the one who is killed, life for the human race, satisfaction for the wronged party, and justice between the killer and the killed. Glory be to Him, whose law is free from opposition to what He has legislated, such as the proposals of corrupt minds and the misguided, oppressive opinions.

As for his saying: "If that were approved by reason, it would be approved in burning his garment, ruining his house, and slaughtering his animal, responding to him with the like." [Responding to destruction with its like in all circumstances is the law of the oppressors.]

The answer to this is that the harm of those crimes is removed by making him compensate with the equivalent of what he destroyed, for the like fills the place of the like in every respect. Thus, responding in kind would become pure corruption, just as it is not permitted for him to kill the son or slave of the other in response to the other having killed his son or slave. This is the law of the oppressive transgressors, from which the law of the Most Wise of judges is free. Moreover, responding in kind when destroying property has some room for ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), and some scholars have adopted it, as has been previously indicated concerning the punishment of the unbelievers by destroying their property when they do that to us, or when it enrages them. This differs from killing his slave when the slave has killed another slave of his, or killing his horse, or hamstringing his horse, for that is oppression toward one who does not deserve it. However, the Sunnah (prophetic practice) required compensation with the like, not destruction of an equivalent, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) made one of his wives, who had broken the vessel of her fellow wife, replace it with a vessel in its place, and said: "A vessel for a vessel." There is no doubt that this causes less corruption and is more beneficial for both parties, because when the owner of the destroyed property takes its equivalent, he becomes as one from whom nothing was lost, and he benefits from what he took in exchange for his property. If we enabled him to destroy the other's property, it would be an increase in the squandering of wealth. What is intended by satisfaction and making the offender taste the pain of destruction is generally achieved by making him pay compensation, and we do not give attention to rare cases in which the offender is not harmed by paying compensation. There is no doubt that this is more fitting to reason, more effective in achieving good, and more in accord with wisdom. Furthermore, if retaliation in property were legislated as a deterrent to the offender, the side of the one who was wronged would remain unconsidered, rather he would remain in pain, aggrieved, and unrecompensated. The Shari'ah has come to both compensate this and deter that.

If it is said: then let the wronged party be given the choice between making the offender pay compensation or destroying an equivalent of what he destroyed, just as you gave him the choice in the case of an injury to his limb, and you gave the heirs of the slain the choice between the offender's destruction of an equivalent and taking the diyah (blood money).

[The wisdom of giving the wronged party the choice in some situations but not others]

It is said: there is no benefit in that for the offender, nor for the wronged party, nor for the rest of people; rather, it is merely an increase in corruption, with no benefit in it except mere satisfaction. Banishing and disciplining the offender suffices for satisfaction. The difference between property and blood in this matter is clear, for an offense against souls and limbs brings into the wronged party and his heirs more rage, fury, and enmity than an offense against property brings, and it brings upon them more disgrace, shame, endurance of humiliation, zealous honor, and burning desire to avenge, which property can never repair. So much so that their children and descendants are reproached for it. The heirs of the slain have an intention in retaliation and in making the offender and his heirs taste what he made the wronged party and his heirs taste, which is not available to one whose garment has been burned or whose horse has been hamstrung. The wronged party and his heirs are aggrieved, and if the offender and his heirs are not made aggrieved and made to swallow the same pain and rage that the first party swallowed, it would not be just.

The Arabs in their pre-Islamic time used to blame those who accepted the diyah and were content with it instead of obtaining vengeance and healing their rage. Such as the saying of one of their poets satirizing one who took camels as diyah:

"And that which you now milk is blood, except that its color is not reddish."

Jarir said, reproaching one who took the diyah and bought with it palm trees:

"Oh, inform the sons of Hujr ibn Wahb that dates are sweet in winter."

Another said:

"When what is in the skin-bag is poured out, know that it is the blood of the elder, so drink the blood of the elder or leave it."

Another said:

"Two friends whose natures differ: I want glory, while he wants fat.
I want the blood of the sons of Malik, while the opinion of al-Mu'alla is the whiteness of milk."

Although the Shari'ah has abolished this, and has brought what is better than it and more beneficial in both this life and the Hereafter, namely giving the heirs the choice between obtaining vengeance and satisfaction on the one hand, and taking the diyah on the other, the intention behind this custom was that the Arabs did not reproach one who took the equivalent of his property, nor did they consider that a weakness or incapacity at all. This is unlike one who took the price of his close relative's blood. Allah has not made the two matters equal in nature, nor in reason, nor in law. A person may tear his garment in anger, slaughter his livestock, or destroy his property, and in doing so he does not suffer the same hardship, anger, and contempt that befall one who kills himself, cuts off his nose, or gouges out his eye.

The comparison applies only to the essence of fasting (sawm, abstaining from food, drink and other things for the sake of God), not to its exact form, measure, or manner.

The fasting person is one whose limbs abstain from sins, whose tongue abstains from lying, obscenity and false speech, whose stomach abstains from food and drink, and whose private parts abstain from sexual misconduct (rafath).

If he speaks, he does not say anything that wounds his fast. If he acts, he does not do anything that spoils his fast. So all his speech is beneficial and righteous, and likewise his deeds. They are like the fragrance that someone sitting with a bearer of musk smells. In the same way, whoever sits with the fasting person benefits from his company and is safe in it from falsehood, lying, wickedness and injustice.

This is the prescribed fasting, not merely refraining from food and drink. In the authentic hadith: "Whoever does not give up false speech, acting upon it, and ignorance, God has no need for him to give up his food and drink." And in another hadith: "How many a fasting person gets from his fast nothing but hunger and thirst."

So fasting is the fasting of the limbs from sins and the fasting of the stomach from drink and food. Just as food and drink break and spoil the fast, sins cut off its reward and spoil its fruit, making the one who fasts like one who did not fast.

[Section on the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning fasting]

[The purpose of fasting and its benefits]

This is a section on the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning fasting. Since the purpose of fasting is to restrain the soul from desires, to wean it from what it is accustomed to, and to moderate its appetitive power, so that it becomes prepared to seek what brings it ultimate happiness and bliss, and to accept what purifies it and in which lies its eternal life. Hunger and thirst break the sharpness and fierce drive of the soul, and remind it of the state of hungry, needy people.

Through narrowing the food and drink channels, the paths of Satan through the servant are narrowed. The powers of the limbs are restrained from their unchecked course, by the natural law concerning what harms them in this life and the next. Fasting calms every limb and every power from its wildness, and bridles them with its bridle. It is the bridle of the God-fearing, the shield of warriors, and the training of the righteous and those brought near (to God). Among all acts, it belongs to the Lord of the worlds in a special way. The fasting person does nothing outwardly; he only leaves his desire, food and drink for the sake of his Worshipped One. It is abandoning what the soul loves and enjoys, preferring the love of God and seeking His pleasure. It is a secret between the servant and his Lord, which no one else knows. People may know him to have abstained from the outward breaking acts, but that he left his food, drink and desire for the sake of his Worshipped One is something no human being can know. That is the true reality of fasting.

Fasting has a remarkable effect on preserving the outward limbs and inner powers, and protecting them from mixing (with harmful things) that brings corrupt matter, which, when it overcomes them, corrupts them, and from expelling the bad matter that prevents them from health. Fasting preserves the health of the heart and the limbs, and returns to them what the hands of desires have seized from them. So it is one of the greatest aids to piety, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183].

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fasting is a shield."

He commanded whoever is overwhelmed by sexual desire and has no ability (to marry) to fast, and made it a protection (wija') against this desire.

The point is that since the benefits of fasting are witnessed by sound minds and upright natures, God prescribed it for His servants out of mercy towards them, kindness to them, and as a protection and shield for them.

The guidance of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning it was the most perfect guidance, the greatest achievement of its purpose, and the easiest on souls.

Since weaning souls from what they are accustomed to and from their desires is among the hardest and most difficult matters, its obligation was delayed until the middle of Islam after the Hijrah (migration), when souls had settled upon monotheism and prayer and had become accustomed to the commands of the Qur'an. So it was transferred to them gradually.

[Section: The wisdom in restricting the concessions (rukhas) to the traveler]

As for his statement: "He permitted the traveler who is at ease on his journey the concession of breaking the fast and shortening the prayer, but not the resident who is exhausted and in extreme hardship," there is no doubt that breaking the fast and shortening the prayer are specific to the traveler, and a resident does not break his fast except due to illness. This is from the perfection of the Lawgiver's wisdom. For travel in itself is a piece of punishment, and it is in itself hardship and exertion, and even if the traveler is among the most comfortable of people, he is still in hardship and exertion in proportion to his state. So it was from the mercy of Allah toward His servants and His kindness to them that He lightened for them half of the prayer and accepted from them only the half, and lightened for them the performance of the obligatory fast during travel and accepted from them its performance while at home, just as He legislated the like in the case of the sick person and the menstruating woman. Thus He did not deprive them of the benefit of the act of worship by dropping it entirely during travel, nor did He obligate them to it during travel in the same way as He obligates them while at home. As for residence, there is no reason to drop any part of the obligation during it or to postpone it, and the hardship and preoccupation that may arise in it are matters that cannot be controlled or confined. If every preoccupied person and every person burdened by hardship were permitted to take concessions, the obligation would be lost and utterly nullified; and if it were permitted for some but not others, it would be uncontrolled, for there is no attribute that determines what concession is permitted and what is not, unlike travel. Moreover, hardship has been attached to it a concession that suits it: if it is the hardship of illness and pain that harms the person, then breaking the fast and praying seated or on one's side are permitted with it, and this is analogous to the shortening of the number (of prayers). If it is the hardship of fatigue, then the interests of this world and the Hereafter are bound up with exertion, and there is no rest for one who has no exertion; rather, rest is in proportion to exertion. Thus the Sharia is harmonious in its rulings and its interests, by the praise and grace of Allah.

(Benefit)

If a person sees someone drowning and cannot rescue him except by breaking his fast, may he break it?

Abu al-Khattab answered: he may break it if he is certain of rescuing him from drowning and he cannot both fast and rescue him.

Ibn al-Zaghuni answered: if he is able to rescue him and it is his strong assumption that he can, then he is obligated to break the fast and rescue him. There is no difference between breaking it by water entering his throat during swimming, or if he finds in himself weakness in rescuing him due to hunger, so that he eats, because he breaks the fast for permissible travel, so breaking it for an obligatory duty is more fitting.

I say: The causes of breaking the fast are four: travel, illness, menstruation, and fear for the destruction of one whose life would be endangered by fasting, such as a nursing or pregnant woman if they fear for their children; and similar to it is the case of the one who rescues the drowning person.

Our shaykh Ibn Taymiyyah permitted breaking the fast in order to strengthen oneself for jihad, practiced it, and issued a ruling on it when the enemy besieged Damascus during Ramadan. Some jurists objected to him and said: "This is not a long journey."

The Shaykh said: "This is breaking the fast to gain strength for fighting the enemy, and it is more fitting than breaking the fast for a two-day journey, whether a permissible journey or a sinful one. When Muslims fight their enemy while fasting, they cannot inflict harm upon them, and perhaps fasting weakens them from fighting, so the enemy seizes the core of Islam.

Would any jurist doubt that breaking the fast here is more fitting than the traveler's breaking it?

And the Prophet ﷺ commanded them during the Conquest campaign to break the fast so that they might be strong against their enemy."

So he gave as the reason strength against the enemy, not travel. And Allah knows best.

I say: If breaking the fast is permitted for the nursing and pregnant woman for fear for their children, and for one who rescues a drowning person, then breaking it for fighters is more deserving of permissibility. And whoever considers this to be among the "unrestricted public interests" (al-maslahah al-mursalah) has erred; rather, this is a matter of analogy of the more fitting kind (qiyas al-awla), and of the indication and allusion of the text (dalalat al-nass wa imaauhu).

The Word of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. In this there are two or more benefits.

The first: if He had said "Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down," the wording would require that the sending down applied to the whole month, as already mentioned from the words of Sibawayh. This contradicts the meaning, because the sending down happened on one night of it, in one hour of that night. How, then, could it cover the entire month? Mentioning "the month," which is not a proper name, fits the meaning, just as you say "I travelled in such-and-such a month," and the travelling does not cover the whole month.

The second benefit: if he had said "Ramadan in which the noble Qur'an was sent down," the ruling of praise and glorification would be restricted to one specific month. As has already been established, this name and what is like it, when it is not accompanied by an indicator showing the continuation of years, has as its reference only the year you are in or the year mentioned before it. So mentioning "the month," which in reality is the crescent (al-hilal), is what is intended, as the poet said:

"And the month is like the paring of a fingernail."

He means the crescent. This ties the ruling, which is glorification, to the crescent and to the month named by this name, whenever it occurs, in whatever year it occurs. Ramadan, and what is like it, does not become a definite name in such a context, because it was not applied to a specific year. Do you not see that the verse is in Surat al-Baqarah, and it is among the last things revealed, while the Qur'an had been sent down years before that? If you said "Ramadan, Zayd performed the pilgrimage in it," meaning in a past Ramadan, you would be asked "which Ramadan?" and you would have to say "he performed the pilgrimage in Ramadan of the Ramadans," until you meant a specific year, as has already been explained.

A third benefit: mentioning the month, which is the explanation of "the appointed days" (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat), because days are explained by days and by the month or the like. They are not explained by the word Ramadan, because its wording is derived from a different root, and it is also a proper name. So it is not appropriate to explain the appointed days by it unless the month is mentioned, which has the same meaning, and then it is added to it.

As for his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever fasts Ramadan," there is also a benefit in omitting the word "month": the fast covers the whole month. If he had said "Whoever fasts or stands in prayer in the month of Ramadan," it would become an adverbial of place or time requiring the preposition "fi" (in), and the standing and the fasting would not cover the whole of it. So "Ramadan" in the hadith is an object (maf'ul) in the broad sense, like His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] during the night﴾, because if it were an adverbial, He would not need to say: ﴿except a little﴾.

If it is said: then the saying "whoever stands in prayer during Ramadan" should be restricted to the year in which it occurs, since you have stated that it is only a proper name when you mean it for your year or for a specific year?

It is said: his saying "whoever fasts Ramadan" is general, addressed to every individual and to the people of every year. So it becomes like your saying "whoever fasts Ramadan every year," as you say "if you come to me every day at dawn, I will give you." The indicator showing continuation stands in place of mentioning "every year." The difference between the two hadith and the verse has become clear to someone who reflects on these sections and contemplates them. Then this benefit, in your view, does not equal the whole world in its entirety, and you have not assessed it at its true worth. And Allah is the One sought for help to give its due thanks. This is the exact text of al-Suhayli's words.

(Benefit)

The meanings of the word (shahida)

In their language, (shahida) has several meanings. The first is presence (al-huduur), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾.

About this there are two views: one is "whoever is present in the town during the month," and the second is "whoever witnesses the month while in the town." These two are mutually implying. The second meaning is report (al-khabar), and from it: "Two trustworthy men testified before me, and the one most pleasing to me among them was Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade prayer after the afternoon prayer and after the dawn prayer." Narrated by Muslim, Ahmad, Abu Dawud and others. The third meaning is awareness of a thing (al-ittila' 'ala al-shay'), and from it: ﴿And Allah is over all things Witness﴾.

If every report is a testimony, then those who require the word "testimony" in it have no evidence from the Book, the Sunnah, consensus or sound analogy. From Ahmad there are three narrations about this. One of them: requiring the wording of testimony. The second: sufficiency of the mere report, which our shaykh chose. The third: a distinction between testimony regarding sayings and testimony regarding actions. Testimony regarding sayings does not require the wording of testimony, while testimony regarding actions does require it, because when someone says "I heard him say," he is like a witness on behalf of the Messenger of Allah regarding what he reports from him.

[Section: The wisdom in distinguishing some days from others]

As for his saying: "He forbade fasting on the first day of Shawwal and made fasting on the last day of Ramadan obligatory, though the two are equal," the first premise is correct, and the second is false. The two days are not equal, even if they share sunrise and sunset. This is a day of the month of fasting which Allah prescribed for His servants, and this is the day of their festival and joy, which Allah, exalted is He, made a thanksgiving for their fasting and its completion. They are His guests on it, glory be to Him, and the generous, noble host loves that his guest accept his hospitality, and dislikes that he refuse to accept his hospitality by fasting or otherwise. And it is disliked for the guest to fast except with the permission of the owner of the house. So among the greatest excellences of the Law is the obligation of fasting on the last day of Ramadan, for it completes what Allah commanded and is the seal of the act. And the prohibition of fasting on the first day of Shawwal, for it is a day on which the Muslims are the guests of their Lord, blessed and exalted is He, and they are thanking Him for His blessing upon them. So what could be more eloquent and better than this combination of obligation and prohibition?

(Benefit)

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted those who attend the festival to sit for the sermon and to leave. He also permitted them, when the festival falls on Friday, to be content with the festival prayer instead of attending the Friday prayer.

He (ﷺ) used to take a different route on the day of the festival: he would go by one road and return by another.

It was said: so that he would greet the people of both roads.

It was said: so that both groups would receive his blessing.

It was said: so that he would fulfil the need of anyone who had a need from either of them.

It was said: so that he would manifest the symbols of Islam in all the wide roads and paths.

It was said: so that he would enrage the hypocrites by their seeing the might of Islam and its people and the establishing of its rites.

It was said: so that the testimony of the places would increase, for the one who goes to the mosque or the musalla, one of his steps raises a degree and the other removes a sin, until he returns to his home.

It was said, and this is the most correct: it is for all of that, and for other wisdoms which his action is never free of.

It is narrated from him that he used to say the takbir from the dawn prayer on the Day of 'Arafah until the afternoon prayer on the last day of the Days of Tashriq: "Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest, and to Allah belongs all praise."

The reason for its revelation is reported to be that the Companions said: "O Messenger of God, is our Lord near, so that we address Him in private, or far, so that we call out to Him?" Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.﴾ This indicates that they were guided to intimate address (munajah) in supplication, not to calling out (nida'), which is raising the voice. They asked about this, and they were answered that their Lord, blessed and exalted, is near. He does not need to be called out to in His supplication and request. Rather, one makes a request to the Near One in intimate address, not to the Distant One by calling out.

This nearness to the supplicant is a particular nearness, not a general nearness shared by everyone. He is near to the one who calls upon Him and near to the one who worships Him, and the servant is nearest to his Lord when he is prostrating. This is more specific than the nearness of turning (qurb al-inabah) and the nearness of response (qurb al-ijabah), which most of the theologians (mutakallimun) did not affirm beyond it. It is rather a particular nearness to the supplicant and the worshipper, as the Prophet ﷺ said, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; and whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom."
