Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. This is His nearness to His worshipper. As for His nearness to the one who supplicates and asks Him, it is as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾, and His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾.

In this verse is the indication and the information about this nearness. As for the nearness of blessed and exalted God to His beloved, it is another kind, another structure, and another matter, as I have mentioned in the book al-Tuhaf al-Makkiyya. However, the expression falls short of it, and the true meaning of it never fully settles in the heart. Yet according to the strength or weakness of love, the servant's affirmation of this nearness is determined. Beware, then beware, of expressing it in other than the Prophetic wording, or of allowing into your heart a meaning other than its intended meaning, lest your foot slip after it has been firm. Many people have weakened in discernment in this station, and their expression has been corrupted, so they fell into kinds of gross errors and ecstatic utterances (shathat). Opposite them stood others whose veil of error led them to deny the servant's love for his Lord altogether, and His nearness to him, reducing that to mere promised reward; in their view, He is only the Beloved who is near, and nothing more. I have mentioned more than one hundred ways of refuting both these and those in the book al-Tuhfa. The purpose here is the discussion of this verse.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 187:

Shu'bah narrated from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, who said: "It is the child." This was also said by al-Hakam, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

The highest-ranked report on this is what Muhammad ibn Hurr narrated from his father: "My uncle told me, from his father, who told me, from my father, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: 'It is the child.'"

Ibn Zayd said: "It is intercourse." Qatadah said: "Seek the concession which Allah has prescribed for you."

There is another report from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr)."

The correct position is to say: when Allah lightened the burden on the Ummah by permitting intercourse during the night of fasting until the break of dawn, and the one having intercourse is typically overcome by desire and the fulfilment of appetite, to the point that nothing else barely occurs to his heart, He, glorified is He, guided them to seek His pleasure in this very pleasure. They should not approach their wives merely by the rule of desire alone, but should seek what Allah has prescribed for them of reward and of offspring who come forth from their loins, worshipping Allah and associating nothing with Him. And they should seek the concession He has permitted them, out of His love for them accepting His concessions. For Allah loves that His concessions be taken, just as He dislikes that His disobedience be committed. Among what Allah has prescribed for them is the Night of Decree, so they were commanded to seek it.

But there remains the question: what is the connection of this to the permission of intercourse with their wives?

It is said: in it is guidance that the permitted intimacy should not distract them from seeking this night which is better than a thousand months. It is as if He, glorified is He, says: fulfil your desire from your wives during the nights of fasting, but let that not distract you from seeking what Allah has prescribed for you of this night, with which He has favoured you. And Allah knows best.

(Benefit)

Al-'Udwan (transgression): it is exceeding the limits of Allah, concerning which He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, those are the wrongdoers.﴾

And He said in another place: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them.﴾ So He forbade transgressing them in one verse and approaching them in another verse. This is because His limits, glorified is He, are the dividing boundaries between the lawful and the unlawful, and the boundary of a thing is at times included within it, so it is part of it, and at times not included within it, so it has the status of what lies opposite. Thus the first consideration gives the prohibition of transgressing them, and the second consideration gives the prohibition of approaching them.

(Benefit concerning the annexation of time-expressions to events)

Time-expressions are annexed to the events that occur within them, as in "the day Zayd stands," because they are periods in which those events take place, and so they are annexed to them due to their specificity to them. This differs from place-expressions, since these are not specific to those events. If they are generally specific, the annexation is good, as in "this is a place where the judge sits," which is equivalent to "the day the judge sits." Sometimes time-nouns are annexed to events that do not occur in them because of their connection to them, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿the night of the fast (laylat al-siyam)﴾. Here "night" (laylah) is a time-expression, and it is annexed to "fasting" (al-siyam), while the fasting does not occur in it. Since in some speech it is permissible to annex a time-expression to a noun that is an event even though the event does not occur in it, they annexed it to a verb in form while it is annexed to the event in meaning, and the verbal word was inserted to affirm the meaning, specify the purpose, and remove the impurities of ambiguity. So when the listener hears your saying "the day Zayd stood," he knows you mean the day on which Zayd stood. Had you said, in place of "the night of the fast," "the night of Zayd's fasting," it would have had no meaning except that fasting occurs at night. It is this which led them to insert the verbal word when they intend to annex time-expressions to events. Analogise the subject and predicate on this.

(Section: The second degree, guarding the limits in what is not harmful)

For the sake of preserving chastity and piety, and ascending above baseness, and to be free from trespassing the limits.

He says: whoever rises from the first degree to this degree of scrupulousness (wara') leaves much of what is not harmful among the permissible, out of preserving his chastity and fearing that its purity be clouded and its light extinguished. For much of the permissible clouds the purity of chastity, takes away its radiance, extinguishes its light, and wears away its beauty and radiance.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, once said to me concerning some permissible matter: "This contradicts the lofty ranks, though its abandonment is not a condition for salvation," or words to this effect.

So the knower (al-'arif) leaves much of the permissible out of preserving his chastity, especially when that permissible thing is a barrier (barzakh) between the lawful and the unlawful, for between them is a barrier, as has preceded. Thus abandoning it, for the possessor of this degree, is as though it were a requirement which cannot be avoided, because it contradicts his degree.

The difference between the possessor of the first degree and the possessor of this one is that the former strives to attain chastity, while this one strives to guard its purity from becoming clouded and its light from being extinguished and departing. This is the meaning of his saying: "out of preserving chastity."

As for ascending above baseness, it is rising above its paths and its deeds.

As for being free from trespassing the limits: the limits are the endpoints, the points where the lawful and unlawful divide. Wherever it ends and stops, that is its limit. Whoever trespasses it falls into disobedience. Allah the Exalted has forbidden transgressing His limits and approaching them. He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

And He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. The limits are meant as the ends of the lawful, and where He forbids approaching, the limits there are the beginnings of the unlawful.

He, glorified is He, says: Do not transgress what I have permitted you, and do not approach what I have forbidden you.

So the scrupulous person (al-wari') is freed from approaching these and transgressing those, and this is trespassing the limits.

Namely, that you refer that matter to the judges and use their ruling as a means to consume it.

If it is said: "Had he intended this meaning, it would have said: 'and bring down [your cases] to the judges concerning them'" — whereas bringing them down to the judges means using bribery to reach them, so that you bribe the judge in order to reach the consumption of wealth unjustly through his bribe.

It is said: the verse encompasses both types, for each of them is a bringing down to the judges by means of them, so the prohibition applies to both together.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 195:

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Three are a right upon Allah to help them: the mujahid (one who strives) in the way of Allah, the mukatab (slave seeking to purchase his freedom) who wishes to pay (his debt of freedom), and the one who marries seeking chastity."

And he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without having fought, and without having entertained the thought of fighting in his soul, dies upon a branch of hypocrisy."

Abu Dawud mentioned from him (ﷺ): "Whoever does not fight, or equip a fighter, or take care of a fighter's family in goodness, Allah will strike him with a calamity before the Day of Resurrection."

And he (ﷺ) said: "When people become stingy with the dinar and the dirham, deal with one another through 'inah (a deceptive form of credit sale), follow the tails of cows, and abandon jihad in the way of Allah, Allah will send down a calamity upon them, and He will not lift it from them until they return to their religion."

Ibn Majah mentioned from him (ﷺ): "Whoever meets Allah, Mighty and Majestic, having no trace of striving in the way of Allah, meets Allah with a flaw in him."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. Abu Ayyub al-Ansari interpreted "throwing oneself with one's hands into destruction" as abandoning jihad. And it is authentically related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, the gates of Paradise are under the shade of the swords."

(Fa'idah)

Ibn 'Aqil was asked: with the widespread corruption today, is it better for a woman to uncover her face while in ihram, or to cover it and pay the expiation (fidyah)?

Yet 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "If the Messenger of Allah had known what the women have introduced, he would have forbidden them from the mosques."

He answered: Uncovering the face is the distinctive mark of a woman's ihram, and abolishing a ruling that was established by the Shari'ah because of newly introduced innovations is not permissible, for that would be abrogation (naskh) by new occurrences, and it would lead to the complete removal of the Shari'ah.

As for the saying of 'Aisha, she referred the matter to the Lawgiver, saying: "Had he seen it, he would have forbidden it," yet she herself did not forbid it. 'Umar also approved of the covering of a slave woman (amah) and said: "Do not imitate the free women."

It is well known that among them there were those who embellished themselves, but when the uncovering of the head was prescribed to distinguish free women from slave women, it became a distinction. So what do you think of an uncovering that is placed between the rites of pilgrimage and the state of being out of ihram? The Shari'ah has urged looking at a woman before marriage and has permitted witnesses to look, so it is no innovation for it to command her to uncover (her face), while commanding men to lower their gaze, so that the trial is greater, just as game was brought close to the hands during ihram and then forbidden.

I say: The cause of this question and answer is the obscurity of some of what the Sunnah has stated concerning the woman in ihram. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not prescribe for her the uncovering of the face in ihram or otherwise. Rather, the text only forbade the niqab specifically, just as it forbade the gloves (qaffazain), and forbade the wearing of the shirt (qamis) and trousers (sarawil). It is well known that his prohibition of wearing these items did not mean that she must be left entirely uncovered. Indeed, the people have agreed that the woman in ihram covers her body with her shirt and her outer garment, and that a man covers his body with the upper wrap (rida') and his lower body with the waist wrap (izar), even though the source of the prohibition regarding the niqab, the gloves, the shirt and the trousers is one and the same. How, then, can something be added to the requirement of the text, and be understood from it that she is legislated to uncover her face openly before people?

What text, implication, generality, analogy or public interest supports this? Rather, the woman's face is like the body of a man: it is forbidden to cover it with something fitted to its shape, such as the niqab or the burqa', and her hand is likewise forbidden to be covered with something fitted to the shape of the hand, such as the glove.

As for covering her with a sleeve, or covering the face with a sheet (mula'ah), a khimar or a garment, this has never been forbidden.

Whoever says that her face is like the head of the muhrim has no text, generality or sound basis for this, and its analogy to the head of the muhrim is not valid, because of the difference that Allah has placed between them.

The saying of some of the early scholars (salaf), "the ihram of the woman is in her face," meant only this sense: that it is not obligatory for her to avoid (ordinary) clothing as it is obligatory for the man, but it is obligatory for her to avoid the niqab, so that her face is like the body of a man. Even if it were supposed that he meant the obligation to uncover it, his saying would not be a proof unless it were established from the Lawgiver that he said this and meant by it the obligation to uncover the face; and there is no way to either of these two meanings.

Mother of the Believers 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "When riders passed by us, one of us would let her jilbab fall over her face." None of them used a stick to place between her face and the jilbab, as some jurists have said, and this is not known from any woman among the Companions' women or the Mothers of the Believers, neither in practice nor in fatwa. It is impossible that this would be a distinctive mark of ihram and not be apparent and well known among them, known to both the elite and the common people. Whoever prefers fairness and follows the path of knowledge and justice will have the preponderant of the views made clear to him from the weak, and the sound from the corrupt. And Allah is the Granter of success and the Guide.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 197:

He combined for them the provision of their journey and the provision of their return, just as He combined the two garments in His saying: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts and as an adornment, but the clothing of righteousness, that is best. That is among the signs of Allah, that they may remember.﴾ [al-A'raf: 26]

So He mentioned, glory be to Him, the adornment of their outward and inward states, and alerted them through the sensory to the immaterial. Understanding this degree goes beyond merely grasping the wording and its placement in the basic usage of the language. And Allah is the One sought for help, the One relied upon, and there is no power and no strength except through Allah.

(Section: Disobedience Affects the Intellect)

Among its punishments is that it specifically affects the diminishing of the intellect. You will not find two intelligent people, one of them obedient to Allah and the other disobedient, except that the intellect of the obedient one is more abundant and more complete, his thinking is sounder, his opinion more correct, and righteousness accompanies him.

For this reason you find that the address of the Qur'an is only with those endowed with intellects and minds, as in His saying: ﴿So fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, and His saying: ﴿So fear Allah, O people of understanding, that you may succeed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100], and His saying: ﴿And none remember except those of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Similar examples are many.

And how can one be intelligent and of abundant intellect when he disobeys the One who is in His grip and in His home, while he knows that He sees him and witnesses him, yet he disobeys Him while He is with his very eye, not hidden from him; and he uses His blessings in the service of what displeases Him, and at every moment calls down His anger upon himself, His curse, His distancing him from His nearness, His expelling him from His door, His turning away from him, His forsaking him, leaving him to his own self and his enemy, his fall from His sight, and his deprivation of the spirit of His pleasure and His love, the delight of the eye in His nearness, the triumph of being in His neighborhood, and gazing upon His face among the company of His friends—up to multiples upon multiples of that of His honor toward the people of obedience, and multiples upon multiples of that of the punishment of the people of disobedience.

So what intellect is there for one who prefers the pleasure of an hour, or a day, or an age, which then passes away as if it were a dream that never was, over this enduring bliss and this great triumph? Rather, it is the happiness of this world and the next. Were it not for the intellect by which the proof is established upon him, he would be in the position of the insane; indeed the insane may be in a better state than him and safer in outcome. This is so from this aspect.

As for its effect in diminishing the intellect of livelihood, were it not for the shared participation in this deficiency, the deficiency of the intellect of our disobedient would be apparent to our obedient; but the calamity is general, and madness has many kinds.

How strange! If intellects were sound, they would know that the path to attaining pleasure, joy, happiness, and good living lies only in the pleasure of the One in whose pleasure is all bliss, and in whose anger and wrath is all pain and torment. In His pleasure is the coolness of the eyes, the joy of souls, the life of hearts, the delight of spirits, the goodness of life, the sweetness of living, and the finest bliss. Were a mithqal of a dharra of it weighed against the bliss of this world, it would not equal it. Indeed, when the heart attains even the smallest share of it, it does not accept this world and all in it as a substitute for it. And yet he enjoys his share of this world more greatly than the enjoyment of those who live in luxury in it, and his enjoyment of that small portion is not mixed with the sorrows, griefs, and opposing anxieties that mix the enjoyment of the people of luxury. Rather, he has obtained the two blisses and awaits two other blisses greater than them, and whatever pains befall him in the midst of that. The matter is as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you suffer pain, then they suffer pain as you suffer pain, and you hope from Allah for what they do not hope﴾ [al-Nisa': 104].

So there is no god but Allah, how diminished is the intellect of one who sells pearls for dung, and musk for dung-droppings, and the companionship of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, for the companionship of those upon whom Allah is wrathful, whom He has cursed, and for whom He has prepared Hell, and evil is the destination.

(Benefit)

Taqwa has three levels:

The first: guarding the heart and the limbs against sins and prohibited things.

The second: guarding them against what is disliked (makruhat).

The third: guarding against superfluities and what does not concern one.

The first gives the servant his life; the second gives him his health and strength; and the third gains him his joy, happiness, and radiance.

**(Benefit)**

If it is asked: why does ʿĀshūrāʾ (the tenth of Muharram) expiate one year, while the Day of ʿArafah expiates two years?

It is answered that there are two reasons:

First: the Day of ʿArafah falls in a sacred month, preceded by a sacred month and followed by a sacred month, unlike ʿĀshūrāʾ.

Second: fasting the Day of ʿArafah is among the distinctive features of our law (sharīʿah), unlike ʿĀshūrāʾ, so its reward was multiplied through the blessings of the Chosen One (ﷺ).

And Allah knows best.

**(Benefit)**

It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "There is no day except that its night precedes it, except the Day of ʿArafah, whose night follows it."

I say: this is among the matters on which opinions differ. It is reported from a group that the night of a day is the night after it, while what is well known among people is that the night of a day is the night before it. Some scholars made a distinction: a night attached to a day, such as the night of Friday, Saturday, Sunday and the rest of the days, belongs to the day preceding it; while a night attached to a place, a state or an action, such as the night of ʿArafah and the night of the departure (from Minā), and similar cases, belongs to what follows it. They based this on the report from Ibn ʿAbbās. But this was refuted by the night of ʿĪd. What the people have understood, in former and recent times, from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Do not single out Friday for fasting among the days, nor the night of Friday for prayer among the nights,"

is that it refers to the night whose morning dawns upon Friday. People hasten to honour it and increase worship in it more than the other nights, so he forbade singling it out for night prayer, just as he forbade singling out its day for fasting. And Allah knows best.

**(Exhortation)**

O you who are present with us out of a desire for leisure, you are not with us. Return to the dens of laziness, for war is thrust and strike.

And O you who bid farewell, turn back, for we have crossed al-ʿUdhayb, and soon our news will reach you shortly.

And O you whose wedding took place at al-Khayf in Minā, the tears teach you how to throw the pebbles at the jamarāt.

The guest of love has no hospitality except the lives (of those who love).

**[The Merit of Standing at ʿArafah on a Friday]**

It is said: some scholars have preferred Friday over the Day of ʿArafah, citing this hadith. Al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā related a narration from Aḥmad that the night of Friday is better than the Night of Qadr. The correct view is that Friday is the best day of the week, and the Day of ʿArafah and the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Naḥr) are the best days of the year, as is the Night of Qadr, and the night of Friday. Therefore, standing at ʿArafah on a Friday has a merit over the other days in several respects.

The first: the coming together of the two days which are the best of days.

The second: that it is the day in which there is an hour whose supplication is certainly answered. Most opinions hold that it is the last hour after ʿAṣr, and all the people of the standing place (al-mawqif) are then standing in supplication and humble entreaty.

The third: that it coincides with the day on which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at ʿArafah.

The fourth: that on it creatures gather from the regions of the earth for the sermon and the Friday prayer, and this coincides with the gathering of the people of ʿArafah on the Day of ʿArafah at ʿArafah. Thus there results, from the gathering of the Muslims in their mosques and at their standing place, supplication and humble entreaty that do not occur on any other day.

The fifth: that Friday is a day of ʿĪd, and the Day of ʿArafah is a day of ʿĪd for the people of ʿArafah. For this reason, fasting it is disliked for those who are at ʿArafah. In al-Nasāʾī from Abū Hurayrah, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade fasting the Day of ʿArafah while at ʿArafah." There is an issue with its chain, for Mahdī ibn Ḥarb al-ʿAbdī is not well known, and the report depends upon him. But it is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from the hadith of Umm al-Fadl: "Some people disputed in her presence on the Day of ʿArafah concerning the fasting of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Some of them said: he is fasting; others said: he is not fasting. So she sent to him a bowl of milk while he was standing on his camel at ʿArafah, and he drank it."

It has been disputed what the wisdom is behind the recommendation of breaking the fast on the Day of ʿArafah while at ʿArafah. A group said: so that he may be strengthened for supplication; this is the view of al-Khiraqī and others. Others, among them Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah, said: the wisdom in it is that it is a ʿĪd for the people of ʿArafah, so fasting it is not recommended for them. He said: the proof for this is the hadith in the Sunan from him (ﷺ) that he said: "The Day of ʿArafah, the Day of Sacrifice, and the days of Minā are our ʿĪd, the people of Islam."

Our shaykh said: the Day of ʿArafah is only a ʿĪd in respect of the people of ʿArafah because they gather on it, unlike the people of the cities, who only gather on the Day of Sacrifice, so that is their ʿĪd. The point is that when the Day of ʿArafah coincides with a Friday, two festivals coincide together.

The sixth: that it coincides with the day on which Allah, the Exalted, completed His religion for His believing servants and perfected His favour upon them, as established in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb who said: "A Jew came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and said: O Commander of the Faithful, there is a verse you recite in your Book; had it been revealed to us, the Jews, we would have taken the day on which it was revealed as a festival. He said: Which verse? He said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favour upon you, and approved Islam as your religion﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3]. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: Indeed I know the day on which it was revealed and the place where it was revealed: it was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at ʿArafah on a Friday, and we were standing with him at ʿArafah."

The seventh: that it coincides with the Day of the Great Gathering and the Greatest Standing on the Day of Resurrection, for the Hour will be established on a Friday, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best day on which the sun has risen is Friday. On it Adam was created, on it he was admitted into Paradise, on it he was expelled from it, and on it the Hour will be established. And in it there is an hour in which no Muslim servant coincides with it while asking Allah for something good except that He gives it to him." For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, legislated for His servants a day on which they gather, and they remember the beginning and the return, Paradise and the Fire. Allah the Exalted reserved for this community the day of Friday, for on it was the beginning and on it is the return. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in his dawn prayer the two sūrahs of (al-Sajdah) and (Hal atā ʿalā al-insān), because they include what was and what will be on this day: the creation of Adam, the mention of the beginning and the return, and entry into Paradise and the Fire. So he would remind the community on this day of what was in it and what will be. Likewise a person remembers, on the greatest standing place of this world, which is the Day of ʿArafah, the greatest standing before the Lord, glorified is He, on this very day, and it will not be split until the people of Paradise settle in their abodes and the people of the Fire in theirs.

The eighth: that the acts of obedience performed by the Muslims on Friday and the night of Friday are more than in the other days, to the extent that most of the people of wickedness respect Friday and its night, and they regard that whoever dares on it to disobey Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has his punishment hastened by Allah and is not given respite. This is a matter that has become established among them and they know it through experience. That is due to the greatness of the day and its nobility in the sight of Allah, and Allah's choosing it from among all the other days. There is no doubt that standing (at ʿArafah) on it has a merit over other days.

The ninth: that it coincides with the Day of Increase (Yawm al-Mazīd) in Paradise, which is the day on which the people of Paradise are gathered in a wide valley, and pulpits of pearls, pulpits of gold, and pulpits of emerald and ruby are set up for them upon dunes of musk. They look upon their Lord, blessed and exalted is He, and He manifests Himself to them, so they see Him clearly. The one who arrives earliest is the one who hastens most to the mosque, and the nearest of them to Him is the nearest to the Imam. The people of Paradise yearn for the Day of Increase in it because of the honour they receive on it, and it is a Friday. So when it coincides with the Day of ʿArafah, it has an additional merit, distinction and excellence that is not for any other.

The tenth: that the Lord, blessed and exalted, draws near in the evening of the Day of ʿArafah to the people of the standing place, then He boasts of them to the angels, saying: "What did these want? I call you to witness that I have forgiven them." And with His drawing near to them, blessed and exalted, there occurs the hour of answered supplication, in which He does not turn away any petitioner who asks for good. So they draw near to Him through their supplication and humble entreaty to Him in that hour. And He draws near to them, exalted is He, in two kinds of nearness: the first is the nearness of certain answer in that hour; the second is His special nearness to the people of ʿArafah and His boasting of them to His angels. The hearts of the people of faith perceive these matters, so their strength increases upon its strength, along with joy, delight and happiness, and hope in the bounty and generosity of their Lord. By these aspects and others, the standing on the day of Friday was given preference over other standings.

As for what has spread on the tongues of the common people, that it equals seventy-two pilgrimages, this is false; it has no basis from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor from any of the Companions or the Successors. And Allah knows best.

Whoever is fair to himself and knows his own deeds is ashamed before God to confront Him with his deed, or to be pleased with it for his Lord, while he knows within himself that if he were doing something for a beloved person among the people, he would expend his sincere advice on it and leave out none of its goodness without doing it.

In sum, this is the state of this servant with his Lord in all his deeds. He knows that he does not fulfil this station its due, so he is always seeking forgiveness from God after every deed. The Prophet ﷺ, when he finished the prayer, would seek forgiveness from God three times.

And the Most High said: ﴿And at the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness﴾.

Al-Hasan said: "They would extend the prayer until the pre-dawn, then sit down seeking forgiveness from their Lord."

And the Most High said: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from God. Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. So He, glorified is He, commanded seeking forgiveness after standing at 'Arafah and at Muzdalifah. And it was prescribed for one who performs ablution to say after his ablution: "O God, make me among those who repent, and make me among those who purify themselves."

This is repentance after ablution, repentance after the pilgrimage, repentance after the prayer, and repentance after the night prayer.

So the possessor of this station is compelled to repentance and seeking forgiveness, as has been made clear. He is never without seeking forgiveness and repentance, and whenever his acts of obedience increase, his repentance and seeking forgiveness increase.

(Section)

The sum of the matter in this is only by perfecting servitude to God, Mighty and Majestic, outwardly and inwardly, so that all the movements of his soul and body are in the things beloved to God. The perfection of a servant's servitude is his agreement with his Lord in loving what He loves, and exerting effort in doing it, and his agreement with Him in disliking what He dislikes, and exerting effort in leaving it. This only occurs for the soul at peace (al-nafs al-mutma'innah), not for the soul that commands to evil (al-nafs al-ammarah) nor for the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah).

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 200:

In it is the command to remember God often and with intensity, because of the servant's great need for it and his inability to do without it even for the blink of an eye. Whatever moment the servant is empty of the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that moment is against him and not for him, and his loss in it is greater than what he gained in his heedlessness of Allah.

One of the knowers of God (al-'arifin) said: "If a servant turns towards Allah, Exalted, for such-and-such years and then turns away from Him for a single moment, what he has lost will be greater than what he has gained."

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from 'A'isha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said:

"No hour passes over a son of Adam in which he does not remember (Allah) except that he will regret it on the Day of Resurrection."

It is also mentioned from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, raising it (to the Prophet), also:

"The regret of the people of Paradise will be only over an hour that passed them in which they did not remember Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

From Umm Habiba, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"All of the speech of the son of Adam is against him and not for him, except enjoining what is good, forbidding what is evil, or remembering Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

From Mu'adh ibn Jabal, he said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which deeds are most beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic?"

He said: "That you die while your tongue is moist with the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Everything has a polish, and the polish of hearts is the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Al-Bayhaqi also mentioned, raised (to the Prophet) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he used to say: "Everything has a polish, and the polish of hearts is the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Nothing is more effective in saving one from the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." They said: "Not even jihad in the way of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Not even if one strikes with his sword until it breaks."

There is no doubt that the heart rusts just as copper, silver and other things rust, and its polish is through remembrance, for it polishes it until it leaves it like a white mirror.

So if it is abandoned, it rusts; and if it is polished, it becomes clear.

And as for placing al-'Azeez (the Almighty) before al-Hakeem (the All-Wise): if it is derived from al-hukm (judgment, meaning decisive separation and command), then the meaning mentioned is correct. If it is derived from al-hikmah (wisdom), which is the perfection of knowledge and will, implying the consistency of His creation and its functioning in the best and most perfect manner, and His placing things in their proper places, and this is the apparent meaning of this name, then the reason for placing it first is that might ('izzah) is the perfection of power (qudrah), and wisdom (hikmah) is the perfection of knowledge ('ilm). He, glory be to Him, is described with every attribute of perfection in its most complete and greatest form and in its ultimate degree. So the attribute of power is mentioned first, because its object is closer to the observation of creation, which are His acts and His signs (ayat).

As for wisdom, its object is generally related to contemplation, reflection and consideration, and it comes after the object of power.

A second reason: contemplation of wisdom comes after contemplation of the act and knowledge of it, so the mind moves from it to contemplating the purposes (hikam) and meanings that He has placed within it.

A third reason: wisdom is the end (ghayah) of the act, so it comes after it in the way that ends come after their means. Power relates to bringing it into existence, and wisdom relates to its end. So the means is placed before the end, because it is prior in external order.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 213:

Sa'id related from Qatadah: "It was mentioned to us that between Adam and Nuh, peace be upon them both, there were ten centuries, all of them upon guidance and upon a law of truth. Then they differed after that, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent Nuh. He was the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth, and he was sent when people differed and abandoned the truth."

And Ibn 'Abbas said: "The people were one nation: they were all upon Islam."

This is the correct view regarding the verse.

'Atiyyah related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They were one nation, they were disbelievers."

This is the view of al-Hasan and 'Ata', who said: "From the time of Adam's death until the sending of Nuh, peace be upon him, the people were one nation upon one creed, which was disbelief. They were all disbelievers, like cattle. Then Allah sent Nuh, Ibrahim, and the prophets."

This view is very weak. It is an interrupted narration (munqati') from Ibn 'Abbas, and what is authentically related from him is the opposite.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Zur'ah related to us, Shaiban ibn Farrukh related to us, Hammam related to us, Qatadah related to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They were all upon Islam."

This is definitely the correct view, for the recitation (qira'ah) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is: "So they differed, and Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners."

This recitation is supported by Allah's words in Surah Yunus: ﴿And mankind was not but one nation, and they differed﴾.

The point is this: the enemy plotted against them and toyed with them until they split into two groups, disbelievers and believers. He plotted against them through the worship of idols and the denial of resurrection.

The first thing through which the enemy plotted against the idol-worshippers was devotion at graves and making images of their people so that they would remember them, as Allah, glorified is He, related their stories in His Book, saying: ﴿And they said, "Do not abandon your gods, and do not abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr"﴾ [Nuh: 13].

Al-Bukhari related in his Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "These are the names of righteous men from the people of Nuh. When they perished, Satan inspired their people: 'Set up at their gathering places, where they used to sit, idols (ansab), and name them after them.' They did so, but they were not worshipped until those (people) perished and knowledge was forgotten, and then they were worshipped."

Ibn Jarir said, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Qays, who said: "They were righteous men from the descendants of Adam, who had followers who emulated them. When they died, their companions, who used to emulate them, said: 'If we made images of them, it would be more inspiring for us to worship, when we remember them.' So they made images of them. When they died and others came after them, Iblis crept up to them and said: 'They only used to worship them, and through them rain was sent down,' so they worshipped them."

(Principle)

A servant's perfection and righteousness are lacking from one of two directions. Either his nature is dry and hard, not soft, not submissive, and not receptive to what brings about its perfection and success; or his nature is soft and submissive, easily led, but not steadfast in that, rather quick to move away from it and frequently changing. So whenever Allah grants a servant submission to the truth and steadfastness upon it, let him receive good tidings, for he has been given every good. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills.

**A Noble Benefit:** The words of the Exalted: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing while it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing while it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ And His words: ﴿And if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing while Allah has placed in it much good.﴾ [4:19]

The first verse concerns jihad, which is the perfection of the irascible faculty (al-quwwa al-ghadabiyya), and the second concerns marriage, which is the perfection of the appetitive faculty (al-quwwa al-shahwaniyya). The servant dislikes confronting his enemy with his irascible faculty, out of fear for himself, yet this disliked thing is good for him in his livelihood and his afterlife. He loves truce and disengagement, yet this loved thing is evil for him in his livelihood and his afterlife. Likewise, he dislikes a woman because of some attribute of hers, while in keeping her there is much good he does not know. He loves a woman because of some attribute of hers, while in keeping her there is much evil he does not know. The human being is as his Creator described him: "a wrongdoer, ignorant" [33:72]. Therefore it is not fitting that the criterion for what harms and benefits him be his inclination, his love, his aversion, and his hatred. Rather, the criterion is what Allah has chosen for him through His command and prohibition. The most beneficial thing for him, absolutely, is obedience to his Lord, outwardly and inwardly, and the most harmful thing for him, absolutely, is disobedience to Him, outwardly and inwardly. When he stands in obedience and servitude to Him, sincerely, then everything that befalls him of what he dislikes becomes good for him. But if he abandons His obedience and servitude, then everything of what he loves that he has is evil for him. Whoever has sound knowledge of his Lord and understanding of His names and attributes will know with certainty that the disliked things that afflict him and the trials that descend upon him contain kinds of interests and benefits that his knowledge and thought cannot count. Indeed, the servant's interest in what he dislikes is greater than in what he loves.

Most of the interests of souls lie in what they dislike, just as most of their harms and causes of destruction lie in what they love. Consider a gardener of a garden, skilled in cultivation, who planted a garden and tended it with watering and care until its trees bore fruit. He then approaches them, cutting their joints and severing their branches, because he knows that if they were left as they are, their fruit would not be good. He feeds them from a tree of good fruit. When they have joined with it, united with it, and yielded their fruit, he comes with his blade and cuts their weak branches that drain their strength, and makes them taste the pain of cutting and the iron, for their benefit and perfection, so that their fruit may be fit to be presented before kings. Then he does not leave them to the impulses of their nature to drink at all times, but makes them thirst at times and waters them at other times, and does not leave water upon them constantly, even though that would make their leaves more lush and their growth faster. Then he deliberately strips away much of the adornment of leaves with which they were adorned, because that adornment comes between their fruit and its full ripening and perfection, as with grapevines and the like. He cuts their limbs with iron and sheds much of their finery, and this is precisely their benefit. If they had discernment and perception like animals, they would imagine that this is corruption for them and harm to them, when in fact it is precisely their benefit.

Likewise is a compassionate father toward his child, knowing what is good for him. If he sees that his benefit lies in drawing out corrupt blood from him, he cuts his skin and severs his veins and makes him taste severe pain. If he sees that healing lies in amputating a limb, he removes it, and this is mercy to him and compassion for him. If he sees that his benefit lies in withholding gifts from him, he does not give to him and does not expand provision for him, knowing that this is the greatest cause of his corruption and destruction. Likewise he restrains him from many of his desires out of protection and for his benefit, not out of stinginess toward him. So the Most Wise of judges, the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Knowing of the knowers, who is more merciful to His servants than they are to themselves and than their fathers and mothers are, when He sends down upon them what they dislike, it is better for them than if He did not send it down, out of His consideration for them, His kindness toward them, and His gentleness with them. Had they been empowered to choose for themselves, they would have been unable to manage their own interests in knowledge, will, and action. But He, glorified be He, has taken charge of their affairs according to the requirement of His knowledge, wisdom, and mercy, whether they love it or dislike it. The certain ones who know His names and attributes recognize this, so they do not suspect Him in any of His rulings. But it was hidden from the ignorant who do not know Him and His names and attributes, so they dispute His management, cast doubt on His wisdom, do not submit to His judgment, and oppose His judgment with their corrupt intellects, false opinions, and unjust policies. They have neither known their Lord nor attained their own interests. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Whenever the servant attains this knowledge, he dwells in this world before the next, in a garden that resembles nothing but the bliss of the Hereafter. He never ceases to be content with his Lord, and contentment (al-ridā) is the garden of this world and the resting place of the gnostics (al-ʿārifīn). He is at ease in soul with what befalls him of decrees, which are in fact Allah's own choice for him, and his heart is tranquil in the acceptance of His religious rulings. This is contentment with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (ﷺ) as messenger. Whoever has not attained this has not tasted the flavor of faith. This contentment is in proportion to his knowledge of Allah's justice, wisdom, mercy, and good choosing. The more he knows of this, the more content he is with it. So the decree of the Lord, glorified be He, regarding His servant revolves between justice, benefit, wisdom, and mercy, and never departs from that at all, as He said in the well-known supplication: "O Allah, I am Your servant, son of Your servant, son of Your female servant. My forelock is in Your hand, Your judgment over me is executed, Your decree concerning me is just. I ask You by every name belonging to You, by which You named Yourself, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept hidden in the knowledge of the unseen with You, to make the Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my chest, the departure of my grief, and the removal of my anxiety and distress." Whoever says it, Allah removes his anxiety and distress and replaces them with relief. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, should we not learn them?" He said: "Yes, whoever hears them should learn them."

The point here is His saying, "Your decree concerning me is just." This encompasses every decree He issues upon His servant, whether punishment or pain, and its cause. He is the One who decreed the cause and decreed the effect, and He is just in this decree. And this decree is good for the believer, as he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, Allah does not decree for the believer any decree except that it is good for him, and this is not the case for anyone except the believer." Ibn al-Qayyim said: "I asked my Shaykh whether this includes the decree of sin, and he said: 'Yes, with its condition.'" The condition is summarized in what follows from the sin of effects beloved to Allah: repentance, humility, remorse, submission, lowliness, weeping, and the like.

**(Section)**

In this verse are several rulings, secrets, and interests for the servant. When the servant knows that what is disliked may bring what is loved, and what is loved may bring what is disliked, he is not secure from harm coming to him from the direction of pleasure, nor does he despair of pleasure coming to him from the direction of harm, because he does not know the outcomes, whereas Allah knows what the servant does not know. This requires several things for the servant:

Among them: there is no benefit for him greater than complying with his Lord's command, even if it is hard for him at first. Because its outcomes are all goods, joys, delights, and pleasures, and although his soul dislikes it, it is better and more beneficial for it. Likewise, nothing is more harmful to him than committing what is forbidden, even if his soul desires it and inclines to it, because its outcomes are all pains, sorrows, evils, and calamities.

Especially, the intelligent person bears a small pain for the great pleasure and abundant good it leads to, and avoids a small pleasure for the great pain and lasting evil it leads to. The view of the ignorant does not go beyond beginnings to their ends, whereas the intelligent and shrewd always look at ends from behind the veils of beginnings, seeing what lies behind those veils of praiseworthy and blameworthy ends. They see the prohibitions as a delicious food into which deadly poison has been mixed, so whenever his desire calls him to eat it, what is in it of poison forbids him. They see the commands as a medicine of bitter taste, leading to health and cure, and whenever the bitterness of its taste forbids him from taking it, the benefit of it commands him to take it. But this requires abundant knowledge, by which one perceives the ends from their beginnings, and strength of patience, by which one prepares oneself to endure the hardship of the path, for the good outcome hoped for at the end. If certainty and patience are lacking, this becomes impossible for him. But when his certainty is strong, every hardship he bears in seeking lasting good and lasting pleasure becomes easy for him.

Among the secrets of this verse: it requires of the servant that he entrust (tafwīḍ) himself to the One who knows the outcomes of affairs, and be content with what He chooses for him and decrees for him, in hope of a good outcome.

Among them: he does not make demands upon his Lord, nor choose over Him, nor ask Him for what he has no knowledge of. Perhaps his harm and destruction lie in it, while he does not know. So he does not choose anything over his Lord, but asks Him for good choice for him, and that He make him content with what He chooses. Nothing is more beneficial to him than this.

Among them: when he entrusts himself to his Lord and is content with what He chooses for him, He strengthens him in what He chooses for him, with power, resolve, and patience, and turns away from him the calamities that are the target of the servant's choosing for himself. And He shows him, of the good outcomes of His choice, what he could never have reached by what he would have chosen for himself.

Among them: it relieves him from the wearying thoughts about the various kinds of choices, and empties his heart of the calculations and schemes by which one ascends one steep path and descends another.

Yet with this, he cannot escape what has been decreed for him. So if he is content with Allah's choice, the decree befalls him while he is praised and thanked, and is treated with kindness in it. Otherwise, the decree befalls him while he is blameworthy in his own eyes, not treated with kindness in it, along with his own choosing for himself.

When his entrusting and contentment are sound, he is surrounded, in what is decreed, by compassion toward him and gentleness with him, so he finds himself between His compassion and His gentleness. His compassion protects him from what he fears, and His gentleness makes easy for him what He has decreed.

When the decree takes effect in the servant, one of its greatest causes of taking effect is his scheming to repel it. So there is nothing more beneficial to him than surrender, and casting himself before the decree, prostrate like a corpse. For the lion does not consent to eat carrion.

**(Section)**

The content one is standing with Allah's choice for him, turning away from his own choice for himself. This comes from the strength of his knowledge of his Lord, exalted be He, and his knowledge of himself.

Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, Sufyan al-Thawri, and Yusuf ibn Asbat once gathered together.

Al-Thawri said: "Before today I used to hate sudden death. But today, I wish I were dead."

Yusuf ibn Asbat said to him: "And why?"

He said: "Because of what I fear of trial."

Yusuf said: "But I do not hate a long life."

Al-Thawri said: "And why do you hate death?"

He said: "Perhaps I will come upon a day in which I repent and do righteous deeds."

Then it was said to Wuhayb: "What do you say?"

He said: "I do not choose anything. Whatever is dearest to me is whatever is dearest to Allah."

Al-Thawri kissed him between the eyes and said: "Spiritual one, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!"

This is the state of a servant for whom the state of life and the state of death have become equal. He stands with Allah's choice for him in both. Wuhayb, may Allah have mercy on him, had a lofty station in contentment and other than it.

**The forty-second:** that he knows that Allah's withholding from His believing servant who loves Him is a gift, and His trial of him is well-being. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "His withholding is a gift." That is because He does not withhold out of stinginess or lack. Rather, He considers the good of His believing servant, so He withholds, by choice and good consideration.

This is as he said. He, glorified be He, does not decree for His believing servant any decree except that it is good for him, whether that decree displeases him or pleases him. So His decree of withholding for His believing servant is a gift, even if it appears as withholding. And it is a blessing, even if it appears as a trial. And His testing is well-being, even if it appears as a calamity. But because of the servant's ignorance and wrongdoing, he counts as gift, blessing, and well-being only what he enjoys in the present and what suits his nature. Were he granted a generous share of knowledge, he would count withholding a blessing and trial a mercy, and he would enjoy trial more than he enjoys well-being, and enjoy poverty more than he enjoys wealth, and in a state of scarcity he would be more thankful than in a state of abundance.

This was the state of the predecessors (al-salaf).

So the intelligent, content person is one who counts trial as well-being, withholding as a blessing, and poverty as wealth.

Allah revealed to one of His prophets: "When you see poverty approaching, say: 'Welcome, emblem of the righteous.' And when you see wealth approaching, say: 'A sin whose punishment has been hastened.'"

So the content one is the one who counts Allah's blessings upon him in what he dislikes as greater and more numerous than His blessings upon him in what he loves, as one of the gnostics said: "O son of Adam, Allah's blessing upon you in what you dislike is greater than His blessing upon you in what you love." And He, exalted be He, said: ﴿But perhaps you dislike a thing while it is good for you.﴾

One of the gnostics also said: "Be content with Allah in all that He does to you. He withheld from you only to give to you. He tested you only to grant you well-being. He made you ill only to heal you. He made you die only to bring you to life. So beware lest you part from contentment with Him for the blink of an eye, lest you fall from His sight."

**(Benefit)**

He, glorified be He, informed that fighting is hateful to them, although it is good for them, because it leads to the greatest and most beneficial of beloved things. Souls, however, are inclined to ease, comfort, and luxury, and that is evil for them because it leads to the loss of what is beloved. The intelligent person does not look at the immediate pleasure of what is beloved and prefer it, nor at the immediate pain of what is disliked and turn away from it, for that may be evil for him. Indeed, it may bring upon him the utmost pain and deprive him of the greatest pleasure. Rather, the intelligent of this world endure hardships they dislike for the pleasure that follows them, even if it is temporary.

Matters are of four kinds: a disliked thing that leads to a disliked thing; a disliked thing that leads to a beloved thing; a beloved thing that leads to a beloved thing; and a beloved thing that leads to a disliked thing. The beloved thing that leads to the beloved has the motive for action gathered in it from two aspects, and the disliked thing that leads to the disliked has the motive for abandonment gathered in it from two aspects.

Two remaining divisions are pulled in opposite directions by the two callers, and these two are the very battleground of trial and testing. The soul prefers whichever of the two is nearest to it in dwelling, namely the immediate, while the intellect and faith prefer whichever is most beneficial and most lasting. The heart lies between the two callers, inclining to this one at one time and to that one at another time. This is the locus of trial, both legal and divinely decreed. The caller of the intellect and faith calls out at every moment: "Hasten to success (ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ)." At dawn, the people praise the night journey (al-surā); and at death, the servant praises piety (al-tuqā). But if the darkness of the night of love grows intense and the authority of desire and will holds sway, the caller says: "O soul, be patient, for it is but an hour, and then it passes, and all of this goes away and vanishes."

(Qāʿidah: a principle)

When God tests His servant with some kind of affliction and trial, and that trial turns him back to his Lord, gathers him to Him, and casts him at His door, this is a sign of his happiness and of God's desire for good for him. Hardship is cut off and has no permanence, however long it lasts; it lifts from him when it lifts, and he has been recompensed in its place with the most sublime and excellent recompense: his return to God after having been averse to Him, his turning to Him after having been turned away, and his prostrating himself at His door after having been opposed to Him, and his having been exposed at the doors of others.

For such a person, the affliction is in truth a blessing, even if it grieves him, his nature dislikes it, and his soul recoils from it. Often what is hateful to the souls becomes, by some cause, the means to what they love, and no means is like it. God's words on this are the cure and the protection: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing while it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾

But if the affliction does not turn him back to Him, and instead his heart strays from Him and he is turned toward creation, and he forgets the remembrance of his Lord, the supplication to Him, the humbling before Him, the repentance, and the return to Him, then this is a sign of his wretchedness and of God's desire for evil for him. So when the affliction lifts from such a person, it returns him to the rule of his nature, the authority of his desire, his insolence and exultation. His nature then brings forth every kind of wickedness, insolence and arrogance, and turning away from thanking the Benefactor for ease just as he turned away from remembering Him and humbling himself to Him in hardship. Thus this person's affliction becomes a burden upon him, a punishment and a deficiency in his case, while the affliction of the first is a purification for him, a mercy, and a perfecting. And success is from Allah.

(Precious point)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾. This is of the type of substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). The question was really about fighting in it, yet the month was mentioned first. Why was the month placed first, when you have said that they mention first what is more important to them and what they care about more? It is said: the question did not come from them until after the fighting had occurred in the month and their enemies had reproached them for it and violated its sanctity. Their concern and attention for the month was therefore greater than their concern for the fighting. The question arose out of reverence for the sacred month, and so it was mentioned first. Its placement first accords with the principle we have mentioned.

If it is said: what is the benefit of repeating the word "fighting" in its explicit form? Why did it not suffice with a pronoun, saying "Say: it is great"? For when you say, "I asked him about Zayd: is he in the house?", it is more concise than saying, "Is Zayd in the house?"

It is said: repeating it in the explicit form has a subtle point, namely that the predicative ruling is attached to the name "fighting" in general. Had he used the pronoun and said "it is great," one might have supposed that the ruling is restricted to that particular fighting about which they asked. That is not the case; rather, it is general to every fighting that occurs in a sacred month. A parallel to this benefit is his saying ﷺ, when he was asked about performing ablution with sea water: "Its water is pure, and its dead animals are lawful" (sahih). He repeated the word "water" and did not confine himself to saying, "Yes, perform ablution with it," lest it be supposed that the ruling is restricted to the questioners by some kind of restriction. So he turned from "Yes, perform ablution" to a general answer that entails the ruling and the purity being attached to the water itself as such, which conveys the continuance of the ruling permanently, attaches it to the generality of the verse, and removes the supposition of restricting it to the occasion. Reflect upon it, for it is subtle.

Likewise in the verse: when He said "fighting in it is great," He made the predicate "great" fall upon "fighting in it," so the ruling is applied to it in general. The pronoun would not convey this.

[Section: The Expedition of Nakhla]

Then ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi was dispatched to Nakhla in Rajab, at the end of seventeen months after the Hijra, with twelve men from the Muhajirun, each two of them taking turns on a camel. They reached Batn Nakhla, lying in wait for a caravan of Quraysh. In this expedition ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh was named "Commander of the Believers." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had written him a letter and ordered him not to look at it until he had travelled two days, then to look at it. When he opened the letter he found in it: "When you have read this letter of mine, proceed until you alight at Nakhla between Mecca and al-Ta'if, and watch there for Quraysh, and bring us news of their affairs." He said: "I hear and obey." He informed his companions of this and told them that he would not compel them; whoever desired martyrdom should go forward, and whoever disliked death should return; as for himself, he would proceed. So they all went on. In the course of the journey Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas and ʿUtba ibn Ghazwan lost a camel that they were taking turns riding, so they stayed behind to search for it, while ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh went on until he alighted at Nakhla. A caravan of Quraysh passed by him, carrying raisins, leather, and merchandise, among them ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami, ʿUthman and Nawfal, the two sons of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughira, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, a client of the Banu al-Mughira. The Muslims consulted among themselves and said: "We are on the last day of Rajab, the sacred month. If we fight them, we violate the sacred month; and if we leave them tonight, they will enter the Haram." Then they agreed to engage them. One of them shot ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami and killed him, and they captured ʿUthman and al-Hakam, while Nawfal escaped. Then they came back with the caravan and the two captives, having set aside from it the fifth (khums), which was the first khums in Islam, the first person killed in Islam, and the first two captives in Islam. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disapproved of what they had done, and the insistence and denunciation of Quraysh intensified; they claimed that they had found a point of argument, saying: "Muhammad has made the sacred month lawful." This weighed heavily on the Muslims, until Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is great, but averting from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, (barring access to) the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it are greater with Allah; and fitnah is greater than killing﴾ [al-Baqara 2:217]. He, glorified be He, says: what you have denounced them for, though it is great, what you yourselves have committed of disbelief in Allah, of barring from His way and from His House, of expelling the Muslims who are its people from it, and of the polytheism you hold, and the fitnah that has arisen from you through it, is greater with Allah than their fighting in the sacred month. Most of the early scholars interpreted fitnah here as polytheism, as in His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqara 2:193]. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Then their fitnah was only that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am 6:23], meaning: the outcome of their polytheism and its end, the final result of their affair, was only that they disowned it and denied it.

Its real meaning is: polytheism that its holder calls others to and fights for, and which punishes whoever does not succumb to it. This is why it is said to them at the time of their punishment with the Fire and their fitnah in it: ﴿Taste your fitnah﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:14]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: your denial.

Its real meaning is: taste the ultimate end of your fitnah, its final outcome and the consequence of its affair, like His saying: ﴿Taste what you used to earn﴾ [al-Zumar 39:24]. Just as they tempted His servants to polytheism, they were tempted into the Fire, and it was said to them: "Taste your fitnah." From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10]. Fitnah here was interpreted as their torturing the believers and burning them with fire, but the word is more general than that. Its real meaning is: they tortured the believers so that they would be turned away from their religion. This is the fitnah attributed to the polytheists.

As for the fitnah which Allah the Exalted attributes to Himself, or which His Messenger attributes to Him, such as His saying: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others﴾ [al-An'am 6:53], and Musa's saying: ﴿It is none but Your fitnah; You send astray thereby whom You will and guide whom You will﴾ [al-A'raf 7:155], that is of another sense: it means trial, testing and affliction from Allah of His servants with good and evil, with blessings and calamities. This is one kind. The fitnah of the polytheists is another kind. The fitnah of the believer in his wealth, children and neighbour is yet another. The fitnah that He causes among the people of Islam, like the fitnah He caused between the companions of ʿAli and Muʿawiya, between the people of the Camel and Siffin, and among the Muslims until they fight one another and abandon one another, is another kind. This is the fitnah of which the Prophet ﷺ said: "There will be a fitnah in which the one sitting is better than the one standing, the one standing is better than the one walking, and the one walking is better than the one running." The hadiths of fitnah in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded withdrawal from the two groups refer to this fitnah.

Fitnah sometimes is intended to mean disobedience, as in His saying: ﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me leave and do not tempt me"﴾ [al-Tawba 9:49]. This was said by al-Jadd ibn Qays when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him to Tabuk; he said: "Grant me leave to stay behind and do not tempt me by exposing me to the daughters of the Banu al-Asfar, for I cannot be patient regarding them." He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Surely, in fitnah they have fallen﴾ [al-Tawba 9:49], meaning: they fell into the fitnah of hypocrisy and fled to it from the fitnah of the daughters of al-Asfar.

The purpose is this: Allah the Exalted judged between His allies and His enemies with justice and equity. He did not absolve His allies of committing sin by fighting in the sacred month; rather, He informed that it is great, and that what His enemies the polytheists are upon is greater and more grievous than merely fighting in the sacred month. Thus they deserve blame, reproach and punishment more. Especially since His allies were interpreting their fighting that way, or were negligent in a kind of negligence that Allah forgives them in light of what they did of tawhid, obedience, emigration with His Messenger, and preferring what is with Allah. They are, as it has been said:

"When the beloved commits one sin, his good qualities come with a thousand intercessors."

How then can he be compared with a hateful enemy who came with every ugliness and did not come with a single intercessor of good qualities?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 218:

Reflect, then, on how He made their hope dependent on their performing these acts of obedience.

The deluded said: "Those who neglect and waste the rights of God, who abandon His commands, who transgress against His servants, and who dare to violate His prohibitions, these are the ones who hope for God's mercy."

The secret of the matter: hope and good opinion of God are only sound when accompanied by the performance of the means that God's wisdom has prescribed in His law, His decree, His reward, and His generosity. The servant performs these means, then has good opinion of his Lord, and hopes that He will not leave him to them, and that He will make them lead to what benefits him, and will turn away whatever opposes them and nullify their effect.

Just as He, glorified is He, made hope for the people of righteous deeds, so too He made fear for the people of righteous deeds. Thus it is known that beneficial hope and fear are only those accompanied by action.

(Section)

Jihad is not complete except with higrah (emigration), and neither emigration nor jihad is complete except with faith, and those who hope for God's mercy are those who have fulfilled these three. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of God—those hope for the mercy of God, and God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Just as faith is obligatory upon every person, so two emigrations are obligatory upon him at all times: an emigration to God, mighty and majestic, through monotheism, sincerity, turning back (to Him), reliance, fear, hope, love, and repentance; and an emigration to His Messenger through following him, submitting to his command, affirming his report, and giving precedence to his command and report over the command and report of others: "Whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for a worldly gain he might obtain or a woman he might marry, his emigration is to what he emigrated for."

And He obligated upon him the struggle against his own self for the sake of God, and the struggle against his Satan. All of this is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) in which no one can substitute for another.

As for fighting the disbelievers and hypocrites, it may suffice that some of the community undertake it if the purpose of jihad is achieved by them.

[Section: The difference between hope (raja') and wishful thinking (tamanni)]

The difference between hope and wishful thinking: hope occurs together with exerting effort and expending one's utmost strength in undertaking the means of success and triumph.

Wishful thinking is the soul's talk of attaining that while neglecting the means that lead to it. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of God—those hope for the mercy of God﴾.

So, glorified is He, He limited the hope with its two wings to these alone.

And the deluded said: "Those who wasted His commands, committed His prohibitions, followed what angers Him, and avoided what pleases Him—those hope for His mercy." This is no strange thing from the delusion of the soul and Satan toward them. Hope in a servant whose heart is filled with faith in God and the Last Day, when what God has promised of His honor and Paradise is set before his eyes, the heart stretches out inclining toward that, out of longing for it and eagerness for it, like one who stretches his neck toward a desired object that has come before his eyes.

The sign of true hope is that the one who hopes fears losing the Paradise and losing his share of it through abandoning what he fears might come between him and entering it. His likeness is that of a man who proposed to a noble woman of rank and honor to her family. When the time of the contract came, with the gathering of the notables and great men and the man's arrival at the gathering, he was informed on the evening of that day so he could prepare to attend, for the woman and the great people would see him. So he set about preparing, adorning and beautifying himself, trimmed the excess of his hair, cleansed and perfumed himself, put on his finest clothes, and went to that house, guarding himself on his way against every filth, pollution, and trace that might touch him, even dust and smoke and whatever is less than that. When he reached the door, its master welcomed him and seated him at the head of the house on the carpets and cushions, and eyes looked at him and honor was directed to him from every side. But if he had gone, after taking this adornment, and sat in the garbage heaps, rolled and smeared himself in them, and filth from dung and dirt stained his body and clothes, entering his hair, skin, and garments, then came in that state to that house, intending to enter for the promise that had been made to her, the doorkeeper would have risen against him with beating, expulsion, and removal, and driven him away from its door and path, so he returned bewildered and humiliated.

The first is the state of the one who hopes, and this is the state of the one who wishes. If you wish, picture the two men's situation with a king who is among the most jealous of people, the most trustworthy, and the best in dealings, such that no one's right is lost before him, and he deals with people from behind a screen that no one sees, while his merchandise, wealth, trade goods, male and female slaves are openly displayed in his house to those who deal with him. Two men entered upon him. One of them dealt with him in truthfulness, trustworthiness, and sincere counsel, never having been found to cheat, betray, or deceive; he sold him all his goods and conducted himself with the king's servants and slave-girls as he ought to. Whenever he came to him with merchandise, he chose for him the best and most beloved of goods, and if he made it with his own hand he exerted his utmost to beautify and refine it, making what was hidden of it better than what was apparent. He received the supplies from whoever he was commanded to receive them from, and complied with what the envoy between him and the king commanded him regarding the measure of what he was to make, its description, form, shape, time, and all its affairs. The other, whenever he entered, came with the basest goods he could find, not purifying them from adulteration, nor giving sincere counsel about them, nor relying in their effect on what the interpreter had conveyed from the king and the envoy between him and the craftsmen and merchants; rather he made them according to his own desire.

Despite this, he would betray the king in his house while he was absent from his sight. No desire appeared without him acting on it, no sanctity of the king was left without his gazing at it and striving to corrupt it, and nothing that angers the king was left without his committing it whenever he was able. They continued in this for a period. Then it was said that the king would appear that day to those who dealt with him, to call them to account and give them their rights. The two men stood before him, and he dealt with each according to what he deserved.

So reflect on these two examples, for the reality corresponds to them. The one who truly hopes, when Paradise has become the object before his eyes, and his hope and aspiration have stretched his heart toward it, strives for it with its striving; for hope is the stretching and inclination of the heart. His hope is realized by complete preparation, fear of loss, and taking precautions.

Its origin is from withdrawal (al-tanahhi), and raja' al-bi'r means its side, and arja' al-sama' means its sides. The stretching of the heart toward the beloved, cut off from what would sever it from him, is a withdrawal from the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah) and its causes and what it calls to. This stretching, inclination, and fear is a characteristic of the tranquil soul (al-nafs al-mutma'innah). When the heart's insight is opened and it sees the Hereafter and what God has prepared there for the people of His obedience and the people of His disobedience, it fears and departs swiftly toward God and the Abode of the Hereafter. Before that it had been at peace with the self, and the self is the mother of desires and of the world. When the veil of the self is lifted from it, it departs swiftly and leaves its neighborhood, seeking the neighborhood of the Mighty, the Merciful, in the Gardens of Bliss. From here, every fearful one becomes hopeful and every hopeful one becomes fearful, and the name of one is applied to the other, for the hopeful one's heart is near to the state of the fearful one. This hopeful one has withdrawn his heart from dwelling with the self and Satan, departing toward God, a banner from Paradise having been raised for him; so he hastens toward it, his whole heart stretched out toward it.

And this fearful one flees from their neighborhood, seeking refuge in God from being imprisoned by them in their prison in this world, for he would be imprisoned with them after death and on the Day of Resurrection, since a man is with his companion in this world and the next. When he heard the threat, he departed from the neighborhood of the evil neighbor in both abodes, so he was given the name of the fearful.
