Abraham, in order to force this counter-argument to its logical conclusion, required him to manipulate the movement of the sun from a direction other than the one from which God brings it, if he (the interlocutor) claimed to be equal to God in giving life and causing death.

So if he was truthful, let him manipulate the sun in a way that would validate his claim. This is not a transition from one proof to a clearer proof, as some of the theologians (nuzzar) have claimed; rather, it is a binding of the claimant to the consequences of his argument, if it is sound.

(Benefit)

In a hadith: "Indeed, in allusions (ma'arid) there is a sufficient alternative to lying." Abraham, the Friend (al-Khalil), used an allusion with the tyrant when he said of his wife, "She is my sister." The Prophet ﷺ used an allusion with a man who asked him on the road, "Who are you people?" and he said, "We are from water." Abu Bakr (al-Siddiq) used an allusion with someone who kept asking him on the road of the migration, "Who is this with you?" and he said, "A guide who guides me to the way."

(Section)

He said: The flight of the elite from report to witnessing, from traces to origins, and from portions (of worldly gain) to detachment.

He means: they are not content for their faith to be based merely on report, until they ascend from it to witnessing what is reported. So they seek to ascend from knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqīn) by report to the eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqīn) by witnessing, just as Abraham the Friend of God, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, asked of his Lord when he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest.﴾ Thus Abraham sought that certainty become direct vision and the known become witnessed. This is the meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) expressed by doubt in his saying: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," where he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ Yet neither the Prophet (ﷺ) nor Abraham doubted; far be it from them both. He merely expressed this meaning in this phrasing.

This is one of the opinions concerning the hadith.

There is a second opinion: that it is in the form of negation, meaning that Abraham did not doubt when he said what he said, and neither did we. This view is also sound: if what he asked for had been due to doubt, we would have had more right to it than he did. But he did not ask out of doubt; he asked for tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah).

The levels are three. Knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqīn) is obtained from report; then the reality of what is reported becomes manifest to the heart or the sight, until knowledge of it becomes eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqīn); then one engages with it and is immersed in it, and it becomes truth of certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn). Our knowledge of Paradise and Hell now is knowledge of certainty. When Paradise is brought near to the righteous at the place of standing, and Hell is made manifest to the deviators, and they witness both directly, that is eye of certainty, as God the Exalted said: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire; then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty.﴾

When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, that is truth of certainty.

This verse serves as an explanation and clarification of the multiplication that Allah grants to the one who lends. Allah set forth this parable to bring the image of multiplication before the minds, through this single grain buried in the earth that produced seven ears, each ear containing a hundred grains, so that the heart looks at this multiplication with its insight just as the eye looks at these ears that came from one grain. Thus the witness of sight joins the witness of faith and the Qur'an, so the faith of the one who spends grows stronger and his soul becomes generous in giving.

Consider how the word for ear (*sunbulah*) is made plural in this verse as *sanabil*, which is the plural of abundance, since the context is one of increase and multiplication. In the verse ﴿and seven green ears and others dry﴾ [Yusuf: 43] it is made plural as *sunbulat*, the plural of paucity, because seven is a small number and there is no reason for emphasizing abundance.

As for His words, ﴿and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾, it has been said: the meaning is that Allah multiplies this multiplication for whom He wills, not for every spender. Rather, He singles out with His mercy whom He wills, and this is due to the variation in the states of spending itself, in the qualities and circumstances of the spender, in the intensity of need, the magnitude of benefit, and the suitability of the place (of expenditure).

It has also been said: ﴿and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ beyond that, so it is not restricted to seven hundred, but He exceeds this measure in multiplication to many times over.

The interpretation of the verse has differed. It has been said: ﴿the example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain﴾ (i.e., the example of the spending itself is like a grain).

And it has been said: the example of those who spend in the way of Allah is like the sower of a grain, so that the likened matches the likened-to.

Here there are four matters: the spender, the spending, the sower, and the seed. Allah mentioned from each side the more important of its two parts. From the side of the likened (the spenders) He mentioned the spender, since the purpose is to mention his condition and his affair, and He omitted mention of the spending because the wording points to it. From the side of the likened-to He mentioned the seed, since it is the place in which the multiplication occurred, and He left out mention of the sower because the loan does not depend on mentioning him.

Reflect on this eloquence, this rhetorical excellence, and this conciseness that contains the ultimate of clarity.

This is common in the parables of the Qur'an; indeed, most of them come in this pattern. Then He concluded the verse with two of His Most Beautiful Names that correspond to its context, namely *al-Wasi'* (the All-Encompassing) and *al-'Alim* (the All-Knowing). So the servant should not find this multiplication improbable, nor should his breast be constricted from it. For the One who multiplies, glory be to Him, is vast in giving, vast in wealth, and vast in bounty. Yet one should not think that the vastness of His giving necessitates that it be realized for every spender, for He is All-Knowing of who is suited to this multiplication and deserving of it, and who is not deserving of it nor suited to it. His generosity and bounty, exalted be He, do not contradict His wisdom; rather, He places His bounty in its proper places according to His vastness and mercy, and withholds it from those who are not fit for it by His wisdom and knowledge.

(Section)

Allah, glory be to Him, likened the spending of the one who spends in His way, whether by this is meant jihad or all the paths of good in every act of piety, to one who sows a seed, from which each grain produced seven ears, each ear containing a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies beyond that for whom He wills, according to the state of the spender, his faith, his sincerity, his excellence, the benefit of his spending, its quantity, and its being placed where it belongs. The reward of spending varies according to what is in the heart of faith, sincerity, and steadfastness at the time of spending. Steadfastness means giving out wealth with a firm heart, whose breast has been expanded to give it, whose soul has consented to it, and which has departed from his heart just as it departs from his hand. He is steady of heart at the time of giving, neither anxious nor distressed, nor one whose soul pursues (the wealth) with trembling hand and heart. And the reward varies according to the benefit of the spending, its avenues, its placement in the right places, and the goodness and purity of the spender.

Under this parable is a point of fiqh (jurisprudence): Allah, glory be to Him, likened spending to sowing.

The one who spends his good wealth for Allah alone and not for anyone else is like one who sows his wealth in fertile soil. Its yield depends on the seed, the goodness of the soil, the tending of the seed with watering, and the removal of weeds and foreign plants from it. When these matters come together and no fire burns the crop nor does any calamity strike it, it comes forth like mountains, and its example is like a garden on a *rabwah*, which is an elevated place where the garden is exposed to the sun and winds, so the trees grow there in the most complete growth. Then a great, continuous rain falls upon it, which waters and nurtures it, and it yields its fruit double what other gardens yield, because of that heavy downpour. But if a heavy downpour does not reach it, then a *tall*, which is a light rain of small drops, suffices it because of the nobility of its place of growth; it grows and develops under the shade. Moreover, mention of the two kinds, the heavy rain and the light rain, is an indication of the two kinds of spending, the abundant and the little.

Among people, some spend in heavy downpour and others spend in light drizzle. And Allah does not waste the weight of an atom. But if something befalls this doer that drowns his deeds and nullifies his good works, he is like a man ﴿who has a garden of date palms and grapevines, beneath which rivers flow, for whom are all kinds of fruits, and old age has struck him while he has weak offspring, and a whirlwind containing fire strikes it and it is burned﴾. So when the Day of accounting of deeds and securing of rewards comes, this doer finds his deed has been struck by what befell the owner of this garden. His regret at that time will be greater than this one's regret over his garden.

This is a parable Allah set forth regarding the regret of the loss of a blessing at the time of great need for it, despite its great worth and benefit. The one whose garden was lost has been struck by old age and weakness, so he is most in need of his blessing. Moreover, he has weak offspring who cannot benefit him nor manage his affairs; rather, they are his dependents. So his need for his blessing at that time is at its greatest, because of his weakness and the weakness of his offspring. How then will the state of this man be if he had a great orchard containing all kinds of fruits and produce, the most noble and beneficial fruits being those of the date palm and the grape? Its yield would sustain him and his offspring. Then one morning he finds it completely burned, like a harvested field. What regret could be greater than his?

Ibn 'Abbas said: this is the parable of one who is concluded with corruption at the end of his life.

Mujahid said: this is the parable of one who neglects obedience to Allah until he dies.

Al-Suddi said: this is the parable of the one who shows off in his spending, who spends for other than Allah, whose benefit is cut off from him at the time he most needs it.

One day 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked the Companions about this verse, and they said: Allah knows best. 'Umar became angry and said: say "we know" or "we do not know." Ibn 'Abbas said: there is something in my heart about it, O Commander of the Faithful. He said: speak, my nephew, and do not belittle yourself. He said: it is a parable for a deed. He said: for what deed? He said: for a wealthy man who does good deeds, then Allah sends Satan to him, and he works at sins until he drowns all his deeds.

Al-Hasan said: by Allah, this is a parable that few people among mankind understand. It is an elderly man whose body has weakened and whose children have multiplied, who is most in need of his garden. Indeed, by Allah, one of you is most in need of his deeds when the world is cut off from him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 262:

This is an explanation of the good loan (al-qard al-hasan): what is it? It is that it be "in the way of Allah" (fi sabil Allah), that is, seeking His pleasure and the paths that lead to it. Among the most beneficial of these paths is the path of jihad. "The way of Allah" is both specific and general, and the specific is a part of the general. And it is that one does not follow one's charity with reminders (mann) or harm (adha). Reminding is of two kinds.

The first: reminding with the heart without expressing it with the tongue. If this does not nullify the charity, it stems from a deficiency in witnessing Allah's favor upon him in giving wealth, in others being deprived of it, and in His granting him success in giving and preventing others from it. So the favor belongs to Allah upon him in every respect. How, then, can his heart witness a favor from someone other than Him?

The second kind: that he reminds the recipient with his tongue, transgressing against the one to whom he has done good, showing him that he has bestowed a favor upon him, that he has made him obligated to him, and placing the burden of obligation around his neck. He says: "Did I not give you such and such?" and enumerates his benefactions to him. Sufyan said: "He says, 'I gave you, but you did not thank me.'"

Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad said: "My father used to say: 'If you give a man something and you see that your greeting weighs heavily on him, then withhold your greeting from him.'" And they (the early scholars) used to say: "If you do a favor, forget it; and if someone does a favor for you, do not forget it." And regarding this it has been said:

"And indeed a man who gives me a favor and reminds me of it once is (as) miserly."

It has also been said: "Safwan (the hard, smooth stone) is one who gives to his requester and reminds him; and one who withholds his gift and is stingy." Allah forbade His servants to remind others of a favor and singled it out as an attribute of Himself, because from the servants it is a cause of distress and reproach, while from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, it is bounty and reminder.

Moreover, He is the true Benefactor in reality, and the servants are intermediaries; He is the One who truly bestows favor upon His servant. Also, reminding of favors is an enslaving, a breaking, and a humiliation of the one upon whom the favor is reminded, and servitude and abasement are fit only for Allah.

Also, reminding of favor is that the giver witnesses that he is the lord of bounty and benefaction, and that he is the patron of blessing and its bestower, when in reality this belongs to none but Allah. Also, the one who reminds of his gift witnesses himself as elevated above the taker, superior over him, independent of him, mighty, and witnesses the taker's humiliation, his need for him, and his poverty; and this is not fitting for a servant. Also, the giver has entrusted his reward to Allah, and Allah has returned to him manifold what he gave, so the compensation for what he gave remains with Allah. What right, then, does he have over the taker? So if he reminds him of it, he has wronged him a clear wrong, and claimed that his right is upon him.

From here, and Allah knows best, his charity was nullified by reminding, for his exchange and dealing were with Allah, and the compensation for that charity was with Him. He was not content with that, and sought compensation from the taker and dealing with him. So when he reminds the one he gave to, his exchange with Allah and his dealing with Him are nullified. Reflect on these counsels from Allah to His servants and His guidance to His lordship and His sole divinity, and that He nullifies the deeds of whoever contends with Him in any part of His lordship and divinity: there is no god but Him, and no lord besides Him.

By His saying: ﴿Then they do not follow what they have spent with reminder or harm﴾, He draws attention to the fact that reminder and harm, even if they come after the charity and their time is prolonged, harm their owner and deprive him of the intended goal of the spending. Had He used the conjunction "wa" and said, "and they do not follow what they spent with reminder and harm," it would have implied restricting this to the state (of the giving). And if reminder and delayed harm nullify the effect of spending and prevent reward, then the accompanying (reminder and harm) is more deserving of this and more appropriate.

Observe how the predicate here is stripped of the particle "fa'" (then): ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾, while in His other saying, ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and openly, for them is their reward with their Lord﴾, it is joined with "fa'". The "fa'" that enters upon the predicate of a subject that is a relative pronoun or a descriptive conveys the meaning of condition and consequence, and that the reward is due by virtue of the attribute or relative clause contained in the subject. Here, since the context calls for specifying the exclusive party entitled to the reward and no other, the predicate is stripped of "fa'". The meaning is that the one who spends his wealth for Allah, without reminder or harm, is the one who deserves the stated reward, not the one who spends for other than Allah and reminds and harms with his spending. So this is not a context of condition and consequence, but a context of specifying who is deserving and no other.

In the other verse, He mentions spending by night and day, secretly and openly. He mentions the generality of times and the generality of states, and brings "fa'" in the predicate to indicate that spending at any time it occurs, by night or day, and in any state it occurs, secretly or openly, is a cause of reward in every condition. So the servant should hasten to it and should not postpone it beyond its time and state, nor delay the night's spending until the day, nor the day's spending until night, nor wait with open spending for a time of secrecy, nor with secret spending for a time of openness. For his spending, at whatever time and in whatever state it occurs, is a cause of his reward and recompense. So reflect on these secrets in the Qur'an; perhaps you will attain them as they pass by you in the exegeses. The favor and grace belong to Allah alone, with no partner.

[Chapter: Showing-off, reminding and harm nullify deeds]

If there arises, among these charitable deeds, what nullifies them, such as reminding, harm and showing-off, then showing-off prevents them from being established as a cause of reward, and reminding and harm nullify the reward for which they were a cause. The likeness of their doer and the nullification of his deed is like the likeness of Safwan, which is the smooth stone, upon which there is dust, and a heavy downpour (wabil, the intense rain) strikes it, leaving it bare with nothing upon it. Reflect on the parts of this eloquent parable and how they correspond to the parts of what it depicts, and you will know the greatness and majesty of the Qur'an. For the stone corresponds to the heart of this showing-off, reminding and harmful person: his heart, in its hardness against faith, sincerity and goodness, is like the stone, and the deed he performed for other than Allah is like the dust upon that stone. The hardness and firmness of what lies beneath prevents it from growing and remaining when the downpour descends. So it has no connected substance that receives water and produces herbage.

Likewise, the heart of the showing-off has no steadfastness at the downpour of the command, the prohibition, the decree and the divine destiny. When the downpour of revelation descends upon it, that little dust that was upon it is uncovered, and what lies beneath appears as a bare stone with no growth in it.

This is a parable that Allah, the Glorified, has struck for the deed and spending of the showing-off, who on the Day of Resurrection cannot obtain the reward of any part of it, at a time when he is most in need of it. And success is from Allah.

Ibn al-Qayyim, Commentary on Surah 2, verse 263:

He informed that "the kind word" (al-qawl al-ma'ruf) is that which hearts recognize and do not reject.

"Forgiveness" (al-maghfirah), which is pardoning those who have wronged you, is better than "charity followed by injury" (al-sadaqah bi'l-adha). The kind word is a form of goodness (ihsan). Charity in the form of speech, and forgiveness, which is goodness by refraining from censure and retaliation, are two kinds of goodness. Charity accompanied by injury is a good deed combined with that which nullifies it, and there is no doubt that two good deeds are better than one nullified good deed. Included in "forgiveness" is forgiving the beggar if some rudeness and harm toward you arose from him because of your refusal; his pardoning him is then better than giving him charity and hurting him. This is according to the more well-known of the two opinions regarding the verse. The second opinion: "forgiveness" refers to forgiveness from Allah, meaning that forgiveness from Allah for you, by means of the kind word and the gracious refusal, is better than charity followed by injury. There is also a third opinion: "forgiveness" and pardon from the beggar, when he is refused and the one asked is excused, is better than that he should obtain charity for himself which is followed by injury. The clearest of these opinions is the first, followed by the second, while the third is very weak, because the address is only to the giver who is asked, not to the beggar who takes. The meaning is: speaking kindly to him, overlooking and pardoning, is better for you than giving to him and hurting him. Then He concluded the verse with two attributes fitting what it contained, so He said: "And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing" (wallahu ghaniyyun halim), and in it there are two meanings.

The first: Allah is free of need from you; nothing of your charities reaches Him. The greater share of benefit in charity belongs to you, its benefit returning to you and not to Him, glorified and exalted is He. So how would one who gives charity boast of his expenditure and injure, when Allah is completely free of need of it and of everything other than Him? And despite this, He is Forbearing, since He does not hasten to punish the one who boasts. Within this is a warning and admonition.

The second meaning: He, glorified and exalted, despite His complete freedom from need in every respect, is described with forbearance and pardon and overlooking, along with His abundant giving and bountiful charity. So how would one of you injure with his boasting, when his giving is small and his means are meager and poor? Then he said:

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 264:

So this verse includes the report that stinginess-reminders (al-mann) and harm (al-adha) nullify charity, and this is evidence that a good deed may be nullified by an evil deed, along with the words of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet or speak to him loudly as you speak to one another, lest your deeds be nullified while you are unaware.﴾

The discussion of this issue has already been presented at the beginning of this treatise, so there is no need to repeat it.

It may be said that the reminders and harm that accompany the charity are what nullify it, without extending to what comes after it; however, there is nothing in the wording that indicates this restriction, and the context indicates that it is nullified by them absolutely. It may also be said that the example of one who shows off, who does not believe in God and the Last Day, indicates that the nullifying reminder and harm are those that accompany the charity, like showing off and disbelief, since showing off, if it comes after the deed, does not nullify it. This is answered in two ways:

The first: the comparison is made in the state in which the deed is nullified, namely the state of the one who shows off and the one who reminds and harms, in that each of the two nullifies the deed.

The second: showing off (riya') occurs only together with the deed, because it is a form of ru'ya (seeing), whose companion acts so that people may see his deed, so it is not delayed. This differs from reminders and harm, which may occur both together with the charity and later, and their delay is more frequent than their accompaniment.

As for His words, «like the one who spends», it may mean "like the nullification of the one who spends," so that the nullification of one is compared to the nullification of another; or it may mean "do not be like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people," so that the spender is compared to the spender.

As for His words, «so his example», meaning the example of this spender whose reward for his spending has become void, it is like a smooth rock (safwan), which is a bare stone, and there are two opinions about it: one says it is singular; the other says it is the plural of safwa. "Upon it is dust, and a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare," meaning the rain (wabil) is intense rain, leaving it smooth (saldan), which is one with nothing upon it of plants or anything else. This is among the most eloquent and finest of examples, for it includes the comparison of the heart of this spender who shows off, whose spending did not issue from faith in God and the Last Day, to the rock, because of its hardness and firmness and the absence of benefit from it; and it includes the comparison of the trace of charity that clings to it to the dust that clung to that rock, and the heavy rain that removed that dust from the rock and took it away, by the obstacle that nullified his charity and removed it, just as heavy rain takes away the dust that is on the rock, leaving it bare, so the spender is unable to obtain anything of its reward, because it has been nullified and removed. There is also another meaning in it: that the one who spends for other than God apparently does a deed for which a reward is recorded and which grows for him, just as the grain that, when sown in good soil, produces seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains; but behind this spending there is a barrier that prevents its growth and increase, just as beneath the soil there is a rock that prevents the seed sown in it from sprouting. So it neither grows nor yields anything.

This is a parable of those whose spending comes from sincerity and truthfulness. For seeking the pleasure of Allah (glorified is He) is sincerity (ikhlas), and firming the soul (at-tathbit) is truthfulness (sidq) in giving. The one who spends faces two afflictions when he spends, and if he is saved from them, his parallel is what this verse mentions.

The first: that he seeks, through his spending, praise, commendation, or some worldly aim of his. This is the state of most spenders.

The second affliction: the weakness of his soul, its laziness and hesitation. Will he act or not?

The first affliction disappears by seeking the pleasure of Allah.

The second affliction disappears through firming (at-tathbit), for firming the soul strengthens it, empowers it, and drives it forward to give. This is its truthfulness, and seeking the pleasure of Allah, desiring His Face alone, is its sincerity. When the source of spending is free of these, its likeness is that of a garden (jannah), which is a densely treed orchard, and he is sheltered by it, meaning concealed by it, not an empty bare plain.

The garden is "on a height" (bi-rabwah), which is an elevated place, because it is more complete than a garden in the lowlands and depressions, for when it is raised it is exposed to the air and winds, and it lies in the sun at its rising, its zenith, and its setting. Thus its fruit is riper, finer, better, and more abundant, since fruit grows sweeter and more wholesome through winds and sunlight, unlike fruit that grows in shade. And when the garden is in an elevated place, it is feared only to lack water and moisture. So He said, Most High: "a heavy rain" (wabil), which is the intense rain of great quantity, so it yielded its fruit and gave its blessing, producing double its fruit compared to other gardens, or double what it used to yield because of that heavy rain. This is the state of the foremost, those brought near.

"But if heavy rain does not reach it, then a light rain (tall)" is less than heavy rain. It suffices it, due to the nobility of its growing place and the goodness of its planting; it is content with the light rain to bring forth its blessing. This is the state of the righteous (al-abrar) and the moderate in spending, and they are of ranks before Allah. The owners of heavy rain are the highest in rank, and they are those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and openly, and prefer others over themselves even though they themselves are in need. The people of the light rain are their moderate ones.

So He illustrated the state of the two categories and their deeds by a garden on a height, and their abundant spending by heavy rain and light rain. Just as each of the two rains requires the purification of the garden's fruit and its like by multiples, so too their spending, whether abundant or little, after it issued from seeking the pleasure of Allah and firming of their souls, is pure, growing, and multiplied before Allah.

There is disagreement about the meaning of "two-fold" (di'fayn). It was said: "di'f" of a thing is its double, and "di'fayn" is its double plus itself, i.e., twice the amount (its equal added to it).

It was also said: "di'fu" of a thing is its double, and "di'fayhi" is three times it, and "thalathat di'afihi" is four times it; each time it increases by "di'f," it increases by an equal amount. What led this speaker to this view is his avoidance of equating the meaning of the singular and dual forms, for he saw that the "di'f" of a thing is its equal plus it, so when it increases to its equal it becomes two equals, and these are the "di'f." Thus if it were said, "lahā di'fān" (for her are two-fold), there would be no difference between singular and dual. So for him, "di'fān" are two equals added to the original, and it follows from this that three times it would be three equals added to the original, and so on endlessly.

The correct view is that "di'fayn" are only two equals: the original and its equal. This is indicated by His saying, "So it yielded its produce two-fold" (fa-ataat ukulaha di'fayn), meaning two equals, and His saying, "Her punishment shall be doubled, di'fayn," meaning two equals.

For this reason He said regarding good deeds: "We shall give her her reward twice (marratayn)."

As for what they supposed about equating the meaning of the singular and dual, it is a misconception arising from the assumption that "di'f" is the equal together with the original; this is not so. Rather, the equal has two considerations: if considered alone, it is "di'f"; if considered together with its counterpart, they are "di'fayn." And Allah knows best.

There is disagreement about the grammatical governing of His saying "fa-tall" (then a light rain):

It was said: it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning "and light rain suffices it."

It was said: it is a predicate whose subject is omitted, its estimate being "so what waters it and reaches it is light rain."

The pronoun in "asabaha" (it reached it) may refer either to the garden or to the height, and these two are mutually implicit.

(Benefit)

If this garden, which is in a lofty place where the sun and winds are not screened from it, and which was struck by heavy rain, so that it yielded its fruit double what others yield, is considered beautiful by reason and sense, then likewise is the spending of one who spends his wealth for the sake of Allah, not for any reward from creatures nor for thanks, but with firmness from his own soul and strength in spending, who does not bring out the expenditure while his heart trembles at its leaving, his hands shake, his heart weakens, and he falters at the time of spending. This is unlike the spending of one who has firmness and strength.

Since people are divided in spending into these two categories, the parable of the spending of the one with sincerity, strength, and firmness is like the heavy rain, and the parable of the other's spending is like the light rain, which is a weak rainfall. This is according to the abundance or scarcity of spending, and the completeness or weakness of sincerity, strength, and certainty in it. Do you not see that He, glorified is He, drew the attention of minds to what is commendable in this and to the ugliness of the first one's conduct?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 266:

Almighty Allah alerted minds to the ugliness of evil deeds, which nullify the reward of good deeds, and He likened them to the condition of an elderly man who has weak offspring, so that he fears for them destitution and for himself as well, and who has a garden that is the source of his livelihood and the livelihood of his offspring, containing date palms, grapes, and all kinds of fruits. Then it (the garden) is struck, at the time when he is most in need of it and most hopeful in it, by a fierce fire that burns it up. Thus He alerted minds to the fact that the ugliness of sins that drown acts of obedience is like the ugliness of this condition. In this way ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them, explained it, regarding a wealthy man who worked in obedience to Allah for a period of time; then Allah sent Satan to him, and he committed sins until he drowned his deeds. Al-Bukhari mentioned it in his Sahih.

Do you not see that He alerted minds to the ugliness of disobedience after obedience, and struck this parable for its ugliness?

(Section)

Al-Hasan said: This is a parable, by Allah, few among people understand it: an elderly man whose body has grown weak and whose children have multiplied, and who is most in need of his garden. Indeed, by Allah, one of you is most in need of his deeds when the world has cut itself off from him.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, on the authority of ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: ʿUmar once asked the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, "About what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms...﴾ [the verse]?"

They said: "Allah knows best." ʿUmar became angry and said: "Say we know or we do not know." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There is something in my heart, O Commander of the Faithful." ʿUmar said: "Speak, O my nephew, and do not belittle yourself." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was given as a parable for a deed." ʿUmar said: "What deed?"

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "For the deed of a man who worked in obedience to Allah, then Allah sent Satan to him, and he committed sins until he burned up his deeds."

As for His saying, ﴿Would any of you like...﴾, it is expressed in the form of a denying interrogative, which is more emphatic than a negation or a prohibition and more subtle in effect, just as you see another doing a repugnant act and you say to him: "No intelligent person would do this; would one who fears Allah and the Last Abode do this?"

And His saying ﴿any of you﴾ uses the singular form because it implies a general denial, just as you say: "Would anyone who has any good do this?" and this is more emphatic in denial than saying "Would they [plural] like..."

His saying ﴿would like﴾ (yawaddu) is more emphatic in denial than if it had said "would want" (yuriddu), because loving and wishing for this condition described is more repugnant and more denied than merely desiring it.

His saying, ﴿to have a garden of date palms and grapes﴾, singled out these two kinds of fruit because they are the noblest kinds of fruit and the most beneficial, for from them come sustenance, food, medicine, drink, and fruit, both sweet and sour, and they are eaten fresh and dried, and their benefits are very numerous.

There has been disagreement about which of the two is more beneficial and superior.

One group preferred the date palm, another group preferred the grape, and each group cited arguments for its view, which we have mentioned in another place.

The decisive word is that this differs according to the lands, for Allah, glorified and exalted, has established the custom that the dominance of one of them does not occur where the dominance of the other occurs.

In the land where the date palm dominates, grapes do not flourish or grow abundantly, because grapes only grow in soft, loose, moderate land, not overly fertile; there they grow and multiply. As for the date palm, its growth and abundance are in hot, saline land, which does not suit grapes. So the palm in its land and place is more beneficial and superior than grapes there.

And grapes in their land and mineral soil are superior to palms there. And Allah knows best.

The purpose is that these two kinds are the best and most noble of fruits.

So the garden containing them is the best of gardens, and despite this, rivers flow beneath this garden. That is more perfect for it and greater in its worth. Yet it lacks none of the desirable kinds of fruit; rather, in it are fruits of every kind, but its main and intended produce is the date palms and grapes. Thus there is no contradiction between it being of date palms and grapes, and in it are fruits of every kind.

A similar example is His saying: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: We granted one of them two gardens of grapes, and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them cultivated land (32). Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth within them (33). And he had fruit﴾.

It has been said that the "fruits" in the verse of al-Kahf and in the verse of al-Baqarah are meant as benefits and wealth, but the context indicates that they are the well-known fruits and nothing else, because of His saying in al-Baqarah: "He has in it of every kind of fruit." Then He said: ﴿Then a whirlwind containing fire struck it﴾, i.e., the garden, ﴿and it was burned﴾. In al-Kahf: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin], so he began to turn his palms over regarding what he had spent upon it, while it lay in ruins on its trellises﴾. And that is none but the fruits of the garden.

Then He said: ﴿And old age has overtaken him﴾. This points to the intensity of his need for his garden and the attachment of his heart to it in several respects.

The first: his age has advanced beyond earning, trade, and the like.

The second: a son of Adam's greed intensifies in old age.

The third: he has offspring, so he is eager to preserve his garden for his own need and the need of his offspring.

The fourth: they are weak, so they are a burden upon him, unable to benefit him with their strength or their activity.

The fifth: his expenditure upon them is because of their weakness and incapacity.

This is the utmost extent of the heart's attachment to this garden, because of its value in itself and the intensity of his and his offspring's need for it. When you picture this condition and this need, how great will be this man's calamity when a whirlwind strikes his garden, a wind that spins on the earth then rises through the layers of the air like a column, and in it is fire, which passes over that garden, burns it, and reduces it to ashes. So, by Allah, al-Hasan spoke truly: "This is a parable, few among people understand it." For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, drew attention to the greatness of this parable and urged hearts to reflect upon it because of their great need for it, when He said: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, that you might reflect﴾.

If the intelligent person reflects upon this parable and makes it the focus of his heart, it would suffice and cure him. Likewise, when a servant performs acts of obedience to Allah and then follows them with what nullifies and burns them of acts of disobedience to Allah, he is like the whirlwind with fire that burns the garden which he planted through his obedience and righteous deeds.

Had the one who disobeys Allah after obeying Him truly conceived this meaning and contemplated it as it should be, his soul would not have enticed him, by Allah, to burn and waste his righteous deeds. But his knowledge must be absent from him at the time of disobedience, and for this reason he deserves the name of ignorance. Everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant.

If it is asked: is the waw in His saying ﴿And old age has overtaken him﴾ a waw of circumstance (al-hal) or a waw of conjunction (al-ʿatf)? And if it is a conjunction, what does it conjoin what follows it to?

I say: there are two views.

One: it is the waw of circumstance, which al-Zamakhshari chose, and the meaning is: "Would any of you like to have a garden whose condition is such and such, while he is old and his offspring are weak?"

The second: that it is a conjunction upon the meaning, for the verb of wishing, which is His saying ﴿Would any of you like﴾, is often used for the past. So the meaning is: "Would he like that he had a garden of date palms and grapes, and old age had overtaken him, and what has been described befell it?"

Consider how Allah, glorified, struck the parable for the hypocritical spender whose spending did not proceed from faith: it is like a smooth rock with dust upon it; nothing at all grows upon it, rather its seed is lost, wasted, because of his lack of faith and sincerity. Then He struck the parable for one who worked in obedience to Allah, sincere in his intention for Allah, then there befell him what nullified his reward: a garden that is among the finest and most pleasant and most blossoming gardens. Then He let loose upon it a fiery whirlwind that burned it. For this one something grew for him and his deed bore fruit, then it burned it; but the first one never obtained anything that the fire could seize.

Blessed is He who made His speech a life for hearts, a cure for breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (Tafsir Ibn al-Qayyim) on Surah 2, verse 267:

He, glorified is He, attributes the earning (kasb) to them, although He is the Creator of their actions, because it is their act that subsists in them; and He ascribes the bringing forth (ikhraj) to Himself, because it is not an act of theirs, nor is it within their power. Thus He ascribes to them what is within their capacity and ascribes to Himself its effect, over which they have no power. Within this is a refutation of those who equate the two kinds and who strip the servant of his power, his action and his agency altogether. And He, glorified is He, singled out these two kinds, namely what comes forth from the earth and what is acquired through trade, over other kinds of livestock. This is either in terms of reality, since these were the greater part of the wealth of the people at that time.

For the Muhajirun were people of trade and earning, and the Ansar were people of tillage and cultivation. He singled out these two kinds for mention because of their need for an explanation of their rulings and because of their general prevalence. Or it is because they are the roots of wealth, and everything else arises from them and originates from them. For earning (kasb) encompasses all trades in their various kinds and types, including clothing, food, slaves, animals, tools, goods, and all else that trade involves. And what comes forth from the earth encompasses its grains, its fruits, its treasure (rikaz) and its minerals. These two are the roots of wealth and the most prevalent of wealth among the people of the earth, so mentioning them was more important.

Then He said: ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it to spend from it﴾. So He, glorified is He, forbade intending to give away the inferior, as is the habit of most souls: keeping the good for themselves and giving the poor the inferior.

His forbidding the intention to do this and his aiming at it contains something resembling an excuse for one who does it not by intention and aim, but by coincidence, when it was what was present at that time, or when his property was of its kind. For such a person did not aim at the bad; rather, he aimed at giving out some of what God had bestowed upon him.

The position of His words ﴿from it you spend﴾ is that of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: do not intend it while spending from it.

Then He said: ﴿And you would not take it except that you close your eyes to it﴾.

That is: if you were the ones entitled to it and it were offered to you, you would not accept it as your right except by overlooking it and being lenient about taking it, from the saying of people: "So-and-so closed his eyes to part of his right" (aghmada fulan 'an ba'di haqqihi).

It is said to the seller: "Aghmid," meaning, do not scrutinize. As if you do not see.

Its origin is from the closing of the eyelid, as the one who sees, out of his dislike for it, does not fill his eye with it, but closes his sight and partially shuts his gaze out of aversion. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Did not a people with the vengeance-seeking of ... tempt us, and men who are content with closing the eyes"

In it are two meanings:

One: How do you give to God and offer Him what you would not be content to be given yourselves, and what none of you would be content to receive as a gift from his companion? God is most worthy to be given the best of things and the choicest of them.

The second: How do you assign to Him what you dislike for yourselves, when He, glorified is He, is good and accepts only what is good?

Then He concluded the two verses with two attributes required by their context, saying: ﴿And know that God is Rich, Praiseworthy﴾.

His richness and praiseworthiness both preclude His accepting the bad. For one who receives the bad and the corrupt either receives it out of need for it, or his self does not refuse it because of its lack of perfection and nobility. As for the One who is free of need, of noble station and perfect attributes, He does not accept it.

﴿And know that God is Rich, Praiseworthy﴾

He, glorified is He, says: I am Rich, free of need of what you spend, so that nothing from it could reach Me; Praiseworthy, deserving of all praises. Your spending does not fill any need of Mine nor does it bring Me any praise. Rather, He is the Rich in Himself, the Praiseworthy in Himself, and in His names and attributes, and your spending benefits only you and returns to you.

It is incumbent upon whoever has not felt in his heart the sweetness of this address, its majesty, its subtle placement, its drawing of hearts and spirits, and its penetrating of them, to treat his heart with piety, to purge from it the corrupt substances that have come between him and his share of this, and to seek the means by which he may attain it: sincere desire, and turning to God that He give life to his heart, purify it, and place in it faith and wisdom. For a dead heart does not taste the flavor of faith, does not find its sweetness, and does not enjoy a good life, neither in this world nor in the next. Whoever wishes to contemplate the roots of blessings, let him graze his herd of remembrance in the gardens of the Qur'an, and let him reflect on what God has enumerated in it of His blessings, and what He has made known of them to His servants from the beginning of the Qur'an to its end: from the creation of the people of the Fire, and His testing them with Iblis and his party, and the empowering of their enemies over them, and their trial with desires, wills and whims, so that the blessing upon them may be magnified through opposing and combating them; the enemies of God against His friends and servants, the most complete and perfect blessing in every thing He has created, whether beloved or hated, blessing and trial alike, and in everything He has brought about on the earth of His encounters with His enemies and His honoring of His friends, and in everything He has decreed and destined. The detailing of this cannot be encompassed by the pens and papers of this world, nor by the powers of servants; what is here is only a reminder and an indication.

Whoever surveys the Most Beautiful Names finds them to be praises and eulogies, whose eloquence falls short of reaching their true reality, and whose comprehension the imaginations fail to encompass even one of them. Yet God, glorified is He, possesses praises, eulogies and kinds of commendation that have not stirred in thoughts, nor passed through hearts, nor appeared to any perceiver, nor occurred to any reflection.

In the supplication of the one who knows his Lord best, and knows His names, attributes and praises most:

"I ask You by every name which You have named Yourself with, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to one of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You, that You make the Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my breast, the removal of my sorrow and the departure of my worry and grief."

And in the Sahih, from him (ﷺ), in the hadith of intercession, when he prostrates before his Lord: he said, "He will open to me of His praises something I do not know well now." And he used to say in his prostration: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your anger, and in Your pardon from Your punishment, I seek refuge in You from You. I cannot count praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself." So no one of His creation can number the praise of Him at all. He has names, attributes, praise and commendation that no near angel nor sent prophet knows, and the proportion of what the servants know of that to what they do not know is like a sparrow's sip from the sea.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 268:

This verse contains an exhortation to spending and an urging towards it in the most eloquent words and the finest meanings. For it includes an explanation of what calls to miserliness, what calls to giving and spending, an explanation of what the caller to miserliness invites to, what the caller to spending invites to, and an explanation of what each of the two callers calls upon.

So He, glory be to Him, informed that what calls them to miserliness and stinginess is Satan, and He informed that his call is through what he promises them and frightens them with, of poverty if they spend their wealth. And this is the caller that prevails over creation.

For one of them intends to give charity and to give out, and he finds in his heart a caller saying to him: "When you take this out, you will be in need of it; you will become poor after bringing it out. Withholding it is better for you, so that you do not remain like the poor man; your wealth is better for you than his wealth." When he portrays this image to him, he commands him with indecency (fahshā'), which is miserliness, the most ugly of indecencies. This is the consensus of the exegetes: that the fahshā' here is miserliness. So this is his promise and this is his command. He is a liar in his promise, a deceiver and a wicked one in his command. So the one who responds to his call is deluded, deceived and defrauded. For he lowers the one who calls him by his deception, then brings him to the worst of destinations, as it has been said:

*He lowered them by deception, then brought them down; indeed the wicked one is a deceiver to whoever befriends him.*

And his promise of poverty is not out of compassion for him, nor as sincere advice, as a man advises his brother, nor out of love for his remaining rich; rather, nothing reaches him from his poverty and need. His promise of poverty to him and his command to him to be miserly are only so that he may think ill of his Lord, and leave what he loves of spending for His sake, so that deprivation becomes his due.

As for Allah, glory be to Him, He promises His servant forgiveness of his sins from Him, and bounty, that He will replace for him more than what he spent, and multiples of it, either in this world or in this world and the Hereafter.

So this is the promise of Allah, and that is the promise of Satan. Let the miser and the spender consider which of the two promises is more trustworthy? And which of them does his heart find rest in and his soul become tranquil?

And Allah grants success to whom He wills, and forsakes whom He wills. And He is the All-Encompassing, the All-Knowing.

And reflect on how He concluded this verse with these two names: ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾.

For He is vast in giving, knowing who deserves His bounty and who deserves His justice; so He gives this one by His bounty and withholds from that one by His justice. And He is Knowing of everything.

So reflect upon these verses and do not consider lengthy elaboration on them to be excessive, for they have a matter that none understands except one who has understood the address of Allah and comprehended His intent.

﴿And these are the parables which We present to mankind, and none understands them except those of knowledge.﴾

And reflect on the conclusion of this surah, which is the summit of the Qur'an, with the rulings on wealth and the categories of the wealthy and their conditions.

And how He divided them into three categories: the one who does good, namely those who give charity. He mentioned their reward and its multiplication, and that lending their wealth to the Reliable Repayer, glory be to Him, is theirs. Then He warned them of what nullifies the reward of their charities and burns them after they have become sound and complete: reminding of favours and harm; and He warned them of what prevents its effect from taking hold initially: showing off (riyā'). Then He commanded them to draw near to Him with the best of it, and not to aim at the worst and most wicked of it. Then He warned them against responding to the call of miserliness and indecency, and informed that their response to His call, glory be to Him, and their trust in His promise, is more fitting for them.

And He informed that this is from His wisdom, which He gives to whom He wills of His servants, and that whoever is given it has been given much good: he has been given what is better and more excellent than the whole world, because He, glory be to Him, described the world as little, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾.

And He, exalted, said: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾, so this indicates that what Allah gives His servant of His wisdom is better for him than the world and what is in it. Not everyone comprehends this, rather none comprehends it except one who has intellect and pure reason. Thus He, exalted, said: ﴿And none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾.

Then He informed that whatever they spend of expenditure or whatever they draw near to Him with through a vow, He knows it, so it is not lost before Him; rather He knows what was done for His sake, and He Himself undertakes to reward it from His vast bounty, and He leaves the reward of one who acts for another to the one for whom he acted, for he is a wrongdoer to himself, and he has no helper.

Then He, glory be to Him, informed about the states of those who give charity for His sake, and that He rewards them for it, whether they display it or conceal it, after it is sincere for His sake. He said: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent﴾, i.e., how excellent a thing they are. This is praise for them, described as being apparent and manifest, so that the one who gives them does not imagine that their effect and reward have been nullified, which would prevent him from bringing them out and cause him to wait for concealment, whereupon they would be lost, or obstacles would intervene and be placed between him and his heart, or between him and bringing them out. So he does not delay his open charity, once its time has arrived, until a time of secrecy. And this was the state of the Companions.

(Lataifah)

He said to the family of His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah and the wisdom﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33].

The wisdom that the messengers brought is the true wisdom, which includes beneficial knowledge and righteous action, guiding to the religion of truth, so that one attains the truth in belief, speech and deed.

Allah, glory be to Him, distributed this wisdom among His prophets and messengers, and gathered it for Muhammad ﷺ, just as He gathered for him the excellent qualities that He had distributed among the prophets before him, and gathered in his Book the sciences and deeds that had been distributed among the books before it.

Were every sound wisdom in the world, from every group, to be gathered, it would be an extremely small portion compared to the wisdom given to him, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, a proportion that humans cannot perceive.

[Chapter: The Station of Wisdom]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of wisdom (ḥikmah).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾

And He the Exalted says: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, and taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [al-Nisa: 113].

And He said concerning the Messiah, peace be upon him: ﴿And He will teach him the Book and wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al Imran: 48].

Wisdom in the Book of Allah is of two kinds: singular, and paired with the Book. The singular is interpreted as prophethood, and interpreted as knowledge of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the knowledge of the Qur'an: its abrogating and abrogated (nasikh and mansukh), its clear and ambiguous (muhkam and mutashabih), its earlier and later, its lawful and unlawful, and its parables.

al-Dahhak said: it is the Qur'an and understanding of it. Mujahid said: it is the Qur'an, knowledge and jurisprudence (fiqh). In another narration from him: it is correctness in speech and action.

al-Nakha'i said: it is the meanings of things and understanding them.

al-Hasan said: it is scrupulousness (wara') in the religion of Allah. It seems he explained it by its fruit and its requirement.

As for wisdom paired with the Book, it is the Sunnah. Likewise al-Shafi'i and other imams said.

It was also said: it is judgment by revelation. Its interpretation as the Sunnah is more general and more well-known.

The best of what has been said about wisdom is the statement of Mujahid and Malik: it is knowing the truth and acting upon it, and correctness in speech and action.

This cannot be achieved except through understanding the Qur'an and jurisprudence in the laws of Islam and the realities of faith.

Wisdom is of two kinds: knowledge-based (ʿilmiyyah) and practical (ʿamaliyyah). The knowledge-based is awareness of the inner realities of things, and knowing the connection of causes to their effects, in creation and command, in decree and law.

The knowledge-based, as the author of "al-Manazil" said, is placing a thing in its proper place.

(Chapter)

Remembrance (tadhakkur) and reflection (tafakkur) are two stations that yield kinds of knowledge and realities of faith and excellence (ihsan). The knower keeps turning his reflection back upon his remembrance, and his remembrance back upon his reflection, until the lock of his heart is opened by the permission of the All-Knowing Opener. al-Hasan al-Basri said: The people of knowledge have always returned remembrance upon reflection and reflection upon remembrance, and made hearts speak until they spoke.

The author of "al-Manazil" said: Remembrance is above reflection, because reflection is seeking, and remembrance is finding.

He means that reflection is seeking the ends from their beginnings, as he said: Reflection is the insight of the heart feeling its way to attain the desired goal.

As for his saying that remembrance is finding, it is because it occurs regarding what was obtained through reflection, then was forgotten through forgetfulness; when he remembers it, he finds it and attains it.

Tadhakkur is a form of tafa''ul from dhikr, which is the opposite of forgetting, and it is the presence of the knowledge-image of the remembered thing in the heart. The pattern tafa''ul was chosen for it because it is achieved after a delay and gradual progression, like tabassur (insight), tafahhum (understanding) and ta'allum (learning).

Thus the station of remembrance relative to reflection is the station of the attainment of the sought-after thing after searching for it. For this reason, the signs of Allah, both recited and witnessed, are called reminders, as He said of the recited: ﴿And We gave Moses the guidance, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book as guidance and a reminder for people of understanding﴾ [Ghafir: 53]; and He said of the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqah: 48]; and He said of His witnessed signs: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it and adorned it and it has no cracks? And the earth — We spread it out and cast into it firm mountains and caused to grow in it of every beautiful pair, as an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ [Qaf: 6-8].

So tabsirah is the instrument of sight, and tadhkirah is the instrument of remembrance. He joined them together and made them for the people of repentance, because when the servant turns in repentance to Allah, he perceives the places of the signs and lessons, and so he takes them as evidence of what they are signs of for him. Thereby aversion is removed by repentance, blindness by insight, and heedlessness by reminder, because insight brings about in him the obtaining of the image of the signified in the heart after his heedlessness of it. So the ordering of the three stations is the best ordering, and each of them supports its companion, strengthens it and makes it fruitful.

He the Exalted also said of His witnessed signs: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in force, and they roamed through the lands — is there any escape? Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf: 36].

People are of three kinds. A man whose heart is dead: he is the one who has no heart, so this verse is not a reminder for him.

The second: a man who has a living, receptive heart, but who does not listen to the recited signs by which Allah informs about the witnessed signs, either because they have not reached him, or they reach him but his heart is occupied with other things and absent from them. He is absent-hearted, not present, so for him too the reminder is not attained despite his receptivity and the existence of his heart.

The third: a man with a living, receptive heart, to whom the signs are recited; he gives ear with his hearing, gives ear and brings his heart present, and does not occupy it with anything other than understanding what he hears. He is a heart that witnesses, one who gives ear, and this category is the one who benefits from the recited and witnessed signs.

The first is like the blind man who does not see.

The second is like the seeing man who directs his gaze away from the direction of what is seen, so neither of them sees it.

The third is like the seeing man who has fixed his gaze toward the direction of what is seen, followed it with his sight, and faced it at a middle distance, neither too far nor too near. This is the one who sees it.

Glory be to Him who made His speech a cure for what is in the breasts.

If it is said: What is the place of "or" (aw) in this structure according to what you have established?

It is said: In it is a subtle secret, and we do not say that it means "and" (waw), as the literalist grammarians say.

Know that a man may have a sharp, kindled heart, full of extracting lessons and deriving judgments. His heart leads him to remembrance and reflection, so when he hears the signs they are light upon light for him. These are the most perfect of Allah's creation and the greatest of them in faith and insight, to the point that what the Messenger informed them of seems witnessed by them, though they did not perceive its details and kinds. It was said: the likeness of the state of al-Siddiq with the Prophet ﷺ is like the likeness of two men who entered a house: one of them saw its details and particulars, and the other his hand fell upon what was in the house without seeing its details or particulars, but he knew that there were great matters in it whose details his sight did not grasp. Then they both came out, and he asked him about what he had seen in the house, and every time he informed him of something, he confirmed it, because of what he had of its evidences. This is the highest of the ranks of siddiqiyyah. Do not consider it far-fetched that Allah, the Bestower, bestows upon a servant the like of this faith, for the bounty of Allah does not fall under any limit or reckoning.

So the possessor of this heart, when he hears the signs while there is in his heart a light of insight, increases in light upon his light. If the servant does not have such a heart, but gives ear and his heart is present and not absent, remembrance is attained for him too: ﴿But if a heavy rain does not reach it, then a light drizzle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265]. The heavy rain and the light drizzle apply to all deeds, their effects and their requirements. The people of Paradise are of the foremost, the brought near, and the people of the right hand, and between them in degrees of excellence is what is between them, to the point that the pure drink of one kind is made good by the drink of the other kind and is mixed with it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, and it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Saba: 6]. Every believer sees this, but the seeing of the people of knowledge of it has one hue, and the seeing of others of it has another hue.

The author of "al-Manazil" said: The structures of remembrance are three: benefiting from admonition, insight through lesson, and attaining the fruit of reflection.

Benefiting from admonition: it is that the striking of fear and hope strikes the heart, so that it moves to action, seeking deliverance from fear and desiring the attainment of what is hoped for.

Admonition (ʿiẓah) is command and prohibition joined with encouragement and warning.

Admonition is of two kinds: admonition through what is heard, and admonition through what is witnessed. Admonition through what is heard is benefiting from the guidance and right direction he hears, and the counsels that came upon the tongues of the messengers and what was revealed to them; likewise benefiting from admonition from every counselor and guide in matters of religion and worldly interests.

Admonition through what is witnessed is benefiting from what he sees and witnesses in the world of the places of lessons, the rulings of decree and its courses, and what he witnesses of the signs of Allah that indicate the truthfulness of His messengers.

As for insight through lesson, it is an increase in insight beyond what it was at the station of reflection, through the strength of recollection, because remembrance holds fast the meanings that were obtained through reflection on the places of signs and lessons. So he attains them through reflection, and they become polished and clear for him through remembrance, and the resolve to proceed grows according to the strength of insight, because it requires determining the consideration of what moves the seeking, for seeking is a branch of awareness. Whenever awareness of the beloved grows strong, the heart's journey toward it intensifies, and whenever reflection occupies itself with it, awareness of it and insight into it and remembrance of it increase.

As for attaining the fruit of reflection, this is a subtle point.

Reflection has two fruits: attaining the sought-after thing completely within what is possible, and acting in accordance with its requirement, observing its right. For the heart, during reflection, had become weary through its labors in obtaining the sought-after thing; when the meanings were obtained for it and fermented in the heart, and the intellect rested, it returned to remember what it had gathered and surveyed, so it rejoiced in it and was pleased with it, and at this station it corrected what it had missed at the station of reflection, because it had come close to it in the station of remembrance, which is higher than it. Then it took up the intended fruit, which is acting upon its requirement, observing its right, for righteous action is the fruit of beneficial knowledge, which is the fruit of reflection.

If you want to understand this by a sensory example: the seeker of wealth, as long as he is earnest in his seeking, is in weariness and toil; when he obtains it, he rests from the exertion of seeking and returns from the journey of trade, surveys what he has gathered and sees it, and in this state corrects what he may have erred in while busy with seeking. When it is sound for him and his gain is pure to him, he begins to spend the wealth on the beneficial ends intended from it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 271:

He informed that giving it to the poor in secret is better for the one who spends than displaying it and making it public..

Reflect on His, the Exalted, restricting concealment specifically to giving to the poor, and He did not say: "And if you conceal them, it is better for you." For among charity there is that whose concealment is not (preferable), such as equipping an army, building a bridge, digging a river, or other things. As for giving it to the poor, concealing it has benefits: covering him (the recipient), not embarrassing him among people, sparing him from being exposed, and that people do not see that his hand is the lower hand and that he has nothing, so that they do not shun dealing and trading with him. This is an added benefit beyond merely doing good to him through charity, along with its including sincerity and the absence of showing off and seeking praise from people. Concealing it for the poor is better than displaying it among people. From this is the Prophet's ﷺ praise of secret charity, his commendation of the one who performs it, and his informing that he is among the seven who will be in the shade of the Throne of the All-Merciful on the Day of Resurrection.

For this reason, He, glory be to Him, made it better for the one who spends, and informed that by that spending He expiates from him some of his misdeeds. Nothing of your deeds or intentions is hidden from Him, glory be to Him, for "He is All-Aware of what you do."

Then He informed that this spending benefits only themselves; it returns to them at the time they most need it. So how can one of you be stingy with himself, when its benefit is exclusively his and returns to him? The spending of the believers is only for seeking His Face sincerely, because it proceeds from their faith, and their spending returns to them in full and complete. "And they will not be wronged even the weight of a speck (of dust)."

This discourse began with the statement that Allah is the Guide, the One who grants success in dealing with Him and preferring His pleasure, and that it is not upon His Messenger to guide them; rather, it is upon him to convey (the message) to them. He, glory be to Him, is the One who grants success to whom He wills toward His pleasure.

Then He mentioned the recipients to whom charity is given.

(Benefit)

As for His, the Exalted, saying: "And He will expiate from you some of your misdeeds" (﴿وَيُكَفِّرُ عَنْكم مِن سَيِّئاتِكُمْ﴾), the word "min" (مِن) here is the partitive "min" (min al-tab'id), because the verse is in the context of the reward for charity, as He said: "If you show your charities, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will expiate from you some of your misdeeds" (﴿إن تبدوا الصدقات فنعما هي وإن تخفوها وتؤتوها الفقراء فهو خير لكم ويكفر عنكم من سيئاتكم﴾).

Charity does not remove all sins. Of this kind is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Let him expiate for his oath and let him do what is better."

Narrated by Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, and al-Bukhari has something similar.

He used "'an" (عن) in the speech to signal the meaning of exiting from the oath, when he mentioned the agent, who is the one exiting. It is as if he said: "Let him exit from his oath through expiation."

And since He did not mention the agent who expiates in His saying: "That is the expiation of your oaths" (﴿ذَلِكَ كَفّارَةُ أيْمانِكُمْ﴾), and did not mention "min," and attributed the expiation to the oaths, this is an idafa of the verbal noun to its object. Although oaths do not expiate; rather, what expiates is the breaking (of the oath) and the sin. But expiation is a release from the binding of the oath, and for this reason it is attributed to the oath, just as release is attributed to a binding, since an oath is a binding and expiation is its release. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 273 (part 1 of 2):

He described them with six attributes:
The first: poverty.
The second: that they confine themselves (ḥabs, "confinement") to the cause of Allah, the Exalted, and to jihad against His enemies and the support of His religion. The root of ḥaṣr is prevention. So they prevent themselves from spending themselves on the affairs of this world, and restrict themselves to giving themselves over to Allah and in His cause.
The third: their inability to travel for earning a livelihood. Ḍarb fi'l-arḍ ("striking the earth") means travel. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel in the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾.
And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾.
The fourth: their great abstinence (ta'affuf), which is their fine patience and their display of self-sufficiency.
﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their abstinence﴾, and their not approaching people and concealing their need.
The fifth: that they are recognized by their marks (sīmā). This is the sign that indicates their state, by which Allah described them. This does not contradict the ignorant person's supposition that they are wealthy, because the ignorant person has only the outward appearance, whereas the one who knows is the one who discerns and reads people by their marks. The discerning ones (al-mutawassimūn) are the elite of the believers, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern (al-mutawassimīn)﴾.
The sixth: their leaving off asking people, so they do not ask them insistently (ilḥāf). Ilḥāf is persistent pressing, and the negation applies to both together, i.e., they do not ask and they do not press. So there is no asking from them that would involve pressing. This is like his saying ﴿a trackless desert whose landmark is not guided by﴾, meaning there is no landmark by which one is guided. In it there is something like an indication that the blameworthy asking is the asking that involves pressing. As for asking to the extent of necessity without pressing, the better course is to leave it, but it is not forbidden.
These are six attributes of those deserving charity, yet most people have disregarded them: they have taken only the outward appearance of poverty and its garb, without its reality.
As for the rest of the attributes mentioned, those who possess them are rare, and whoever recognizes them is rarer still. Allah singles out for His success whom He wills. These, then, are the ones who do good with their wealth.
The second category: the wrongdoers, who are the opposite of these. They are the ones who slaughter the needy and the distressed.
When need drives someone to them, they do not relieve his distress except with an addition over what they give him. These are the people of usury (ribā). Allah, the Exalted, therefore mentioned them after this, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest, if you should be believers (278)﴾.

[Section: The Station of Poverty (faqr)]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of poverty.
This station is the most noble, the highest and the most exalted of the stations of the path according to the people (of Sufism). Indeed, it is the spirit of every station, its secret, its kernel, and its goal.
This is known only by knowing the reality of poverty, and this group means by it something more specific than its original meaning. The word faqr occurs in the Qur'an in three places.
The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For the poor who have been confined in the cause of Allah, who cannot travel in the land. The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their abstinence﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], i.e., the charities are for these. The poor among the Emigrants were about four hundred. They had no dwellings in Medina, nor tribes. They had confined themselves to jihad in the cause of Allah. So they were available for every expedition that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched. They were the People of the Bench (Ahl al-Ṣuffa). This is one of the opinions regarding their being "confined in the cause of Allah."
It was said: it is their confining themselves to obedience to Allah. It was said: it is that poverty and destitution confine them from jihad in the cause of Allah.
It was said: when they opposed the enemies of Allah and fought them for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, they were confined from striking the earth to seek livelihood. Thus they are unable to strike the earth.
The correct view is that, because of their poverty, weakness and frailty, they are unable to strike the earth, and because of their perfect chastity and self-restraint, whoever does not know their condition thinks them wealthy.
The second place: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Charity is only for the poor﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60] – the verse.
The third place: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah﴾ [Fāṭir: 15].
So the first category is the elite of the poor. The second is the poor of the Muslims, both their elite and their common. The third is the general poverty of all the people of the earth: their rich and their poor, their believers and their disbelievers.
The poor described in the first verse are opposed by the people of means (ahl al-jidda), by those who are not confined in the cause of Allah, and by those who do not conceal their poverty out of abstinence. Their opposite is more numerous than the opposite of the second category.
The second category is opposed by the wealthy, the people of means. It includes the abstinent and others, and the one confined in the cause of Allah and others.
The third category has no opposite. Rather, Allah alone is the Rich, and everything other than Him is poor toward Him.
The people's meaning of poverty is something more specific than all of this. It is the realization of servitude and the constant need of Allah, the Exalted, in every state.
This meaning is too exalted to be called poverty. Rather, it is the reality and kernel of servitude, and the removal of the self from competing with lordship (rubūbiyya).
