Yaḥyā ibn Mu'ādh was asked about it, and he said: "Its reality is that one is not self-sufficient except by Allah, and its definition is: the absence of all means." He means: the absence of trust in them and of standing with them. It is, as some shaykhs said: "something that Allah places only with those He loves, and drives toward whom He wills."
Ruwaym was asked about poverty, and he said: "Releasing the self to the rulings of Allah."
This is praised only in releasing it to the religious and destined rulings which one is not commanded to repel or guard against.
Abū Ḥafṣ was asked: "With what does the poor man come before his Lord?" He said: "The poor man has nothing to come before his Lord with except his poverty."
The reality of poverty and its perfection, as one of them said when he was asked: "When does the poor man deserve the name of poverty?" He said: "When no remnant of himself is left in him." It was said to him: "And how is that?" He said: "If he has something, then he does not have it. And if he does not have it, then it is his."
This is one of the finest expressions of the meaning of poverty that the people point to: that all of him becomes for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. No remnant of his self, his portion, or his desire is left in him. So whenever some ruling of his self remains in him, his poverty is flawed.
Then this was explained by his saying: "If he has something, then he does not have it," i.e., if it belongs to his self, then it is not for Allah; and if it does not belong to his self, then it is for Allah.
So the reality of poverty is that you are not for yourself, and nothing of you is for it, such that you are wholly for Allah. And if you are for yourself, then there is ownership and self-sufficiency, which contradicts poverty.
This poverty they point to is not negated by wealth or possessions. The messengers of Allah and His prophets were at its peak together with their wealth and dominion, such as Abraham the Friend (ﷺ), who was the father of guests; he had wealth and livestock. Likewise were Solomon and David, peace be upon them. Likewise was our Prophet (ﷺ), who was as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 8]. So they were rich in their poverty, poor in their richness.
The real poverty is the continuance of need of Allah in every state, and that the servant witness, in every atom of his outward and inward being, complete need of Allah, the Exalted, in every respect.
Poverty is intrinsic to the servant. It only renews for him through his witnessing and his existence as a state; otherwise it is a reality.
As Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his spirit, said:
"Poverty for me is an attribute of essence, necessary forever, just as wealth is forever an intrinsic attribute of Him."
It has effects, signs, requirements and causes, most of which the people's allusions point to, such as the saying of one of them: "The poor man's resolve does not outpace his step." He means: he is the son of his state and his time, so his resolve is confined to his time and does not exceed it.
It was said: the pillars of poverty are four: knowledge that guides it, scrupulousness that restrains it, certainty that carries it, and remembrance that comforts it.
Al-Shiblī said: "The reality of poverty is that one is not self-sufficient by anything apart from Allah."
Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh was asked: "When does the poor man find rest?" He said: "When he sees for himself no time other than the one he is in."
Abū Ḥafṣ said: "The best thing by which the servant seeks a means to Allah is the continuance of need of Him in all states, the constant adherence to the Sunnah in all actions, and seeking sustenance from a lawful source."
It was said: among the rulings of poverty is that one has no desire. If he must have some, his desire should not exceed his sufficiency.
It was said: the poor man is one who owns nothing and is not owned. More complete than this: one who owns but is not owned by any owner.
It was said: whoever desires poverty for the nobility of poverty dies poor; and whoever desires it so that nothing distracts him from Allah dies rich.
Poverty has a beginning and an end, and an outward and an inward. Its beginning is humiliation, and its end is honor. Its outward is lack, and its inward is richness. As a man said to another: "Poverty and humiliation?" He said: "No, rather poverty and honor." He said: "Poverty and wealth?" He said: "No, rather poverty and a throne." Both are correct.
The people agreed that the continuance of need of Allah, together with mixing (with other things), is better than the continuance of purity together with seeing oneself and self-admiration, though there is no purity with those two.
When you know the meaning of poverty, you know that it is the very essence of richness in Allah.
So there is no sense in the question of one who asks: "Which of the two states is more perfect: need of Allah, or self-sufficiency in Him?"
This is an invalid question, for self-sufficiency in Him is the very essence of need of Him.
This question was put to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Farghānī, and he said: "When need of Allah, the Exalted, is sound, self-sufficiency in Allah is sound; and when self-sufficiency in Allah is sound, richness in Him is perfected."
So it is not said which of them is superior, need or self-sufficiency, because they are two states, neither of which is complete except with the other.
As for their discussion of the question of the patient poor and the grateful rich, and preferring one over the other:
According to the people of verification and knowledge, preference does not return to the essence of poverty and wealth themselves. Rather, it returns to deeds, states and realities. So the question itself is corrupt in its own right, for preference with Allah, the Exalted, is by piety and the realities of faith, not by poverty or wealth, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you with Allah is the most pious of you﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 13], and He did not say "the poorest of you" or "the richest of you."
Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his spirit, said: "Poverty and wealth are a trial from Allah for His servant, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and gives him favor, he says, 'My Lord has honored me.' But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says, 'My Lord has humiliated me'﴾ [al-Fajr: 15-16]. Nay, i.e., not everyone to whom I extend and give, have I honored, and not everyone whom I constrict and restrict, have I humiliated. Honor is that Allah honors the servant by His obedience, faith in Him, love of Him and knowledge of Him. Humiliation is that He strips him of that."
He – meaning Ibn Taymiyya – said: "Preference does not occur by wealth or poverty, but by piety. If the two are equal in piety, they are equal in rank." I heard him say that.
They discussed this question in the presence of Yaḥyā ibn Mu'ādh, and he said: "Neither poverty nor wealth will be weighed tomorrow; rather, patience and gratitude will be weighed."

(Benefit)
Insistence (ilḥāf) contradicts the state and description of contentment. Allah, glorified is He, praised those who do not ask people insistently. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their abstinence; you recognize them by their marks; they do not ask people insistently﴾.
A group said: they ask people for what their need calls them to ask, but they do not press. So Allah negated from them the asking of pressing, not asking in general.
Ibn ʿAbbās said: "If he has lunch, he does not ask for dinner; if he has dinner, he does not ask for lunch."
Another group – among them al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ and others – said: rather, the verse requires leaving asking entirely, because they were described as abstinent and as recognized by their marks, without openly asking. For if they had openly asked, the ignorant one would not have thought them wealthy.
Then they differed about the meaning of His saying: ﴿They do not ask people insistently﴾.
Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that there is no asking from them, so pressing does not occur, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48], i.e., there will be no intercession that benefits. And as in His saying: ﴿No ransom will be accepted from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123], i.e., there will be no ransom that is accepted, and its like. Imru' al-Qays said:
"Upon a trackless road whose landmark is not guided by"
i.e., there is no landmark by which one is guided.
Ibn al-Anbārī said: the interpretation of the verse is: they do not ask at all, so that asking would not lead them at some times to pressing. This is like your saying: "So-and-so, his good is not hoped for," i.e., he has no good so that it could be hoped for.
Abū ʿAlī said: no asking from them is established in this verse, because the meaning is: there is no asking from them, so there would be no pressing from them. He said: a similar thing is the saying of the poet:

A poet says:

*"Its terrors do not frighten the hare,
And you do not see the dabb (spiny-tailed lizard) hide away in it."*

That is, there is no hare in it to be frightened by its terror, nor a dabb to hide in its burrow.

Al-Farra' said: "He negated insistent begging (ilhaf) from them." He meant the negation of all asking.

(Section)

**The ruling on asking (al-masala)**

Asking is basically forbidden (haram). It is permitted only out of need and necessity, because it is an injustice in three respects: an injustice toward the Lordship (al-rububiyyah) of Allah, an injustice toward the one asked, and an injustice toward the one who asks.

As for the first: he has displayed his request, his poverty, his humility and his seeking of gifts to other than Allah, and that is a kind of worship. So he has placed the request in other than its proper place, and directed it to other than its rightful people. He has wronged his monotheism (tawhid) and his sincerity, and his need of Allah, his reliance upon Him and his contentment with His decree. He has become self-sufficient by asking people instead of asking the Lord of people. All of this diminishes the right of tawhid, extinguishes its light and weakens its strength.

As for his wronging the one asked: he has asked him for what he does not have, and by his request he has imposed upon him a right that he did not owe him, and exposed him to the hardship of giving or the blame of refusing. If he gives, he gives reluctantly; if he refuses, he refuses with embarrassment and evasion. This applies when he asks for what is not owed. But if he asks for a right that the other person owes him, then he is not included in this, and he has not wronged him by asking.

As for his wronging himself: he has spilled the water of his face, humbled himself to other than his Creator, placed himself in the lower of two stations, and accepted for it the basest of two conditions. He has consented to the loss of the honour of his self, the dignity of his restraint and the ease of his contentment. He has sold his patience, his contentment, his reliance, his satisfaction with what has been allotted to him, and his independence from people, for asking them. This is exactly his wronging of himself, for he has put himself in other than its proper place, diminished its nobility, lowered its rank, removed its might, belittled and demeaned it, and accepted that his self should be beneath the self of the one asked and his hand beneath the hand of that one. Were it not for necessity, this would not be permitted in the Shari'ah.

It is established in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will not cease asking people until he comes on the Day of Resurrection with no flesh on his face."

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever asks people for their wealth to increase his own, is only asking for live coals. So let him ask little or ask much."

In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, that one of you should take his rope and gather firewood on his back, then give it in charity to the people, is better for him than that he should come to a man and ask him, whether he gives or refuses."

In Sahih Muslim, also from him, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That one of you should go out in the morning, gather firewood on his back, give it in charity, and be independent of people, is better for him than that he should ask a man, whether he gives or refuses. That is because the upper hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with those you are responsible for." Imam Ahmad added: "And that he should take dust and put it in his mouth is better for him than that he should put in his mouth what Allah has forbidden him."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from al-Zubair ibn al-Awwam, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "That one of you should take his rope and come with a bundle of firewood on his back, sell it, and Allah restrains his face thereby, is better for him than that he should ask people, whether they give him or refuse him."

In the two Sahihs, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that some of the Ansar asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he gave them. Then they asked him again and he gave them, then they asked him again and he gave them, until what he had was exhausted. Then he said to them, when he had spent everything in his hand: "Whatever good I have, I will not withhold from you. Whoever seeks to be chaste, Allah will keep him chaste; whoever seeks independence, Allah will make him independent; whoever exercises patience, Allah will give him patience. No one has been given a gift better and more comprehensive than patience."

From Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, while on the pulpit, mentioning charity, abstinence and asking: "The upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is the giving hand, and the lower hand is the asking hand." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

From Hakim ibn Hizam, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he gave me. Then I asked him again and he gave me. Then he said: 'O Hakim, this wealth is green and sweet. Whoever takes it with a generous soul, it will be blessed for him; and whoever takes it with a greedy soul, it will not be blessed for him, and he will be like one who eats but is never satisfied. The upper hand is better than the lower hand.'" Hakim said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by Him who sent you with the truth, I will never ask anyone for anything after you until I depart this world.'" Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to call Hakim to receive a gift, but he refused to accept it from him. Then 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, called him to give him something, but he refused to accept anything from him. 'Umar said: "I call you to witness, O assembly of Muslims, against Hakim: I offer him his right from this fay' (booty), and he refuses to take it." So Hakim, may Allah be pleased with him, did not ask anyone from the people after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he died." Agreed upon as authentic.

It is narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: My scribe of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah told me: "Mu'awiyah wrote to al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah: 'Write to me something you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' So he wrote to him: 'I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: Allah dislikes three things for you: gossip, squandering wealth, and excessive asking.'" Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

From Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not persist in asking. By Allah, none of you will ask me for anything and I give him something while I am unwilling, except that what I give him will be taken away from its blessing." 

In another wording: "I am only a treasurer. Whoever I give to with a good heart, it will be blessed for him; and whoever I give to out of asking and greed, will be like one who eats and is never satisfied." Narrated by Muslim.

From Abu Muslim al-Khawlani, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The beloved, trustworthy one told me (as for him, he is beloved to me, and as for him in my estimation, he is trustworthy): 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nine, or eight, or seven of us, and he said: 'Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of Allah?' We had only recently given our pledge to him, so we said: 'We have already pledged to you, O Messenger of Allah.' Then he said: 'Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of Allah?' We said: 'We have already pledged to you, O Messenger of Allah.' Then he said: 'Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of Allah?' He said: So we extended our hands and said: 'We have pledged to you, O Messenger of Allah. On what, then, should we pledge to you?' He said: 'That you worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and the five prayers, and obey Allah'—and he said a word quietly—'and that you do not ask people for anything.' I saw some of those men, when the whip of one of them fell, not asking anyone to hand it to him." Narrated by Muslim.

From Samurah ibn Jundub, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Asking is a scratch by which a man scratches his face, except that a man asks a ruler, or in a matter that is unavoidable." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

The passage mentions the generality of times and the generality of states, and He brought the particle "fa" (then/so) in the predicate so as to indicate that spending, at whatever time it occurs, whether by night or by day, and in whatever state it occurs, whether secretly or openly, is a cause for reward in every case. So the servant should hasten to it, and should not postpone it to another time or state. He should not delay the spending of the night until the day arrives, nor the spending of the day until the night. He should not defer the spending that is open until a time of secrecy, nor the spending that is secret until a time of openness. For his spending, at whatever time and in whatever state it occurs, is a cause of his recompense and reward. So reflect upon these secrets in the Qur'an, for perhaps you will not attain them through what passes by you in the tafsir books. The grace and favour belong to Allah alone, with no partner.

[Section: The wisdom in distinguishing between unity and difference of kind in the prohibition of riba]

As for his statement: "He prohibited selling a mudd of wheat for a mudd and a handful, and permitted selling it for a qafiz of barley," this is among the excellences of the Shari'ah which none can discern except those of abundant intellect. We will point to the wisdom behind it as far as our weak minds and limited expressions allow, while the Lord's legislation and wisdom are above our intellects and expressions. So we say:

Riba is of two types: apparent (jali) and hidden (khafi). The apparent is prohibited because of the great harm in it, and the hidden is prohibited because it is a means (dhari'ah) to the apparent. Thus the prohibition of the first is intended directly, and the prohibition of the second is a means. As for the apparent, it is riba al-nasi'ah (riba of delay), which is what they used to practice in the Jahiliyyah: one postpones his debt and increases it in wealth, and whenever he postpones it the wealth increases, until a hundred becomes thousands upon thousands. Generally, only one who is destitute and in need does this. When the creditor sees that the one owed postpones his demand and waits for him with an increase he gives him, he strains to give it in order to ransom himself from the captivity of demand and imprisonment, and to delay from time to time. So his harm intensifies, his calamity grows, and debt overtakes him until it consumes all that he possesses. Thus wealth swells upon the needy without any benefit reaching him, and the wealth of the usurer increases without any benefit coming from him to his brother. So he devours his brother's wealth falsely, and his brother receives the utmost harm. From the mercy of the Most Merciful of the merciful, His wisdom, and His kindness to His creation is that He prohibited riba, cursed its consumer, its payer, its scribe, and its two witnesses, and declared war from Him and His Messenger upon whoever does not abandon it. No such threat has come concerning any other major sin, and for this reason it is among the greatest of the major sins. Imam Ahmad was asked about the riba about which there is no doubt, and he said: it is that a man has a debt and says to him: "Will you pay or will you increase?" If he does not pay, he increases it in wealth and the other increases it in term. God, glorified is He, has made riba the opposite of charity, so the usurer is the opposite of the one who gives charity. God, Exalted, said: ﴿God deprives riba of blessing and makes charities grow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], and He said: ﴿And what you give in riba to increase within the wealth of people does not increase with God; but what you give in zakah, seeking the Face of God, those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ [al-Rum: 39], and He said: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume riba, doubled and redoubled, and fear God that you may succeed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 130] ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 131].

Then He mentioned the Garden prepared for the God-fearing who spend in ease and in hardship, and these are the opposite of the usurers. So He, glorified is He, forbade riba, which is injustice to people, and commanded charity, which is kindness to them.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, from Usamah ibn Zayd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Riba is only in delay (nasi'ah)." Such a statement is intended to restrict perfection, that the complete riba is only in delay, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely﴾ [al-Anfal: 2], up to His saying: ﴿Those are the believers truly﴾ [al-Anfal: 4], and like the saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "The scholar is only one who fears God."

[Section: Riba al-fadl]

As for riba al-fadl, its prohibition is from the category of blocking the means (sadd al-dharai'), as he explicitly stated in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not sell a dirham for two dirhams, for I fear for you al-rimma," and al-rimma is riba. So he prevented them from riba al-fadl because of what he feared for them from riba al-nasi'ah. That is because when they sell a dirham for two dirhams, this is only done because of the difference between the two types, whether in quality, in minting, in weight and lightness, or otherwise; they progress from immediate profit in them to deferred profit, which is exactly riba al-nasi'ah. This is a very near means, so from the wisdom of the Lawgiver is that He blocked this means for them, and prevented them from selling a dirham for two dirhams, whether cash or deferred. This is a wisdom that is intelligible and conforms to reason, and it closes the door of harm for them.

Having clarified this, we say: the Lawgiver explicitly stated the prohibition of riba al-fadl in six items: gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates, and salt. The people agreed on the prohibition of excess in them when the kind is the same, and they differed concerning other things. One group restricted the prohibition to these alone, and the earliest transmitted of this view is Qatadah; it is the position of the Zahiriyyah, and the choice of Ibn 'Aqil at the end of his works, though he held qiyas; he said: because the 'illahs (effective causes) of the qiyas-based views in the matter of riba are weak 'illahs, and when the 'illah does not appear clearly, qiyas is impossible.

Another group prohibited it in every measured or weighed item of the same kind; this is the position of 'Ammar, Ahmad in the apparent of his school, and Abu Hanifah. Another group restricted it to food even if it is neither measured nor weighed; this is the view of al-Shafi'i and a narration from Imam Ahmad. Another group restricted it to food if it is measured or weighed; this is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, a narration from Ahmad, and a view of al-Shafi'i. Another group restricted it to staple food and what sustains it; this is the view of Malik, and it is the most preponderant of these views, as you will see.

As for dirhams and dinars, one group said: the 'illah in them is that they are weighed; this is the position of Ahmad in one of his two narrations and the position of Abu Hanifah. Another group said: the 'illah in them is thamaniyyah (being a currency); this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Malik, and Ahmad in the other narration, and this is the correct view, indeed the right one. For they unanimously agreed on the permissibility of exchanging them (as salam) for weighed items such as copper, iron, and others; if copper and iron were ribawi, it would not be permissible to sell them on credit for dirhams in cash. Whatever is subject to the rule of exchange, when its kind differs, excess is permitted in it without deferment; and when a 'illah is violated without any influential distinction, this indicates its invalidity.

Moreover, the 'illah of weighing has no suitability (munasabah); it is pure tardid (mere concomitance). Unlike the 'illah of thamaniyyah, for dirhams and dinars are the prices of goods, and the price is the standard by which the valuation of property is known. It must therefore be fixed and controlled, neither rising nor falling; for if the price rose and fell like commodities, we would have no price by which to measure goods, and everything would be merchandise. The people's need for a price by which they measure goods is a general necessary need, and this cannot be achieved except by a value by which things are known, and that does not happen except by a currency by which things are valued, which remains in one state and does not itself get valued by something else; otherwise it becomes a commodity that rises and falls, and people's transactions are corrupted, disputes arise, and harm intensifies, as you have seen of the corruption of their dealings and the harm befalling them when fulus were taken as merchandise, prepared for profit, so harm spread and injustice occurred. If you make a single price that does not increase or decrease, but by which things are valued while it is not valued by others, the affairs of people are set right. So if riba al-fadl were permitted in dirhams and dinars, such as giving sound coins and taking broken ones, or light ones and taking heavier ones in excess, it would become a trade, or it would inevitably lead to riba al-nasi'ah in them. Currencies are not desired for their own sake, but for the purpose of reaching goods by them; if they themselves become goods desired for their own sake, the affairs of people are corrupted. This is an intelligible meaning specific to currencies and does not extend to all other weighed items.

[Section: The wisdom in the prohibition of riba al-nasi'ah in foodstuffs]

As for the four foodstuff categories, people's need for them is greater than their need for others, because they are the sustenance of the world and what sustains it. Among the consideration of the people's interests is that they were forbidden from selling some of them for others on credit, whether the kind is the same or different, and they were forbidden from selling some of them for others immediately with excess even if their qualities differ; and they were permitted excess among them when their kinds differ.

The secret of this, and God knows best, is that if selling some of them for others on credit were permitted, no one would do it except when he profits; and then his soul would be willing to sell them immediately out of greed for profit, so food would become scarce for the needy and their harm would intensify, while most people on earth do not have dirhams or dinars, especially the people of the tents and the deserts, who only exchange food for food. So it was from the Lawgiver's mercy toward them and His wisdom that He forbade them riba al-nasi'ah in them, as He forbade it in currencies; for if He had permitted credit in them, the statement "either you pay or you increase" would enter, so one sa' would become several qufzan. They were weaned from credit, then weaned from selling them with excess hand to hand, since the sweetness of profit and the lure of gain would drag them to trading in them on credit, which is exactly the harm. This differs from two distinct kinds, for their realities, qualities, and purposes differ; so obliging them to equality in exchanging them would harm them, and they would not do it; and permitting credit between them is a means to "either you pay or you increase." So it was part of the full consideration of their interests that He restricted them to selling them hand to hand however they wished, so they gained the benefit of exchange and the harm of "either you pay or you increase" was averted. This differs from when they are sold for dirhams or other weighed items on credit, for need calls for that; if they were prevented from it, it would harm them, and the salam contract, which is among their interests in what they need more than others, would be impossible; and the Shari'ah does not bring this. They have no need in selling these categories for each other on credit, and it is a near means to the harm of riba. So they were permitted in all that their need calls for, which is not a means to a dominant harm, and they were prevented from what need does not call for and what usually leads to a dominant harm.

This is clarified by the fact that whoever has one of these kinds and needs another kind, he needs to sell it for dirhams to buy the other kind, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Sell the mixed dates for dirhams, then buy with the dirhams janib (superior dates)," or he sells it for that same kind at its equivalent value. In both cases he needs to sell it immediately. This differs from when credit is allowed, for then he sells it at a surplus and needs to buy the other kind at a surplus, because the holder of that kind takes excess from him as he took excess from others; so harm arises from credit to each of them, and credit here is between two kinds, and in the first type it is within one kind, and both are the source of harm and corruption.

If you reflect on what credit has been prohibited in, you will see that it is either one kind or two kinds whose purposes are one or close, such as dirhams and dinars, wheat and barley, dates and raisins. When purposes are distant, credit is not prohibited, such as wheat and clothing, iron and olive oil.

This makes it clear that if a person were permitted to sell a mudd of wheat for two mudds, that would be a spot trade. Souls would then seek the deferred trade for the pleasure and sweetness of gain. So they were forbidden from that, and even from parting before taking possession, in order to complete this wisdom and safeguard this interest. The two contracting parties may agree on immediate payment, and it is customary for one of them to be patient with the other. Just as the people of stratagems (ḥiyal) do, they conclude the contract openly while having agreed on something else. They likewise conclude a marriage contract while having agreed on a tahlil (a marriage arranged to make a previously divorced woman lawful to her former husband), and they sell a commodity on credit while having agreed that it will be returned to the seller without that price. So if they were allowed to part before taking possession, they would conclude the sale as a cash sale and postpone the demand for the sake of profit, and thus fall into the very thing that is forbidden.

The secret of the matter is that they were forbidden from trading currency for the same kind of currency, because that would defeat the purpose of currency for them. They were also forbidden from trading staple foods for the same kind of staple food, because that would defeat the purpose of staples for them. This same meaning is present in the sale of raw gold (tibr) and minted gold ('ayn), because raw gold has no craftsmanship for which it is valued, so it is in the position of dirhams, concerning which the Lawgiver intended that they should not be exchanged at a difference. For this reason he said: "Its bullion and its minted coin are equal." Thus the wisdom behind the prohibition of ribā al-nasī'ah (riba of deferment) in a single kind or in two kinds, and ribā al-faḍl (riba of excess) in a single kind, became clear. The prohibition of the former is a prohibition of ends, and the prohibition of the latter is a prohibition of means and the blocking of pretexts (sadd al-dharā'i'). For this reason, none of ribā al-nasī'ah was permitted.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 276:

God punishes the one who devises a way to consume people's wealth through riba by causing his wealth to be destroyed, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿God deprives riba of blessing and makes charities grow.﴾

Thus the wealth of the one who deals in riba must certainly be destroyed, however much it may reach.

The root of this is that God, glorified is He, made the punishments of the perpetrators of crimes the opposite of what they intended by those crimes. He made the punishment of the liar the nullification of his speech and its rejection against him.

He made the punishment of one who embezzles from the spoils of war, seeking to increase his wealth through ghulul (misappropriation of booty): the deprivation of his share and the burning of his goods.

He made the punishment of one who hunts in the Sacred Precinct (haram) or while in the state of ihram: the prohibition of eating what he hunted, and his being made to pay its equivalent.

He made the punishment of one who is arrogant toward accepting the truth and submitting to it: that he be made to suffer humiliation and abasement in proportion to what he was arrogant toward of the truth.

He made the punishment of one who is proud against His worship and obedience: that He makes him a slave to those who worship and obey Him.

He made the punishment of one who terrifies the road and cuts off the highway: that his limbs be cut off, and that all roads be cut off to him by banishment from the land, so that he travels in it only in fear.

He made the punishment of one whose whole body and soul take pleasure in unlawful intercourse: that his body and soul be made to suffer through flogging and stoning, so that the pain reaches where the pleasure reached.

The Prophet (ﷺ) prescribed the punishment for one who looks into another's house: that his eye be gouged out with a stick or the like, as a corruption of the organ that betrayed him, and that entered his home without permission and looked upon what is forbidden to him.

He punishes every traitor by causing his scheming to go astray and be nullified, so that it does not achieve its intended goal, even if it attains some of it. What he attains becomes a cause of increasing his punishment and disappointment: ﴿And indeed God does not guide the scheming of the traitors.﴾ [Yusuf: 52]

He punished the one who eagerly seeks leadership, command and judgeship by prescribing that he be prevented and deprived of what he coveted, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We do not entrust this work of ours to one who asks for it."

For this reason He punished the father of mankind, Adam (peace be upon him), by expelling him from Paradise when he disobeyed by eating from the tree in order to remain there forever. So his punishment was his expulsion from it, the opposite of what he hoped for.

He punished the one who takes another god alongside Him, seeking support and strength through it, by making it an opponent to him through which he is humiliated and forsaken, as He said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides God that they might be for them a source of might. No! They will deny their worship of them and will be opposed to them.﴾ [Maryam: 81-82] And He said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides God, hoping they would be helped. They are unable to help them, and they are for them an army brought forward.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74-75]

And He said: ﴿Do not make with God another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾ [al-Isra: 22]

This is the opposite of what the polytheist hoped for by taking a god: victory and praise.

He punishes people when they cheat in measure and weight by the oppression of the ruler over them, who takes from their wealth many times what they cheated one another of.

He punishes them when they withhold zakat and charity out of preference for their wealth, by withholding rain from them, so that their wealth is destroyed thereby, and their rich and poor become equal in need.

He punishes them when they turn away from His Book and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ) and seek guidance from other than them: by leading them astray and closing off the doors of guidance to them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the hadith of Ali (may God be pleased with him), narrated by al-Tirmidhi and others, in which he mentioned the Qur'an:

"Whoever among the tyrants abandons it, God will break him; and whoever seeks guidance in other than it, God will lead him astray."

Whoever turns away from the Qur'an either does so out of arrogance, and his recompense is that God breaks him, or he seeks guidance from elsewhere, and his recompense is that God leads him astray.

This is a very broad and greatly beneficial principle. Whoever reflects upon it will find that it includes God's punishment, glorified is He, of whoever leaves His obedience, by reversing his intention upon him both legally and in decree, in this world and the Hereafter. His universal custom, glorified is He, among His servants has been consistent: whoever schemes with falsehood, it is schemed against him; whoever devises a plot, a plot is devised against him; and whoever deceives another, he is deceived.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites try to deceive God, but He is the one who deceives them.﴾ [an-Nisa: 142]

And He said: ﴿And the evil scheme does not encompass anyone except its own people.﴾ [Fatir: 43]

Thus you will not find a schemer except that he is schemed against, nor a deceiver except that he is deceived, nor a plotter except that a plot is devised against him.

(Benefit)

God, glorified is He, divided His creation into rich and poor, and their interests are not completed except by filling the need of the poor. So He obligated, in the surplus of the wealth of the rich, that which fills the need of the poor, and He forbade riba, which harms the needy. Thus His command to give charity and His prohibition of riba are two full brothers. For this reason God combined them in His saying: ﴿God deprives riba of blessing and makes charities grow﴾, and His saying: ﴿And whatever you give in riba to increase the wealth of people does not increase with God; but what you give in zakat, seeking the countenance of God — those are the ones who receive multiplied reward.﴾ [ar-Rum: 39] God, glorified is He, mentioned the rulings of people concerning wealth at the end of Surah al-Baqarah, and they are three: justice, injustice, and bounty. Justice is trade, injustice is riba, and bounty is charity. He praised the givers of charity and mentioned their reward, and He censured the practitioners of riba and mentioned their punishment, and He permitted trade and lending for a specified term.

The verse opens with a command to fear Allah, which is the opposite of riba, and He commanded them to abandon whatever riba remained after the revelation of the verse. He pardoned them for what they had taken through it before the prohibition; otherwise they would have had to return what they had taken through it before the prohibition. He made this compliance conditional upon their having faith.

Whatever is conditional becomes void when the condition is absent.

Then He emphasized the prohibition upon them with the most severe and harshest thing: it is warring against Allah and His Messenger on the part of the one who deals in riba.

In this threat is contained that the one who deals in usury is at war with Allah and His Messenger, and Allah has declared war upon him. This threat has not come concerning any major sin other than usury, highway robbery, and striving in the land with corruption, because each of these two (usury and highway robbery) is corrupting in the land and cuts off the way for people: the one by his overpowering them and dominating over them, and the other by his refusal to relieve their distresses except by loading them with distresses even harder than them.

So He informed about highway robbers that they wage war against Allah and His Messenger. And these (usurers), if they do not abandon usury, are declared as warriors against Him and against His Messenger.

Then He said: ﴿And if you repent, then for you is your principal (rus amwalikum)﴾, meaning: if you abandon usury and repent to Allah from it, after you had contracted it, then you are only entitled to your principal, not increasing upon it, so that you do not wrong the one who takes it, and not decreasing from it, so that he who takes it does not wrong you. If this recipient is in hardship, then it is obligatory to give him respite until a time of ease. And if you give it as charity to him and remit it, that is better and more beneficial for you. But if your souls refuse and are stingy with the obligatory justice or the recommended graciousness, then remind them of a day on which you will return to Allah and meet your Lord, who will fully repay you for your deeds, at the time when you most need it.

So He mentioned the benefactor, who is the one giving charity, and then followed him with the wrongdoer, who is the usurer.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾

[Section: The reason Khuzaymah was singled out, his testimony alone being accepted]

As for his statement, "And He made the testimony of Khuzaymah ibn Thabit equal to two testimonies, over others who were better than him," there is no doubt that this was among his special distinctions. Had he testified before the Prophet ﷺ or before anyone else, his testimony would have counted as that of two witnesses. This singling out was due to a specific reason that called for it: his hastening, ahead of the Companions present, to bear witness that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had indeed made the pledge with the Bedouin. Every one who heard this account was obliged to bear witness that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had made the pledge with the Bedouin, for that is among the requirements of faith and of bearing witness to his truthfulness ﷺ, and this is established for every Muslim. But Khuzaymah perceived that this particular matter falls under the general scope of testimony to his truthfulness in everything he reports. There is no difference between what he reports from Allah and what he reports from others in regard to his truthfulness in this and that, and faith is not complete except by affirming him in both this and that. When Khuzaymah perceived this, unlike those present, he deserved that his testimony be made equal to two testimonies.

The saying of Allah, may He be remembered: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other can remind her﴾. This contains evidence that if a witness forgets his testimony and another reminds him of it, he does not return to the other's statement until he himself recalls it. He is not permitted to merely follow (taqlid) the other. For He, glorified be He, said: "so that one of them may remind the other," and He did not say "so that she may inform her."

There are two readings of it: with the doubling (tathqil) and without (takhfif). The correct view is that both mean the same thing, from "remembrance" (dhikr). Further removed is the one who says it means "makes her remember" in both wording and meaning. For He, glorified be He, made this a cause of error, which is the opposite of remembrance. Thus, if she errs or forgets, the other reminds her, and so she remembers.

His saying, ﴿that one of them errs﴾, its meaning according to the Kufans is: "lest one of them err." They apply this throughout all occurrences of this construction, such as His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ and similar.

The Kufans' interpretation is challenged by the accusative in His saying ﴿so that one of them may remind the other﴾, for the implied meaning would be: "lest you go astray" and "lest she remind." The Basrans explained it by an implied verbal noun, namely: intention, aversion, or caution, and similar terms, so they said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, that you may not go astray﴾ means: out of caution that you go astray, or out of aversion that you go astray, and so on.

This explanation is problematic for them in His saying ﴿that one of them errs﴾: if they take it as "aversion that one of them errs," then the conjoined clause, "so that one may remind the other," would share its ruling and become something disliked. And if they take it as "intention that one of them errs," then error would be intended.

The answer to this is that the statement is to be taken according to its meaning, and the implied sense is: "that one reminds the other if she errs." And this is certainly intended.

Shaykh Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of them errs, the other can remind her﴾.

This contains evidence that two women may stand in place of one man, for the purpose of reminding one of them if she errs.

This applies only where error occurs ordinarily, which is forgetfulness and lack of precision.

To this meaning the Prophet ﷺ alluded when he said: "As for the deficiency in their intellect: the testimony of two women equals that of one man."

He thereby clarified that the halving of their testimony is due to weakness of intellect, not weakness of religion. From this it is known that the justice of women is on a par with the justice of men.

Their intellect is only less than that of men. So whatever testimony does not ordinarily involve fear of error is not subject to being half that of a man.

Those matters in which their testimony is accepted alone are things they see with their eyes, touch with their hands, or hear with their ears, without reliance on intellectual reasoning, such as childbirth, the infant's cry at birth, breastfeeding, menstruation, postnatal bleeding, and defects hidden under clothing. Such things are not ordinarily forgotten, and knowing them does not require complete intellect, unlike the meanings of statements one hears, such as the professions of faith and other things. For these are intellectual meanings, and the time since hearing them can be long in general.

Had this verse not required a journey to explain it on its own, I would have mentioned some of its interpretation. The aim here is only alerting and pointing out. He has also mentioned the just person, who takes back his capital from his debtor without addition or reduction.

Then He concluded the surah with this great ending, which is from a treasure beneath His Throne. The devil flees from the house in which it is recited. It contains knowledge, insights, foundations of Islam, principles of faith, and stations of excellence, the explanation of which would require a separate book.

(Benefit)

Allah, the Exalted, said regarding testimony on wealth: ﴿from among those whom you accept as witnesses﴾, and He said regarding bequest and revocation: ﴿two persons of justice from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. This is because the one seeking testimony there is the rights-holder, so he brings whom he accepts to preserve his right. If that person is not just, it is he who loses his right. But the one seeking testimony here seeks testimony for a right established with him, so his acceptance alone does not suffice; the witness must be just in himself. Also, Allah, glorified and exalted, said there: ﴿from among those whom you accept as witnesses﴾ because the rights-holder is the one who guards his property by one whom he accepts. If the one owing the right says, "I accept this man's testimony against me," there is dispute over its acceptance, while the verse indicates that it is accepted. This differs from revocation and divorce, for these involve a right of Allah; likewise bequest involves the right of an absent party.

(Another benefit)

In His saying, ﴿except that it be a present trade which you conduct among yourselves﴾ there is guidance toward the trick of 'inah and similar devices. For the commodity circulates between the two contracting parties in order to escape usury.

They said: The Sunnah has shown that a person may be permitted to escape a statement for which he would sin or fear, by means of ambiguous expressions (ma'arid), which is a stratagem in speech, just as that is a stratagem in actions.

Qays ibn al-Rabi' narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Indeed in ambiguous speech there is what suffices a man from lying."

Al-Hakam narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "I would not be pleased with ambiguous speech in exchange for red camels."

Al-Zuhri narrated from Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, from his mother Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who was among the early emigrants: "I did not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ grant a concession in anything that people call a lie except in three: a man who reconciles between people, a man who lies to his wife, and lying in war."

The meaning of lying in this is ambiguous speech, not outright lying.

Mansur said: They had speech by which they warded off punishment and calamities from themselves. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ met a scout of the polytheists while he was with a group of his Companions, and the polytheists said: "Who are you?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "We are from water." Then some of them looked at others and said: "The tribes of Yemen are numerous; perhaps they are among them," and they departed.

By his ﷺ saying "we are from water," he meant the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿created from gushing water﴾ [al-Tariq: 6].

When Abdullah ibn Rawahah had relations with his slave-girl, his wife saw him, took a knife and came to him, but found that he had finished his need. She said: "If I had seen you where you were, I would have struck you in the neck with it." He said: "What did you do?" She said: "If you are truthful, recite the Qur'an." He said:

"I bear witness that the promise of Allah is true, and that the Fire is the abode of the disbelievers.
And that the Throne floats above the water, and above the Throne is the Lord of the worlds.
And it is carried by mighty angels, the angels of the Lord, marked out."

She said: "I believe in the Book of Allah and I deny my own sight."

This reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he laughed until his molars showed.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: This is firmly established from Abdullah ibn Rawahah.

It is reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I am amazed at one who knows ambiguous speech, how can he lie?"

Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, was invited to a meal and said: "I am fasting." Then they saw him eating. They said: "Did you not say you were fasting?" He said: "Did not the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Fasting three days of every month is like fasting the whole year'?"

When Muhammad ibn Sirin's creditor demanded payment and he had nothing with him, he would say: "I will give you on one of the two days, God willing." Thus one would think he meant his day and the one following it, but he meant the two days of this world and the Hereafter.

al-A'mash reported from Ibrahim that a man said to him: "So-and-so ordered me to go to such-and-such a place, and I cannot reach that place. What is the stratagem?" He said: "Say: 'By Allah, I see nothing except what another has guided me to,'" meaning: except what your Lord has made you see.

Hammad reported from Ibrahim concerning a man seized by another, who said: "I have a right against you." He said: "No." The other said: "Swear by walking to the House of Allah." He said: "I swear by walking to the House of Allah," and intended the mosque of his quarter.

Hisham ibn Hassan reported from Ibn Sirin that a man was afflicted with the evil eye. He saw Shurayh's mule and wanted to cast his eye upon it, but Shurayh noticed him. Shurayh said: "When it lies down, it will not rise until it is made to rise." The man said: "Uff, uff," and the mule was safe. Shurayh meant that Allah, the Exalted, is the One who makes it rise.

al-A'mash reported from Ibrahim that he was asked about a man who hears that another has said something about him and asks him about it. He said: Say: "By Allah, Allah surely knows that there is none of that thing," meaning by "that" (ma): "that which" (alladhi).

Uqbah ibn al-Mughirah said: We used to visit Ibrahim, and he feared al-Hajjaj. When we left him, he would say: "If you are asked about me and sworn to, then swear by Allah that you do not know where I am, nor do you have any knowledge of him, nor in what place he is. Intend that you do not know in what place I am, whether standing or sitting," and you will have spoken truly.

A man came to him and said: "I struck an animal and it died, so I took another, and they want to make me swear that it is the same animal I struck." He said: "Ride it, and strike it on its belly while you are riding, then swear that it is the animal you struck."

Abu 'Awanah reported from Abu Maskin: I was with Ibrahim while his wife was rebuking him about a slave-girl of his, and he had a fan in his hand. He said: "I call you to witness that she belongs to her." When we left, he said: "What did you bear witness to?" We said: "We bore witness that you had given the slave-girl to her." He said: "Did you not see me gesture toward the fan? I only said to you, 'Bear witness that she belongs to her,' and I meant the fan."

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan reported from Umar ibn Dharr from al-Sha'bi: "Whoever swears an oath without making an exception, then righteousness and sin in it are according to his knowledge." I said: "What do you say about stratagems (hiyal)?" He said: "There is no harm in stratagems in what is lawful and permissible. Stratagems are only something by which a man escapes from what is unlawful and reaches what is lawful. Whatever is of this kind, or similar, there is no harm in it. We only dislike that a man should devise a stratagem against another's right until he nullifies it, or devise a stratagem in falsehood until he makes it appear true, or devise a stratagem in something until he introduces doubt into it. As for what is in the manner we have described, there is no harm in it."

Hammad, may Allah have mercy on him, whenever someone came to him whom he did not wish to meet, would place his hand on his molar and say: "My molar, my molar."

Al-Rashid sent a man to Shurayk to bring him, but Shurayk asked him to leave and to excuse his absence, and he did so. Then al-Rashid detained him, then sent another messenger and brought him, and asked him why he had not come when the messenger came. He swore to him with emphatic oaths that he had not seen the messenger on the day he had been sent, intending by that the second messenger, and he was believed, and ordered the man released.

al-Thawri was brought to the assembly of al-Mahdi, and wanted to stand but was prevented. He swore by Allah that he would return, so he left his sandal and went out, then came back and put it on and did not return. Al-Mahdi said: "Did he not swear that he would return?" They said: "He did return, and took his sandal."

They said: There is no school of the followed imams that does not include many matters of stratagems.

Yet the people most distant from saying this were Malik and Ahmad. Ahmad was asked about al-Marwazi while al-Marwazi was with him, and he did not wish to go out to the questioner, so Ahmad put his finger in his palm and said: "al-Marwazi is not here. What would al-Marwazi do here?"

Ahmad was asked about a man who swore by divorce that he would have intercourse with his wife during the day of Ramadan, and he said: He should travel with her and have intercourse with her on the journey.

The author of al-Mustawʿab said: I found in the hand of our shaykh Abu Hakim: It is related that a man asked Ahmad about a man who swore that he would not break his fast in Ramadan. He said to him: "Go to Bishr ibn al-Walid, ask him, then come back and inform me." He went and asked him. Bishr said: "When your family breaks their fast, sit with them and do not break yours. When it is the time of suhur, eat," and he cited the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Come to the blessed morning meal." Ahmad approved of it.

They said: Allah taught His Prophet Yusuf, peace be upon him, the stratagem by which he reached the taking of his brother: by displaying that he was a thief and placing the cup in his brother's bag, though he was not such in reality, but he showed it as a means to take his brother and keep him with himself. Allah, may He be exalted, described that as a scheme (kayd) which He devised for Yusuf so that he might take his brother. Then He, glorified be He, informed that it was of the knowledge by which He raises degrees whomever He wills, and that people differ in it: ﴿and above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾.

(Benefit: The difference between testimony and transmission)

The ruling of transmission (riwayah) applies generally to the narrator and others across the passing of times, whereas testimony is specific to the one against whom and in whose favor it is given, and does not extend beyond them except by mere consequence. Imposing obligation on a specific person may provoke enmity, the desire for benefit, and the suspicion that requires rejection. Therefore testimony was guarded by number and maleness, and was rejected in cases of kinship, enmity and the arising of suspicions. Such precautions were not taken in transmission, whose ruling is general and not specific, so no number or maleness was required for it. Rather, what was required is what makes the reporter's truthfulness predominant in assumption: justice that prevents lying, and alertness that prevents the dominance of forgetfulness and confusion.

The testimony of women and slaves: since women are deficient in intellect and religion, they were not among the people of testimony. When need calls for it, a woman is strengthened by another like her, because then it is further from her forgetfulness and error, since her companion reminds her.

As for the requirement of freedom, it is extremely far-fetched, and there is no evidence for it from the Book, the Sunnah, or consensus.

Ahmad has related from Anas ibn Malik that he said: "I know of no one who rejected the testimony of a slave, while Allah accepts his testimony over the nations on the Day of Resurrection. How then would his testimony not be accepted against his like among the responsible adults?"

His testimony is accepted in transmission from the Messenger, so how would it not be accepted against a man concerning a dirham?

This is not refuted by women, because their testimony is accepted together with another like them, for the reason we mentioned. The factor preventing acceptance of a woman's testimony alone is absent in the slave.

Upon this principle are several issues. First: reports of the sighting of the crescent of Ramadan. Whoever is satisfied with one witness regards it as transmission, because of its generality to the responsible persons, so it is like the call to prayer.

Whoever requires a number of witnesses for it assimilates it to testimony, because it does not generalize across the ages or the regions, but specifies that year and that locality, according to one of the two opinions.

This is refuted by the call to prayer, a refutation from which there is no escape.

Second: reports of lineage through the physiognomists (qafah). Insofar as it is a particular report about a particular person, which is specific and not general, it takes the course of testimony. Whoever treats it as transmission is mistaken, for it has no place here. Rather the correct view is that, insofar as one stands publicly for the people in a general way, and his statement rests on a matter specific to him among the evidences and signs, he takes the course of a judge, so his statement is a judgment, not a transmission.

(Impugnment of the narrator and the witness)

From this, the impugnment of a narrator or a witness: is one person sufficient for it, treating it as a judgment, or must there be two, treating it as testimony, according to the difference of opinion? As for treating it as transmission, that is not valid.

And as for [testimony] concerning narration and impugning [a narrator], it is only that one impugns him by his own *ijtihad* (independent legal judgment), not by what he relates from others. Whether *tarjamah* (conveying or translating) for a fatwa, writing (*khatt*), testimony, and other things require plurality is built upon this. But its being built upon narration and testimony is correct, and the ruling has no place here.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 2, verse 286:

﴿It shall have what it earned, and it shall bear what it has deserved.﴾ He means: of evil deeds. This is because sins are reached through desire, Satan, and whim, whereas good is attained through the bestowal of God without the intermediary of desire or the enticement of an enemy. This is the distinction between them as stated by al-Suhayli. There is, however, a better distinction than this, namely that iktisab (acquiring, deliberate acquisition) requires effort, striving, and exertion, so that nothing is placed upon the servant except what comes about through his striving, exertion, and effort. Kasb (earning), on the other hand, is attained with the slightest involvement, even merely by intending a good deed and the like. Thus evil is specified with iktisab, while good is described with the more general kasb. This accords with the sound hadith: "When My servant intends a good deed, write it down for him; and if he intends an evil deed, do not write it down."

Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

As for the hadith, "the intermediary and its absence," it is weak, because good also comes through the intermediary of the Messenger, the angel, inspiration, and divine success. So this is set against the intermediaries of the condition. The distinction is what we have mentioned, and God knows best.

(Benefit)

Iktisab is more emphatic than kasb, and for this reason it is used for what falls upon its doer, while kasb is used for what benefits its doer. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿It shall have what it earned, and it shall bear what it has deserved.﴾ This alerts that reward is obtained for it with minimal striving and earning, while punishment comes only from its acquiring, its manipulation, and what it exerts itself in.

Once this is known, then delighting in trial and rejoicing in God's choice, glorified be He, is not restricted to patient endurance (al-istibar), but occurs along with patience (al-sabr) and with self-restraint (al-tasabbur).

However, since al-istibar is more emphatic and stronger than al-sabr, this delight and rejoicing is more fitting for it. And God knows best.

﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes.﴾

(Benefit)

Naskh (abrogation) also has another meaning: naskh of the understandings of the addressees, meaning the removal from their understanding of what they grasped that was not intended and that the wording did not indicate, even if it gave that impression. Thus the Companions applied the term naskh to His saying: ﴿And whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, God will call you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.﴾ They said: "It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes,﴾ to the end of the verse."

This is abrogation of understanding, not abrogation of a ruling that is established, for being called to account does not necessitate punishment in the Hereafter or in this world either. For this reason He made the accounting general, then stated afterward that He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. So they understood from the verse that the blame, which is punishment, is a burdening of them beyond their capacity, and so this meaning was removed from their understanding by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes,﴾ to its end. Thus this is the lifting of an understanding not intended, from the angel's inspiration, and that is the lifting of what something other than the angel cast into their hearing or into their wishful thinking.
